cram.def: Stops a threat BEFORE it occurs. Examples: firewall, lock, ACL, MFA.
Identifies threats AS they happen. Examples: IDS, CCTV, audit logs.
Reduces damage AFTER an incident and restores systems. Examples: backups, patches.
Discourages attackers without physically stopping them. Examples: warning signs, visible guards.
Alternative used when primary control can't be implemented. Examples: extra logging instead of MFA.
Instructs people on required behavior via policy. Examples: acceptable use policy, mandatory training.
Technology-based controls. Examples: firewalls, IDS/IPS, encryption, authentication systems.
Administrative/policy controls. Examples: risk assessments, security policies, security planning.
Controls carried out by people and procedures. Examples: guards, change management, IR drills.
Tangible real-world controls. Examples: locks, fences, mantraps, bollards, badge readers.
IDS = Detective (alerts only). IPS = Preventive (blocks traffic). Know this for the exam.

matching.prompt: CCTV monitoring a server room
Firewall blocking inbound traffic
Restoring from backup after ransomware
'No unauthorized access' warning sign
Extra logging when MFA unavailable
Mandatory password policy document
Encryption on a hard drive
Annual risk assessment process
Security guard patrolling perimeter

questions.q: Which control type is designed to stop a threat BEFORE it occurs?
opts: Detective
Corrective
Preventive
Compensating
questions.exp: Preventive controls stop threats before they happen — firewalls, ACLs, locks, MFA.

questions.q: A CCTV camera monitoring a server room is which control type?
opts: Preventive
Corrective
Detective
Directive
questions.exp: Detective controls identify and record events. CCTV logs intrusions but doesn't stop them.

questions.q: Extra logging added because MFA can't be funded is a _____ control.
opts: Corrective
Deterrent
Physical
Compensating
questions.exp: Compensating controls substitute for a primary control when it can't be implemented.

questions.q: A security guard patrolling a data center falls under which control CATEGORY?
opts: Technical
Managerial
Operational
Physical
questions.exp: Physical controls are tangible, real-world measures — guards, fences, locks, badge readers.

questions.q: Annual security awareness training is best classified as which control category?
opts: Technical
Physical
Operational
Managerial
questions.exp: Managerial controls are administrative — policies, risk assessments, security planning.

questions.q: A warning sign reading 'Unauthorized Access Prohibited' is primarily which control type?
opts: Preventive
Deterrent
Corrective
Directive
questions.exp: Deterrent controls discourage attackers by highlighting consequences without physically stopping them.

questions.q: IT restores from a clean backup after a malware infection. This is which control type?
opts: Preventive
Corrective
Detective
Compensating
questions.exp: Corrective controls minimize damage and restore systems after an incident.

questions.q: An IDS that alerts the SOC to suspicious traffic is which control type?
opts: Preventive
Corrective
Detective
Deterrent
questions.exp: An IDS detects and alerts only — unlike IPS it doesn't block, making it a detective control.

questions.q: A mantrap at a data center entrance is primarily which control type?
opts: Detective
Preventive
Directive
Corrective
questions.exp: A mantrap physically prevents unauthorized entry one person at a time — preventive.

questions.q: Which control category includes security guards, incident response procedures, and change management?
opts: Technical
Managerial
Operational
Physical
questions.exp: Operational controls are executed by people following procedures — guards, IR drills, change management.

questions.q: A policy stating 'All employees must wear ID badges' is which control type?
opts: Directive
Detective
Corrective
Compensating
questions.exp: Directive controls instruct personnel on required behavior through policy.

questions.q: Fencing, bollards, and exterior lighting around a corporate campus are examples of which control category?
opts: Managerial
Technical
Physical
Deterrent
questions.exp: Physical controls are tangible, real-world barriers — fencing, bollards, lighting, locks, fences, mantraps. While these same controls also act as a Deterrent in the Type axis, the question asks for the CATEGORY (Managerial / Operational / Technical / Physical), not the Type (Preventive / Deterrent / Detective / Corrective / Compensating / Directive). Every control sits at the intersection of one Category AND one Type — they are independent axes.

questions.q: An organization deploys motion detectors, fingerprint biometric scanners, and an intrusion detection system (IDS) across its facility. These tools are which control category?
opts: Operational
Technical
Physical
Managerial
questions.exp: Technical controls are electronic or hardware-based systems — motion sensors, biometric readers, IDS/IPS, firewalls, encryption. Operational controls are human-driven processes (guard patrols, change management, incident-response drills). The hardware of an IDS is Technical even when an Operational SOC team monitors its alerts; CompTIA classifies based on the control itself, not the process around it.

questions.q: A company's information security policy requires all employees to complete annual security training and to acknowledge the acceptable use policy at hire. These mandates are which control type?
opts: Directive
Detective
Managerial
Preventive
questions.exp: Directive controls instruct personnel on required behavior through policy, training, and acknowledgements. They are distinct from Preventive (active stops like firewalls or locks) and from Managerial — Managerial is a Category that describes WHO/WHAT the control acts on, while Directive is a Type that describes HOW the control works. A written policy is Managerial in Category AND Directive in Type.

questions.q: A facility installs two security cameras: a visibly-mounted dome camera in the lobby ceiling, and a concealed pinhole camera covering a server-room corridor. The two cameras serve which control types, respectively?
opts: Both are Preventive — physically installed cameras stop unauthorized access from occurring
Visible camera = Detective; concealed camera = Deterrent — both record events, but only the hidden one is preventive
Both are Detective — cameras only record activity, regardless of whether they are visible or concealed
Visible camera = Deterrent (it discourages because it's seen); concealed camera = Detective (it records without warning)
questions.exp: Visible cameras deter — attackers who notice them are discouraged from acting because they expect to be recorded. Concealed cameras detect — they record without warning, so they don't deter (no one knows to be discouraged), but they capture evidence after the fact. The Type assignment depends on whether the camera is announcing its presence. The Category for both is Technical (electronic recording systems).

scenarios.q: A financial services firm is deploying new security tools after a recent breach. Leadership asks for a control that will STOP unauthorized database connections, not just notify staff after the fact. Which of the following BEST addresses this requirement?
opts: A SIEM rule that alerts on anomalous database logins
A network firewall rule that blocks the application subnet from reaching the database except via the API tier
Database activity monitoring with nightly exception reports
A monthly access review of database service accounts
scenarios.exp: Leadership wants a control that prevents the activity before it happens — that is a preventive control. A firewall rule that blocks the forbidden network path prevents the connection itself. SIEM alerting and DAM reports are detective (they notice the activity after it starts), and access reviews are administrative/detective. Only the firewall rule stops the connection.

scenarios.q: A retailer's payment-processing terminals run an embedded OS that the vendor will not patch for six more months, even though a critical vulnerability was just disclosed. The terminals cannot be taken offline during the holiday season. Which control type BEST describes isolating those terminals on a dedicated VLAN with strict egress filtering until the patch arrives?
opts: Preventive control
Detective control
Compensating control
Corrective control
scenarios.exp: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the primary control (here, patching) cannot be applied. Isolating the vulnerable terminals on a restricted VLAN mitigates risk until the vendor patches. Preventive describes the patch itself once available; corrective is what you apply after an incident; detective only observes. CompTIA uses 'compensating' specifically for this stop-gap scenario.

scenarios.q: After a successful phishing campaign went undetected for several weeks, a company's audit team asks for a control whose PRIMARY purpose is to discover similar incidents sooner next time. Which implementation BEST fits that request?
opts: A SIEM use case that correlates suspicious inbox-rule creation with anomalous sign-in locations and alerts the SOC
Quarterly user awareness training delivered to all staff on identifying phishing attempts
A spam filter at the email gateway that quarantines suspected phishing messages before delivery
A written security policy that prohibits clicking links in unsolicited external email
scenarios.exp: The audit team explicitly wants to discover similar events sooner — that is the definition of a detective control. A SIEM correlation rule that surfaces suspicious mailbox activity is detective. The spam filter is preventive (it blocks the message before delivery); awareness training is preventive/administrative (it reduces the chance of clicks); a written policy is directive. Only the SIEM rule is designed to detect incidents already underway.

scenarios.q: A newly hired security analyst is asked to classify the organization's controls by category for an upcoming audit. Which of the following is BEST described as a managerial control rather than a technical, operational, or physical control?
opts: A written acceptable use policy reviewed and signed annually by all employees
A Group Policy setting that enforces a 15-minute screen lock on all workstations
A firewall rule set that blocks outbound traffic to known command-and-control IP addresses
A security guard who patrols the data center perimeter during overnight hours
scenarios.exp: Managerial (administrative) controls are documented decisions — policies, standards, procedures, risk management artifacts. A signed acceptable use policy is the classic example. The Group Policy screen-lock and the firewall rule are technical controls (enforced by technology). The perimeter guard is a physical control. Only the AUP belongs in the managerial category.

scenarios.q: A ransomware incident encrypted several user file shares before the SOC contained it. The immediate priority is to return the affected shares to service with minimal data loss. Which action is BEST described as a corrective control in this situation?
opts: An intrusion detection system alert that originally notified the SOC of the ransomware activity
The mandatory annual security awareness training attended by all staff earlier in the quarter
Restoring the encrypted shares from last night's verified immutable backup onto a rebuilt file server
The firewall rule that blocks outbound SMB traffic from user workstation subnets
scenarios.exp: A corrective control acts after an incident to restore normal operation or reduce damage. Restoring encrypted shares from a verified backup is a textbook corrective action. The IDS alert is detective — it identified the incident but did not correct it. The awareness training and outbound SMB firewall rule are both preventive. Only the restore actively reverses damage that has already occurred.

scenarios.q: A facilities manager asks the security team to recommend a low-cost addition to the parking lot and building perimeter that will discourage casual trespassers without relying on active monitoring or physically blocking access. Which recommendation BEST describes a deterrent control?
opts: A biometric palm reader on the employee entrance door that is the only sanctioned way to enter the building
Motion-activated floodlights paired with clearly visible signage stating the area is under video surveillance
A line of concrete bollards installed along the frontage to block unauthorized vehicles from approaching the entrance
An SOC analyst assigned to watch the parking-lot camera feeds continuously on a 24/7 rotation
scenarios.exp: Deterrent controls discourage bad behavior by signaling consequences, rather than physically blocking, detecting, or responding. Floodlights and visible surveillance signage are classic deterrents — they make a would-be trespasser choose a softer target without ever touching the attacker. A biometric door lock is preventive (it actually stops entry). Concrete bollards are physical/preventive. A 24/7 camera analyst is detective. Only the signage + lighting combination is primarily a deterrent.

scenarios.q: A bank installs a biometric palm-reader at its data-center vestibule. The same device is referenced in two compliance reports: one classifies it as part of the data-center's access-control infrastructure (electronic identity verification), and the other classifies it as a measure that stops unauthorized personnel from reaching the server racks. In CompTIA's SY0-701 framework, which classification pair is correct?
opts: Category = Physical; Type = Deterrent — the device is a tangible wall-mounted unit that discourages approach
Category = Technical; Type = Preventive — biometrics electronically authenticate AND stop unauthorized entry
Category = Operational; Type = Detective — the device logs each attempt as part of the security process
Category = Technical; Type = Detective — biometrics electronically detect and record each entry attempt
scenarios.exp: Biometric palm-readers are electronic identity-verification systems (Technical Category) whose primary purpose is to allow or deny entry (Preventive Type). The same device also logs each attempt (a Detective side-effect), but CompTIA classifies controls by their PRIMARY purpose — for access-control devices that's Preventive. Every control sits at the intersection of one Category AND one Type; the two axes are independent.

questions.q: Brady is developing the architecture for a new data loss prevention system that his organization will use to prevent the exfiltration of sensitive information over the network. What category of control is Brady implementing?
opts: Managerial
Technical
Operational
Detective
questions.exp: The control categories recognized by CompTIA are technical, operational, managerial, and physical. Data loss prevention systems use technology to achieve security control objectives and are, therefore, technical controls.

questions.q: Carl’s organization is subject to PCI DSS. He determines that he will be unable to meet one of the PCI DSS objectives due to technical limitations and has obtained permission from his merchant bank to implement an alternative mechanism in place of the PCI DSS requirement. What type of control is Carl implementing?
opts: Preventive
Compensating
Detective
Corrective
questions.exp: The scenario does not tell us whether the control is preventive, detective, or corrective. We do know, however, that it is being used in place of another control requirement that Carl’s organization is unable to meet and is, therefore, a compensating control.

questions.q: Jill is reviewing the security controls that her organization uses to protect a sensitive network segment. She determines that the network is lacking adequate IDS capability. What type of control deficiency has Jill identified?
opts: Detective
Corrective
Preventive
Deterrent
questions.exp: An intrusion detection system (IDS) identifies potential intrusions that may be taking place on a network and is, therefore, an example of a detective control. An intrusion prevention system (IPS), on the other hand, might actually block the attack and would be an example of a preventive control.

cram.def: The three foundational security goals: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.
Only authorized users can access data. Controls: encryption, access controls, MFA, need-to-know.
Data has not been altered without authorization. Controls: hashing, digital signatures, permissions.
Systems and data accessible when needed. Controls: redundancy, backups, failover, load balancing.
Encryption scrambles data so only authorized parties can read it.
A hash changes if data is altered — used to verify data hasn't been tampered with.
DDoS attacks flood a system to make it unavailable — attacking availability.

matching.prompt: DDoS attack primary target
Encryption primarily protects
Hashing primarily protects
Attacker modifying records undetected
Hospital system offline during emergency
Unauthorized data disclosure
Redundant servers and backups support

questions.q: What does the CIA triad stand for?
opts: Control, Integrity, Access
Cyber, Intelligence, Authority
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Confidentiality, Identity, Access
questions.exp: CIA = Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three foundational goals of information security.

questions.q: Which CIA component ensures data is only accessible to authorized users?
opts: Integrity
Availability
Confidentiality
Authentication
questions.exp: Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized disclosure — encryption and access controls support this.

questions.q: A hospital's records system going offline during surgery violates which CIA component?
opts: Confidentiality
Integrity
Non-repudiation
Availability
questions.exp: Availability ensures systems are accessible when needed — critical outages directly violate this.

questions.q: An attacker modifying financial records without detection violates which CIA component?
opts: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication
questions.exp: Integrity ensures data has not been altered in an unauthorized way.

questions.q: Encryption primarily protects which CIA component?
opts: Integrity
Availability
Non-repudiation
Confidentiality
questions.exp: Encryption scrambles data so only authorized parties can read it — directly protecting confidentiality.

questions.q: A DDoS attack primarily targets which CIA component?
opts: Confidentiality
Integrity
Authentication
Availability
questions.exp: DDoS floods a target to make it unavailable — directly attacking availability.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST supports availability?
opts: Redundant systems and backups
Strong password policies for all administrative accounts
Encrypting data at rest with AES-256 storage
Strict access control lists on shared drives
questions.exp: Redundancy and backups ensure services remain available even during failures or attacks.

questions.q: Hashing is primarily used to protect which CIA component?
opts: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
Non-repudiation
questions.exp: Hashing verifies data hasn't changed — any modification produces a different hash, protecting integrity.

scenarios.q: An energy utility's control engineers notice that a field device is reporting sensor readings that drift several seconds out of sync with reality. Attackers appear to be altering the values in transit between the device and the SCADA server. Which pillar of the CIA triad is MOST directly under attack?
opts: Integrity of the sensor readings in transit
Confidentiality of the sensor readings in transit
Availability of the sensor readings at the SCADA server
Non-repudiation of the field device's submissions
scenarios.exp: Tampering with sensor readings in transit violates integrity — the receiving system trusts data that no longer reflects what the device actually sent. Confidentiality is about secrecy (reading data), availability is about reachability (data arriving at all), and non-repudiation is about proving who sent a message (and is not a CIA pillar). Integrity is the most direct answer here.

cram.def: Proof that an action occurred and the actor CANNOT deny it. Critical for legal/audit purposes.
Sender hashes the message, encrypts hash with their PRIVATE key. Provides authentication + integrity + non-repudiation.
You sign with YOUR private key. Only you have it — so only you could have signed it.
Anyone verifies your signature with YOUR public key. If valid, it proves you signed it.
HMAC uses shared key — both parties could have created it, so NO non-repudiation. Digital signatures use private key — only one party could sign.
A trusted authority certifies when a document was signed. Proves the document existed at that time.
Non-repudiation is closely related to integrity — you can't deny something that's cryptographically proven.

matching.prompt: Prevents a sender denying they sent a message
Key used to CREATE a digital signature
Key used to VERIFY a digital signature
Provides integrity + authentication but NOT non-repudiation

audit_d_review.note: HMAC; same as item 1 (1.2 Non-repudiation umbrella).

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: HMAC (Hash-Based Message Authentication Code)

sb_fix_2.note: Index-confirmed at p.217-218. Glossary references HMAC under HOTP entry. Non-repudiation requires single-party proof; shared-key HMAC cannot provide it - exactly the testable point. Strong Tier 1.

matching.prompt: CIA component non-repudiation is most tied to
Technology that provides non-repudiation

questions.q: Non-repudiation ensures that:
opts: A sender cannot deny sending a message
Data is encrypted in transit
Only authorized users can read data
Systems remain available during attacks
questions.exp: Non-repudiation proves an action occurred and prevents the actor from denying it.

questions.q: Which technology provides non-repudiation?
opts: Symmetric encryption
Digital signatures
Hashing alone
VPN tunnels
questions.exp: Digital signatures use asymmetric cryptography to bind a message to its sender — providing non-repudiation.

questions.q: A digital signature is created using the sender's:
opts: Public key
Shared key
Private key
Session key
questions.exp: Senders sign with their PRIVATE key. Only they possess it, so only they could have signed.

questions.q: Non-repudiation is most closely related to which CIA component?
opts: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
All three equally
questions.exp: Non-repudiation is a property of integrity — implemented via digital signatures and tamper-evident logs.

questions.q: Why does HMAC NOT provide non-repudiation?
opts: It uses asymmetric keys that anyone can verify with a public key
Both parties share the same key so either could have created it
It only verifies integrity but not the origin of the message
It depends on a centralized timestamp authority that may not exist
questions.exp: Non-repudiation requires that only one party could have created the proof. HMAC's shared key means either party could have.

audit_d_review.note: HMAC + non-repudiation; 1.2 Non-repudiation IS umbrella; HMAC is the foil concept used to teach what does/doesn't provide non-repudiation.

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: HMAC (Hash-Based Message Authentication Code)

sb_fix_2.note: Same Sybex home as Item 1 (p.217-218). Strong Tier 1.

questions.q: If Alice signs a message with her private key, what can Bob verify using her public key?
opts: That the message body has been encrypted by Alice for him
Bob's own identity has been authenticated to Alice's system
Alice sent it and the content hasn't been altered
That the message will reach Bob without delay or loss
questions.exp: Bob verifying with Alice's public key confirms she signed it (authentication) and the content is intact (integrity).

questions.q: Which BEST supports non-repudiation in a corporate email system?
opts: TLS encryption on email transport
Mandatory email archiving with retention policy
SPF records published in DNS for the sending domain
S/MIME digital signatures on emails
questions.exp: S/MIME applies digital signatures to emails — binding the sender's identity to the message cryptographically.

scenarios.q: A purchasing manager claims they never approved a $40,000 wire transfer, even though the workflow shows their account signed off. The security team must determine whether the approval can be definitively tied to the manager and not just anyone with their password. Which control provides the STRONGEST non-repudiation?
opts: Username and password audit logging in the application
Time-stamped server logs forwarded to a central SIEM
A scanned image of the manager's handwritten signature attached to the approval PDF
A digital signature applied with the manager's private key stored on a hardware token
scenarios.exp: Non-repudiation requires cryptographic evidence that only the private key holder could have produced. A hardware-token-backed digital signature binds the action to the physical device, not just the account — passwords alone can be stolen. Server logs and audit trails are evidence but can be undermined by credential theft; scanned handwritten signatures are trivially copyable and provide no cryptographic binding.

cram.def: Verifying WHO you are. Methods: passwords, biometrics, tokens, certificates.
Determining WHAT you can do. Enforced via ACLs, RBAC, permissions after authentication.
Tracking WHAT YOU DID. Logs: login times, commands run, resources accessed. Critical for forensics.
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service. Centralized AAA server for network access control.
Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus. Cisco-preferred AAA protocol. Separates AuthN, AuthZ, Accounting.
Knowledge factor: password, PIN, passphrase, security question.
Possession factor: smart card, hardware token, OTP app, phone.
Inherence/biometric factor: fingerprint, retina scan, facial recognition, voice.
Multi-Factor Authentication: uses two or more DIFFERENT factor types. Two passwords = not MFA.

matching.prompt: Verifying a user's identity at login
Granting access to a specific file share after login
Logging what commands a user ran
Centralized AAA server protocol
Smart card — which factor type?
Fingerprint scan — which factor type?
Password — which factor type?

questions.q: What does AAA stand for in network security?
opts: Authentication, Access, Auditing
Authority, Access, Accountability
Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
Assurance, Authorization, Auditing
questions.exp: AAA = Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what can you do?), Accounting (what did you do?).

questions.q: Which AAA component verifies a user's identity?
opts: Authorization
Authentication
Accounting
Access control
questions.exp: Authentication answers 'who are you?' — verified via passwords, biometrics, tokens.

questions.q: Which AAA component determines what resources a user can access?
opts: Authentication
Authorization
Auditing
Accounting
questions.exp: Authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?' — enforced via ACLs, roles, permissions.

questions.q: Which AAA component tracks what actions a user performed?
opts: Authentication
Accounting
Authorization
Administration
questions.exp: Accounting logs user activity — login times, commands run, resources accessed. Critical for forensics.

questions.q: RADIUS is primarily used for which function?
opts: Centralized AAA for network access
Encrypting all data at rest on internal servers
Generating digital certificates
Hashing user passwords for secure storage
questions.exp: RADIUS provides centralized AAA for network access control — widely used with 802.1X.

questions.q: Which of the following is 'something you have'?
opts: Password
Fingerprint
Hardware token
PIN
questions.exp: Hardware tokens and smart cards are possession factors — something you physically carry.

questions.q: A user provides a password AND a fingerprint. This is:
opts: Single-factor authentication only
Two-factor authentication
Authorization for resource access
Identification claim by the user
questions.exp: Two different factor types (knowledge + inherence) = two-factor authentication, a form of MFA.

questions.q: Using a PIN and a password together is:
opts: Not MFA because both are 'something you know'
MFA because two factors are used
Always sufficient for high-security systems
A form of biometric authentication
questions.exp: PIN and password are both knowledge factors — using two of the same factor type is NOT MFA.

scenarios.q: A helpdesk technician successfully logs into a ticketing platform with their corporate SSO credentials, but when they try to reassign a ticket to the system administrator group, the platform returns 'access denied.' Which stage of AAA is blocking the action?
opts: Authentication, because the credentials were invalid
Accounting, because the action was not logged successfully
Authorization, because the user's role lacks the required permission
Identification, because the username could not be resolved
scenarios.exp: Logging in succeeded, so authentication passed. What failed is authorization — the stage that checks whether the authenticated identity is permitted to perform the requested action. Accounting is the audit/logging step and does not block actions; identification (resolving the username) is part of the authentication stage, not a separate block on action.

cram.def: Identifies the difference (gap) between current security posture and a desired target state.
The target or desired state used for comparison. Often a security framework or regulatory requirement.
NIST CSF, ISO 27001, CIS Controls, PCI DSS, HIPAA.
A prioritized remediation roadmap listing what needs to be done to close each identified gap.
Pen test actively exploits. Gap analysis reviews documentation and controls against a framework.

matching.prompt: Current state vs desired state comparison
The target state used for comparison
Output of a gap analysis
NIST CSF or ISO 27001 used as
Gap analysis vs pen test — key difference
matching.answer: Gap analysis reviews controls; pen test actively exploits

questions.q: A gap analysis in security is used to:
opts: Actively exploit known vulnerabilities
Classify data sensitivity levels
Monitor real-time network traffic
Compare current security posture to a desired baseline
questions.exp: A gap analysis identifies the difference between where you are and where your security baseline requires you to be.

questions.q: Which document is commonly used as a baseline for a security gap analysis?
opts: A vulnerability scan report from last quarter
A risk register listing accepted residual risks
A security framework like NIST CSF or ISO 27001
A firewall ruleset showing currently allowed traffic
questions.exp: Security frameworks define desired security states that organizations compare their current posture against.

questions.q: After a gap analysis, the organization should produce:
opts: A prioritized remediation plan to close identified gaps
An immediate report to regulators on all findings
A full penetration test against critical assets
A new firewall ruleset blocking flagged ports
questions.exp: The primary output of a gap analysis is a prioritized remediation roadmap.

questions.q: How does a gap analysis differ from a penetration test?
opts: A gap analysis is always automated using vulnerability scanning tools
A gap analysis and a penetration test are essentially the same exercise
A gap analysis tests technical controls; a pen test reviews policies and procedures
Gap analysis reviews controls against a standard; pen test actively exploits vulnerabilities
questions.exp: Gap analysis compares documentation and controls to a framework. Pen testing actively attempts exploitation.

cram.def: 'Never trust, always verify.' No implicit trust for any user, device, or network location.
Traditional perimeter model: inside the network = trusted. Zero Trust eliminates this assumption.
Divides the network into small isolated zones. Limits lateral movement if a segment is compromised.
Zero Trust continuously re-evaluates trust — not just at login. Considers device health, behavior, location.
Makes access decisions. Includes identity provider, policy engine, trust algorithm.
Enforces access decisions made by the control plane. Includes policy enforcement points (PEP).
The component that evaluates access requests against policy and grants or denies access.

matching.prompt: Core Zero Trust principle
Divides network into isolated zones
Makes access decisions in Zero Trust
Enforces access decisions in Zero Trust
Internal user treated how in Zero Trust?
matching.answer: Same as external — no implicit trust

questions.q: The core principle of Zero Trust is:
opts: Trust all internal network traffic
Block all external traffic by default
Never trust, always verify
Use VPNs for all connections
questions.exp: Zero Trust assumes no user or device is trusted by default — every access request must be verified.

questions.q: A Zero Trust model treats internal network users:
opts: As fully trusted by default after VPN login
As administrators by default within the corporate LAN
With higher trust than external users
The same as external users — requiring verification
questions.exp: Zero Trust eliminates implicit trust for internal users — every request is authenticated and authorized.

questions.q: Micro-segmentation in a Zero Trust architecture is used to:
opts: Encrypt all data at rest on internal corporate servers
Replace traditional firewalls with software-defined perimeters
Speed up authentication across enterprise applications
Divide networks into small isolated zones to limit lateral movement
questions.exp: Micro-segmentation contains breaches — a compromised segment cannot easily reach other segments.

questions.q: Which BEST aligns with a Zero Trust approach?
opts: Allowing all intranet traffic without authentication
VPN granting full network access after login
Per-application MFA with continuous device health checks
Trusting devices on a known subnet
questions.exp: Zero Trust requires per-resource authentication with strong factors and continuous verification.

questions.q: Continuous verification in Zero Trust means:
opts: Trust is re-evaluated throughout a session, not just at login
Passwords must be changed continuously
All traffic is encrypted at all times
Users must re-authenticate every minute
questions.exp: Zero Trust continuously evaluates device health, user behavior, and context — not just at initial authentication.

questions.q: In a Zero Trust architecture following NIST SP 800-207, an identity-aware proxy that inspects each user request and either permits or blocks the connection is acting as which component?
opts: Policy Administrator (PA) — it issues the session token after the decision is made
Policy Engine (PE) — it generates the trust score that drives the access decision
Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) — it sits inline with the traffic and enforces the access decision
Resource server — it hosts the application the request is destined for
questions.exp: An identity-aware proxy that allows or denies traffic in real time is the PEP — it sits on the data plane. The PE makes the decision; the PA communicates it; the proxy enforces it. The resource server is what the PEP is protecting, not the enforcement point itself.

questions.q: In a Zero Trust architecture, the component that evaluates context — including device posture, user identity, and threat intelligence — to produce an allow-or-deny decision is the:
opts: Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) — it sits inline with traffic and applies whatever decision was made
Policy Administrator (PA) — it issues a session credential after the decision has been reached
Policy Engine (PE) — it consults the trust algorithm to decide whether the request should be granted
Resource Server — it hosts the protected data the subject is trying to access
questions.exp: The PE is the brain of Zero Trust: it consumes signals (identity, device posture, threat intel) and consults the trust algorithm. The PA acts on the PE's decision by issuing a session credential; the PEP enforces it on traffic; the resource server is what the PEP is protecting.

questions.q: In a NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust deployment, which statement BEST distinguishes the Policy Engine from the Policy Enforcement Point?
opts: The Policy Engine handles authentication; the Policy Enforcement Point handles authorization
The Policy Engine sits inline with traffic; the Policy Enforcement Point lives in the control plane
The Policy Engine and Policy Enforcement Point are interchangeable terms for the same component
The Policy Engine decides whether to grant access; the Policy Enforcement Point applies that decision to live traffic
questions.exp: PE = decision; PEP = enforcement. PE lives on the control plane and consults the trust algorithm; PEP lives on the data plane and applies the verdict to live traffic. Crucially, neither replaces authentication or authorization — Zero Trust is an architecture for HOW access decisions are made and enforced, not the AAA process itself. The PE consumes signals (after authn), produces an authorization decision, and the PEP enforces it.

questions.q: In a Zero Trust architecture, what is the specific role of the Policy Administrator (PA)?
opts: Inspecting each request against firewall and proxy rules and blocking disallowed traffic
Evaluating user identity, device posture, and contextual signals to compute a trust score
Storing the protected data and serving it to subjects after authorization succeeds
Communicating the Policy Engine's decision to the enforcement point and issuing or revoking the session credential
questions.exp: PA bridges the PE's decision and the PEP's enforcement: once the PE says 'allow,' the PA generates a session-specific credential or token, hands it to the PEP, and tracks the session. When trust changes mid-session, PA revokes the credential. The PA's role is most clearly articulated in NIST SP 800-207; some Zero Trust framings collapse PA into PE on the control plane.

scenarios.q: A company is moving away from a legacy 'castle-and-moat' VPN model in which authenticated users gain broad access to the internal network. The security team is implementing a zero trust architecture. Which change BEST reflects a zero trust principle?
opts: Expanding the VPN concentrator capacity so more remote users can authenticate simultaneously at peak times
Reducing the number of firewall rules by trusting all traffic that originates inside the corporate WAN
Extending the internal VLAN reach into every branch office so users have the same flat network experience everywhere
Requiring per-application access decisions that evaluate identity, device posture, and request context on every request
scenarios.exp: Zero trust replaces implicit network-location trust with explicit per-request verification of identity, device posture, and context. Making access decisions at each request, per application, is the core zero trust pattern. Expanding VPN capacity perpetuates the old implicit-trust model; extending a flat VLAN and trusting internal WAN traffic move in the opposite direction by enlarging the trust zone.

scenarios.q: An IT architect is implementing Zero Trust at a financial services firm. The team deploys a SIEM that ingests endpoint telemetry, identity provider events, and threat intelligence feeds; an existing reverse proxy at the application edge is configured to consult an internal API before forwarding any HTTP request, and a small service tracks active sessions and revokes their tokens when a device's compliance status changes. In NIST SP 800-207 terms, which mapping is correct?
opts: SIEM/risk feeds → Policy Engine inputs; reverse proxy → Policy Enforcement Point; session-token service → Policy Administrator
Reverse proxy → Policy Engine; SIEM → Policy Enforcement Point; session-token service → resource server
All three are different views of the Policy Engine — NIST 800-207 treats the control plane as a single PE
Reverse proxy → Policy Administrator; SIEM → Policy Engine; session-token service → Policy Enforcement Point
scenarios.exp: The SIEM feeds risk signals into the PE's trust algorithm; the PE produces the decision. The reverse proxy sits inline with HTTP traffic and applies the decision — that's the PEP. The session-token service that issues and revokes credentials is the PA, the bridge between PE decisions and PEP enforcement. NIST 800-207 explicitly splits the control plane into PE and PA; collapsing them or swapping the planes is the most common student error.

cram.def: Two-door entry system — only one door open at a time. Prevents tailgating into secured areas.
Sturdy posts that prevent vehicles from ramming buildings or restricted areas.
'Something you have' physical access control. Logs who enters/exits and when.
Detective control. Deters and records — supports investigations after an incident.
Shielded enclosure that blocks electromagnetic signals — protects against RF attacks.
Requires two people present for sensitive operations — prevents insider threats in high-security areas.
Physically tether laptops and devices to fixed structures — prevents theft.

matching.prompt: Prevents tailgating with two-door entry
Prevents vehicle ramming attacks
Physical access token — 'something you have'
Blocks electromagnetic signals
Requires two people for sensitive operations
Physically secures a laptop to a desk

audit_d_review.note: Cable lock; 1.2 Physical Security IS umbrella for physical security mechanisms.

sb_fix_2.note: Chapter-level Tier 3. Ch 9 Site Security is the TOC home for physical locks; 'cable lock' not named in glossary/index/practice tests. Term may be in chapter prose. partial-depth retained.

questions.q: A mantrap (access control vestibule) is designed to:
opts: Prevent tailgating by allowing only one person through at a time
Monitor video footage from CCTV cameras at the entrance
Encrypt all physical media leaving the secure building
Alert the SOC after detecting an unauthorized entry attempt
questions.exp: A mantrap forces one-at-a-time entry through two interlocked doors — preventing tailgating.

questions.q: Which physical security device prevents vehicle-based attacks on buildings?
opts: Cable lock
Bollard
Faraday cage
Mantrap
questions.exp: Bollards are sturdy posts placed to stop vehicles from ramming into buildings or restricted areas.

questions.q: A Faraday cage is used to:
opts: Prevent unauthorized physical entry into a secured area
Log all physical access events to secured rooms
Block electromagnetic signals to prevent RF eavesdropping
Store encryption keys in a tamper-resistant module
questions.exp: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic fields — protecting against RF attacks and signal interception.

questions.q: Two-person integrity requires:
opts: Two passwords to be entered for system login
Two-factor authentication on every critical account
Two people present to perform sensitive operations
Two security guards on patrol at all entry points
questions.exp: Two-person integrity prevents insider abuse by requiring a witness for high-security operations.

questions.q: Motion-activated perimeter lighting is primarily which type of security control?
opts: Preventive
Detective
Deterrent
Corrective
questions.exp: Lighting deters intruders and improves camera footage — primarily a deterrent control.

scenarios.q: A regional office stores backup tapes for the primary data center. Management requires three things: only authorized staff may enter the tape vault, unauthorized entries must generate an alert, and the organization must be able to identify who entered after the fact. Which combination of physical controls BEST satisfies all three requirements?
opts: A single pin-pad entry using a shared numeric code that is rotated quarterly among staff
A badged card reader plus an interior motion sensor alarm, with card-reader logs retained for 90 days
A padlock and key, with the key held by the facilities manager and signed out as needed
A visitor sign-in sheet at the lobby desk that all visitors complete before proceeding to the vault
scenarios.exp: The requirements demand authentication (who), alerting (detection), and attribution (records). A badged card reader authenticates individuals and logs entries for attribution; an interior motion sensor alarms on unauthorized entry. A shared pin-pad code defeats attribution because everyone uses the same code. A padlock has no detection or individual logging. A lobby sign-in sheet neither protects the vault nor reliably attributes entries. Only option B satisfies all three needs.

cram.def: A single decoy system designed to attract attackers. Used to detect intrusions and study attacker techniques.
A network of honeypots simulating a realistic environment. Provides richer intelligence than a single honeypot.
A decoy file that alerts when accessed. No legitimate user would open it.
Fake data (credentials, records, API keys) that triggers an alert when used. Any access = intrusion.
Redirects malicious DNS queries to a controlled IP — neutralizes C2 (command and control) communication.
DETECTION and INTELLIGENCE — not blocking. Alert when attackers interact with decoys.

matching.prompt: Single decoy server to lure attackers
Network of decoy systems
Decoy file that alerts when opened
Fake credentials that alert when used
Redirects C2 DNS traffic to a controlled IP
Primary purpose of deception technologies

questions.q: A honeypot is best described as:
opts: A decoy system designed to lure and study attackers
A signature-based malware scanning system
A firewall rule set that blocks known attackers
A centralized password vault for admin accounts
questions.exp: Honeypots are intentionally vulnerable decoy systems that attract attackers so their techniques can be analyzed.

questions.q: Which deception technique redirects malicious DNS queries to neutralize C2 communications?
opts: Honeypot
Honeynet
Honeytoken
DNS sinkhole
questions.exp: DNS sinkholes intercept malicious domain lookups and redirect them to a controlled IP, cutting off C2 channels.

questions.q: A honeytoken is:
opts: A fake decoy server in the DMZ designed to attract attackers
A small piece of malware planted by attackers to test detection
A network monitoring agent that detects unusual access patterns
A decoy piece of data (credentials, file, API key) that alerts when accessed or used
questions.exp: Honeytokens are fake data items — any access reveals an attacker's presence since no legitimate use exists.

questions.q: The primary purpose of deception technologies is to:
opts: Detect attackers and gather intelligence about their techniques
Replace traditional firewalls and IPS appliances
Block attacks immediately at the network edge
Automatically patch vulnerabilities upon detection
questions.exp: Deception tech is about detection and intelligence — not blocking. Attackers interacting with decoys reveal themselves.

questions.q: Which deception technology would BEST help detect attackers who have already breached the perimeter?
opts: Honeytokens and honeyfiles placed on internal systems
Firewall rules at the network perimeter
An IDS deployed at the network perimeter
DNS filtering of known-malicious domains
questions.exp: Internal honeytokens detect lateral movement — an attacker accessing them reveals they are inside.

scenarios.q: An SOC lead wants earlier warning when attackers who have already bypassed the perimeter begin exploring the internal network. Budget is tight and there is no room for large new infrastructure. Which deception technique BEST fits these constraints while producing a high-confidence alert?
opts: Deploying a full-scale honeynet that mirrors the production environment for attackers to explore
Publishing the company's internal IP ranges to an external threat feed to mislead attackers during reconnaissance
Adding an additional next-generation firewall in front of existing NGFWs for deeper defense in depth
Seeding the environment with honeytokens — plausible but unused credentials, files, and API keys that alert when accessed
scenarios.exp: Honeytokens are deliberately planted bait artifacts — unused credentials, fake API keys, decoy files — that generate high-confidence alerts because no legitimate user has any reason to touch them. They are extremely low cost to deploy. A full honeynet provides richer data but exceeds the stated budget and infrastructure constraints. Adding another firewall is defense in depth, not deception. Publishing internal IP ranges externally is neither standard practice nor helpful.

questions.q: Brian ran a penetration test against a school’s grading system and discovered a flaw that would allow students to alter their grades by exploiting a SQL injection vulnerability. What type of control should he recommend to the school’s cybersecurity team to prevent students from engaging in this type of activity?
opts: Confidentiality
Integrity
Alteration
Availability
questions.exp: By allowing students to change their own grades, this vulnerability provides a pathway to unauthorized alteration of information. Brian should recommend that the school deploy integrity controls that prevent unauthorized modifications.

questions.q: What factor is a major reason organizations do not use security guards?
opts: Reliability
Training
Cost
Social engineering
questions.exp: Security guards can be one of the costliest physical security controls over time, making the cost of guards one of the most important deciding factors guiding when and where they will be employed. Reliability, training, and the potential for social engineering are all possible issues with security guards, but none of these is the major driver in the decision process.

questions.q: Megan wants to deploy a sensor that is inexpensive, yet will allow her to detect humans entering and moving in a secured room. Which of the following should she select?
opts: An infrared sensor
A microwave sensor
An ultrasonic sensor
A pressure sensor
questions.exp: Infrared sensors balance lower cost with the ability to detect humans entering and moving in a space. Microwave sensors are more expensive but can provide better coverage, including traveling through some barriers. Ultrasonic sensors are rarely used for this purpose, and pressure sensors are limited to the pad where they are deployed, making them expensive and challenging to use for rooms or larger spaces.

questions.q: Kathleen wants to discourage potential attackers from entering the facility she is responsible for. Which of the following is not a common control used for this type of preventive defense?
opts: Fences
Lighting
Platform diversity
Video surveillance
questions.exp: Fences, lighting, and video surveillance can all help discourage potential malicious actors from entering an area, although a determined adversary will ignore or bypass all three. Platform diversity can help make it harder for attackers to succeed, but this is primarily a resilience tactic, and remains more costly to maintain and implement.

questions.q: What type of physical security control is shown here?
opts: A Faraday cage
An access control vestibule
A bollard
An air gap
questions.exp: An access control vestibule uses a pair of doors. When an individual enters, the first door must be closed and secured before the second door can be opened. This helps prevent tailgating, since the person entering will notice anybody following them through the secured area. A Faraday cage is used to stop electromagnetic interference (EMI), a bollard prevents vehicular traffic, and an air gap is a physical separation of networks or devices.

questions.q: Mike wants to stop vehicles from traveling toward the entrance of his building. What physical security control should he implement?
opts: An air gap
A hot aisle
A robotic sentry
A bollard
questions.exp: Bollards are physical security controls that prevent vehicles from accessing or ramming doors or other areas. They may look like pillars, planters, or other innocuous objects. An air gap is a physical separation of technology environments; a hot aisle is the aisle where systems in a datacenter exhaust warm air; and unlike in movies, robotic sentries are not commonly deployed and aren’t ready to stop vehicles in most current circumstances.

questions.q: What component of a zero‐trust architecture forwards requests from subjects and acts on whether subjects are allowed to access resources?
opts: Policy administrators
Policy enforcement points
Policy engines
Policy gateways
questions.exp: Policy enforcement points communicate with policy administrators to forward requests from subjects and to receive instructions from them about connections to allow or end. Policy administrators are components that establish or remove the communication path between subjects and resources, including creating session‐specific authentication tokens or credentials as needed. Policy engines make policy decisions based on both rules and external systems. Policy gateways are not reference components for zero‐trust designs.

questions.q: Ben wants to observe malicious behavior targeted at multiple systems on a network. He sets up a variety of systems and instruments to allow him to capture copies of attack tools and to document all the attacks that are conducted. What has he set up?
opts: A honeypot
A beartrap
A honeynet
A tarpit
questions.exp: A honeynet is a group of systems that intentionally exposes vulnerabilities so that defenders can observe attacker behaviors, techniques, and tools to help them design better defenses.

questions.q: Chris wants to use geolocation technology to find where phones issued by his organization are located. Which of the following is not commonly used as part of geolocation techniques?
opts: Bluetooth
GPS
NFC
Wi‐Fi
questions.exp: Nearfield communication (NFC) is not typically used for geolocation because of its extremely short range. Geolocation services may use GPS, Wi‐Fi, and Bluetooth to identify areas, access points, Bluetooth beacons, and other items that help with location services.

questions.q: The network that Jaime is connecting to requires each device to protect itself from potential threats both from outside the local security zone and from systems that share the same network zone with it. What security design concept requires this type of configuration?
opts: Security zones
Zero trust
Screened subnet
Security tagging
questions.exp: A zero‐trust network does not trust systems or individuals, even if they are already inside the network's security perimeter. This means that each device or system must be secure and defended, rather than creating a harder outside security shell at security boundaries like many traditional networks did. Security zones are a high‐level concept based on the level of security for a network segment or other logical division. Screened subnets, also called DMZs, are used to allow access from public or lower‐security zones to resources such as web servers. Security tagging is not a specific technical term.

questions.q: Samantha has configured an unused network segment at her company to appear to be vulnerable and has added instrumentation and data‐gathering capabilities so that she can observe and analyze what attackers do while attempting to exploit that network. What type of environment has she set up?
opts: A honeynet
A black hole
A honeypot
A tarpit
questions.exp: A honeynet is a network that is built to have intentional vulnerabilities that will attract attackers whose actions can then be recorded and studied. A honeypot is a system or device configured in a similar way. A black hole is a network location where traffic is sent that will not be further forwarded. A tarpit is a system configured to slow down attackers.

questions.q: Phil is investigating a security incident where the attackers shut down his organization’s database server. They do not appear to have actually gained access to the system, but shut it down using some type of remote exploit. What principle of cybersecurity was most directly violated during this incident?
opts: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
Nonrepudiation
questions.exp: This is an example of an availability breach. By shutting down the database server, the attackers were able to deny authorized users access to the server. Confidentiality was not compromised as data was not accessed. And since data was not accessed, it was not changed either, keeping data integrity intact. Nonrepudiation does not play a role in this scenario since we are not concerned with proving data source identity to a recipient.

questions.q: Ian is designing an authorization scheme for his organization’s deployment of a new accounting system. He is considering putting a control in place that would require that two accountants approve any payment request over $100,000. What security principle is Ian seeking to enforce?
opts: Two‐person integrity control
Separation of duties
Least privilege
Security through obscurity
questions.exp: It is sometimes difficult to distinguish between cases of least privilege, separation of duties, and two‐person control. Least privilege means that an employee should have only the access rights necessary to perform their job. That is not the case in this scenario because accountants need to be able to approve payments. Separation of duties occurs when the same employee does not have permission to perform two different actions that, when combined, could undermine security. That is not the case here because both employees are performing the same action: approving the payment. Two‐person control occurs when two employees must jointly authorize the same action. That is the case in this scenario. Security through obscurity occurs when the security of a control depends on the secrecy of its mechanism.

questions.q: Norm is evaluating the security of his organization’s datacenters and notices that there is a hole in the barbed wire fence protecting the facility. What type of control flaw has Norm identified?
opts: Physical
Detective
Corrective
Compensating
questions.exp: A fence is an example of a physical control. Norm has identified a deficiency in a physical control that may be remediated by repairing the fence. A detective control helps pinpoint errors after an event has taken place. Corrective controls make up for an error and help restoration functions. A compensating control is an alternative method with which to implement an alternative substitute control in place of a complicated one that would take longer to implement.

questions.q: Tina is applying a digital signature to a contract so that the recipient can prove that she agreed to its terms. What goal of cryptography most directly describes Tina’s actions?
opts: Nonrepudiation
Confidentiality
Integrity
Authentication
questions.exp: Nonrepudiation ensures that individuals can prove to a third party that a message came from its purported sender. Although Tina may also achieve other goals with her approach, this goal is her stated intention.

questions.q: Susan is designing the physical security controls for her organization’s new building. She would like to ensure that the front doors are protected from a vehicle being used to ram through them. Which physical security control can Susan effectively utilize?
opts: A moat
A wall
Bollards
A fence
questions.exp: Bollards are pillars or other structures placed in designated locations to prevent vehicles from passing through an area. Whereas many bollards look like metal poles or concrete pillars, planters, large boulders, and other structures can also serve as bollards. A moat is not a typical security control unless your organization has a castle, and walls and fences are more frequently used to prevent access by people.

questions.q: Chuck wants to deploy a sensor in his datacenter that will detect humans who enter the space. He has a relatively low budget, so he wants the best coverage he can get inexpensively. What type of sensors should he purchase?
opts: Infrared
Microwave
Pressure
Ultrasonic
questions.exp: Chuck knows that infrared sensors are typically less expensive and are well suited to detect humans moving in a space. Microwave sensors typically cost more per sensor but are less likely to be influenced by temperature variations and can work through some substances, allowing them to monitor areas that infrared sensors cannot. Pressure sensors are deployed in specific locations and are not well suited to monitoring a larger facility like a datacenter, and ultrasonic sensors are rarely used in enterprise environments for this type of purpose.

questions.q: Kirk wants to learn more about attacker techniques, and to do so he sets up a system that appears to be vulnerable to attacks he is curious about. He carefully instruments the system and captures all attacker data and actions. What type of system has Kirk set up?
opts: A darknet
A honeypot
A tarpit
A beartrap
questions.exp: Kirk has set up a honeypot, an intentionally vulnerable and instrumented system designed to allow defenders to analyze attacker tools and techniques. A darknet is unused network space that is instrumented to allow the observation of network probes and attacks, particularly those that target network space by iterating through IP address ranges. Tarpits are systems that are designed to slow attackers down, such as those that respond to vulnerability scans very slowly with a service on every port. Beartrap is not a security term.

questions.q: What component of a zero‐trust reference design makes decisions based on rules set as part of the zero‐trust configuration?
opts: The policy enforcement point
The policy engine
The policy administrator
The policy enforcer
questions.exp: In a zero‐trust reference design, a subject’s use of a system that is untrusted connects through a policy enforcement point allowing trusted transactions to the enterprise resources. A policy engine makes policy decisions based on rules that are then acted on by policy administrators. Policy enforcer is not a part of the reference design.

cram.def: Controlled process to assess, approve, implement, and document IT changes — minimizing unintended security impacts.
Formal document describing a proposed change: what, why, impact, rollback plan, timeline.
Group of stakeholders who review and approve significant changes before implementation.
Pre-defined steps to revert to the previous working state if a change causes problems.
Period during which no changes are permitted — e.g. end of financial year, major events.
Pre-approved, low-risk, routine change that doesn't require full CAB review each time.
Urgent change (e.g. zero-day patch) — expedited approval process but still requires documentation.

matching.prompt: Formal document requesting a system change
Group that approves major changes
Plan to undo a failed change
Routine pre-approved low-risk change
Period when no changes are permitted

questions.q: The primary purpose of change management in IT security is to:
opts: Speed up software deployments by removing review and approval bottlenecks from release pipelines
Ensure changes are assessed, approved, and documented to minimize risk
Replace vulnerability scanning by enforcing automated configuration drift detection on every host
Automate patch deployment so emergency security fixes can roll out without management oversight
questions.exp: Change management provides a controlled process for evaluating and approving changes to reduce unintended security impacts.

questions.q: A rollback plan is used to:
opts: Speed up future deployments by caching the binaries from prior successful releases
Train new engineers by giving them documented examples of past production changes
Archive old configurations indefinitely so auditors can reconstruct historical state
Revert to the previous working state if a change fails
questions.exp: A rollback plan defines how to undo a change quickly if it causes problems, minimizing downtime.

questions.q: Which group reviews and approves significant changes before implementation?
opts: The CISO acting alone — no committee review is required for production changes
The penetration testing team that validates the security posture of each proposed change
Help desk staff who escalate changes to the on-call engineer for after-hours review
Change Advisory Board (CAB) — committee that reviews and approves significant changes
questions.exp: The CAB reviews proposed changes, assesses risk and impact, and approves or rejects before implementation.

questions.q: An emergency patch for a critical zero-day should:
opts: Follow an expedited change management process and be documented afterwards
Skip all documentation since the urgency justifies bypassing every review step
Bypass testing entirely — emergency patches are pre-validated by the vendor
Require no approval — engineering teams self-authorize emergency security work
questions.exp: Even emergency changes require an expedited process and post-implementation documentation.

questions.q: Which type of change is pre-approved, low-risk, and routine?
opts: Emergency change
Major change
Standard change
RFC
questions.exp: Standard changes are pre-approved routine changes that don't require CAB review every time.

questions.q: A change freeze is implemented because:
opts: All vulnerabilities have been patched and no further changes are technically required
The rollback plan has failed in testing and engineers cannot ship without one
The CAB has not met recently and requires fresh quorum before approving anything
A high-risk period requires stability — no changes permitted
questions.exp: Change freezes prevent changes during critical business periods to reduce risk.

questions.q: An administrator changes a firewall rule without submitting an RFC or getting CAB approval. This is:
opts: Acceptable for minor changes since firewall rule edits rarely cause production impact
Standard practice for firewall administrators with senior-level operational privileges
Required in emergency situations — the RFC step can always be skipped under time pressure
An unauthorized change that violates change management policy
questions.exp: Unauthorized changes bypass review processes and can introduce vulnerabilities, outages, or compliance violations.

scenarios.q: A web application team needs to deploy a security patch within two hours to address an actively exploited zero-day. Which change management path BEST fits this situation while still preserving governance?
opts: Standard change with full CAB review scheduled for next week
Normal change with the usual 48-hour stakeholder notification period
Skip change management entirely because it is a security issue
Emergency change with post-implementation CAB review
scenarios.exp: Emergency changes are a recognized category specifically for urgent fixes that cannot wait for the normal CAB cadence. They still require governance, but the CAB review happens after implementation rather than before. Skipping change management abandons oversight, and standard or normal changes follow a slower pre-approval cadence that cannot meet a two-hour window.

scenarios.q: A proposed change will replace the authentication provider used by the company's core financial application. The change advisory board meets tomorrow. Which group is MOST critical to include in the impact analysis for this change?
opts: The finance team that owns the application, the identity team that owns the auth provider, and the owners of any downstream systems integrated via SSO
The HR department alone, because authentication ultimately affects employee access
The facilities team alone, because physical access decisions are related to authentication
The desktop support team alone, because they will field any user help tickets that result from the change
scenarios.exp: Change impact analysis must cover the application owner, the platform owner of the component being changed, and downstream integrations that could break. The finance application owners, identity team, and SSO-integrated system teams together represent all three categories. Any single team by itself — HR, facilities, or desktop support — misses critical stakeholder scope, and narrow stakeholder scoping is one of the most common causes of botched changes.

scenarios.q: A mid-sized organization's change advisory board keeps rejecting proposed changes because they arrive without documented test results from a staging environment. One team pushes back, arguing that their change is 'too small to bother testing.' Which response BEST aligns with sound change management practice?
opts: Accept the team's assessment because small changes statistically rarely cause production problems
Move the change straight to production so its outcome can be observed in the real environment and rolled back if needed
Carve out a standing exemption so changes the team self-classifies as small can bypass the CAB entirely
Require documented test results regardless of change size, because the CAB cannot assess risk without evidence that the change actually worked in a non-production environment
scenarios.exp: Test results are a required input to the CAB's risk decision — without them, the board is guessing. 'Too small to test' is exactly the category of change that tends to cause outages because risk is assumed away rather than evaluated. Accepting the team's claim, carving out a self-classified bypass, or skipping straight to production all remove the evidence that the change process depends on. Requiring documented test results for every change preserves the governance contract.

cram.def: Only approved applications can execute. Default-deny. Strongest application control.
Known bad applications are blocked. Default-allow. Less secure than allow listing.
Documented standard secure state of a system. Deviations are detected and remediated.
Tracks every change to code and configurations (git, SVN). Enables rollback, auditing.
Mirrors production — used to test changes safely before deploying to production.
Isolating an application or process to prevent it from affecting the rest of the system.
Instead of patching running systems, replace them with new pre-configured instances.

matching.prompt: Only approved software can execute
Known bad software is blocked, rest allowed
Standard secure configuration of a system
Tracks all changes to code over time
Safe environment for testing before production
Isolates an application to prevent system impact

questions.q: Which process ensures only approved software versions can execute in production?
opts: Allow listing — defining an explicit set of approved software versions cleared to execute
Change management — approving the introduction of new software through CAB review
Vulnerability scanning — checking installed software versions for known CVEs and CVSS scores
Penetration testing — attempting to bypass installed software controls during scheduled engagements
questions.exp: Allow listing (whitelisting) ensures only explicitly approved software can execute — everything else is blocked.

questions.q: A configuration baseline is used to:
opts: Document and enforce the standard secure state of a system
Define maximum user permissions allowed across each role in the directory
Scan for vulnerabilities by comparing installed software versions to a CVE feed
Apply default operating-system security profiles to every newly imaged endpoint at enrollment time
questions.exp: A configuration baseline documents the standard secure configuration — deviations trigger alerts and remediation.

questions.q: Allow listing is considered more secure than block listing because:
opts: It requires less ongoing maintenance than maintaining a long block list of bad files
It does not require administrative rights to enforce on standard endpoint workstations
It is faster to implement initially because the list of approved apps is usually small
It blocks everything by default and only permits approved applications
questions.exp: Allow listing is default-deny — only explicitly approved applications run. Block listing is default-allow, which is weaker.

questions.q: Sandboxing a suspicious file is used to:
opts: Execute it in an isolated environment to observe behavior without risking production systems
Encrypt the file using a key derived from its hash for safe long-term archival storage
Permanently delete the file by zeroing its disk blocks before the next backup window
Forward the file directly to the antivirus vendor for inclusion in their signature feed
questions.exp: Sandboxing isolates execution so any malicious behavior cannot affect the host system or network.

questions.q: An immutable infrastructure approach means:
opts: Production systems are deployed once at install and then never receive any updates whatsoever
Operating systems are configured so administrators cannot change any settings after deployment
All data on running systems is automatically encrypted at rest using filesystem-level encryption
Instead of patching running systems, they are replaced with pre-configured new instances
questions.exp: Immutable infrastructure replaces systems rather than patching them in place — eliminating configuration drift.

scenarios.q: A database administrator is about to apply a complex schema migration to a production system during the approved maintenance window. Which element is MOST critical to include in the technical change plan before work begins?
opts: A color-coded Gantt chart of all recent database changes this quarter
A post-implementation screenshot of the updated schema for audit records
A documented backout plan with rollback steps that have been tested in a non-production environment
A list of all developers who have accessed the database in the past 90 days
scenarios.exp: A tested rollback plan is the single most critical technical artifact for a complex change — without it, a failed migration can leave production in an unrecoverable state. Gantt charts and developer access lists are supporting governance artifacts, not recovery tools. Post-implementation screenshots document what happened but do not help if the change must be reversed mid-window.

scenarios.q: A DevOps team needs to update a shared TLS cipher configuration across 200 web servers. They propose applying the change through their version-controlled configuration management system, with every change tracked as a reviewed pull request. Which statement BEST describes the advantage of this approach over ad-hoc changes made directly on each server?
opts: It eliminates the need for a documented backout plan, because version control itself can always roll a change back cleanly
It allows the team to bypass the organization's normal maintenance window requirements, because automated changes are low risk
It removes the need for a change advisory board review, because the changes are delivered through automation rather than by hand
It provides an auditable history of configuration changes, consistent application across every server, and a reviewable diff before the change is applied
scenarios.exp: Version-controlled configuration management delivers three concrete properties for technical change management: an auditable change history (who changed what, when), consistent application across all servers (no snowflake hosts), and a reviewable diff before the change merges. It does not replace a tested backout plan, CAB review, or maintenance windows — those governance and recovery requirements remain regardless of the delivery mechanism. Option B captures the real advantages without overstating them.

questions.q: Tim is working on a change to a web application used by his organization to fix a known bug. What environment should he be working in?
opts: Test
Development
Staging
Production
questions.exp: Developers working on active changes to code should always work in the development environment. The test environment is where the software or systems can be tested without impacting the production environment. The staging environment is a transition environment for code that has successfully cleared testing and is waiting to be deployed into production. The production environment is the live system. Software, patches, and other changes that have been tested and approved move to production.

questions.q: What do many organizations use to schedule and coordinate changes for information systems?
opts: Impact analysis
Backout plans
Maintenance windows
Version control
questions.exp: Many organizations use scheduled maintenance windows to coordinate changes to information systems. These windows are preplanned and announced times when all non‐emergency changes will take place and often occur on evenings and weekends. A change management process ensures that personnel can perform a security impact analysis. Experts evaluate changes to identify any security impacts before personnel deploy the changes in a production environment. A backout plan allows personnel to undo the change and return the system to its previous state if necessary. Version control ensures that developers and users have access to the latest versions of software and that changes are carefully managed throughout the release process.

questions.q: Erica is documenting potential concerns about patching as part of the change management for her organization’s security practices. Which of the following is not a common technical implication of patching?
opts: Legacy applications
Downtime
Service restarts
Application restarts
questions.exp: Downtime as well as the need for applications and services to restart are common technical implications of patching processes. Patching doesn’t create legacy applications, but legacy applications are unlikely to have new patches available.

cram.def: Same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast. Problem: secure key exchange. Examples: AES, DES, 3DES.
Public/private key pair. Slower. Solves key exchange. Examples: RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman.
Shared freely. Used to ENCRYPT data sent TO you, and to VERIFY your digital signature.
Never shared. Used to DECRYPT data sent to you, and to CREATE your digital signature.
Public Key Infrastructure. System for managing digital certificates — issuance, renewal, revocation.
Trusted third party that issues, signs, and revokes digital certificates.
Top of the PKI hierarchy. Its certificate is self-signed. Trust anchor.
Subordinate CA that issues certificates on behalf of the root CA. Protects the root CA.
A copy of private keys stored securely with a third party — allows recovery if keys are lost.

matching.prompt: Same key for encryption and decryption
Public/private key pair
Key used to encrypt data sent TO you
Key used to decrypt data sent to you
Issues and signs digital certificates
Top of PKI hierarchy — self-signed cert
Stored copy of private keys with third party

questions.q: In asymmetric encryption, which key is used to encrypt data being sent to a recipient?
opts: The recipient's private key
The recipient's public key
The sender's private key
A shared symmetric key
questions.exp: Encrypt with the recipient's PUBLIC key — they then decrypt with their PRIVATE key.

questions.q: PKI is used to manage:
opts: Firewall rules
Password hashes
Digital certificates and key pairs
Network routing tables
questions.exp: PKI manages the lifecycle of digital certificates — creation, distribution, renewal, and revocation.

questions.q: Symmetric encryption is preferred for bulk data encryption because:
opts: It is more secure than asymmetric
It is significantly faster than asymmetric encryption
