It does not require key exchange
It uses public/private key pairs
questions.exp: Symmetric algorithms (AES) are much faster than asymmetric (RSA) — used for bulk data; asymmetric used for key exchange.

questions.q: Which key must NEVER be shared in asymmetric cryptography?
opts: Public key
Session key
Private key
Shared key
questions.exp: The private key must never be shared — it is used to decrypt incoming data and to create digital signatures.

questions.q: An intermediate CA in a PKI hierarchy is used to:
opts: Self-sign and issue root certificates for the entire PKI tree
Maintain the master Certificate Revocation List for the entire PKI
Store the root CA private keys in protected hardware escrow
Issue certificates on behalf of the root CA, protecting the root from direct exposure
questions.exp: Intermediate CAs issue certificates while the root CA remains offline — protecting the critical trust anchor.

questions.q: Key escrow means:
opts: Storing a copy of private keys with a trusted third party for recovery purposes
Destroying old private keys immediately after rotation so they cannot be used to decrypt anything later
Wrapping each user's private key under an organization-wide master key so all keys share one root of trust
Publishing the public certificate to a directory so revoked keys can be detected by relying parties
questions.exp: Key escrow allows recovery of encrypted data if keys are lost — required in some regulated industries.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of asymmetric encryption?
opts: AES-256
3DES
ChaCha20
RSA
questions.exp: RSA is asymmetric (public/private key pair). AES, 3DES, and ChaCha20 are all symmetric algorithms.

scenarios.q: A browser shows a certificate warning when users visit a new internal web portal, even though the certificate was issued by the company's internal CA and is not expired. The CA's root certificate has not yet been distributed to user devices. What is the MOST likely cause of the warning?
opts: The server certificate has expired and needs to be reissued
The browser does not trust the issuing CA because its root certificate is not in the device's trust store
The certificate was issued with the wrong common name for the portal hostname
The web server is negotiating a weak cipher suite that the browser rejects
scenarios.exp: PKI trust flows from the client's local root store. An internal CA's root certificate must be pushed to each device (via GPO, MDM, or manual install) before browsers will trust the certificates it issues — otherwise every chain terminates in an unknown root and the browser warns. Expiry, wrong common name, and weak ciphers all produce more specific error messages than the generic untrusted-issuer warning described here.

cram.def: Stored data — on drives, databases, USB, backups. Encrypted with AES-256 typically.
Data moving across a network. Protected by TLS, HTTPS, VPN, SSH.
Data actively being processed in memory/CPU. Hardest to protect. Secure enclave helps.
Encrypts entire storage device. BitLocker (Windows), FileVault (macOS). Protects stolen devices.
Protects data in transit. Replaced SSL. Used by HTTPS (port 443).
Advanced Encryption Standard. Symmetric block cipher. Standard for data at rest. AES-256 strongest.
Destroying the encryption key makes encrypted data permanently unreadable — secure data deletion method.

matching.prompt: Encrypted data stored on a hard drive
TLS protects data in which state
Data being processed in RAM
BitLocker encrypts the entire drive
Standard encryption algorithm for data at rest
Destroying the key to make data unreadable

questions.q: Data encrypted while stored on disk is called:
opts: Data at rest
Data in use
Data in transit
Data in process
questions.exp: Data at rest refers to stored data — on drives, databases, and backups. Typically encrypted with AES.

questions.q: TLS protects data in which state?
opts: In transit
In use
At rest
In backup
questions.exp: TLS encrypts data moving across networks — protecting data in transit between clients and servers.

questions.q: Full disk encryption (FDE) primarily protects against:
opts: Unauthorized access to data when a device is lost or stolen
Network eavesdropping while data is in transit
Malware execution after the system has booted
Phishing attacks targeting user credentials
questions.exp: FDE encrypts the entire drive — stolen devices cannot have their data read without the decryption key.

questions.q: Which state of data is most difficult to protect with encryption?
opts: Data at rest
Data in transit
Data in use
Data in backup
questions.exp: Data in use (in RAM/CPU) is actively being processed — it must be decrypted to be used, making it hard to protect.

questions.q: Cryptographic erasure is:
opts: Destroying the encryption key to render encrypted data permanently unreadable
Physically destroying the storage media using shredding
Overwriting all data on the disk multiple times with random patterns
Deleting the file system index from the storage device
questions.exp: Cryptographic erasure destroys only the key — the encrypted data remains but is permanently inaccessible.

questions.q: Which protocol replaced SSL and is now used to protect HTTPS traffic?
opts: SSH
TLS
IPsec
SFTP
questions.exp: TLS (Transport Layer Security) replaced SSL and is the standard for encrypting web traffic — HTTPS uses TLS.

scenarios.q: A compliance auditor reviews a database holding patient records. The database resides on an encrypted volume, but the auditor flags a concern about data protection during backup replication to an offsite site over the public Internet. Which protection MOST directly addresses the auditor's concern?
opts: Increasing the complexity and rotation frequency of the database administrator's password
Enabling TLS for the replication connection so that data is encrypted in transit between the primary and the offsite site
Rotating the volume-level encryption key on the primary database server every month
Adding row-level access controls inside the database so only specific roles can read patient records
scenarios.exp: The auditor's concern is specifically about replication traffic traversing the public Internet — that is a data-in-transit problem, not a data-at-rest problem. The encrypted volume and any at-rest key rotation protect the disk where the data lives, not the wire between sites. Row-level access controls enforce authorization, not confidentiality on the network. TLS on the replication connection encrypts the data as it moves between sites, which is exactly what the auditor flagged.

cram.def: How do you securely share a symmetric key when you have no secure channel yet? Diffie-Hellman solves this.
Allows two parties to derive a shared secret over a public channel without transmitting the secret itself.
Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral. Generates new key pair for each session — provides Perfect Forward Secrecy.
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral. Stronger security with smaller key sizes. Used in modern TLS.
Each session uses a unique ephemeral key. Compromising the long-term private key doesn't expose past sessions.

matching.prompt: Solves secure key exchange over public channel
Unique key per session — provides PFS
Past sessions protected even if private key compromised
DH variant using elliptic curves — smaller keys
Older key exchange — no PFS

questions.q: Diffie-Hellman is used to:
opts: Sign digital certificates with the issuer's private key
Establish a shared secret over an insecure public channel
Hash user passwords stored in a database
Encrypt email attachments using a public key
questions.exp: Diffie-Hellman allows two parties to derive a shared secret over a public channel without transmitting the secret.

questions.q: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) ensures that:
opts: Encryption keys never expire and remain valid forever
One key is reused for every encryption session over time
All keys are stored permanently in a key escrow database
Compromising the long-term private key does not expose past session keys
questions.exp: PFS uses ephemeral session keys — even if the server's private key is later stolen, past sessions remain safe.

questions.q: Why is RSA key exchange being phased out of modern TLS in favor of DHE/ECDHE?
opts: RSA key exchange is no longer mathematically secure against modern computers
RSA encryption is too slow for modern hardware speeds
RSA key exchange requires a separate certificate per session
RSA key exchange does not provide Perfect Forward Secrecy
questions.exp: RSA key exchange uses the same server private key for all sessions — compromising it exposes all past sessions. DHE/ECDHE provide PFS.

questions.q: DHE stands for:
opts: Dynamic Hash Encryption
Diffie-Hellman Exchange
Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral
Distributed Hash Encryption
questions.exp: DHE = Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral. 'Ephemeral' means a new key pair is generated for each session — enabling PFS.

scenarios.q: Two systems need to establish a shared symmetric session key to encrypt a large data transfer. Their only communication path is the public Internet and they have never pre-shared any secret. Which cryptographic technique BEST solves this key establishment problem?
opts: Agreeing in advance that both endpoints will use the same symmetric algorithm, such as AES-256 in GCM mode
An ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (or ECDHE) key exchange, which lets each side compute the same shared secret without ever transmitting it over the wire
Each side independently hashing a fixed shared password with SHA-256 and using the resulting digest as the session key
The sender encrypting a randomly chosen session key with a pre-shared password and emailing it to the recipient before the transfer begins
scenarios.exp: Diffie-Hellman (and its elliptic-curve variant ECDHE) lets two parties derive the same shared secret over a public channel without ever transmitting the secret — which is exactly the situation described. Agreeing on an algorithm like AES-256 is not a key exchange. Hashing a shared password assumes a pre-shared secret, which the scenario explicitly rules out. Emailing a password-wrapped key also assumes a pre-shared password and exposes the key to anyone who intercepts the email and guesses that password.

cram.def: Hardware chip on motherboard. Stores encryption keys, certificates, passwords. Tied to specific hardware. Used by BitLocker.
Dedicated enterprise device for secure key generation, storage, and cryptographic operations.
TPM = built into a single device. HSM = external/network device, enterprise-grade, high-performance.
Isolated CPU region for sensitive operations. Apple Secure Enclave, ARM TrustZone, Intel SGX.
Storage device with built-in encryption hardware. Encryption/decryption happens at drive level.

matching.prompt: Hardware chip on motherboard storing crypto keys
Enterprise external device for key management
Isolated CPU region — resistant to OS compromise
BitLocker relies on this hardware component
Drive with built-in encryption hardware

questions.q: A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) is used to:
opts: Provide secure internet access through a trusted hardware module
Block malware at the corporate network perimeter via firewall rules
Securely store cryptographic keys and support hardware-based encryption tied to a device
Manage user passwords centrally in Active Directory user groups
questions.exp: TPM is a hardware chip that stores keys, certificates, and passwords — bound to the specific device it's installed in.

questions.q: BitLocker relies on which hardware component to verify boot integrity before releasing the encryption key?
opts: HSM
TPM
UEFI only
Smart card exclusively
questions.exp: BitLocker uses the TPM to seal the volume encryption key — it checks system integrity at boot before decryption.

questions.q: A secure enclave is:
opts: A physically locked and access-controlled secure server room with biometrics
An encrypted backup storage location managed entirely by the OS itself
A type of VPN tunnel used for secure remote administration of the device
An isolated processor area that protects sensitive code and data from the main operating system
questions.exp: Secure enclaves are isolated execution environments resistant to OS-level attacks.

questions.q: Which of the following provides the BEST protection for private keys in a high-security enterprise environment?
opts: A dedicated HSM — tamper-resistant hardware purpose-built for enterprise key protection
TPMs deployed per-workstation as the enterprise key store for end-user devices
An AES-256 encrypted key file on a hardened internal file server
An enterprise password manager with role-based access controls and audit logging
questions.exp: HSMs are the gold standard for enterprise key protection — tamper-resistant, high-performance, with strict access controls.

scenarios.q: A financial company must store the root signing key for its internal certificate authority in such a way that the key can still be used for signing operations but cannot be extracted, even by a privileged administrator with full access to the host server. Which technology BEST meets this requirement?
opts: A hardware security module (HSM) that stores the key in tamper-resistant hardware and exposes only signing operations to the CA, never the key material itself
A software-encrypted key file on the CA server, protected by a strong administrative passphrase that only trusted staff know
A TPM-sealed key file tied to the boot state of the CA server, so the key is only accessible when the expected boot environment is measured
A Windows DPAPI-protected blob stored in the CA service account's user profile, automatically unlocked when the service logs on
scenarios.exp: A hardware security module stores cryptographic keys in tamper-resistant hardware and exposes only operations (sign, encrypt, decrypt), not the key material — privileged administrators of the host cannot extract the key. Software-encrypted key files and DPAPI blobs are ultimately only as strong as the administrator account that protects them. A TPM-sealed file provides strong platform binding but is designed for boot-state attestation, not non-extractable custody of a CA root key that must survive hardware refresh and remain usable by the CA.

cram.def: Hiding secret data WITHIN ordinary non-secret files (images, audio, video). The existence of the message is concealed.
Replaces sensitive data with a random non-sensitive token. Original data stays in a secure vault. Used in PCI DSS.
Replaces real data with realistic-looking fake data for dev/test environments. Original data preserved.
Encryption mathematically secures data. Obfuscation hides it. Both can be used together.
Payment card data — token used in transactions, real card number never stored by merchant.
Developers need realistic data for testing without using real customer PII.

matching.prompt: Hiding a message inside an image file
Replacing a credit card number with a random token
Showing fake but realistic data to developers
Token maps to real data stored in secure vault
Original data preserved but not shown

questions.q: Steganography is the practice of:
opts: Encrypting data with a strong symmetric key so the contents are unreadable without it
Generating digital certificates that bind a public key to a verified identity for trust
Hashing passwords with a per-user salt before storage so plaintext is never written to disk
Hiding secret data within ordinary non-secret files such as images or audio
questions.exp: Steganography hides messages inside ordinary files — the existence of the secret message is itself concealed.

questions.q: Tokenization replaces sensitive data with:
opts: A random non-sensitive token that maps back to the original in a secure vault
An encrypted version of the original data using AES-256
A cryptographic hash of the original data using SHA-256
A compressed version of the original data using zlib compression
questions.exp: Tokenization substitutes sensitive data (e.g. credit card numbers) with a random token — the original stays in a secure vault.

questions.q: Data masking is used to:
opts: Permanently delete and overwrite sensitive data records in production
Monitor and audit-log all access to sensitive data files for review
Encrypt backup data at rest using strong industry-standard ciphers
Replace real data with realistic-looking fake data so developers can test without real PII
questions.exp: Data masking provides realistic test data without exposing real customer information to developers or testers.

questions.q: How does steganography differ from encryption?
opts: Steganography is always cryptographically stronger than encryption
Steganography hides the existence of the message; encryption hides its content
They are essentially the same cryptographic technique
Steganography is more efficient than encryption for protecting large files
questions.exp: Encryption makes the message unreadable. Steganography hides the fact that a message exists at all.

scenarios.q: A developer needs to share a production database snapshot with an offshore analytics vendor so the vendor can tune query performance. Real customer names and Social Security numbers cannot leave the production environment, but the column structure and realistic-looking data distributions must be preserved so that query plans behave the same way as in production. Which technique BEST fits this need?
opts: Full-disk encryption applied to the exported snapshot file before it is handed off to the vendor
Compressing and password-protecting the snapshot archive with a strong passphrase shared out of band with the vendor
Hashing every sensitive field with SHA-256 before export so that the original values are irreversible on the vendor side
Data masking that replaces sensitive fields with realistic but fictional values while preserving the column schema, data types, and distributions
scenarios.exp: Data masking replaces sensitive values with realistic-but-fictional substitutes while preserving column types, formats, and distributions — the vendor sees data that behaves like production for query-plan purposes without exposing any real customer. Encryption and password-protected archives only hide data in transit or at rest; once decrypted, the real PII is visible again. Hashing destroys distributions and is still vulnerable to dictionary attacks on low-entropy fields like Social Security numbers.

cram.def: One-way (can't reverse), deterministic (same input = same hash), avalanche effect (small change = completely different hash).
128-bit hash. BROKEN — collision vulnerabilities. Not used for security. Still used for checksums.
256-bit hash. Part of SHA-2 family. Current standard for most security applications.
Random value added to a password BEFORE hashing. Unique per user. Defeats rainbow tables.
Precomputed hash-to-plaintext mapping. Defeated by salting passwords.
Hash-based Message Authentication Code. Hash + shared secret key. Provides integrity + authentication.
1. Hash the message. 2. Encrypt hash with private key. 3. Recipient decrypts with public key. 4. Compare hashes.

matching.prompt: 128-bit hash — broken, collision vulnerabilities
256-bit hash — current standard
Random value added before hashing passwords
Precomputed hash table — defeated by salts
Hash + shared secret for integrity + authentication
Small input change produces completely different hash
Step 1 of creating a digital signature

questions.q: Which hashing algorithm produces a 256-bit hash and is considered the current standard?
opts: MD5
SHA-256
SHA-1
SHA-512
questions.exp: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest and is part of the SHA-2 family — widely used and considered secure.

questions.q: What is added to a password BEFORE hashing to defend against rainbow table attacks?
opts: IV
Salt
Pepper
Nonce
questions.exp: A salt is a unique random value added per user before hashing — making precomputed rainbow table attacks useless.

questions.q: Why is MD5 no longer recommended for security purposes?
opts: It produces fixed-length 128-bit output regardless of input size
It cannot be used with a salt to defend against rainbow tables
It was deprecated by NIST in 2008 due to quantum computing threats
It produces collision vulnerabilities — different inputs can produce the same hash
questions.exp: MD5 has known collision vulnerabilities — two different inputs can produce the same hash, breaking integrity guarantees.

questions.q: A digital signature is verified using the sender's:
opts: Public key
Shared key
Private key
Session key
questions.exp: The sender's PUBLIC key is used to verify their signature — anyone can verify, but only the private key holder could have signed.

questions.q: HMAC provides which security properties?
opts: Message encryption and compression of payload data
Non-repudiation and full message confidentiality
Integrity and authentication using a shared secret key
Key exchange and digital signature generation
questions.exp: HMAC combines hashing with a shared secret — verifying both that the data hasn't changed and that the sender knows the key.

questions.q: What is the correct order for creating a digital signature?
opts: Encrypt the message, then hash it
Hash the message, then encrypt the hash with the sender's private key
Hash the message, then encrypt it with the recipient's public key
Encrypt with symmetric key, then sign with public key
questions.exp: Digital signing: hash the message → encrypt the hash with your private key. Verification: decrypt with public key → compare hashes.

scenarios.q: A software vendor publishes an installer along with a SHA-256 hash posted on the same download page. A customer wants assurance not only that the installer has not been altered in transit, but also that it actually came from the vendor and not from an attacker who compromised the download page. Which additional artifact BEST provides that assurance?
opts: A digital signature on the installer that can be verified against the vendor's public certificate obtained from a trusted source
A second SHA-256 hash of the installer posted to a different section of the same vendor website
A larger hash algorithm such as SHA-512 used in place of SHA-256 for the published hash value
A password-protected ZIP archive wrapping the installer, with the password emailed separately to registered customers
scenarios.exp: A hash alone proves integrity only if the hash source itself is trustworthy — if the attacker can modify the installer on the page, they can replace the posted hash too. A digital signature binds the file to the signer's private key, and verifying it against a public certificate obtained from a trusted source (CA chain or pre-installed trust store) establishes both integrity and authenticity. A stronger hash algorithm has the same provenance weakness; a password-protected ZIP does not prove the signer's identity.

cram.def: Distributed, immutable ledger. Each block contains data + hash of previous block. Tampering breaks the chain.
Copies exist on many nodes simultaneously. No single point of failure or control.
Once recorded, blockchain data cannot be altered without invalidating all subsequent blocks.
How nodes agree on valid transactions. Examples: Proof of Work (PoW), Proof of Stake (PoS).
Blockchain primarily provides INTEGRITY and NON-REPUDIATION. Not confidentiality by default.

matching.prompt: Primary security property blockchain provides
What makes blockchain tamper-evident
matching.answer: Each block hashes the previous block

matching.prompt: Copies on many nodes simultaneously
Once written, cannot be changed without detection
How nodes agree on valid transactions

questions.q: A blockchain is best described as:
opts: A centralized encrypted database for storing all transactions
A distributed immutable ledger where each block contains a hash of the previous block
A type of symmetric encryption algorithm used widely in banking
A certificate authority that issues and revokes digital certificates
questions.exp: A blockchain is a distributed ledger — each block cryptographically links to the previous, making tampering detectable.

questions.q: What makes blockchain records tamper-evident?
opts: They are stored with AES-256 encryption — altering a record requires breaking the cipher first
They use symmetric keys for signing — only the symmetric key holder can produce valid signatures
Each block contains a hash of the previous block — altering any block invalidates all subsequent blocks
Each block carries a synchronized network timestamp — any backdated modification would be detectable
questions.exp: Altering any block changes its hash, which invalidates the next block's stored hash — breaking the entire chain.

questions.q: Which security property does blockchain primarily provide?
opts: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity and non-repudiation
Authentication
questions.exp: Blockchain's cryptographic chaining provides strong integrity — records cannot be altered undetected.

scenarios.q: A consortium of shipping suppliers wants a shared ledger that records each parcel's custody transfers between companies. Any participant must be able to read the full ledger, no single participant should be able to retroactively alter past entries without detection, and there is no central authority to control the system. Which technology BEST fits these requirements?
opts: A shared SQL database hosted in the data center of the largest consortium member, with read-write accounts issued to the other members
A shared SFTP folder where each supplier uploads a digitally signed CSV of its custody transfers at the end of each business day
A centralized document management system where every supplier is granted read-write access to a single shared folder of custody records
A distributed blockchain ledger in which each block is cryptographically chained to the previous block and replicated across participating nodes
scenarios.exp: A distributed blockchain ledger provides all three properties the scenario explicitly requires: tamper evidence (each block is hashed and chained to the previous one, so altering a past entry invalidates every subsequent hash), shared readability across all participants, and no single controlling authority. A central SQL database or document system concentrates trust in one participant. A shared SFTP folder of signed CSVs provides integrity per file but allows silent rewrites of history and does not produce a single consortium-visible ordered ledger.

cram.def: Binds a public key to an identity. Signed by a CA. Contains: subject, public key, issuer, validity dates.
Standard format for digital certificates. Used in TLS, S/MIME, code signing.
Generated by requester. Contains public key + identity info. Sent to CA for signing.
Domain Validation. Only proves ownership of domain. Fastest to obtain. Basic HTTPS.
Extended Validation. Rigorous identity check. Highest assurance.
*.example.com covers ALL first-level subdomains. One cert for many subdomains.
Subject Alternative Name. Single cert covers MULTIPLE different domain names.
Published list of revoked certificates. Clients download and check against it.
Real-time certificate revocation checking. Client queries OCSP responder for specific cert status.
Server includes OCSP response in TLS handshake — reduces client lookup latency.
Application hardcodes expected certificate/public key. Rejects any other cert — prevents MITM.
Signed by its own private key (not a CA). Browsers show warnings. Used in internal/dev environments.

matching.prompt: Only proves domain ownership — fastest
Highest assurance — rigorous organization verification
Single cert covering all subdomains of a domain
Single cert covering multiple different domains
Real-time revocation checking protocol
Published list of revoked certificates
Server includes OCSP response in TLS handshake
App hardcodes expected certificate to prevent MITM
Document sent to CA requesting certificate issuance

questions.q: Which protocol provides REAL-TIME certificate revocation status checking?
opts: CRL
LDAP
OCSP
SCEP
questions.exp: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) allows clients to query the revocation status of a specific certificate in real time.

questions.q: A wildcard certificate (*.example.com) covers:
opts: All first-level subdomains of example.com
Only the example.com root domain itself
Multiple unrelated domains in one certificate
Only internal IP addresses on the LAN
questions.exp: A wildcard cert covers any first-level subdomain: mail.example.com, www.example.com, app.example.com, etc.

questions.q: A self-signed certificate is signed by:
opts: The entity that owns it, using its own private key
An intermediate certificate authority in the PKI
A trusted root CA at the top of the chain
A separate registration authority entity
questions.exp: Self-signed certs are signed by the entity itself — not a trusted third-party CA, so browsers display warnings.

questions.q: Certificate pinning is used to:
opts: Prevent MITM attacks by hardcoding the expected certificate or public key in an application
Speed up TLS handshakes by skipping the certificate validation step
Automatically renew certificates before they reach their expiration date
Generate Certificate Signing Requests to send to the CA for signing
questions.exp: Certificate pinning rejects any certificate not matching the hardcoded expected value — even a valid CA-signed cert.

questions.q: What is a CSR (Certificate Signing Request)?
opts: A formal revocation notice sent from the certificate holder to the issuing CA
A cryptographic hash of an existing certificate used for fingerprint comparison
A firewall rule that controls HTTPS traffic flow to a specific application
A document generated by the requester containing their public key and identity info, sent to a CA for signing
questions.exp: A CSR is generated by the requester — it contains their public key and identifying info, and is sent to a CA to be signed.

questions.q: OCSP stapling improves performance by:
opts: Caching trusted certificates locally on each client browser to allow reuse later
Compressing the certificate chain data using standard zlib compression algorithms
Having the server include the OCSP revocation response in the TLS handshake, eliminating a separate client lookup
Reducing the public key size used during handshake to speed up TLS processing
questions.exp: OCSP stapling has the server provide the pre-fetched OCSP response during the handshake — no extra round trip for the client.

scenarios.q: A private key for a production web server's TLS certificate was accidentally committed to a public code repository and briefly indexed by a search engine. The team has already removed the file and reissued a new certificate bound to a new key pair. Which action is MOST important to complete to protect users who may still encounter the old certificate in caches or from attackers replaying it?
opts: Submit the compromised certificate to the issuing CA for revocation and ensure the revocation is published through both CRL and OCSP
Rotate the server's administrative SSH key pair used by the operations team to log into the host
Rename the old certificate and key files on the server's file system so that Apache or nginx cannot accidentally load them again
Send an email to all customers asking them to clear their browser caches and restart their devices before visiting the site again
scenarios.exp: Once a private key has been exposed publicly, the compromised certificate must be revoked through the issuing CA so that clients performing CRL or OCSP checks see the certificate as invalid — otherwise an attacker holding the leaked key can still impersonate the server to clients that trust the cert. Rotating SSH keys addresses an unrelated credential. Renaming files on the server does not reach any external client. Asking customers to clear caches is neither reliable nor scalable and is not a certificate lifecycle control.

questions.q: Mike is sending David an encrypted message using a symmetric encryption algorithm. What key should he use to encrypt the message?
opts: Mike’s public key
Mike’s private key
David’s public key
Shared secret key
questions.exp: In symmetric encryption algorithms, both the sender and the receiver use a shared secret key to encrypt and decrypt the message, respectively.

questions.q: Acme Widgets has 10 employees and they all need the ability to communicate with one another using a symmetric encryption system. The system should allow any two employees to securely communicate without other employees eavesdropping. If Acme Widgets switched to an asymmetric encryption algorithm, how many keys would be required to add the 11th employee?
questions.exp: In an asymmetric encryption algorithm, each employee needs only two keys: a public key and a private key. Adding a new user to the system requires the addition of these two keys for that user, regardless of how many other users exist.

questions.q: What type of digital certificate provides the greatest level of assurance that the certificate owner is who they claim to be?
opts: DV
OV
UV
EV
questions.exp: Extended validation (EV) certificates provide the highest available level of assurance. The CA issuing an EV certificate certifies that they have verified the identity and authenticity of the certificate subject.

questions.q: Glenn recently obtained a wildcard certificate for *.mydomain.com. Which one of the following domains would not be covered by this certificate?
opts: mydomain.com
core.mydomain.com
dev.www.mydomain.com
mail.mydomain.com
questions.exp: Wildcard certificates protect the listed domain as well as all first‐level subdomains. dev.www.mydomain.com is a second‐level subdomain of mydomain.com and would not be covered by this certificate.

questions.q: Which one of the following servers is almost always an offline CA in a large PKI deployment?
opts: Root CA
Intermediate CA
RA
Internal CA
questions.exp: Root CAs are highly protected and not normally used for certificate issuance. A root CA is usually run as an offline CA that delegates authority to intermediate CAs that run as online CAs.

questions.q: Which one of the following certificate formats is closely associated with Windows binary certificate files?
opts: DER
PEM
PFX
P7B
questions.exp: The PFX format is most closely associated with Windows systems that store certificates in binary format, whereas the P7B format is used for Windows systems storing files in text format.

questions.q: What type of security solution provides a hardware platform for the storage and management of encryption keys?
opts: HSM
IPS
SIEM
SOAR
questions.exp: Hardware security modules (HSMs) provide an effective way to manage encryption keys. These hardware devices store and manage encryption keys in a secure manner that prevents humans from ever needing to work directly with the keys.

questions.q: David would like to send Mike a message using an asymmetric encryption algorithm. What key should he use to encrypt the message?
opts: David’s public key
David’s private key
Mike’s public key
Mike’s private key
questions.exp: When encrypting a message using an asymmetric encryption algorithm, the person performing the encryption does so using the recipient’s public key.

questions.q: When Mike receives the message that David encrypted for him, what key should he use to decrypt the message?
opts: David’s public key
David’s private key
Mike’s public key
Mike’s private key
questions.exp: In an asymmetric encryption algorithm, the recipient of a message uses their own private key to decrypt messages that they receive.

questions.q: If David wishes to digitally sign the message that he is sending Mike, what key would he use to create the digital signature?
opts: David’s public key
David’s private key
Mike’s public key
Mike’s private key
questions.exp: The sender of a message may digitally sign the message by encrypting a message digest with the sender’s own private key.

questions.q: When Mike receives the digitally signed message from David, what key should he use to verify the digital signature?
opts: David’s public key
David’s private key
Mike’s public key
Mike’s private key
questions.exp: The recipient of a digitally signed message may verify the digital signature by decrypting it with the public key of the individual who signed the message.

questions.q: Norm is using full‐disk encryption technology to protect the contents of laptops against theft. What goal of cryptography is he attempting to achieve?
opts: Integrity
Non‐repudiation
Authentication
Confidentiality
questions.exp: Norm’s actions are designed to protect against the unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information. This is a clear example of protecting confidentiality.

questions.q: Brian discovers that a user suspected of stealing sensitive information is posting many image files to a message board. What technique might the individual be using to hide sensitive information in those images?
opts: Steganography
Homomorphic encryption
Replay attack
Birthday attack
questions.exp: Steganography is the art of using cryptographic techniques to embed secret messages within another file.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about cryptographic keys is incorrect?
opts: All cryptographic keys should be kept secret.
Longer keys are better than shorter keys when the same algorithm is used.
Asymmetric algorithms generally use longer keys than symmetric algorithms.
Digital certificates are designed to share public keys.
questions.exp: All of these statements are correct except for the statement that all cryptographic keys should be kept secret. The exception to this rule are public keys used in asymmetric cryptography. These keys should be freely shared.

questions.q: What type of cipher operates on one character of text at a time?
opts: Block cipher
Bit cipher
Stream cipher
Balanced cipher
questions.exp: Stream ciphers operate on one character or bit of a message (or data stream) at a time. Block ciphers operate on “chunks,” or blocks, of a message and apply the encryption algorithm to an entire message block at the same time.

questions.q: Vince is choosing a symmetric encryption algorithm for use in his organization. He would like to choose the strongest algorithm from these choices. What algorithm should he choose?
opts: DES
3DES
RSA
AES
questions.exp: AES is the successor to 3DES and DES and is the best choice for a symmetric encryption algorithm. RSA is a secure algorithm, but it is asymmetric rather than symmetric.

questions.q: Kevin is configuring a web server to use digital certificates. What technology can he use to allow clients to quickly verify the status of those certificates without contacting a remote server?
opts: CRL
OCSP
Certificate stapling
Certificate pinning
questions.exp: The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) provides real‐time checking of a digital certificate’s status using a remote server. Certificate stapling attaches a current OCSP response to the certificate to allow the client to validate the certificate without contacting the OCSP server. Certificate revocation lists (CRLs) are a slower, outdated approach to managing certificate status. Certificate pinning is used to provide an expected key, not to manage certificate status.

questions.q: Acme Widgets has 10 employees and they all need the ability to communicate with one another using a symmetric encryption system. The system should allow any two employees to securely communicate without other employees eavesdropping. If an 11th employee is added to the organization, how many new keys must be added to the system?
questions.exp: When the 11th employee joins Acme Widgets, they will need a shared secret key with every existing employee. There are 10 existing employees, so 10 new keys are required.

questions.q: Jim configures a Windows machine with the built‐in BitLocker full‐disk encryption tool that uses a TPM chip. When is the machine least vulnerable to having data stolen from it?
opts: When the machine is off
When the machine is booted and logged in but is locked
When the machine is booted and logged in but is unlocked
When the machine is booted and logged in but is asleep
questions.exp: Jim knows that once a BitLocker‐enabled machine is booted, the drive is unlocked and could be accessed. He would be least worried if the machine were off and was stolen, or if the drive itself were stolen from the machine, since the data would not be accessible in either of those cases.

questions.q: Oliver wants to store and manage secrets in his cloud service provider’s environment. What type of solution should he look for as part of their offerings?
opts: A TPM
A secure enclave
A KMS
A Titan M
questions.exp: Oliver should look for a key management system, or KMS, which will allow him to securely create, store, and manage keys in a cloud environment. TPMs, secure enclaves, and Google’s Titan M are all local hardware solutions.

questions.q: What technique is used to ensure that DNSSEC‐protected DNS information is trustworthy?
opts: It is digitally signed.
It is sent via TLS.
It is encrypted using AES256.
It is sent via an IPSec VPN.
questions.exp: DNSSEC does not encrypt data but does rely on digital signatures to ensure that DNS information has not been modified and that it is coming from a server that the domain owner trusts. DNSSEC does not protect confidentiality, which is a key thing to remember when discussing it as a security option. TLS, an IPSec VPN, or encryption via AES are all potential solutions to protect the confidentiality of network data.

questions.q: What is the key difference between hashing and checksums?
opts: Both can validate integrity, but a hash also provides a unique digital fingerprint.
A hash can be reversed, and a checksum cannot be.
Checksums provide greater security than hashing.
Checksums have fewer message collisions than a hash.
questions.exp: Although both a checksum and a hash can be used to validate message integrity, a hash has fewer collisions than a checksum and will also provide a unique fingerprint for a file. Checksums are primarily used as a quick means of checking that that integrity is maintained, whereas hashes are used for many other purposes such as secure password validation without retaining the original password. A checksum would not be useful for proving a forensic image was identical, but it could be used to ensure that your work had not changed the contents of the drive.

questions.q: In some encryption algorithms, an initial connection is set up using an asymmetric key pair. Immediately upon the establishment of that session, the two parties create a new symmetric key that is used for the remainder of the connection. What term best describes this type of symmetric key?
opts: One‐time keys
Ephemeral keys
Private keys
Public keys
questions.exp: Ephemeral, short‐lived keys, are used with key establishment. Public and private keys are part of that exchange. A one‐time key is not an encryption term, but one‐time pads are cryptographic ciphers that are used once and then discarded.

questions.q: What is the key difference between checksums and hashes?
opts: Checksums are unique to every file; hashes are not.
Hashes are reversible and can be used to generate the original file or data; checksums cannot be used to re‐create the original file.
Checksums are a small value used to detect errors, whereas hashes map to an arbitrarily sized output that is unique to each file hashed.
There is no difference—checksums and hashes are the same.
questions.exp: A checksum is a computation that is used to determine whether a file or message has been changed, allowing error detection. A hash generates a unique value for a file and is a one‐way function—it cannot be reversed to re‐create the original file.

questions.q: Which one of the following algorithms is primarily used for the exchange of encryption keys?
opts: PBKDF2
AES
OCSP
Diffie–Hellman
questions.exp: Diffie–Hellman is a key exchange algorithm used to create a common shared secret key. The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a symmetric encryption algorithm used to protect data. Password‐Based Key Derivation Function 2 (PBKDF2) is a key stretching algorithm used to create strong keys from short passwords. The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) is used to verify the validity of digital certificates.

questions.q: Fred wants to implement trusted boot and knows that he needs to make sure that his workstations and laptops have the appropriate hardware to support it. What hardware should he ensure is built into the systems he is purchasing?
opts: TPM
HSM
IPS
NGFW
questions.exp: A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is used by UEFI as part of the boot process to validate the boot objects and programs or to document what is started so that boot attestation can occur. A hardware security module (HSM) is used to create, store, and manage encryption keys and certificates. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) and a next‐generation firewall (NGFW) are both network security devices.

questions.q: Renee would like to send Christopher an encrypted message using an asymmetric encryption algorithm. What key should she use to encrypt the message?
opts: Christopher’s public key
Christopher’s private key
Renee’s public key
Renee’s private key
questions.exp: When encrypting a message using an asymmetric encryption algorithm, the person performing the encryption does so using the recipient’s public key.

questions.q: Grace received a digitally signed message from Richard and would like to verify the digital signature. What key should she use to perform this verification?
opts: Richard’s public key
Richard’s private key
Grace’s public key
Grace’s private key
questions.exp: The recipient of a digitally signed message may verify the digital signature by decrypting it with the public key of the individual who signed the message.

questions.q: What emerging cryptographic technology is commonly used to create a distributed and immutable public ledger?
opts: Quantum computing
Perfect forward secrecy
Homomorphic encryption
Blockchain
questions.exp: The blockchain is, in its simplest description, a distributed and immutable public ledger. This means that it can store records in a way that distributes those records among many different systems located around the world and do so in a manner that prevents anyone from tampering with those records. The blockchain creates a data store that nobody can tamper with or destroy.

questions.q: Rhonda needs a digital certificate for a new web server that she is putting online this afternoon. If she has no prior relationship with a CA, what type of certificate can she obtain most quickly?
opts: OV
EV
DV
UV
questions.exp: Domain validation (DV) certificates require only verification of domain ownership, which can normally be done through an automated process. Other types of certificates require more thorough and time‐consuming verification steps.

questions.q: Jim wants to centrally create, store, and manage certificates and cryptographic keys for his entire organization. What sort of appliance‐based hardware solution should he select?
opts: An HSM
A TPM
An XDR
A Secure Enclave
questions.exp: Hardware security modules (HSMs) are used to create, store, and manage cryptographic certificates and keys in a secure manner. Trusted platform modules (TPMs) are used to help protect the boot process for systems. XDR (extended detection and response) describes technologies that correlate incident and security event information across a wide range of platforms and systems, and then provide analytics and response capabilities. A secure enclave is a dedicated secure element that is built into Apple’s system on chip modules (SOCs). They provide hardware key management, which is isolated from the main CPU, protecting keys throughout their life cycle and usage.

questions.q: Greg’s desktop system stores hashes of the system’s firmware, bootloader, drivers, and other components that are loaded at boot in the TPM, and then boots. The OS then uses a remote attestation client to send that information to a server. What type of boot process is he using?
opts: BIOS boot
UEFI hashing
Secure boot
Measured boot
questions.exp: This is a UEFI measured boot process. Secure boot validates hashes against known good hashes for those boot elements. BIOS does not support either of these processes. UEFI hashing was made up for this question.

questions.q: Jared wants to exchange keys with a third party in a secure manner. Why is key exchange a concern for cryptographic systems?
opts: Key length makes transferring keys difficult due to size.
Asymmetric encryption require extra security when sending private keys.
Symmetric encryption keys are all identical, meaning that they can be easily transferred.
Users may not have a preexisting secure means of communication.
questions.exp: How to exchange keys between two users or systems that have never interacted before is a key problem in cryptographic systems. Protocols like Diffie–Hellman key exchange address this issue for cryptographic systems, allowing users to securely exchange secret keys even if they have no preexisting trusted channel. Key length, even for long keys, does not create inordinately large files. Asymmetric encryption does not require the exchange of private keys, only public keys. Symmetric encryption keys are identical but must be protected, making exchange more challenging.

questions.q: Veronica would like to use a service from her cloud provider that will allow her to create, store, and manage the encryption keys used in her environment. What technology would best meet this goal?
opts: TPM
PKI
GPG
HSM
questions.exp: Hardware security modules (HSMs) are special‐purpose computing devices that manage encryption keys and also perform cryptographic operations in a highly efficient manner. Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) do manage encryption keys, but they are specific to a device and are not available in the cloud. The Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the set of policies, procedures, hardware, and software used to issue and create, distribute, store, revoke and manage public keys and security certificates. GPG, also known as GnuPG, implements Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) and uses public and private keys for data encryption and signing.

questions.q: Christopher received a message from Renee that was encrypted using an asymmetric encryption algorithm. What key should he use to decrypt the message?
opts: Christopher’s public key
Christopher’s private key
Renee’s public key
Renee’s private key
questions.exp: In an asymmetric encryption algorithm, the recipient of a message uses their own private key to decrypt messages that they receive.

questions.q: Jan is concerned that attackers might use a rainbow table attack against her organization’s stored passwords. What is the most effective defense against this type of attack?
opts: Pinning
Key escrow
Input validation
Salting
questions.exp: Rainbow table attacks attempt to reverse hashed password value by precomputing the hashes of common passwords. The attacker takes a list of common passwords and runs them through the hash function to generate the rainbow table. They then search through lists of hashed values, looking for matches to the rainbow table. The most common approach to preventing these attacks is salting, which adds a randomly generated value to each password prior to hashing.

questions.q: Mike wants to make it harder to break the encryption for a file that needs to stay secure for a number of years. Which of the following solutions should he select?
opts: Digitally sign the file.
Increase the key length.
Hash the file before encrypting it.
Encrypt the file before hashing it.
questions.exp: A longer key is generally stronger for modern cryptosystems, and a longer key will be harder to crack. Signing the file helps with nonrepudiation but not resistance to cracking the encryption. Hashing the file before encrypting it or hashing it after will not help in this scenario.

questions.q: Nadean is a software developer who is preparing a new application for release. She wishes to use code signing for the application file that will be deployed to a customer. What key should she use to sign the application?
opts: Her organization’s public key
Her organization’s private key
The customer’s public key
The customer’s private key
questions.exp: Digital signatures are always created using the private key of the person or organization creating the digital signature. In this case, Nadean should use her organization’s private key to sign the application.

cram.def: Government-backed. Most resources, most sophisticated. Motivated by espionage, disruption, or strategic advantage.
Ideologically motivated. Goal: disruption or publicity for a cause. Examples: Anonymous.
Financially motivated. Organized crime. Ransomware, fraud, data theft for resale.
Low skill. Uses pre-made tools without understanding them. Opportunistic, unsophisticated.
Current or former employee/contractor with legitimate access who abuses it. Intentional or unintentional.
Corporate espionage. Steals IP, trade secrets, or business intelligence.
Long-term, stealthy, targeted campaign. Usually nation-state or organized crime. Maintains persistent access.
Unauthorized hardware/software used inside an organization without IT approval — creates unmanaged risk.

matching.prompt: Government-backed, most sophisticated
Ideologically motivated, wants publicity
Primarily motivated by financial gain
Uses tools they don't understand
Has legitimate access and abuses it
Long-term stealthy targeted campaign
Unsanctioned technology used without IT approval

questions.q: Which threat actor typically has the most resources and sophisticated capabilities?
opts: Unskilled attacker
Hacktivist
Nation-state
Insider threat
questions.exp: Nation-state actors have government backing, large budgets, and the most advanced TTPs.

questions.q: A hacker defacing websites to protest corporate environmental practices is a:
opts: Nation-state actor
Unskilled attacker
Cybercriminal
Hacktivist
questions.exp: Hacktivists are motivated by ideology or political causes — not financial gain.

questions.q: Which threat actor uses pre-written tools and exploits without truly understanding them?
opts: Unskilled attacker
Hacktivist
Insider threat
APT
questions.exp: Unskilled attackers rely on existing tools — low skill, opportunistic, often causing unintended damage.

questions.q: An employee stealing customer data before resigning is which type of threat actor?
opts: Hacktivist
Unskilled attacker
Nation-state
Insider threat
questions.exp: Insider threats have legitimate access and abuse it — making them uniquely dangerous.

questions.q: APT stands for:
opts: Advanced Phishing Tactic
Automated Penetration Tool
Advanced Persistent Threat
Application Protection Technology
questions.exp: APT = Advanced Persistent Threat — long-term stealthy campaigns, typically nation-states or organized crime.

questions.q: Financial gain is the PRIMARY motivation for which threat actor?
opts: Cybercriminal
Nation-state
Hacktivist
Unskilled attacker
questions.exp: Cybercriminals are primarily financially motivated — ransomware, fraud, data theft for resale.

questions.q: What most distinguishes an insider threat from external attackers?
opts: High technical skill level beyond what most external attackers can match
Legitimate existing access to systems and data
Financial motivation as the dominant driver behind their attacks
Exclusive use of zero-day exploits provided by nation-state sponsors
questions.exp: Insider threats already have authorized access — bypassing perimeter controls that stop external attackers.

questions.q: Shadow IT refers to:
opts: Malware that hides from antivirus software using rootkit techniques to evade detection
Dark web forums where attackers trade stolen credentials and ready-made exploit kits
A category of nation-state actor specializing in covert long-running cyber operations
Unauthorized hardware or software used inside an organization without IT approval
questions.exp: Shadow IT creates unmanaged risks — IT can't patch, monitor, or secure what it doesn't know exists.

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes an APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) from a typical opportunistic cyberattack?
opts: APT actors target the broadest attack surface they can reach; opportunistic attackers focus on small numbers of pre-selected high-value targets
APT campaigns prioritize long-term stealthy access and persistence; opportunistic attacks prioritize fast visible impact (deface, ransom, smash-and-grab)
APT actors are typically motivated by short-term financial gain; opportunistic attackers pursue strategic intelligence over months
APTs exclusively use zero-day exploits while opportunistic attacks rely only on known and already-patched CVEs
questions.exp: Advanced Persistent Threats are characterized by long-term, stealthy access where the goal is to remain undetected and exfiltrate or position over time — typical of nation-state and named groups (APT29, Lazarus). Opportunistic attacks prioritize speed and impact: ransomware deployment, defacement, credential harvesting that monetizes quickly. The reversed-target distractor (A), reversed-motivation distractor (C), and zero-day-only distractor (D) are common confusions; in reality APTs use whatever access works, including phishing and known CVEs alongside zero-days.

scenarios.q: A company's finance director receives an email appearing to come from the CEO requesting an urgent $150,000 wire transfer to a new vendor account. The CEO is traveling and unreachable by phone. What type of threat actor technique is MOST likely being used?
opts: A hacktivist disrupting financial operations
An insider threat exploiting travel absence
A nation-state actor conducting espionage
A cybercriminal conducting Business Email Compromise
scenarios.exp: BEC (Business Email Compromise) is a financially motivated cybercriminal technique — impersonating executives to authorize fraudulent wire transfers. Urgency, travel context, and financial request are classic BEC indicators.

scenarios.q: A security analyst notices that a recently terminated employee's VPN credentials were used to access internal systems three days after termination, downloading 40GB of files. Which threat actor category does this BEST represent?
opts: Insider threat — a former employee exploiting delayed de-provisioning
Unskilled attacker exploiting a default account
Nation-state actor using stolen credentials
Hacktivist conducting data disclosure
scenarios.exp: Former employees whose access isn't immediately revoked remain insider threats post-termination. The 3-day window is a de-provisioning failure — the most dangerous insider threat window.

scenarios.q: An organization's SOC detects a low-and-slow intrusion active for 8 months. The attacker has pivoted through 12 systems, established multiple backdoors, and exfiltrated intellectual property in small encrypted chunks. No ransom demand has been made. Which threat actor profile BEST fits?
opts: Unskilled attacker using automated scanning tools
Cybercriminal conducting ransomware staging
Hacktivist building public embarrassment
Nation-state APT conducting long-term espionage
scenarios.exp: APT characteristics: long dwell time, multiple persistence mechanisms, intellectual property focus, no financial demand, slow exfiltration. Nation-state actors prioritize persistence over speed.

scenarios.q: A developer installs an unapproved cloud storage app on their work laptop to share large files with clients. IT discovers the app is syncing internal project documents to a personal cloud account. The developer had no malicious intent. Which risk category BEST describes this?
opts: Insider threat — deliberate data exfiltration
Shadow IT creating an unmanaged data exposure risk
Nation-state supply chain attack via the cloud app
Cybercriminal malware disguised as a productivity tool
scenarios.exp: Shadow IT: the developer isn't malicious — they're solving a real problem. But IT can't monitor, control, or secure tools they don't know exist. The exposure is real even without malicious intent.

scenarios.q: Security researchers discover a threat group has been compromising industrial control systems at energy utilities across three countries over two years, causing minor undetected calibration errors that could eventually cause equipment failures. No financial demand has been made. This MOST closely resembles:
opts: A nation-state actor with strategic infrastructure disruption objectives
Hacktivists protesting energy policy
Unskilled attackers using script-based automation
Organized cybercriminals staging for ransomware
scenarios.exp: Nation-state characteristics: multi-year campaign, critical infrastructure target, geographic scope, sabotage without financial motive, and operational technology focus. This aligns with state-sponsored strategic disruption objectives.

questions.q: Ken is conducting threat research on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and would like to consult the authoritative reference for the protocol’s technical specification. What resource would best meet his needs?
opts: Academic journal
Internet RFCs
Subject matter experts
Textbooks
questions.exp: All of these resources might contain information about the technical details of TLS, but Internet Request for Comments (RFC) documents are the definitive technical standards for Internet protocols. Consulting the RFCs would be Ken’s best option.

questions.q: Which one of the following threat research tools is used to visually display information about the location of threat actors?
opts: Threat map
Predictive analysis
Vulnerability feed
STIX
questions.exp: Threat maps are graphical tools that display information about the geographic locations of attackers and their targets. These tools are most often used as interesting marketing gimmicks, but they can also help identify possible threat sources.

questions.q: Ursula recently discovered that a group of developers are sharing information over a messaging tool provided by a cloud vendor but not sanctioned by her organization. What term best describes this use of technology?
opts: Shadow IT
System integration
Vendor management
Data exfiltration
questions.exp: The developers in question are using unapproved technology for business purposes. This is the classic definition of shadow IT. It is possible to describe this as data exfiltration, but there is no indication that the data security has been compromised, so shadow IT is a better description here.

questions.q: Which one of the following motivations is most commonly attributed to hacktivists?
opts: War
Financial gain
Political/philosophical beliefs
Ethical
questions.exp: Hacktivists are defined by the motivation behind their actions—advancing their political or philosophical beliefs. They engage in cyberattacks that they believe will advance their causes.

questions.q: Which one of the following attackers is most likely to be associated with an APT?
opts: Nation-state actor
Hacktivist
Unskilled
Insider
questions.exp: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are most commonly associated with nation-state actors. It is unlikely that an APT group would leverage the unsophisticated services of an unskilled script kiddie type attacker.

questions.q: Which of the following threat actors typically has the greatest access to resources?
opts: Nation-state actors
Organized crime
Hacktivists
Insider threats
questions.exp: Nation-state actors are government sponsored, and they typically have the greatest access to resources, including tools, money, and talent.

questions.q: Which one of the following is the best example of a hacktivist group?
opts: Chinese military
U.S. government
Russian mafia
Anonymous
questions.exp: The Chinese military and U.S. government are examples of nation-state actors and advanced persistent threats (APTs). The Russian mafia is an example of a criminal syndicate. Anonymous is the world’s most prominent hacktivist group.

questions.q: What type of assessment is particularly useful for identifying insider threats?
opts: Behavioral
Instinctual
Habitual
IoCs
questions.exp: Behavioral assessments are very useful when you are attempting to identify insider threats. Since insider threats are often hard to distinguish from normal behavior, the context of the actions performed—such as after-hours logins, misuse of credentials, logins from abnormal locations, or abnormal patterns—and other behavioral indicators are often used.

questions.q: Which one of the following threat actors typically has the lowest level of sophistication?
opts: Organized crime
Unskilled attacker
Hacktivist
Nation‐state
questions.exp: Unskilled attackers are unsophisticated by definition. They simply use tools that are available for download and lack technical expertise. The other attack sources listed here range in sophistication, but all are more sophisticated than unskilled attackers.

questions.q: Which one of the following threat actors is most likely to have access to a zero‐day exploit?
opts: Nation‐state
Hacktivist
Organized crime
Unskilled attacker
questions.exp: Zero‐day vulnerabilities are difficult to discover and their use is the hallmark of sophisticated, well‐resourced nation‐state groups. It is far less likely that organized crime, a hacktivist, or an unskilled attacker would have access to a zero‐day vulnerability.

questions.q: Which one of the following situations would be described as Shadow IT?
opts: Using an unapproved code repository
Hiring an unqualified systems administrator
Configuring inappropriate access controls
Using a product discontinued by the vendor
questions.exp: All of these situations pose a security risk. However, only the use of an unapproved code repository fits the definition of shadow IT—the adoption and use of unapproved technologies by an organization’s employees.

questions.q: Sally works for a government agency that works with classified information. What threat actor motivation is likely to be her highest concern from nation‐state actors?
opts: Ethical
Espionage
Revenge
Financial gain
questions.exp: Espionage is a common motivation for nation‐state actors. Data exfiltration, disruption and chaos, and war are also likely potential motivations for nation‐state actors. Ethical motivations are more commonly associated with hacktivists, whereas revenge is most often associated with insider threats. Financial gain is typically connected to organized crime and insider threats.

questions.q: Patrick is a security analyst with a government agency who believes that his organization was targeted by a sophisticated foreign government attack that used a zero‐day exploit. What term best describes this threat actor?
opts: Hacktivist
Nation‐state
Criminal syndicate
Insider
questions.exp: This attack was waged by a foreign government using a sophisticated zero‐day attack. The group waging this attack clearly qualifies as nation‐state, often called an advanced persistent threat (APT).

cram.def: The path or method an attacker uses to gain unauthorized access to a system.
The total set of points (vectors) where an attacker can try to enter or extract data.
Disable unnecessary services, close unused ports, remove default accounts, patch vulnerabilities.
Email, SMS, IM — used for phishing, malware delivery, social engineering.
Malicious macros in Office documents, malicious PDFs, infected executables.
Infected USB drives, external drives — baiting attacks.
Factory-set admin/admin — must be changed immediately on all devices.
Compromising software or hardware before it reaches the target — e.g. SolarWinds.

matching.prompt: Path an attacker uses to gain access
All points where an attacker can enter
admin/admin left unchanged on a router
Malware injected into a software update
Infected USB drive left in car park
Malicious macro in Word document

questions.q: Which BEST defines a threat vector?
opts: A category of malware (virus, worm, trojan) classified by how it infects and propagates across endpoints
The path or method an attacker uses to gain unauthorized access (e.g. email attachment, removable media, exposed RDP, supply chain)
A numeric vulnerability severity score that quantifies the impact and exploitability of a discovered weakness
A category of threat actor (e.g. nation-state, hacktivist, insider) ranked by typical motivation and technical capability
questions.exp: A threat vector is the route or method by which an attacker reaches a target — common vectors include email, removable media, exposed remote services (RDP, SSH), supply chain components, and direct network access. Distinguishing it from related concepts: malware is the payload that arrives; CVSS is the severity score; threat actor is who is conducting the attack. The vector is the HOW-IT-GETS-IN axis specifically, distinct from the WHO and the WHAT.

questions.q: Reducing the attack surface involves:
opts: Adding more network security monitoring tools at the perimeter layer
Eliminating unnecessary services, closing unused ports, removing default accounts
Increasing user permissions and access rights to improve productivity
Deploying additional honeypots to detect ongoing reconnaissance attempts
questions.exp: Reducing attack surface removes unnecessary entry points — fewer ways in means less risk.

questions.q: Default credentials on a newly deployed network device represent which type of vulnerability?
opts: Physical access attack vector
Supply chain vulnerability
Configuration-based attack vector
Social engineering vector
questions.exp: Default credentials (admin/admin) are a well-known configuration weakness — change them on first login.

questions.q: Which threat vector involves malicious code injected into a legitimate software update before delivery?
opts: Phishing vector
Social engineering
Supply chain attack
Insider threat vector
questions.exp: Supply chain attacks inject malware into legitimate software or hardware before it reaches the target — e.g. SolarWinds.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST reduces the risk from open service ports?
opts: Installing a honeypot on each open port
Monitoring port traffic passively
Disabling unnecessary services and closing unused ports
Requiring stronger passwords for service accounts
questions.exp: Closing unused ports and disabling unnecessary services eliminates those attack vectors entirely.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester hired by a retail company finds that the company's customer-facing web application, employee VPN portal, a forgotten staging server, and 3 IoT-connected security cameras are all accessible from the internet. The tester flags this before attempting exploitation. What concept does this BEST illustrate?
opts: A single critical vulnerability requiring immediate patching
A large attack surface with multiple potential entry points
A misconfigured firewall allowing all inbound traffic
Shadow IT created by the security camera vendor
scenarios.exp: Attack surface is the sum of all points where an attacker could try to enter. Four separate internet-facing systems — especially the forgotten staging server and IoT cameras — represent unnecessary exposure that should be reduced.

scenarios.q: A new branch office deploys 20 switches. The IT team configures VLANs and firewall rules but forgets to change default admin credentials. Six months later, an attacker gains admin access using credentials from the vendor's publicly available setup guide. Which threat vector did the attacker exploit?
opts: An unpatched firmware vulnerability in the switch OS
A supply chain attack on the switch firmware
Default credentials left unchanged — a misconfiguration vector
Physical access to the switch management ports
scenarios.exp: Default credentials are a configuration-based threat vector. The attacker didn't need to find a vulnerability — the organization handed over access by failing the most basic hardening step.

scenarios.q: A security team receives an alert that malware was found on 12 workstations. All affected machines opened the same vendor invoice PDF sent via email two weeks ago. The PDF exploited an unpatched vulnerability in the PDF reader. Which combination of threat vectors does this attack chain use?
opts: Removable media vector leading to network propagation
Voice-based vector followed by a web-based exploit
Message-based vector (email) delivering a file-based payload
Supply chain vector through the vendor's email system
scenarios.exp: Two-stage vector chain: email (message-based vector) as the delivery mechanism, with a malicious PDF (file-based vector) as the payload. The PDF exploited a client-side vulnerability — a classic phishing-to-file-exploit chain.

scenarios.q: A security architect reviewing internet-facing services finds: a public website, a customer portal, an API used by mobile apps, an RDP server used by remote admins, a legacy FTP server no longer actively used, and an exposed Elasticsearch database with no authentication. What is the MOST effective first action without purchasing new tools?
opts: Deploy an IDS to monitor all six services — alerting the SOC on any suspicious activity
Patch the public website and customer portal first — addressing known CVEs in those services
Disable or remove the legacy FTP server and the unauthenticated Elasticsearch instance — reducing the attack surface
Require MFA for the RDP server only — leaving other internet-facing services as configured
scenarios.exp: Attack surface reduction: removing unnecessary services eliminates the attack vector entirely. The legacy FTP server and unauthenticated Elasticsearch are the highest-risk, lowest-justification exposures — they shouldn't exist at all.

scenarios.q: An attacker sends a malicious Word document to 500 employees via a spoofed vendor email. The document contains a macro that downloads a RAT from a compromised website and establishes a C2 connection. Three employees enable the macro. Which combination of threat vectors is used?
opts: Message-based → file-based → web-based
Voice-based → removable media → network
Supply chain → insider threat → physical
File-based → DNS-based → wireless
scenarios.exp: Multi-vector chain: email (message-based) delivers the Word doc (file-based), the macro downloads from a compromised site (web-based), establishing C2. Understanding how vectors combine is key to the exam.

cram.def: Mass fraudulent emails impersonating trusted entities to steal credentials or install malware.
Targeted phishing at a specific person or group. Personalized to seem more legitimate.
Spear phishing targeting senior executives (CEO, CFO, CISO). High-value targets.
Voice phishing — social engineering over phone calls. Often impersonates IT support or banks.
SMS phishing — malicious links or requests sent via text message.
Redirects users to a fake website even if they type the correct URL — DNS poisoning or hosts file modification.
Sender Policy Framework. DNS record listing authorized sending mail servers. Prevents spoofed sender addresses.
DomainKeys Identified Mail. Cryptographic email signature. Proves email came from the domain.
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance. Builds on SPF + DKIM.

matching.prompt: Mass email impersonating a bank
Targeted email at a specific individual
Targeted at a CEO or CFO
Phishing via phone call
Phishing via SMS text message
Redirects correct URL to fake site
DNS record listing authorized sending mail servers
Cryptographic email signature per domain
Policy for handling SPF/DKIM failures

questions.q: A highly targeted phishing email sent to a CEO is called:
opts: Whaling
Spear phishing
Smishing
Vishing
questions.exp: Whaling targets high-value executives. Spear phishing is targeted but at a broader group.

questions.q: SMS-based phishing is called:
opts: Vishing
Smishing
Whaling
Spear phishing
questions.exp: Smishing = SMS phishing — malicious links or requests delivered via text message.

questions.q: Vishing is phishing conducted via:
opts: Voice phone calls
SMS text messages
Email messaging
Social media DMs
questions.exp: Vishing uses phone calls — attackers often impersonate IT support, financial institutions, or government agencies.

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes pharming from phishing?
opts: Pharming subverts DNS or hosts-file resolution so a user typing the correct URL is sent to a fake site; phishing requires the user to click a malicious link
Pharming uses email lures while phishing exploits DNS resolution; the two attacks share the same goal but use opposite delivery channels
Pharming targets only executives via spear-phishing techniques while phishing is broad-spectrum across the workforce
Pharming requires browser zero-day exploits while phishing requires no software exploits at all to succeed
questions.exp: Pharming poisons name resolution (DNS cache, hosts file, or DNS server itself) so a user typing the correct URL gets sent to an attacker-controlled site — no user error needed beyond visiting their normal destination. Phishing requires the user to click a malicious link or visit an attacker URL. The reversed distractor (B — 'pharming uses email') is the most common confusion because the two terms sound similar; the targeting axis (C) and the exploit-required axis (D) are not the defining differences.

questions.q: Which email security standard publishes a list of authorized sending mail servers in DNS?
opts: DKIM
DMARC
SPF
TLS
questions.exp: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) publishes authorized sending servers in DNS — receiving servers reject mail from others.

questions.q: DKIM provides which security property for email?
opts: Cryptographically signs the email to verify it came from the domain and wasn't altered in transit
Encrypts the email body content end-to-end between sender and recipient
Publishes a list of authorized sender mail servers in DNS TXT records
Blocks phishing emails automatically based on sender reputation scoring
questions.exp: DKIM applies a cryptographic signature to emails — verifying the sending domain and detecting tampering.

questions.q: DMARC builds on which two standards?
opts: TLS and SSL
SPF and DKIM
DNSSEC and HTTPS
MFA and SSO
questions.exp: DMARC extends SPF and DKIM — defining what to do (reject, quarantine, report) when emails fail both checks.

scenarios.q: An employee receives an email warning that their Office 365 account will be suspended in 24 hours unless they verify credentials immediately. The link goes to a convincing Microsoft login replica. The employee's manager received the same email. What type of attack is this, and what email control would MOST directly have blocked it?
opts: Spear phishing; blocked by DKIM signing of outbound email
Vishing; blocked by caller ID verification
Whaling; blocked by requiring MFA on the email account
Mass phishing; blocked by SPF/DMARC rejecting email spoofing Microsoft's domain
scenarios.exp: Mass phishing (not targeted) impersonating Microsoft. SPF/DMARC rejects spoofed sender domains — if Microsoft has DMARC p=reject, receiving mail servers reject email falsely claiming to be from microsoft.com.

scenarios.q: The CFO receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the company's external auditors, requesting network credentials to run a remote audit tool. The caller knows the CFO's name, the auditor firm's name, and the upcoming audit date. What attack is being attempted, and what should the CFO do?
opts: Smishing attack — hang up and report to IT security
Vishing attack — verify the caller's identity through an independently sourced phone number before providing anything
