questions.q: Which BEST explains why firmware vulnerabilities are particularly difficult to remediate?
opts: Firmware vulnerabilities can only be patched by replacing the entire physical device because modern hardware does not support in-field firmware updates
Firmware is written in low-level assembly that defenders cannot read, so vulnerability researchers cannot publish proof-of-concept exploits or patches at all
All firmware vulnerabilities are zero-days by definition because firmware never has a previous version to compare against for binary diffing
Firmware operates below the OS and persists through OS reinstalls; vendor updates are infrequent, risky to apply (bricking), and many devices receive no firmware updates after the first product cycle
questions.exp: Firmware sits below the OS — BIOS/UEFI, NIC firmware, drive controller firmware, IPMI/BMC firmware — so wiping and reinstalling the OS does not touch it. Vendor update cadence is much slower than software updates (often quarterly or longer if at all), updates can brick the device if interrupted, and many devices receive no firmware patches after the first product cycle. This combination makes firmware exposure long-lived. The other distractors are wrong: defenders DO read firmware (binary reverse engineering is mature); zero-day status is per-vulnerability not per-class; modern devices generally support firmware updates (replacement is rarely required).

questions.q: A side-channel attack extracts information by:
opts: Analyzing physical signals such as power consumption or electromagnetic emissions — without attacking the software directly
Injecting malicious shellcode directly into the application's process memory
Intercepting network traffic between client and server using a MITM proxy attack
Exploiting SQL injection vulnerabilities in the application's database query layer
questions.exp: Side-channel attacks exploit physical characteristics of hardware rather than software vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Spectre and Meltdown are examples of:
opts: Software-based code injection attacks against running applications
CPU hardware vulnerabilities exploiting speculative execution to read protected memory
Firmware vulnerabilities found in BIOS or UEFI boot components
Social engineering attacks targeting end users with phishing emails
questions.exp: Spectre and Meltdown are CPU hardware-level vulnerabilities — they exploit speculative execution to leak protected memory contents.

audit_d_review.note: Spectre/Meltdown are canonical hardware-vulnerability examples — partial-depth shape, not partial-adjacent. Same SB1.6 pattern as the loose-flag pool. Don't move; flag for SB-fix-2 partial-depth review.

scenarios.q: A network-attached storage device reached end-of-life two years ago. A new vulnerability allowing unauthenticated remote code execution is discovered. The organization has 40 of these devices. What is the MOST appropriate response?
opts: Ignore the vulnerability — the devices have worked fine for two years and a CVE alone doesn't justify the operational cost of replacing them
Apply the firmware patch from the vendor's website immediately and continue using the devices in their existing network segment
Continue normal operations and purchase cyber insurance to cover the financial risk if the EOL devices are exploited later
Since no patch is available for EOL hardware, isolate the devices from the broader network, implement strict firewall rules limiting access, and accelerate replacement planning
scenarios.exp: EOL hardware with no patch available: you cannot patch away the vulnerability. Compensating controls — network isolation, strict firewall rules, enhanced monitoring — reduce risk while replacement is planned. This is the standard approach for unpatched embedded systems.

scenarios.q: A cryptography researcher recovers a 256-bit AES encryption key from a device by measuring power consumption patterns during encryption operations — without accessing the key directly or breaking AES mathematically. What type of attack is this?
opts: A brute-force attack exploiting weak key generation
A birthday attack on the AES key space
A side-channel attack
A supply chain attack on the device's crypto library
scenarios.exp: Exploiting physical emanations from the device rather than attacking the cryptographic algorithm itself. Side-channel attack: the attack doesn't break AES (which is computationally secure) — it exploits physical characteristics of the implementation. Power consumption correlates with operations on key bits. The AES algorithm is fine; the hardware implementation leaks information.

scenarios.q: During a security audit of new servers, a researcher discovers some contain undocumented chips soldered to the motherboard that appear to report system information to external IP addresses. The vendor denies knowledge of the chips. What type of threat does this represent?
opts: A firmware vulnerability — patching the server BIOS will remove the chip and its reporting behavior
Shadow IT — an employee added the chips to the motherboards after delivery to bypass official IT procurement
A rootkit installed during initial server configuration that modifies firmware to add the chips at boot
A hardware supply chain attack — malicious components inserted during manufacturing or distribution, before the servers reached the buyer
scenarios.exp: Hardware supply chain attack: malicious components inserted before the product reached the customer. Distinct from firmware attacks (software). The buyer had no opportunity to detect or prevent this through software security controls. Mitigations include hardware attestation and buying from trusted suppliers with verified chain of custody.

cram.def: Attacker breaks out of a VM to access the hypervisor or other VMs on the same host — most serious virtualization attack.
Uncontrolled growth of VMs — forgotten, unpatched VMs become security risks.
Sensitive data from one VM remaining in shared resources (memory, CPU cache) accessible by another VM.
Runs directly on bare metal hardware. Examples: VMware ESXi, Hyper-V.
Runs on top of a host operating system. Examples: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

matching.prompt: Breaking out of a VM to reach the hypervisor
Uncontrolled growth of unmanaged VMs
Type 1 hypervisor runs on
Type 2 hypervisor runs on

questions.q: VM escape is:
opts: An attacker breaking out of a VM to access the hypervisor or other VMs on the same physical host
Moving a VM from one host to another
A VM shutting down unexpectedly
Migrating VMs between cloud regions
questions.exp: VM escape is the most serious virtualization attack — the attacker gains access to the hypervisor and potentially all VMs on the host.

questions.q: Which BEST captures the SECURITY concern with VM sprawl (vs operational concerns like cost or performance)?
opts: Hypervisor CPU oversubscription forces VMs to share execution slices, allowing one tenant's process to read another tenant's CPU register state via timing side channels
VMs proliferate without clear ownership and then get forgotten — they go unpatched, unhardened, and unmonitored over time, becoming easy targets that no team is responsible for fixing
VM-to-VM network traffic stays inside the hypervisor and never reaches the network monitoring stack, creating a permanent monitoring blind spot regardless of inventory state
Each additional VM costs licensing fees and consumes datacenter cooling capacity, raising IT operational costs faster than the security team's budget grows
questions.exp: The defining security concern with VM sprawl is unmanaged ownership: VMs spin up for testing, projects, demos, then no one updates the inventory, no team patches them, no one monitors their behavior. Over months/years, those VMs accumulate unpatched CVEs and weak configurations that an attacker reaching the network can pivot through. The fix is asset management, ownership tagging, and lifecycle policies — not raw VM count limits. Distractor B (CPU side-channel timing attacks) is a different topic — the Meltdown/Spectre family of hardware vulnerabilities, unrelated to VM sprawl. Distractor C is wrong — modern virtual networking exposes VM-to-VM traffic via vSwitch port mirroring/SPAN. Distractor D is the operational concern the stem explicitly dismisses.

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes a Type 1 hypervisor from a Type 2 hypervisor?
opts: Type 1 is software-based and runs as an application on the host OS; Type 2 is hardware-based with its own embedded kernel and direct hardware access
Type 1 runs directly on bare metal hardware with its own minimal kernel; Type 2 runs as an application on top of a host operating system that mediates hardware access
Type 1 hypervisors are designed for desktop and developer use; Type 2 hypervisors are designed for production data center virtualization workloads
Type 1 supports only paravirtualized guest operating systems; Type 2 supports only fully virtualized guest operating systems with no overlap
questions.exp: A Type 1 hypervisor (bare-metal) installs directly on hardware and contains its own minimal OS kernel — examples include VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V Server, and KVM. A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on top of an existing host OS — examples include VMware Workstation, VirtualBox, and Parallels Desktop. The reversed-software-vs-hardware distractor (B) is the classic misconception. The use-case reversal (C) confuses where each is typically deployed (Type 1 = production, Type 2 = developer/desktop). Para vs full virtualization (D) is a different axis.

scenarios.q: A cloud hosting provider's security researcher demonstrates that a malicious VM they control can read data from memory regions belonging to another customer's VM running on the same physical host. Which vulnerability does this represent?
opts: Resource reuse vulnerability — residual data from one VM's memory pages is accessible to another VM
VM escape — the attacker's VM has broken out of its isolation boundary to access the hypervisor
VM sprawl — too many VMs on the same host causing resource conflicts
A hypervisor type confusion error causing VMs to share address spaces
scenarios.exp: Resource reuse: hypervisors allocate and deallocate memory pages between VMs. If memory isn't properly zeroed before being assigned to a new VM, the new VM may read residual data from the previous VM. Mitigations include secure memory wiping between allocations.

scenarios.q: A security team finds 47 VMs created for projects over 3 years that are no longer actively monitored and haven't received OS updates in over a year. What risk does this represent, and what is the recommended action?
opts: High performance risk — idle VMs consume resources unnecessarily across the cluster
VM sprawl — unmanaged VMs accumulate vulnerabilities; recommend inventory + decommission process
Low risk — unused VMs that aren't actively serving traffic can't be exploited by attackers
VM escape risk — idle VMs are more likely to allow hypervisor escape because of stale guest tools
scenarios.exp: Unmanaged VMs are unpatched attack surfaces within the network. Recommended: inventory all VMs, decommission unused ones with proper data handling, bring required ones into the patch management program. VM sprawl creates unmanaged attack surfaces — forgotten VMs often have default configurations, no patches, and no monitoring. An attacker who compromises one has internal network access. Proper VM lifecycle management — inventory, justify, patch, and decommission — is essential.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester gains access to a VM in a cloud environment and attempts an advanced exploit targeting the hypervisor's memory management to break out of the VM and access the host system. If successful, what attack has occurred and what is the most critical impact?
opts: VM sprawl — the attacker created additional VMs for persistence
A supply chain attack on the hypervisor software
Resource reuse — the attacker reads memory from adjacent VMs without escaping
VM escape
scenarios.exp: The most critical impact is that the attacker could access all other VMs on the same physical host and potentially the entire hypervisor infrastructure. VM escape is the most serious virtualization attack. A successful escape gives the attacker access to the hypervisor, which controls all VMs on that host. All co-resident tenants are potentially compromised. This is why hypervisor patching is critical.

cram.def: Cloud security responsibilities split between provider and customer. Provider secures infrastructure; customer secures data/config.
#1 cloud security risk. Exposed S3 buckets, open security groups, public APIs. Customer responsibility.
Cloud services accessed via APIs — poorly secured APIs are a major attack vector.
Data must remain in specific geographic regions due to legal requirements — cloud complicates this.

matching.prompt: #1 cloud security risk
Provider secures infrastructure; customer secures data
Publicly accessible S3 bucket with sensitive data
Legal requirement for data to stay in specific regions

questions.q: In the cloud shared responsibility model:
opts: The cloud provider is responsible for all security
The customer is responsible for all security
The provider secures the infrastructure; the customer is responsible for data, configurations, and access management
Responsibilities are always equal between provider and customer
questions.exp: The shared responsibility model divides duties — providers secure infrastructure; customers secure what they put on it.

questions.q: Which is the MOST common cause of cloud data breaches?
opts: Nation-state attackers using novel zero-day exploits to breach the cloud provider's infrastructure directly
Misconfiguration by the customer — publicly accessible storage buckets, overly permissive IAM policies, exposed admin endpoints
Weak encryption algorithms used by the cloud provider for data-at-rest and data-in-transit protection across services
Outdated cloud platform software running on the provider's hypervisor and management plane unpatched against known CVEs
questions.exp: Verizon DBIR, Mandiant M-Trends, and most cloud-provider incident reports consistently cite customer misconfiguration as the leading cause of cloud data breaches — exposed S3 buckets, overly permissive IAM roles, default-public storage settings, exposed management endpoints. Nation-state attacks on provider infrastructure, provider crypto weaknesses, and provider software vulnerabilities are all real but represent a much smaller share of actual breaches. The shared responsibility model places configuration squarely on the customer side, and customer misconfiguration is where the volume actually is.

questions.q: An organization finds their cloud storage bucket is publicly accessible and contains customer data. This is an example of:
opts: An API vulnerability
A supply chain attack
A cloud misconfiguration
A virtualization escape
questions.exp: Publicly accessible cloud storage is a misconfiguration — a customer-side security failure in the shared responsibility model.

scenarios.q: A startup stores customer data in an AWS S3 bucket. A developer sets the bucket to 'public-read' for testing, intending to change it before launch. They forget. Three months later, 50,000 customer records are found on a breach forum. Under the shared responsibility model, who bears primary responsibility?
opts: AWS — they should have prevented public-bucket configuration through stricter defaults
The customer (startup) — under AWS shared responsibility, customers own configuration
Split equally between AWS and the customer regardless of who configured the bucket
The developer personally — the company itself bears no organizational responsibility
scenarios.exp: S3 bucket configuration and access control are the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model. Shared responsibility: AWS secures the infrastructure and the S3 service itself. The customer is responsible for what they do with the service — including bucket permissions and data classification. Misconfiguration is the customer's responsibility.

scenarios.q: A security team reviewing cloud posture finds: an S3 bucket with versioning disabled containing DB backups, an EC2 security group allowing inbound RDP from 0.0.0.0/0, an IAM role with AdministratorAccess attached to a Lambda that only needs to read from one S3 bucket, and an API Gateway endpoint with no authentication. Which should be addressed FIRST?
opts: API Gateway first, then S3 bucket, then IAM role, then EC2 security group — based on perceived public-facing exposure
All four findings are equal in priority and should be addressed simultaneously without ranking by exposure or impact
S3 bucket first, then IAM role, then API Gateway, then EC2 security group — prioritizing data-loss risk over network exposure
EC2 security group (RDP open) and API Gateway (no auth) are critical — immediate unauthenticated exposure. IAM role high; S3 versioning medium
scenarios.exp: Prioritize direct exposure paths: open RDP to internet (automated scanners find this in minutes) and unauthenticated API endpoint (immediate data exposure risk) are critical. Overprivileged IAM is high. Disabled versioning is a resilience issue but not an immediate external risk.

cram.def: Compromising a product or service during manufacturing, distribution, or update — before it reaches the target.
Compromising an MSP to access all their clients — e.g. Kaseya VSA attack.
A list of all components in a software product — helps identify vulnerable dependencies.
Contractual right to examine vendor security practices.

matching.prompt: Attack on software update mechanism
Compromising IT provider to reach all their clients
List of all components in a software product
Contractual right to examine vendor security

questions.q: An attacker compromises a widely-used IT management product so that the vendor's signed update pushes a backdoor to thousands of customers via the normal update channel. This is BEST described as:
opts: A watering hole attack — the attacker compromises a website that the target population is known to visit, infecting visitors via the trusted site
A supply chain attack — the attacker compromises an upstream component (vendor product, dependency, hardware) so the malicious payload reaches downstream customers via legitimate trust relationships
A direct phishing campaign — the attacker sends crafted emails to each affected target organization individually with malicious links or attachments
An insider threat — a malicious employee at each affected customer organization independently installed the backdoor on production systems
questions.exp: Supply chain attacks compromise an upstream element — software dependency, vendor product, hardware component — that downstream consumers trust by default. The compromise then propagates to many targets via legitimate update or distribution channels (signed updates, package managers, vendor downloads). Watering hole targets a specific website; direct phishing requires per-target outreach; insider threat is a per-organization compromise. The signature of supply chain attacks is that ONE upstream compromise reaches many downstream victims through their normal trust relationships.

questions.q: An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) helps organizations:
opts: Track physical hardware inventory and asset tags across all enterprise data centers
Monitor live network traffic flows for anomalous communication patterns continuously
Identify all software components and dependencies so they can assess and respond to vulnerabilities in those components
Manage user access rights and group memberships across all enterprise applications
questions.exp: An SBOM lists all components in software — when a vulnerability is found in a library, organizations with SBOMs know if they're affected.

questions.q: Which contractual clause gives an organization the right to examine a vendor's security practices?
opts: Right-to-audit clause
Service Level Agreement
Non-disclosure agreement
Memorandum of Understanding
questions.exp: Right-to-audit clauses allow organizations to verify their vendors' security practices — important for supply chain risk management.

scenarios.q: A widely-used open-source library has a critical RCE vulnerability. An organization's custom web application uses this library but doesn't know it — it was included as a transitive dependency. How would an SBOM have helped?
opts: An SBOM lists all components including transitive dependencies — the organization would have known they used the library and could have responded immediately when the vulnerability was announced
An SBOM would have automatically patched the vulnerability by triggering an update of the affected library across all dependent applications
An SBOM would have prevented the vulnerable library from being included by automatically rejecting any unapproved dependencies at build time
An SBOM is only useful for hardware components — software supply chain visibility requires a separate specialized inventory and tracking tool
scenarios.exp: SBOM value: transitive dependencies are the blind spot. When Log4Shell dropped, organizations with SBOMs knew within hours whether they were affected. Organizations without them spent days doing manual inventory. SBOM is the prerequisite for rapid supply chain vulnerability response.

scenarios.q: An MSP that manages IT for 200 small businesses is compromised via a vulnerability in their RMM software. The attacker uses the MSP's legitimate admin access to deploy ransomware to all 200 client environments simultaneously. What does this demonstrate about supply chain risk?
opts: The RMM software vendor is solely responsible for all 200 businesses' losses, since the vulnerability was in their product, not the MSP's configuration
MSPs should only be used by large enterprises with dedicated in-house security teams who can independently audit every administrative action the MSP performs
All 200 businesses should have run their own RMM software internally instead of outsourcing to an MSP, even if the operational cost is significantly higher

MSP compromise is a high-leverage supply chain attack — compromising one provider gives attackers access to all clients simultaneously. Clients should assess MSP security rigorously and limit the scope of MSP access
scenarios.exp: MSP as supply chain risk: the attacker didn't compromise 200 businesses — they compromised the one entity with access to all 200. Mitigations: vet MSP security (SOC 2 Type II, right-to-audit), segment MSP access, monitor MSP activity, have IR plans that assume MSP compromise.

cram.def: Incorrect security settings that leave systems vulnerable. Often human error. One of the most common vulnerability sources.
Unchanged factory passwords on devices and services. Easily exploited.
Using outdated/weak encryption algorithms (SSL, DES, MD5) when stronger ones are available.
Center for Internet Security — prescriptive configuration guides for securing various OS and applications.

matching.prompt: Factory-set admin/admin left unchanged
Using SSL instead of TLS for HTTPS
Prescriptive secure configuration guides

questions.q: Which of the following is BEST classified as a misconfiguration vulnerability (vs another vulnerability category)?
opts: A zero-day exploit in the OS kernel that no vendor patch yet exists for and no public details have been disclosed
A supply chain attack in which a software dependency is compromised upstream and the malicious payload reaches consumers via signed updates
A buffer overflow in a web application's image-upload handler that allows attacker-supplied input to overwrite return addresses
Leaving default vendor credentials (admin/admin) unchanged on a newly deployed network device that is reachable from the production network
questions.exp: A misconfiguration vulnerability is one introduced by HOW a system is set up — default credentials left in place, overly permissive firewall rules, public-by-default storage buckets, exposed admin endpoints. The fix is configuration management, not code or supply-chain action. Other categories: zero-day (A) is an unknown vendor-side defect; buffer overflow (C) is a code defect; supply chain (D) is an upstream compromise. Knowing the category matters because remediation paths differ — misconfig means reconfigure; code defect means patch; supply chain means vendor response and software bill of materials review.

questions.q: CIS Benchmarks are used to:
opts: Conduct routine penetration tests against all deployed systems
Classify vulnerability severity rankings by overall business impact
Provide prescriptive secure configuration guidance for operating systems and applications
Monitor live network traffic for threat indicators in real time
questions.exp: CIS Benchmarks provide detailed, prescriptive security configuration recommendations.

questions.q: Which approach BEST prevents misconfiguration vulnerabilities at scale?
opts: Manual review of each system individually by a system admin
Configuration management using secure baselines and automated compliance scanning
Replacing all systems with brand new hardware every year
Using only fully managed cloud services for all infrastructure
questions.exp: Configuration management with secure baselines applied consistently and verified automatically is most effective.

scenarios.q: A new IT team member sets up a network switch — configures VLANs and port assignments and brings it online — but forgets to change the default admin credentials. Two weeks later, an attacker uses the switch's web admin interface with credentials from the vendor's public setup guide. What is the primary failure, and what should have prevented it?
opts: The VLANs were incorrectly configured, creating a security gap that the attacker leveraged to access the management interface
Failing to change default credentials during initial setup — a device hardening checklist should require credential changes before production deployment
The switch firmware was unpatched and the attacker exploited a known firmware CVE to bypass authentication entirely
The switch should not have had a web admin interface enabled at all, since CLI-only management is more secure
scenarios.exp: Default credentials: the most basic hardening step was missed. A device hardening checklist or new device setup SOP should require: change default credentials, disable unnecessary interfaces, update firmware — before the device touches production. This is a process failure, not just an individual one.

scenarios.q: An organization fails a PCI DSS audit. The finding states several servers in the cardholder data environment are running TLSv1.0 and 3DES cipher suites. The IT team says these were the standards when the servers were configured five years ago. What type of vulnerability is this, and what remediation is required?
opts: A misconfiguration — outdated TLS/cipher settings persisted; remediate by upgrading to TLS 1.2+/AES
A zero-day vulnerability — apply emergency vendor patches across all servers in the cardholder environment
A supply chain vulnerability — the TLS library was shipped with weak defaults that nobody changed
A hardware vulnerability — the network cards' built-in TLS accelerators are responsible for the legacy cipher use
scenarios.exp: Using deprecated, weak cryptographic protocols when stronger alternatives are available and required. Remediation: disable TLSv1.0 and 3DES, enforce TLSv1.2+ with strong cipher suites. Cryptographic misconfiguration: TLSv1.0 and 3DES have known vulnerabilities and are explicitly prohibited by PCI DSS 4.0. Configuration drift — the environment was once compliant but became non-compliant as standards evolved while the config stayed static.

cram.def: Removing iOS security restrictions to run unsigned code. Voids warranty, removes security controls.
Gaining root/superuser access on Android. Bypasses manufacturer security restrictions.
Installing apps from outside the official app store. Increases risk of malicious apps.
Enterprise tool to enforce policies, wipe, and manage mobile devices.
Attacker social engineers carrier to transfer victim's number to attacker-controlled SIM.
Unauthorized data access via Bluetooth.

matching.prompt: Removing iOS restrictions to run unsigned apps
Gaining root access on Android
Installing apps from outside the official store
Attacker convinces carrier to transfer victim's phone number
Unauthorized data access via Bluetooth

questions.q: Which BEST captures the SECURITY risk of jailbreaking an iOS device?
opts: Jailbreaking voids the manufacturer warranty, removing the user's option to seek vendor repair if the device develops a hardware fault later
Jailbreaking removes iOS's app-sandbox and code-signing enforcement, allowing unsigned (potentially malicious) code to run with full device access; most platform security controls are disabled
Jailbreaking permanently slows the device by approximately 30% because the bypassed security checks consume CPU cycles when re-enabled by background apps
Jailbreaking exposes the user's iCloud password to Apple Support staff, who can then read it during any subsequent support interaction
questions.exp: Jailbreaking strips out iOS's defense-in-depth: the app sandbox that isolates apps from each other and from system data, the code-signing enforcement that ensures only signed apps run, and various kernel-level mitigations. Once removed, malicious apps from non-App-Store sources can run with full device access. Jailbroken devices also often stop receiving iOS security updates because update flows assume an unmodified system. The warranty distractor (B) is real but is a legal/business concern, not a security concern. Performance and Apple-Support-iCloud claims (C, D) are fabricated.

questions.q: A SIM swapping attack involves:
opts: Physically cloning a SIM card using a specialized hardware reader device
Intercepting SMS messages while they are in transit between mobile carriers
Social engineering a mobile carrier into transferring a victim's phone number to an attacker-controlled SIM
Installing malware on a phone via a malicious app from the official store
questions.exp: SIM swapping redirects the victim's phone number to the attacker — enabling interception of SMS-based MFA codes.

questions.q: MDM helps secure mobile devices by:
opts: Enforcing security policies, detecting jailbroken/rooted devices, and enabling remote wipe
Physically securing devices using lockable hardware containers
Encrypting all Bluetooth connections between devices automatically
Preventing SIM swapping attempts at the mobile carrier level
questions.exp: MDM provides centralized control — enforcing encryption, PIN requirements, remote wipe, and detecting compromised devices.

scenarios.q: An employee's company iPhone is lost. IT remotely wipes the device via MDM. The employee later recovers the phone and is upset that all their personal photos (three years' worth) were also deleted. What MDM capability was missing?
opts: Remote wipe should not be used — it's too destructive
MDM containerization should have been implemented — a corporate wipe would remove only the corporate container (email, apps, data) leaving personal content intact
The employee should have backed up to iCloud before reporting the loss
MDM remote wipe is always an all-or-nothing operation
scenarios.exp: Container-based MDM: corporate data exists in a managed container; personal data is outside it. A selective/corporate wipe removes only the container — email, corporate apps, documents — leaving personal photos and apps untouched. This is the correct BYOD configuration.

scenarios.q: An attacker calls a user's mobile carrier, impersonates the user using social media-sourced personal information, and convinces the carrier to transfer the phone number to a new SIM. The attacker then triggers a bank password reset and intercepts the SMS verification code. What attack occurred and what would have prevented it?
opts: Smishing — the user should not respond to unsolicited SMS messages from unknown sources
A replay attack — the SMS verification code was captured and reused after expiry
SIM cloning — the SIM card data was physically duplicated to a second SIM held by the attacker
SIM swapping — a phone-number takeover would have been prevented by app-based MFA instead of SMS codes
scenarios.exp: The bank should offer phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/authenticator app) as an alternative to SMS OTP, and the carrier should require stronger identity verification for SIM changes. SIM swapping: the attacker socially engineered the carrier, not the bank. SMS MFA is vulnerable because the phone number is the second factor — and phone numbers can be hijacked. Better alternatives: TOTP authenticator apps (tied to a device) or FIDO2 hardware keys (cannot be SIM-swapped).

cram.def: A flaw unknown to the vendor — no patch exists. The vendor has had 'zero days' to fix it.
Attack code that targets a zero-day vulnerability — extremely dangerous as there is no patch defense.
Patch quickly when released, network segmentation, least privilege, EDR/behavioral detection, WAF.
Researcher notifies vendor privately and allows time to patch before public disclosure.
Organizations pay researchers who find and responsibly disclose vulnerabilities.

matching.prompt: Vulnerability unknown to the vendor with no patch
Researcher notifies vendor before going public
Pay researchers to find and report vulnerabilities
Public database of known vulnerabilities
Best mitigation when no patch exists

questions.q: Which BEST defines a zero-day vulnerability?
opts: Has been patched for zero days since the public disclosure date — i.e. the patch dropped on day zero of disclosure
Is unknown to the vendor at the time it is exploited and has no available patch — defenders have zero days to prepare a fix
Affects zero deployed systems currently because zero-day refers to the day the vulnerability is first deployed in the wild
Is rated 0.0 on the CVSS scale because zero-day vulnerabilities have not yet been scored by NVD at the time of discovery
questions.exp: A zero-day vulnerability is one that the vendor doesn't know about (or hasn't patched) at the time it is being exploited — defenders have 'zero days' between learning of the vulnerability and needing to defend against active exploitation. The 'zero' in zero-day refers to the defender's preparation time, NOT to the patch age, system count, or CVSS score (the wordplay distractors). Zero-days are particularly dangerous because no signature/IoC exists yet, so detection relies on behavioral anomaly. Once the vendor releases a patch and the CVE is public, it becomes an 'n-day' vulnerability where n = days since disclosure.

questions.q: Responsible disclosure means:
opts: Immediately publishing vulnerability details to warn the public
Notifying the vendor privately and allowing reasonable time to develop a patch before public disclosure
Selling the vulnerability to the highest bidder
Reporting the vulnerability to law enforcement first
questions.exp: Responsible disclosure balances the public's right to know with giving vendors time to patch — preventing immediate exploitation.

questions.q: When a zero-day vulnerability is actively being exploited with no patch available, the BEST mitigations include:
opts: Defense-in-depth
Waiting for the vendor to release a patch
Purchasing cyber insurance
Disconnecting all systems from the internet
questions.exp: Network segmentation, least privilege, behavioral EDR, and temporary workarounds. Without a patch, layered defenses — segmentation, least privilege, behavioral detection — reduce but cannot eliminate risk.

scenarios.q: A vendor releases a critical patch for a zero-day VPN vulnerability being actively exploited. Your organization uses this VPN for all remote access. The patch requires a 2-hour maintenance window during business hours. The CISO wants to deploy immediately; the COO is concerned about the 2-hour outage affecting 800 remote workers. What is the MOST defensible approach?
opts: Implement compensating controls (restrict VPN access, enhanced logging, block known malicious IPs) and patch within 24 hours on an emergency change basis
Deploy immediately during business hours — active exploitation makes any delay unacceptable
Schedule for the next maintenance window — standard change management procedures must be followed
Delay patching until the weekend — 2 hours of exposure is acceptable
scenarios.exp: Risk-tiered response for active exploitation: emergency change management — compress the process, don't eliminate it. Meanwhile, compensating controls reduce exposure during the brief delay. Document everything. This balances urgency with process discipline.

scenarios.q: Threat intelligence indicates a zero-day exists in your web server software, being actively exploited against targets in your industry. No patch is available. Your web servers are public-facing. What combination of compensating controls provides the MOST meaningful risk reduction?
opts: Disconnect the web servers until a patch is available
Change the web server software to a different product immediately
Purchase cyber insurance to cover potential breach costs
Deploy a WAF with custom rules targeting the known exploit patterns, implement enhanced monitoring for indicators of compromise, and restrict server-side capabilities to minimum required
scenarios.exp: Compensating controls for no-patch-available zero-day: WAF custom rules target the specific exploit technique; enhanced monitoring detects exploitation attempts; minimizing server capabilities reduces what an attacker can do if they succeed. Disconnecting isn't viable for public customer services. Changing software immediately introduces more risk than it mitigates.

questions.q: Cindy is concerned that her organization may be targeted by a supply chain attack and is conducting a review of all of her vendor and supplier partners. Which one of the following organizations is least likely to be the conduit for a supply chain attack?
opts: Hardware provider
Software provider
Managed service provider
Talent provider
questions.exp: Supply chain attacks are typically associated with vendors and suppliers that provide technology infrastructure or services that may be compromised. This would include hardware and software providers as well as managed service providers (MSPs). Talent providers, who help with staffing solutions, are generally not considered common avenues for supply chain attacks.

questions.q: Tom’s organization recently learned that the vendor is discontinuing support for their customer relationship management (CRM) system. What should concern Tom the most from a security perspective?
opts: Unavailability of future patches
Lack of technical support
Theft of customer information
Increased costs
questions.exp: Tom’s greatest concern should be that running unsupported software exposes his organization to the risk of new, unpatchable vulnerabilities. It is certainly true that they will no longer receive technical support, but this is a less important issue from a security perspective.

questions.q:
Upon further inspection, Joe finds a series of thousands of requests to the same URL coming from a single IP address. Here are a few examples:

http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=1
http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=2
http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=3
http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=4
http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=5
http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=6

What type of vulnerability was the attacker likely trying to exploit?
opts: Insecure direct object reference
File upload
Unvalidated redirect
Session hijacking
questions.exp: The series of thousands of requests incrementing a variable indicate that the attacker was most likely attempting to exploit an insecure direct object reference vulnerability.

questions.q: Precompiled SQL statements that only require variables to be input are an example of what type of application security control?
opts: Parameterized queries
Encoding data
Input validation
Appropriate access controls
questions.exp: A parameterized query (sometimes called a prepared statement) uses a prebuilt SQL statement to prevent SQL‐based attacks. Variables from the application are fed to the query, rather than building a custom query when the application needs data. Encoding data helps to prevent cross‐site scripting attacks, as does input validation. Appropriate access controls can prevent access to data that the account or application should not have access to, but they don’t use precompiled SQL statements. Stored procedures are an example of a parameterized query implementation.

questions.q: During a web application test, Ben discovers that the application shows SQL code as part of an error provided to application users. What should he note in his report?
opts: Improper error handling
Code exposure
SQL injection
A default configuration issue
questions.exp: Improper error handling often exposes data to users and possibly attackers that should not be exposed. In this case, knowing what SQL code is used inside the application can provide an attacker with details they can use to conduct further attacks. Code exposure is not one of the vulnerabilities we discuss in this book, and SQL code being exposed does not necessarily mean that SQL injection is possible. While this could be caused by a default configuration issue, there is nothing in the question to point to that problem.

questions.q: The application that Scott is writing has a flaw that occurs when two operations are attempted at the same time, resulting in unexpected results when the two actions do not occur in the expected order. What type of flaw does the application have?
opts: Dereferencing
A race condition
An insecure function
Improper error handling
questions.exp: The application has a race condition, which occurs when multiple operations cause undesirable results due to their order of completion. De‐referencing accesses or uses a memory pointer, an insecure function would have security issues in the function itself, and improper error handling would involve an error and how it was displayed or what data it provided.

questions.q: What component of a virtualization platform is primarily responsible for preventing VM escape attacks?
opts: Administrator
Guest operating system
Host operating system
Hypervisor
questions.exp: Virtual machine (VM) escape vulnerabilities are the most serious issue that can exist in a virtualized environment, particularly when a virtual host runs systems of differing security levels. In an escape attack, the attacker has access to a single virtual host and then manages to leverage that access to intrude upon the resources assigned to a different virtual machine. The hypervisor is supposed to prevent this type of access by restricting a virtual machine’s access to only those resources assigned to that machine.

questions.q: Lin’s hardware manufacturer has stopped selling the model of device that Lin’s organization uses and has also stopped providing security or other updates. What phase of the hardware life cycle is the device in?
opts: End‐of‐life
Legacy
End‐of‐sales
Senescence
questions.exp: Legacy hardware is unsupported and no longer sold. End‐of‐life typically means that the device is no longer being made but is likely to still have support for a period of time. End‐of‐sales means the device is no longer being sold, but again, may have support for some time. Senescence is not a term typically used in hardware life cycles.

questions.q: Alaina wants to modify operating system settings and features on her iOS device and to install applications that are not permitted or available via the Apple App Store. What would she need to do to accomplish this?
opts: Deploy an MDM tool to the phone.
Jailbreak the phone.
Keymod the phone.
Install a third‐party operating system.
questions.exp: Jailbreaking will allow Alaina to obtain administrator access to the underlying phone operating system and to modify operating system settings and options as well as to install applications that are not available via the App Store. Deploying an MDM does not permit all of this, keymodding is not a term used in this context, and installing a third‐party OS would allow access but would change the OS.

questions.q: A member of Jake’s team tells him that he sideloaded applications on his Android‐based company owned phone. What has occurred?
opts: Malware was installed on the phone.
The phone was rooted to allow administrative access.
Applications were installed by copying them instead of via an app store.
The organization’s MDM was disabled to avoid its management controls.
questions.exp: Sideloading is the process of copying files between two devices like a phone and a laptop, desktop, or storage device. Jake’s team member has loaded an application without using the Android application store. Sideloading does not necessarily imply malware, rooting, or disabling an MDM, although an MDM may be configured to prevent sideloading.

questions.q: Which one of the following attacks is an example of a race condition exploitation?
opts: XSRF
TOCTOU
SSRF
XSS
questions.exp: The time‐of‐check‐to‐time‐of‐use (TOCTTOU or TOC/TOU) issue is a race condition that occurs when a program checks access permissions too far in advance of a resource request. An example of a cross‐site request forgery (XSRF) is when you have multiple tabs open on your browser and you are logged into your bank portal. An XSRF attack might use your present login status to send a command to transfer money out of your account. An example of a server‐side request forgery (SSRF) is when an attack is made to the internal network of an organization through a web browser. An example of a cross‐site scripting (XSS) attack would be having an attacker’s code executed when you are visiting a website.

questions.q: Which one of the following approaches, when feasible, is the most effective way to defeat injection attacks?
opts: Input block lists
Input allow lists
Browser‐based input validation
Signature detection
questions.exp: Input allow list approaches define the specific input type or range that users may provide. When developers can write clear business rules defining allowable user input, allow listing is definitely the most effective way to prevent injection attacks. Block lists achieve the same goal but attempt to block malicious content rather than allow approved content so they are less effective. Browser‐based input validation is not a good practice because an attacker can easily bypass that validation. Signature detection is generally not used for injection attacks but rather for antivirus software.

questions.q: Christine has been notified that a firewall device has reached its end of life. What should Christine do?
opts: Immediately purchase a new device to replace it.
Begin planning to replace the device when a new version is announced.
Budget for a future replacement before end of support.
Plan to replace the device after end of support.
questions.exp: Most organizations plan to replace a device before it reaches end of support. Running devices past their end of support places the organization at risk because no support will be available if something goes wrong. End of life typically means that the device will no longer be sold, but it will continue to receive updates, patches, and support for some time to come.

questions.q: Nathaniel believes that he has discovered a race condition in an application. What term associated with race conditions describes the issue that occurs when a value is validated?
opts: Time‐of‐use
Target‐of‐evaluation
Time‐of‐check
Target‐of‐change
questions.exp: Time‐of‐check (TOC) is the term that describes when a value is validated. If the value is then changed before it is used (time of use), this can allow a race condition to occur. Target‐of‐evaluation is typically associated with testing or audits, and target‐of‐change is not a commonly used term related to race conditions.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements is not true about zero‐day attacks?
opts: They may be found in software or hardware.
They have a limited window of use.
They are generally unpatchable.
They are often widely publicized.
questions.exp: Zero‐day attacks are generally known only to a small group of researchers who discover the vulnerabilities. They are not known to the general public and would likely be patched by the vendor if they became widely known. Zero‐day vulnerabilities may exist in any technology component: software or hardware. They are only effective during the limited window of opportunity when they remain unpatchable before the vendor issues a fix.

cram.def: Encrypts victim files and demands payment (cryptocurrency) for decryption key.
Lives entirely in memory — no file written to disk. Harder to detect with traditional AV.
Infrastructure attackers use to communicate with and control compromised systems.
Artefacts indicating a system may be compromised: known malicious IPs/hashes/domains, unusual behavior.
Maintain regular offline or offsite backups not connected to the main network.

matching.prompt: Encrypts files and demands payment
Exists only in memory, no disk file
Infrastructure for controlling compromised systems
Best defense against ransomware data loss
Evidence a system may be compromised

questions.q: Which BEST describes ransomware's primary business impact?
opts: Silently exfiltrating credentials, browser session tokens, and saved authentication material to enable downstream account takeover
Deleting system logs and audit trails to obscure the attacker's prior activity and prevent forensic reconstruction of the compromise
Granting an attacker persistent remote interactive access to the compromised host, enabling lateral movement and additional payload delivery
Encrypting the organization's data and demanding cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key, disrupting operations until pay-or-restore-from-backup
questions.exp: Ransomware's primary business impact is operational disruption from encrypted data — the organization cannot access its files, systems, or both, and faces the choice of paying the ransom or restoring from backup (which often takes days and may itself fail). The other options describe primary impacts of OTHER malware categories: info-stealers take credentials covertly; RATs provide persistent remote control; log deletion is post-compromise cleanup. Modern ransomware often combines categories (steal-then-encrypt double-extortion), but the defining impact is still encryption-and-extortion.

questions.q: The BEST defense against ransomware data loss is:
opts: Maintaining regular offline or offsite backups not connected to the main network
Enforcing strong unique passwords across all user and service accounts
Paying the ransom quickly to restore data and minimize total downtime
Installing endpoint antivirus software with up-to-date malware signatures
questions.exp: Offline backups that ransomware cannot reach allow recovery without paying the ransom.

questions.q: Which BEST explains why fileless malware evades traditional signature-based antivirus?
opts: It uses living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins like PowerShell, certutil, regsvr32) — legitimate signed Windows tools that traditional AV does not flag as malicious by default
It never writes the malicious payload to disk — execution stays in process memory; persistence rides registry keys, WMI subscriptions, or scheduled-task XML rather than executable files
It disguises itself as legitimate system files in protected directories so signature scans treat it as benign system content rather than a candidate for inspection
It changes its signature every hour through polymorphic encoding so AV signature databases cannot maintain coverage of the current variant in time
questions.exp: Signature-based AV scans files at rest and at execution-write — its detection model is 'compare file bytes against malware hash database.' Fileless malware never writes the malicious payload to disk: it injects shellcode into a running process's memory, persists via registry keys or WMI subscriptions or scheduled-task XML, and runs in memory. With no file to scan, the AV's scanning model has no input. LOLBin abuse (B) is a related evasion technique but not the defining 'fileless' property. System-file disguise (C) is a different stealth technique. Polymorphism (D) is a different evasion technique. Modern AV/EDR adds behavioral and memory-scanning detection to address the fileless gap.

questions.q: C2 (Command and Control) infrastructure is used by attackers to:
opts: Remotely communicate with and issue commands to compromised systems
Encrypt stolen victim data on disk before demanding a ransom payment
Conduct phishing campaigns to harvest corporate user credentials at scale
Store harvested data and stolen credentials on attacker-controlled servers
questions.exp: C2 servers communicate with malware on victim systems — receiving stolen data and sending instructions.

scenarios.q: A hospital's file servers are encrypted by ransomware at 2am on a Saturday. The attacker demands $500,000. The hospital has offline backups from 48 hours ago and IT says they can restore within 6 hours. A board member argues for paying the ransom to restore faster. What factors should drive the decision NOT to immediately pay?
opts: Always pay the ransom — it's faster than restoring from backups and insurance covers it anyway
Never pay the ransom under any circumstances, regardless of operational impact or regulatory risk
The decision depends on backup viability, recovery-time tolerance, regulatory rules, and likelihood the attacker actually decrypts
Pay if the ransom is less than the cost of recovery from backups by any meaningful margin
scenarios.exp: Whether backups can restore to an acceptable state, legal obligations (ransomware payment compliance), whether patient safety is at immediate risk, and law enforcement notification — not just recovery speed. Ransomware response decision framework: (1) Can backups actually restore? (verify first) (2) Is the 48-hour data gap a patient safety risk? (3) Legal — some ransomware groups are sanctioned, making payment illegal (4) Law enforcement engagement. Ransom is the last resort, not an automatic choice.

scenarios.q: Six months after deploying EDR, a security analyst notices hundreds of legitimate PowerShell automation scripts triggering daily alerts. The analyst begins dismissing alerts without investigating to manage the volume. What risk does this create, and what is the better approach?
opts: No risk — if the scripts are known to be legitimate, dismissing alerts without review is correct practice
Alert fatigue — better approach: tune the EDR to suppress benign repeating alerts via baseline allow-listing
The EDR should be replaced with a different solution that generates substantially fewer alerts daily
PowerShell should be disabled organization-wide to eliminate the source of the alert volume entirely
scenarios.exp: Legitimate high volumes causing analysts to dismiss alerts creates a blind spot where malicious PowerShell activity (LOLBins) is ignored. Better approach: tune the EDR to suppress known-good scripts by hash or path, retaining alerts on anomalous PowerShell behavior. Alert fatigue is a critical security operations failure mode. The solution isn't to ignore alerts — it's to tune detection logic so known-good activity is suppressed and truly anomalous activity surfaces clearly. EDR tuning is an ongoing operational requirement.

cram.def: Malware that attaches to a host file. Requires USER ACTION to execute and spread. Cannot self-replicate without host.
Self-replicating malware. Spreads AUTOMATICALLY across networks. No host file required.
Changes its code/signature with each infection to evade signature-based detection.
Completely rewrites its own code with each infection — most evasive type.

audit_d_review.note: Metamorphic virus; 2.4 Viruses and Worms IS umbrella for virus types.

questions.q: Which malware type replicates itself across networks WITHOUT requiring a host file or user action?
opts: Virus
Worm
Trojan
Rootkit
questions.exp: Worms self-replicate and spread automatically — no host file needed and no user action required to propagate.

questions.q: Which malware type REQUIRES user interaction (such as opening a file) to execute and spread?
opts: Worm
Virus
Rootkit
Ransomware
questions.exp: Viruses attach to host files and require user action to execute — they cannot spread without being triggered by a user.

questions.q: A polymorphic virus is designed to:
opts: Replicate across networks without requiring a host file or user execution
Change its code or signature with each infection to evade signature-based antivirus detection
Encrypt files on the infected host until the victim pays a ransom
Operate entirely in system memory without writing any payload to disk
questions.exp: Polymorphic viruses mutate their signature — making them harder to detect with traditional signature-based AV.

questions.q: WannaCry spread rapidly without user interaction because it behaved like a:
opts: Trojan — disguised as legitimate software requiring user execution
Polymorphic virus — changing its signature on each infection to evade AV
Worm — exploiting SMBv1 to self-propagate across networks
Rootkit — establishing kernel-level concealment after exploitation
questions.exp: WannaCry used the EternalBlue SMBv1 exploit to self-propagate automatically — classic worm behavior.

scenarios.q: A worm is spreading across an organization's network, exploiting an SMBv1 vulnerability to propagate without user interaction. It has reached 400 of 1,200 workstations in 3 hours. What is the MOST effective immediate containment action?
opts: Shut down all affected workstations individually as IT teams reach each one — preventing further spread of the worm process
Run antivirus scans on all 1,200 workstations simultaneously to detect and quarantine the worm before more endpoints are infected
Deploy a patch for the SMBv1 vulnerability to all systems immediately, including those already showing infection signs
Implement network segmentation controls to isolate affected segments and disable SMBv1 on unaffected systems — blocking the propagation vector while containing the spread
scenarios.exp: Worm containment: the worm spreads via network (SMBv1). The containment lever is network isolation — segment the network to prevent east-west propagation, and block/disable SMBv1 on unaffected systems. Patching is the right long-term fix but takes time to deploy at scale.

scenarios.q: An antivirus vendor updates signatures to detect a specific ransomware strain. The ransomware authors release a new variant that changes a few bytes of non-functional code on each infection cycle. Each infected system has a slightly different file hash. What type of malware is this, and why does it evade signature-based detection?
opts: A worm — it spreads by exploiting network vulnerabilities, which changes its hash
A rootkit — it modifies the OS to hide itself from AV signature scans
A polymorphic virus — it alters its signature with each infection while preserving functionality, staying ahead of hash-based signature updates
Fileless malware — it operates in memory where AV can't scan
scenarios.exp: Polymorphic malware: the code changes enough to produce a different hash each infection, defeating signature matching. Functionality is preserved. Detection requires heuristic or behavioral analysis (what does it do?) rather than signature matching (what does it look like?).

cram.def: Secretly monitors user activity and sends data to attacker — keystrokes, screenshots, browsing history, credentials.
Records keystrokes — captures passwords, credit card numbers, messages. Hardware or software.
Displays unwanted advertisements. May redirect browser, slow system.
Pre-installed unwanted software by manufacturer. Uses resources, may include privacy-invasive software.
Gives attacker remote control of victim system — spyware capabilities plus remote command execution.

matching.prompt: Secretly records keystrokes
Displays unwanted advertisements
Pre-installed unwanted manufacturer software
Full remote control of victim machine

questions.q: Spyware primarily does which of the following?
opts: Encrypts files on the host system and demands ransom payment for decryption
Creates a persistent backdoor for remote attacker access to the compromised host
Displays unwanted pop-up advertisements while the user is browsing the web
Secretly monitors user activity and transmits data (keystrokes, screenshots, credentials) to an attacker
questions.exp: Spyware silently collects and exfiltrates sensitive information — running in the background without the user's knowledge.

questions.q: Which BEST captures why a Remote Access Trojan is particularly dangerous?
opts: It self-propagates from host to host like a worm, infecting every reachable machine on the network without needing user action
It encrypts the victim's files in place and demands cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key, treating extortion as the primary monetization path
It gives the attacker interactive remote control of the victim's system — full access to keyboard, screen, camera, microphone, and file system, persisting as long as the channel survives
It deletes itself after first execution to leave no forensic trace, ensuring the attacker's activity cannot be reconstructed even if the compromise is later detected
questions.exp: A RAT's danger is interactive remote control — the attacker sees what the user sees and can drive the keyboard/mouse, capture camera/microphone feeds, browse the filesystem, install additional payloads, and pivot from the compromised host. The persistence and full-environment access make RATs much more dangerous than single-purpose malware. Distractors describe other malware categories: worms self-propagate (A); ransomware encrypts and extorts (C); self-deleting malware (D) is a separate stealth pattern not specific to RATs. Common RAT examples include njRAT and Quasar, all built around the remote-control primitive.

scenarios.q: An employee installs a free system optimization tool from a third-party website. After installation: the browser homepage has changed, new toolbars appeared, they're seeing more advertisements, and performance has degraded. No ransomware or credential theft is observed. What type of malware is this, and what is the BEST remediation?
opts: Ransomware — pay the ransom to restore normal browser function and remove the toolbars
A keylogger — immediately change all passwords used since the optimizer was installed
Adware/PUP — uninstall via system tools, reset browser settings, and run an anti-malware scan
A rootkit — reformat the entire system since rootkits cannot be removed reliably otherwise
scenarios.exp: Remove the optimization tool and associated browser extensions, scan with an anti-malware tool, reset browser settings to defaults. Adware/PUP indicators: browser hijacking, unwanted toolbars, excessive ads, performance degradation. No data theft indicators. Removal: uninstall the source application, remove browser extensions, scan with malware removal tools, reset browser settings. Full reformat is disproportionate for adware.

cram.def: Disguised as legitimate software. Requires user to install it. Contains hidden malicious payload.
Hides the presence of malware by intercepting OS calls. Operates at kernel level. Very hard to detect.
Malicious code that executes when a specific condition is met (date, user login, event). Often planted by insiders.
Network of compromised systems (bots) controlled via C2 server. Used for DDoS, spam, credential stuffing.
Hidden access method installed by attacker for persistent re-entry — bypasses normal authentication.
Uses victim's CPU/GPU to mine cryptocurrency without consent — causes performance degradation.

questions.q: Which BEST describes Trojan horse malware?
opts: Self-propagating malware that spreads from host to host across networks without requiring user action
Stealthy malware that hides its presence by intercepting OS calls and concealing files, processes, and registry keys
Malware that encrypts the victim's data and demands cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key to restore access
Malicious code disguised as legitimate software that requires the user to install or execute it (a delivery mechanism, not a payload category)
questions.exp: A Trojan is malicious code packaged inside something the user wants to install or run — pirated software, a fake app installer, a bundled 'free' tool. The defining axis is that it requires user-initiated execution and is a DELIVERY MECHANISM rather than a self-propagating category. A Trojan can CARRY ransomware, a backdoor, or other payloads, but the Trojan IS the disguise. The distractors describe distinct other categories: worms self-propagate (A); ransomware encrypts and extorts (C); rootkits hide presence (D). Confusing the delivery mechanism (Trojan) with the payload (ransomware/worm) is the most common error.

questions.q: Which BEST describes a rootkit's primary purpose?
opts: Encrypt user files and demand cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key — the defining behavior of the ransomware category
Self-propagate from host to host across the network without requiring any user interaction — the defining behavior of the worm category
Record every keystroke a user types and exfiltrate the captured input to an attacker — the defining behavior of the keylogger category
Hide the presence of malware and the attacker's activity by intercepting OS calls and concealing files, processes, and registry keys
questions.exp: A rootkit's defining function is concealment — it operates at a privileged level (kernel or hypervisor) and intercepts OS calls (file enumeration, process listing, network connection listing) to hide malicious files, processes, and network activity from system tools and many security products. Other malware categories have different primary purposes: ransomware encrypts and extorts (A); worms self-propagate (B); keyloggers capture user input (D). Rootkits are often combined with other malware to provide stealth — a rootkit may hide a keylogger or a backdoor, for example.

questions.q: A logic bomb is:
opts: Malware that always executes immediately upon installation on the target system
Malicious code that lies dormant and executes only when a specific trigger condition is met
A type of distributed denial-of-service amplification attack using public reflectors
A hardware-level firmware vulnerability in BIOS or UEFI components below the OS
questions.exp: Logic bombs trigger on conditions like a specific date, a user logging in, or a file being deleted — often planted by disgruntled insiders.

questions.q: Why are rootkits particularly difficult to detect?
opts: They use strong end-to-end encryption to obscure their network communications
They operate at the kernel level and intercept OS calls — hiding themselves from the very tools used to detect them
They change their executable code or signature with each new system infection
They infect only BIOS or UEFI firmware below the operating system, not user-space
questions.exp: Rootkits modify how the OS reports system information — making infected files, processes, and connections invisible to standard tools.

scenarios.q: A forensic analyst discovers a script embedded in a legitimate backup software installation that monitors whether a specific IT administrator account is still active in Active Directory. If the account is removed, the script triggers and deletes critical database backups. The script was planted by a contractor 14 months ago. What type of malware is this?
opts: A rootkit — it hid itself for 14 months
Ransomware staged for activation at a specific time
A backdoor — the contractor used it to maintain access after the contract ended
A logic bomb
scenarios.exp: Malicious code that executes when a specific trigger condition is met (the admin account being deleted). Logic bomb: the trigger condition is the removal of a specific account. This is a classic insider threat technique — planting a logic bomb before departure. Detection is difficult because the code is dormant until triggered. Code review of all contractor-written code is the mitigation.

scenarios.q: A user reports their computer is extremely slow. Investigation reveals: CPU pegged at 95-100%, the culprit process is named 'svchost.exe' but its path is %AppData% rather than System32, and it's making outbound connections to multiple external IPs. No ransom demand has been made and files appear intact. What is MOST likely occurring?
opts: A legitimate Windows update running in the background — nothing to do beyond letting it complete
Ransomware encrypting files — the ransom demand hasn't appeared yet because encryption is mid-stream
A worm propagating across the network using SMB to spread laterally to other workstations
A cryptominer — the disguised binary uses CPU cycles for unauthorized cryptocurrency mining
scenarios.exp: Hijacking CPU resources to mine cryptocurrency, disguised as svchost.exe but running from an unusual path. Cryptominer indicators: maxed CPU, no file encryption, outbound connections, disguised as a legitimate process name but running from an unexpected path (%AppData% instead of System32). Cryptominers need the CPU for mining — no interest in ransoming or destroying data.

questions.q: RFID cloning is used to:
opts: Replay captured Wi-Fi authentication frames against a wireless access point
Copy the data from an RFID access card to create a duplicate that bypasses physical access controls
Disrupt the RFID reader's radio signal so legitimate badges cannot authenticate to it
Brute-force the PIN entry on a smart-card reader using a programmable USB device
questions.exp: RFID cloning captures and duplicates the data on proximity cards — the cloned card can then be used to bypass access controls.

questions.q: Dumpster diving is a physical attack that involves:
opts: Filling a server room with water
Searching through discarded material for sensitive information like documents or hardware
Overloading physical security systems
Dropping infected USB drives in car parks
questions.exp: Organizations discard sensitive documents without shredding — dumpster diving recovers this information. Mitigated by shredding policies.

questions.q: An employee enters their banking PIN at a self-service kiosk in an open lobby and notices someone standing close behind them. Which mitigation is MOST effective at preventing this specific class of disclosure?
opts: Encrypt the device's local storage so that any captured screen image or input log stored on the kiosk cannot be read offline by an attacker who later seizes it
Enforce multi-factor authentication on the account so that a stolen PIN alone cannot grant the attacker access to the underlying banking session
Replace the static PIN with a stronger 12-character alphanumeric password to increase entropy and resist credential-guessing attacks
Physical and visual mitigations specific to the threat: privacy filter on the screen, body-shield the keypad, and reposition the kiosk away from common over-the-shoulder sightlines
questions.exp: Shoulder surfing is observation of credential entry by a person physically present. The threat axis is visual exposure during entry, so the effective mitigations are physical and visual: privacy filters that narrow the viewing angle, body-shielding the keypad, and kiosk positioning that prevents over-the-shoulder visibility. MFA addresses what an attacker can do AFTER capturing the PIN but does not stop the disclosure. A stronger password is still equally visible to the surfer. Encryption addresses an entirely different threat (offline data access). Students often default to MFA or stronger credentials for any 'stolen credential' scenario; for shoulder surfing the threat is in-the-moment observation and the mitigation must address that specifically.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester walks into a financial firm's building alongside a group of employees returning from lunch, and proceeds to an unlocked conference room where they access an unattended laptop. They printed official-looking visitor badges with a major consulting firm's logo. What TWO physical attack techniques did the tester use?
opts: Shoulder surfing the user's typed laptop password and RFID cloning the visitor's lobby badge
Skimming credit-card details at the front lobby and social engineering the receptionist via phone
Dumpster diving through visitor logs in the bin and baiting employees with branded malicious USB drives
Tailgating (following employees through access control without authenticating) and impersonation (fake visitor badge from a known vendor)
scenarios.exp: Two techniques: (1) Tailgating — followed the legitimate employee group through access control. (2) Impersonation — the fake badge from a recognized firm reduced scrutiny. Mitigations: mantrap (prevents tailgating), verify all visitors at reception regardless of badge, enforce clean desk/screen lock policy.

scenarios.q: An attacker attaches a device to an ATM's card reader that stores magnetic stripe data from every card inserted. A small camera captures PIN entry. Three weeks later, the attacker creates cloned cards. What attacks were used and what mitigations protect against this?
opts: Card skimming and physical camera for PIN capture — mitigated by chip-and-PIN cards (chip cannot be cloned from the stripe), PIN pad shields, and ATM physical inspection programs
RFID cloning and shoulder surfing — mitigated by Faraday cages
Vishing and impersonation — mitigated by caller ID authentication
Bluetooth sniffing and keylogging — mitigated by disabling Bluetooth on ATMs
scenarios.exp: Skimming and PIN camera capture. Chip-and-PIN (EMV) was specifically designed to defeat skimming — the chip generates a unique transaction code each time and cannot be cloned from the magnetic stripe. PIN pad shields make camera capture harder. Banks run ATM inspection programs to detect skimmers.

Targets specific web application — HTTP flood, Slowloris. Hard to distinguish from legitimate traffic.
Sends many SYN packets without completing handshake — exhausts server connection table (half-open connections).

questions.q: How does a DDoS attack differ from a basic DoS attack?
opts: DDoS attacks always use encryption to mask their malicious payloads in transit
DDoS attacks require the attacker to have physical access to the target's network
DDoS attacks only target web applications and never affect network or transport layers
DDoS originates from many distributed sources (botnet), making it much harder to block by IP
questions.exp: DDoS uses thousands of compromised systems as sources — blocking one IP has no effect, unlike a single-source DoS.

Flooding a target with large UDP packets
Amplifying traffic using DNS servers
Disrupting application-layer HTTP requests
questions.exp: SYN floods leave many half-open TCP connections — eventually the server's connection table is full and it can't accept legitimate connections.

questions.q: An attacker generates a 50 Gbps DDoS flood at a target by sending small DNS queries (with the victim's address spoofed as the source) to thousands of open recursive DNS resolvers. The mechanism that BEST explains how a small attacker pipe produces large victim-side traffic is:
opts: DNS responses are inherently larger than queries because the protocol is inefficient; this inefficiency by itself is the amplification mechanism, no other components required
The DNS protocol uses TCP for amplification queries, which the attacker floods with SYN packets; each TCP connection consumes more victim resources than a UDP packet would

Three effects combined: spoofed source IP reflects responses to the victim, small queries elicit ~50x larger responses (EDNS0/DNSSEC), and open recursive resolvers act as unwitting amplifiers using their bandwidth
The attacker compromises the victim's authoritative DNS server and uses it to respond to internet DNS queries, reflecting traffic at the victim from every DNS-using client globally
questions.exp: DNS amplification combines three mechanisms. (1) REFLECTION: the attacker spoofs the victim's IP as the query source, so DNS responses go to the victim instead of the attacker — the attacker never sees the responses, which is fine because the attack goal is consumption of the victim's bandwidth. (2) AMPLIFICATION: a small ~64-byte query elicits a much larger ~3000+ byte response when DNSSEC and EDNS0 are involved — typical amplification factor ~50x. (3) THIRD-PARTY BANDWIDTH: open recursive DNS resolvers (misconfigured to answer any source) are the unwitting amplifiers — the attacker's small upload becomes the resolvers' large download to the victim. Removing any one component defeats the attack: source-IP filtering at the resolver kills reflection; response-rate limiting reduces amplification; closing open recursors removes the third-party bandwidth pool.

scenarios.q: An organization's e-commerce website becomes unavailable during a major sale event. Analysis shows the web servers are receiving 50,000 requests per second — 40x normal — all appearing to be legitimate HTTP GET requests for the product catalog. The requests come from 200,000 different IP addresses globally. What type of attack is this, and why is IP blocking ineffective?
opts: A volumetric DDoS using UDP flood — block all UDP traffic
A DNS amplification attack — block all DNS traffic
A SYN flood — increase the SYN backlog queue on web servers
An application layer DDoS (HTTP flood)
scenarios.exp: IP blocking is ineffective because the attack uses 200,000 distributed source IPs (a botnet). Blocking individual IPs doesn't scale. Application layer DDoS: HTTP requests look legitimate. IP blocking is ineffective against a 200,000-IP botnet — each IP contributes minimally but collectively overwhelm the server. Mitigations: rate limiting per IP, challenge-response (CAPTCHA), CDN/DDoS scrubbing service, and geo-IP filtering if the sale is region-specific.

scenarios.q: A SYN flood sends 100,000 TCP SYN packets per second without completing the three-way handshake. After 30 seconds, the server's connection table is full and it cannot accept legitimate connections. What mitigation technique specifically addresses the resource exhaustion aspect of SYN floods?
opts: Increase the server's RAM to hold more half-open connections
SYN cookies — the server doesn't allocate resources until the handshake is completed, encoding state cryptographically into the initial SYN-ACK response
Block all inbound SYN packets — this prevents legitimate connections too
Rate limit TCP connections to 10 per second from any single IP
scenarios.exp: SYN cookies: instead of allocating state for each SYN, the server encodes connection information into the ISN of the SYN-ACK. No memory is allocated until the ACK arrives completing the handshake. Legitimate clients complete the handshake; attackers' spoofed packets never do — eliminating resource exhaustion.
