Attacker gains control of a domain registration — changes DNS records to redirect all traffic.
Redirecting malicious domain lookups to a controlled IP — blocks malware C2 communication.
DNS Security Extensions — cryptographically signs DNS records to prevent poisoning/spoofing.
Hiding data exfiltration or C2 traffic within DNS queries — often overlooked by firewalls that allow DNS.

questions.q: DNS cache poisoning works by:
opts: Inserting false DNS records into a resolver's cache — causing users to be redirected to attacker-controlled IP addresses
Flooding a DNS server with requests until it crashes and stops responding to legitimate lookups
Intercepting DNS traffic with an on-path attack to read but not modify resolution responses

Blocking all external DNS queries from corporate clients at the perimeter firewall
Cryptographically signing DNS records so resolvers can verify their authenticity
Requiring DNS queries to be performed only over IPv6-enabled resolvers

Resolve hostnames faster by bypassing the standard recursive DNS hierarchy entirely

Poison the DNS cache of a recursive resolver to redirect users to a malicious destination
questions.exp: DNS tunneling encodes data within DNS queries — many firewalls allow all DNS traffic, making it a covert channel.

scenarios.q: Employees report that when they visit the company's banking portal (internalbank.company.com), they're seeing a certificate error and the site looks different. Investigation reveals the DNS resolver used by workstations is returning an incorrect IP for internalbank.company.com. Internal DNS zone files are correct. What attack is occurring?
opts: DNS cache poisoning of an upstream or internal resolver — the resolver has been fed false records. DNSSEC would allow resolvers to verify the authenticity of DNS responses
Domain hijacking — the attacker has taken over the domain registration
A watering hole attack on the banking portal itself
BGP hijacking redirecting traffic before DNS resolution
scenarios.exp: DNS cache poisoning: the resolver's cache has been poisoned with false records. Internal zone files being correct rules out domain hijacking. DNSSEC cryptographically signs zone data — a resolver can verify the DNS response came from the authoritative source. Certificate errors on the fake site are a detection opportunity — train users to report them.

scenarios.q: A security team finds an endpoint making hundreds of DNS queries per hour for subdomains of a domain with no web presence. The subdomains are all long random-looking strings (a3f7b2c1d8e4.attacker.com, b9d2e7f3a1c4.attacker.com). DNS responses return valid IPs but no traffic goes to those IPs. A worm using DNS to propagate by generating random subdomains as it searches for other vulnerable hosts
DNS tunneling — the endpoint is exfiltrating data encoded in DNS query subdomains, with responses potentially carrying C2 commands back
Legitimate CDN behavior generating random subdomain lookups for cache-busting and load distribution
scenarios.exp: DNS tunneling: data is encoded in subdomain labels of DNS queries. The 'random' subdomains are actually encoded data. Responses carry C2 commands back. Most firewalls allow DNS — attackers exploit this. Detection: anomalously high DNS query volume, long/random subdomain strings, queries for domains with no legitimate web presence.

questions.q: Which is the BEST mitigation for WPS-related wireless attacks (e.g. Reaver-style PIN brute-force)?
opts: Using WPA3 exclusively across the network and removing WPA2 backwards compatibility from every access point in the environment
Hiding the network SSID so attackers cannot see the wireless network exists during a passive site survey of the area
Using a stronger WPS PIN with more digits and a mix of letters and symbols to resist brute-force attempts
Disabling WPS on all access points — the WPS PIN exchange is the attack surface, and turning it off eliminates the brute-force path entirely
questions.exp: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) was designed to make wireless setup easier — but the PIN-based variant has a fundamental flaw: the 8-digit PIN is split into two 4-digit halves checked separately, reducing brute-force complexity from 10^8 to ~11,000 combinations. Tools like Reaver exploit this directly. The only effective mitigation is to DISABLE WPS entirely; the PIN cannot be made resistant within the WPS spec. Moving to WPA3 helps but doesn't directly address WPS (you can run WPS on top of WPA3-Personal too); hiding the SSID is security theater (passive listeners see SSIDs in beacon frames or association requests anyway); a stronger PIN doesn't help because the protocol still leaks information about each half independently.

questions.q: Capturing a WPA2 4-way handshake allows an attacker to:
opts: Immediately gain network access
Inject traffic into the wireless network
Decrypt all previously captured network traffic
Perform offline brute-force or dictionary attacks against the pre-shared key
questions.exp: The captured handshake contains enough information for offline cracking — the attacker can test passwords without further network interaction.

scenarios.q: During a wireless assessment, a tester sets up a rogue AP with the same SSID as 'CorpWiFi' with a stronger signal than legitimate APs. Employee laptops automatically connect to the rogue AP. The tester intercepts all their traffic. What attack is this, and what would have prevented automatic connection?
opts: A deauthentication attack — prevented by management frame protection
A WPS PIN attack — prevented by disabling WPS on corporate APs
An evil twin attack — prevented by requiring WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X) which validates the server certificate, so clients refuse to connect to APs presenting unexpected certificates
A Bluetooth pairing attack — prevented by requiring PIN authentication
scenarios.exp: Evil twin: WPA2-Personal (PSK) has no way for clients to verify the AP's identity. WPA2-Enterprise with EAP-TLS or PEAP requires the AP to present a certificate signed by a trusted CA — a rogue AP without that certificate is rejected. Enterprise wireless should use 802.1X, not PSK.

scenarios.q: A wireless penetration tester uses aireplay-ng to send deauthentication frames to clients, forcing them to reconnect. The tester captures the 4-way handshake and takes it offline for dictionary attack. What is the tester doing, and what wireless standard was designed to address the handshake capture vulnerability?
opts: Performing a WPS PIN attack — WPA3 removes WPS entirely so the 8-digit PIN offline brute-force is no longer possible
Performing a Bluetooth attack — Bluetooth 5.0 addresses the handshake-capture vulnerability via encrypted pairing protocols
Capturing a WPA2 4-way handshake via forced deauthentication for offline cracking — WPA3 with SAE provides forward secrecy; capturing the exchange doesn't enable cracking
Conducting ARP poisoning on the wireless network — WPA3 isolation features prevent ARP-level Layer 2 attacks reliably
scenarios.exp: WPA2 handshake capture: deauth forces reauthentication, the 4-way handshake contains enough information for offline password cracking. WPA3's SAE replaces the PSK exchange — it's a zero-knowledge proof that prevents offline cracking even with a full capture of the authentication exchange.

Inject deauthentication frames into wireless broadcast traffic to disconnect legitimate clients

questions.q: ARP poisoning enables an on-path attack by:

Sending fake ARP replies that associate the attacker's MAC address with a legitimate IP — redirecting LAN traffic through the attacker
Forging ICMP redirect messages so each victim updates its routing table to send traffic via the attacker
Hijacking DHCP responses on the LAN to assign the attacker as the default gateway for client traffic
questions.exp: ARP poisoning corrupts the ARP cache of victims — they send traffic to the attacker thinking it's going to the legitimate destination.

Requiring strict TLS certificate pinning enforced at the browser-application level
Blocking all non-HTTPS traffic at the corporate edge firewall before it leaves the network
Instructing browsers to always use HTTPS for a domain — refusing to downgrade to HTTP
questions.exp: HSTS tells browsers the site must always be accessed via HTTPS — browsers refuse to connect over HTTP even if redirected.

scenarios.q: A user can access their bank account fine at home, but on public WiFi the bank's website shows HTTP instead of HTTPS and their credentials may have been captured. Later they find unauthorized transactions. What attack likely occurred, and what should the bank have implemented?
opts: SSL stripping — the attacker used a MITM position to intercept the initial HTTP request and prevent upgrade to HTTPS. HSTS with preloading would have caused the browser to refuse HTTP connections to the bank domain
DNS poisoning at the coffee shop's router — DNSSEC would have prevented this
A rogue certificate authority — certificate pinning would have prevented this
Packet sniffing of unencrypted WiFi — WPA3 with OWE would have encrypted the WiFi traffic
scenarios.exp: SSL stripping on public WiFi: HSTS tells browsers 'always use HTTPS for this domain' — preloaded HSTS means even the first connection is forced to HTTPS before any server response. No HTTP connection is ever made, nothing to strip.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester sends gratuitous ARP replies claiming their MAC address is associated with the default gateway's IP. Within seconds, all workstations send traffic to the tester instead of the actual gateway. The tester forwards traffic to the real gateway while recording it. What attack is this, and what Layer 2 control prevents it?
opts: DNS cache poisoning — DNSSEC prevents this through signed-record validation
IP spoofing — firewall egress filtering at the network boundary prevents this
ARP poisoning/spoofing — Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches prevents this
BGP hijacking — route filtering on border routers prevents this between AS peers
scenarios.exp: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches prevents it by validating ARP packets against a trusted DHCP snooping database. ARP poisoning: ARP has no authentication. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) is the Layer 2 control: the switch inspects ARP packets and compares them against the DHCP snooping binding table. Gratuitous ARP replies that don't match legitimate bindings are dropped.

Capturing an NTLM password hash and replaying it for authentication — no need to crack the hash.

questions.q: A replay attack works by:
opts: Capturing and retransmitting valid authentication packets to gain access without needing the actual credentials
Guessing authentication credentials through high-speed brute force against the login endpoint
Injecting malicious payloads into authentication packets so the server executes attacker code
Cracking encrypted session keys offline using GPU-accelerated cipher analysis to forge tokens
questions.exp: Replay attacks capture valid auth packets and replay them — the system accepts them as legitimate since they passed authentication originally.

questions.q: Which BEST explains why pass-the-hash is classified as a type of replay attack?
opts: The attack only works against web applications that use form-based authentication and stores the captured session hash in a session cookie
The attacker first cracks the captured hash offline to recover the cleartext password, then replays the cleartext to the target service to authenticate
The attack requires the attacker to be on the same Layer 2 broadcast domain as both the original session and the target service for the replay to succeed
The captured NTLM hash is replayed directly to a service for authentication — no need to crack or recover the original password; the hash itself is the authentication credential
questions.exp: Pass-the-hash exploits Windows authentication's design: the NTLM/NTLMv2 hash IS the authentication credential, so an attacker who captures the hash (from memory dump, lsass, etc.) can authenticate to any service that accepts NTLM by replaying the hash directly — no password recovery step needed. The cracking distractor describes a different attack flow (offline brute force then password use). The same-network distractor is wrong — pass-the-hash works across network boundaries as long as the attacker can reach the target service. Web/cookie scope is wrong — pass-the-hash targets Windows authentication, not web sessions.

questions.q: Nonces prevent replay attacks by:
opts: Encrypting all authentication traffic between client and server using TLS in transit
Requiring biometric authentication factors during the initial login session establishment
Adding a unique random value to each authentication request — old requests with invalid nonces are rejected
Limiting login attempts and locking out accounts after repeated authentication failures
questions.exp: Each nonce is unique and single-use — replaying an old authentication packet fails because the nonce has already been used.

scenarios.q: An attacker captures network traffic during a user's authentication to a web application and records the session cookie. An hour later, the attacker injects the captured cookie into their own browser and gains access. What attack occurred and what implementation choices would have prevented it?
opts: Session hijacking via cookie theft
A CSRF attack — prevented by CSRF tokens
A replay attack on the password hash — prevented by NTLM challenge-response
A SQL injection providing direct database access
scenarios.exp: Prevented by: Secure flag (HTTPS-only transmission), HttpOnly flag (no JavaScript access), short session timeout, and binding sessions to the client's IP or browser fingerprint. Session hijacking: the cookie was captured in transit (Secure flag would have prevented transmission over HTTP). The attack succeeded because the cookie has no expiry context or binding — it works anywhere. Session binding and short timeouts limit the replay window.

scenarios.q: A Windows domain uses NTLM authentication for legacy applications. An attacker compromises one workstation and uses Mimikatz to extract NTLM hashes from memory. They then authenticate to a file server using only the captured hash — without cracking it. What technique is this, and what architectural change most effectively prevents it?
opts: Credential stuffing — prevented by MFA on the legacy authentication endpoint
A replay attack on Kerberos tickets — prevented by short ticket lifetimes and key rotation
Pass-the-hash — prevented architecturally by removing NTLM; require Kerberos/AES and Protected Users group
Mimikatz itself is the vulnerability — prevented by patching Mimikatz signatures in AV
scenarios.exp: Most effectively prevented by transitioning from NTLM to Kerberos, implementing Protected Users security group to prevent hash caching, and restricting lateral movement via network segmentation. Pass-the-hash exploits NTLM's design — the hash IS the credential. Mitigations: Kerberos doesn't have the same hash-replay issue. Protected Users group prevents NTLM fallback and credential caching. Windows Credential Guard stores hashes in an isolated environment. Network segmentation limits what the attacker can reach even with valid hashes.

questions.q: Which BEST describes a dropper malware's primary function?
opts: Encrypting the victim's files in place and demanding cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key (the ransomware function)
Serving as a small initial payload that downloads, decrypts, and installs the main malicious component on the compromised host
Exfiltrating the victim's stored credentials, browser session tokens, and saved authentication material to attacker infrastructure (the info-stealer function)
Providing the attacker with persistent interactive remote desktop access to the compromised host for hands-on-keyboard activity (the RAT function)
questions.exp: A dropper is a small staged payload designed to land first on a compromised system and then fetch/install the main malware. The dropper itself is intentionally minimal — small footprint, sometimes obfuscated specifically to evade initial detection — because its job is just to bridge from the initial-access payload (e.g. a phishing attachment) to the larger second-stage malware. Distractors describe primary functions of OTHER categories: ransomware (A), info-stealer (C), RAT (D). Modern attack chains often involve a dropper then loader then main malware sequence, with each stage doing a different job.

A CSRF attack is manipulating server-side commands by forging requests on behalf of the admin user
A web shell has been uploaded to the server — the attacker is executing OS commands through HTTP requests to the malicious script

The shell accepts commands via POST and executes them with the web server's privileges. Incident response: isolate the server, find how the shell was uploaded, remove it, identify what was accessed.

A worm using legitimate system tools to propagate
A rootkit modifying the Windows task scheduler

Living-off-the-land using PowerShell with encoded commands via a scheduled task — effective because PowerShell is a legitimate admin tool, base64 encoding evades simple string-based detection, and the scheduled task provides persistence without a persistent file

Base64 encoding hides the payload from string-matching rules. Scheduled tasks are legitimate persistence mechanisms. Detection requires PowerShell ScriptBlock logging (which decodes base64) and monitoring for scheduled task creation events.

questions.q: Which is the PRIMARY mitigation for CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attacks?
opts: Input validation on all form fields to reject script tags, SQL syntax, and other characters that should not appear in legitimate user input
Unique, unpredictable anti-CSRF tokens issued per session and included in every state-changing request, validated server-side before the action is processed
Content Security Policy (CSP) headers that restrict which domains a page can load scripts and stylesheets from to prevent script injection
HTTPS encryption between the browser and the server to prevent on-path attackers from observing or modifying the request in flight over the network
questions.exp: CSRF works by tricking an authenticated user's browser into submitting an attacker-crafted request to a site where the user is logged in (the browser includes session cookies automatically). The PRIMARY mitigation is anti-CSRF tokens: a unique, unpredictable token tied to the session that must be included in every state-changing request — the attacker's cross-site form cannot include the token because they cannot read it from the legitimate session. Input validation addresses XSS and injection, not CSRF. CSP is for XSS / script-source-restriction. HTTPS prevents on-path attacks but does not stop CSRF, which exploits the user's already-authenticated session. SameSite cookie attributes are a complementary modern mitigation.

IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
Directory traversal — the account number is used as a file path
scenarios.exp: The application exposes a direct reference to internal objects without verifying the requester owns that object. Fix: verify server-side that the authenticated user owns the requested account before returning data. IDOR: the application uses a predictable identifier (account number) as a direct database reference without an authorization check. Fix is server-side: before returning account 10453's data, verify the authenticated session belongs to the owner of account 10453. Client-side controls don't help — attackers modify HTTP requests directly.

scenarios.q: A developer builds a web preview feature where users provide a URL and the server fetches content to display. A researcher provides: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and receives the application's cloud instance metadata including IAM credentials. What vulnerability is this?
opts: CSRF — the server is making requests on behalf of the user
SQL injection — the URL parameter is passed to a database query
Directory traversal — the URL traverses to internal file paths
SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
scenarios.exp: The server fetches attacker-specified URLs, giving access to internal resources (including cloud metadata services) only accessible from the server itself. SSRF: the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254 is accessible only from within the cloud instance — not from the internet. But the server IS the cloud instance. By making the server fetch that URL, the attacker accesses internal resources as if they were the server. Fix: validate/restrict URLs the server will fetch, block private IP ranges.

scenarios.q: Authenticated users can submit support tickets. A researcher discovers they can embed JavaScript in a ticket that executes when a support agent views it in the admin console. The researcher uses this to capture the admin's session cookie. What type of XSS is this, and why is it particularly dangerous?
opts: Stored XSS — particularly dangerous because the payload runs for every admin who views the ticket, no per-victim lure required
Reflected XSS — dangerous because it affects all users who click a crafted link from the attacker
DOM-based XSS — dangerous because it bypasses server-side filtering and runs entirely client-side
CSRF — the ticket submission forges requests on the admin's behalf using cached session cookies
scenarios.exp: Particularly dangerous because it targets privileged admin accounts. A support agent viewing the ticket executes the attacker's script with admin session privileges, enabling account takeover of a high-privilege user. Stored XSS targeting admins: the payload is stored in the ticket and executes when a privileged user views it. This is privilege escalation via XSS — an unprivileged user executing code in a privileged user's browser context. This is how many high-profile compromises begin.

cram.def: Exploits probability that two different inputs produce the same hash (collision). Easier than brute force at large scale.
Forces communication to use a weaker, older, vulnerable protocol version.
Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption — exploits SSLv3 via protocol downgrade.

audit_d_review.note: 2.4 Cryptographic Attacks IS umbrella; POODLE IS a cryptographic attack. Same pattern as SSL stripping / SYN flood / evil twin.

cram.def: Precomputed hash-to-plaintext database. Defeated by salting.
bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2 — deliberately slow hashing algorithms making brute force impractical.

Deliberately slow hashing to resist brute force

questions.q: A birthday attack exploits the fact that:
opts: Users tend to use birthdays as passwords
Finding two inputs that produce the same hash is much easier than brute-forcing a specific hash
Birthday data is stored in databases
Attackers can guess birthdays from social media
questions.exp: The birthday problem shows that hash collisions occur far sooner than intuition suggests — exploited to break MD5 and SHA-1.

questions.q: A downgrade attack forces a connection to:
opts: Use a newer untested protocol with unknown vulnerabilities still present in the codebase
Use stronger encryption keys without negotiating cipher suites with the server first
Disconnect entirely and force the user to authenticate again from scratch
Use a weaker, older, vulnerable protocol version that the attacker can then exploit
questions.exp: Downgrade attacks exploit backward compatibility — forcing use of deprecated protocols like SSLv3 that have known vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Key stretching algorithms like bcrypt mitigate brute force attacks by:
opts: Encrypting the password before hashing
Being deliberately computationally slow
Using asymmetric keys for password storage
Requiring a separate hardware token at login
questions.exp: Making large-scale password cracking impractical. Key stretching applies many iterations of hashing — taking milliseconds per attempt is fine for login but makes billions of guesses per second impractical.

scenarios.q: An organization uses MD5 to verify software download integrity. A researcher demonstrates they can create a malicious file with the same MD5 hash as the legitimate file. Users download and verify the hash — it matches — and install the malware. What cryptographic attack made this possible?
opts: A brute-force attack against MD5 — use longer MD5 hashes
A downgrade attack forcing MD5 instead of SHA-256
A rainbow table attack against MD5 — salt the download hashes
A hash collision attack
scenarios.exp: MD5 has known collision vulnerabilities allowing two different inputs to produce the same hash. Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 which are collision-resistant. Collision attack on MD5: it's computationally feasible to find two different inputs with the same MD5 hash. MD5 was broken for this purpose in 2004. SHA-256 (and SHA-3) are collision-resistant. For software integrity verification, SHA-256 is the minimum.

scenarios.q: A TLS connection between a client and server negotiates to TLS 1.0 with RC4 cipher despite both supporting TLS 1.3. An attacker on the network modified the ClientHello, altering the supported cipher suites list before forwarding it to the server. What attack is this and how should the server prevent it?
opts: A downgrade attack — prevented by enforcing TLS 1.2+/AEAD only on the server and rejecting older negotiations
An SSL stripping attack — prevented by enabling HSTS with includeSubDomains and a long max-age
A replay attack on the TLS handshake — prevented by tracking and rejecting reused random nonces
A birthday attack on the RC4 stream cipher — prevented by rotating session keys after each handshake
scenarios.exp: The server should be configured to reject connections using TLS versions below 1.2, refusing to negotiate with the modified ClientHello regardless of what the client claims to support. Protocol downgrade attack: the attacker manipulates negotiation to force use of a weaker protocol the server still supports. Fix: remove TLS 1.0 and 1.1 from the server's supported versions entirely — if the server won't negotiate TLS 1.0, the downgrade can't succeed. Also remove RC4 and other weak ciphers.

cram.def: Try ONE common password against MANY accounts — avoids lockout. E.g. 'Password1' on all accounts.
Using stolen username/password pairs from one breach to try on other services (exploits password reuse).

audit_d_review.note: Cross-packet precedent: SB-fix-1a #56 was kept-as-is-sb16-candidate (Pass-the-hash).

Stolen credentials tried on other services

matching.answer: One guess per account — never triggers lockout threshold

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes password spraying from a traditional brute-force attack?
opts: Password spraying targets only enterprise SSO endpoints while traditional brute force targets only individual workstation login screens
Password spraying tries a small number of common passwords across many user accounts to evade per-account lockout thresholds; traditional brute force tries many passwords against a single account
Password spraying requires the attacker to already have a valid password hash for offline cracking; traditional brute force is performed online against the live login service
Password spraying succeeds only when MFA is disabled on the target accounts while traditional brute force succeeds even when MFA is enforced
questions.exp: Password spraying inverts the brute-force pattern: instead of many passwords times one account (which triggers lockout fast), the attacker uses a few common passwords (Password123!, Spring2026!, Welcome01) times many accounts. Each account sees only one or two attempts, staying under the lockout threshold. Spraying does not require offline hashes, is not platform-limited to SSO, and the MFA framing is not the differentiator. Detection requires watching for a small set of failed-login passwords distributed across many accounts within a window.

questions.q: Which BEST explains why credential stuffing attacks are effective?
opts: Attackers guess a few common passwords across many user accounts to find an account where the guess matches (this is password spraying)
Many users reuse the same username and password across multiple services — credentials breached from one site work directly against many other services without any guessing
Attackers buy or steal a password hash database from a target site and try every account with the recovered credentials (this is database theft + cracking)
Attackers crack stolen NTLM hashes offline using GPU rigs and then replay the recovered cleartext passwords against the original target (offline cracking)
questions.exp: Credential stuffing exploits PASSWORD REUSE across services. The attacker takes a username/password list breached from one site (or bought from a leak market) and replays it against many other sites. Wherever the user reused the credential, the login succeeds — no guessing, no cracking. Defense: unique passwords per site (password manager), MFA on every account, breach-credential monitoring at signup. Distractors describe related but distinct attacks: spraying (B), database theft + cracking (C), offline hash cracking (D). The defining reuse axis is what makes stuffing effective at scale.

questions.q: Which attack is MOST effectively mitigated by MFA but NOT account lockout?
opts: Brute force
Password spraying
Pass-the-hash
Credential stuffing
questions.exp: Credential stuffing uses valid credentials — account lockout won't trigger. MFA prevents access even with correct credentials.

questions.q: Which BEST captures why pass-the-hash is particularly dangerous in Windows enterprise environments?
opts: Pass-the-hash succeeds against modern Kerberos-based authentication out of the box, so even a fully Kerberos-enforced domain provides no protection against the technique
A captured NTLM hash authenticates as the target user against any NTLM-accepting service — no cracking needed, no rotation defeats it; lateral movement is one tool away wherever the user is logged in
NTLM hashes can be decrypted to cleartext passwords by anyone who knows the published Microsoft decryption key, so the hash itself acts like a cleartext credential
Pass-the-hash gives the attacker raw kernel access on the target, allowing them to load any driver and disable EDR before performing the actual authentication attempt
questions.exp: Pass-the-hash is dangerous because the hash IS the credential — capturing it (from lsass memory, SAM database, or domain controller replication) gives the attacker authenticated access to every NTLM-accepting service the user can reach. Because NTLM hashes don't change unless the user changes their password, and because Windows admin accounts are often used to log into many hosts (each leaving a hash in memory), one hash capture often unlocks broad lateral movement. This is why credential hygiene (admin tier separation, no admin logon to workstations, LAPS, strict NTLM restrictions) is critical. Kerberos-only enforcement DOES help (B is wrong); NTLM hashes are NOT reversible (C is wrong); kernel access is a different attack class (D is wrong).

scenarios.q: An attacker obtains 10 million leaked username/password pairs from a social media breach. A script tests these credentials against a financial institution's login page. 23,000 pairs succeed — users who reused their social media password for their bank account. What attack is this, and what control would have been MOST effective?
opts: Brute force attack — prevented by account lockout after 5 failed attempts
Password spraying — prevented by monitoring for single passwords across multiple accounts
Dictionary attack — prevented by requiring complex passwords
Credential stuffing — most effectively prevented by MFA, which makes the correct password insufficient on its own
scenarios.exp: Credential stuffing exploits password reuse — it uses correct passwords, so account lockout and complexity requirements don't help. MFA is the most effective control: even with the correct password, the attacker needs the second factor they don't have.
