scenarios.q: A SOC team notices in their authentication logs: between 9-11am each day, exactly one failed login attempt occurs against each of 3,000 user accounts, using the password 'Welcome1'. No accounts are locked out. What attack is occurring and why does it evade traditional brute-force detection?
opts: Password spraying — evades brute-force detection because each account sees only one attempt; lockout thresholds never trigger
A brute-force attack — it's just particularly slow, and would still trip per-account lockout policies
Credential stuffing — the attacker has a database of valid credentials gathered from a prior breach
Dictionary attack — the attacker is working through a password list one entry at a time per target account
scenarios.exp: It deliberately stays below account lockout thresholds (one attempt per account per day) while testing a common password against many accounts. Lockout policies count failed attempts PER ACCOUNT, not per password. Password spraying: lockout policies count failures per account. Spraying makes only ONE attempt per account — never triggering per-account lockout. Detection requires correlation across accounts (one password, many accounts). Mitigations: MFA, block commonly-used passwords like 'Welcome1', anomaly detection on authentication patterns.

cram.def: Login from two distant cities minutes apart — account likely compromised (credential theft).
Unexpected CPU/GPU/bandwidth spike — possible cryptominer or data exfiltration.
Large data transfers to unusual destinations — possible data exfiltration or C2 communication.
MD5/SHA-256 hash of known malware. Exact match detection. Easily evaded by polymorphic malware.
Known malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs. Used in firewall rules and DNS sinkholes.
Gaps in logs, log deletion, unusually large logs — sign of cover-up or active attack.

matching.prompt: Login from two distant cities minutes apart
Unexpected CPU spike on a server
Large data transfer to unknown external IP
Gaps or deletions in system logs
Known malicious file hash
Known malicious IP address or domain

questions.q: An impossible travel alert fires when:
opts: A user account shows logins from geographically impossible locations within a short time — indicating credential compromise
A user logs in multiple times within a single calendar day from their normal office location
A backend server suddenly runs out of available disk space and stops accepting new writes
A user downloads a single very large file from an internal corporate file share over the VPN
questions.exp: Impossible travel detects when the same account logs in from locations too far apart for human travel — strong indicator of credential theft.

questions.q: An on-call engineer notices a production server pinning 100% CPU at 3am with no scheduled jobs, no expected backups, and no user load. Which is the MOST likely cause to investigate FIRST?
opts: Routine background maintenance running on the server's monthly maintenance schedule that the on-call engineer has not yet noticed in the runbook documentation overnight
Possible cryptomining or other resource-intensive malicious workload — off-hours timing plus full CPU saturation plus no expected load is the classic crypto-jacking pattern
A failed software update that is silently retrying installation in a tight loop, consuming CPU until the next reboot or manual intervention by the support team
Another administrator already debugging the issue with strace or perf attached to a hot process, consuming CPU as the diagnostic instrumentation collects samples
questions.exp: The combination of '3am, no scheduled work, full CPU saturation' is the classic cryptojacking IoC pattern: malicious crypto-mining processes typically run when defenders aren't watching and use all available CPU because mining throughput depends on it. First-hour investigation: list running processes (top, ps), look for unfamiliar binaries or system processes spawning unusual children, check outbound connections (netstat, NetFlow) for mining-pool destinations (port 3333 stratum), and check sudden onset time. Benign causes (A routine maintenance, C failed-update loop, D admin debugging) are real possibilities and should be ruled out — but the scenario asks what to investigate FIRST, and the cryptojacking signature is most actionable.

questions.q: File hash IoCs are easily evaded by:
opts: Adding new firewall block rules at the network perimeter
Encrypting all malware command-and-control communications
Polymorphic malware that changes its code
Stolen legitimate code-signing certificate signatures
questions.exp: And therefore its hash — with each infection. Hash-based IoCs match exact files — polymorphic malware changes its hash with each infection, evading hash-based detection.

scenarios.q: A SIEM alert fires: 'User jsmith logged in from London at 09:00 and from Singapore at 09:45.' The user's manager confirms jsmith is in the London office today. What does this IoC indicate, and what are the IMMEDIATE response actions?
opts: A misconfigured SIEM rule generating false positives — tune the rule and close the alert
Standard VPN usage — the Singapore IP is likely a VPN endpoint

An impossible travel alert strongly indicating credential compromise. Immediate actions: disable jsmith's account, force session termination on all active sessions, require credential reset via verified out-of-band channel, check what was accessed from the Singapore session
An NTP synchronization error causing timestamp confusion
scenarios.exp: Impossible travel is a strong credential compromise indicator. Immediate actions matter: disable the account first (stop active damage), terminate all sessions, then investigate. The out-of-band channel for credential reset is important — if email is compromised, emailing a reset link helps the attacker.

scenarios.q: A threat hunter reviews DNS logs and notices an internal workstation making periodic DNS queries every 60 seconds to a domain registered 3 days ago that has no web presence. The workstation's user has not reported any issues. What does this pattern suggest?
opts: Beaconing — periodic check-in traffic from C2-infected endpoint; investigate process and isolate
Normal software update checking behavior — no action needed beyond confirming the destination is benign
A DNS tunneling attack exfiltrating data in the queries themselves — payload encoded in subdomain labels
A botnet scanning behavior — automated reconnaissance of network ranges for vulnerable hosts
scenarios.exp: Malware periodically checking in with C2 infrastructure using a recently registered domain (a common evasion technique). Isolate the workstation, collect memory dump, review all processes and network connections, trace what was executed in the past 3 days. Beaconing IoC: regular interval (60 seconds = timer-based), newly registered domain (threat feeds don't have it yet), no legitimate purpose. This is characteristic malware C2 check-in behavior. The user reporting no issues is expected — modern malware is designed to be silent. Memory forensics will reveal the malicious process.

questions.q: Vince recently received the hash values of malicious software that several other firms in his industry found installed on their systems after a compromise. What term best describes this information?
opts: Vulnerability feed
IoC
TTP
RFC
questions.exp: Specific details of attacks that may be used to identify compromises are known as indicators of compromise (IoCs). This data may also be described as an adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTP), but the fact that it is a set of file signatures makes it more closely match the definition of an IoC.

questions.q: Ryan wants to prevent logic bombs created by insider threats from impacting his organization. What technique will most effectively limit the likelihood of logic bombs being put in place?
opts: Deploying antivirus software
Using a code review process
Deploying endpoint detection and response (EDR) software
Disabling autorun for USB drives
questions.exp: Logic bombs are embedded in code, so Ryan’s organization would get the most benefit from a code review process for any code that goes into production. Antivirus and EDR are unlikely to detect logic bombs created by staff in Ryan’s organization.

questions.q: A system in Elaine’s company has suddenly displayed a message demanding payment in Bitcoin and claiming that the data from the system has been encrypted. What type of malware has Elaine likely encountered?
opts: Worms
A virus
Ransomware
Rootkit
questions.exp: Ransomware demands payment to be made while typically using encryption to make data inaccessible. Worms, viruses, and rootkits are not defined by behavior like this.

questions.q: Rick believes that a system he is responsible for has been compromised with malware that uses a rootkit to obtain and retain access to the system. When he runs an antimalware tool’s scanner, the system doesn’t show any malware. If he has other data that indicates the system is infected, what should his next step be if he wants to determine what malware may be on the system?
opts: Rerun the antimalware scan.
Mount the drive on another system and scan it that way.
Disable the systems antivirus because it may be causing a false negative.
The system is not infected and he should move on.
questions.exp: Rootkits are designed to hide from antimalware scanners and can often defeat locally run scans. Mounting the drive in another system in read‐only mode or booting from a USB drive and scanning using a trusted, known good operating system can be an effective way to determine what malware is on a potentially infected system.

questions.q: A recently terminated developer from Jaya’s organization has contacted the organization claiming that they left code in an application that they wrote that will delete files and bring the application down if they are not employed by the company. What type of malware is this?
opts: Ransomware
Extortionware
A logic bomb
A Trojan
questions.exp: Jaya’s former employee is describing a logic bomb, malicious code that will cause harm when a trigger or specific action occurs. In this case, the former employee is claiming that the trigger is them not being employed at the company. Jaya will need to assess all of the code that the employee wrote to determine if a logic bomb exists. Ransomware is a type of malicious software that typically uses encryption to extort a ransom. Extortionware is not a commonly used term. Trojans appear to be useful or desirable software but contain malicious code.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a worm and a virus?
opts: What operating system they run on
How they spread
What their potential impact is
The number of infections
questions.exp: The key difference between worms and viruses is how they spread. Worms spread themselves, whereas viruses rely on human interaction.

questions.q: Which of the following defenses is most likely to prevent Trojan installation?
opts: Installing patches for known vulnerabilities
Preventing downloads from application stores
Preventing the use of USB drives
Disabling autorun from USB drives
questions.exp: Trojans are often found in application stores where they appear to be innocuous but desirable applications or are listed in confusingly similar ways to legitimate applications. Many organizations choose to lock down the ability to acquire applications from app stores to prevent this type of issue. Since Trojans do not self‐spread and rely on user action, patching typically won’t prevent them. While users may try to transfer files via USB, this isn’t the most common means for modern Trojans to spread.

questions.q: Jason’s security team reports that a recent WordPress vulnerability seems to have been exploited by malware and that their organization’s entire WordPress service cluster has been infected. What type of malware is most likely involved if a vulnerability in the software was exploited over the network?
opts: A logic bomb
A Trojan
A worm
A rootkit
questions.exp: Worms often spread via networks, taking advantage of vulnerabilities to install themselves on targeted systems and then to propagate further. Trojans require human interaction to install software that appears desirable. Logic bombs are embedded in code and perform actions when triggers like a date or event occur. Rootkits are used to hide malware and to conceal attacker’s actions.

questions.q: Hui’s organization recently purchased new Windows computers from an office supply store. The systems have a number of unwanted programs on them that load at startup that were installed by the manufacturer. What type of software is this?
opts: Viruses
Trojans
Spyware
Bloatware
questions.exp: Unwanted, typically preinstalled programs are known as bloatware. They take up space and resources without providing value, and many organizations either uninstall them or install clean operating system images to avoid them. There is no indication of malicious activity in the question, so these are most likely not viruses, Trojans, or spyware.

questions.q: What type of malware connects to a command and control system, allowing attackers to manage, control, and update it remotely?
opts: A bot
A drone
A vampire
A worm
questions.exp: Bots connect to command and control (C&C) systems, allowing them to be updated, controlled, and managed remotely. Worms spread via vulnerabilities, and drones and vampires aren’t common terms for malware.

questions.q: Yasmine believes that her organization may be dealing with an advanced rootkit and wants to write IoC definitions for it. Which of the following is not likely to be a useful IoC for a rootkit?
opts: File hashes
Command and control domains
Pop‐ups demanding a ransom
Behavior‐based identifiers
questions.exp: Rootkits are intended to be stealthy, and a pop‐up demanding ransom works against that purpose. File hashes, command and control details, and behavior‐based identifiers are all useful IoCs likely to be relevant to a rootkit.

questions.q: Randy believes that a system that he is responsible for was infected after a user picked up a USB drive and plugged it in. The user claims that they only opened one file on the drive to see who might own it. What type of malware is most likely involved?
opts: A virus
A worm
A trojan
A spyware tool
questions.exp: Randy knows that viruses spread through user interaction with files on thumb drives. A worm would spread itself, a Trojan would look like a useful or desirable file, and there is no indication of spyware in the question.

questions.q: Nathan works at a school and notices that one of his staff appears to have logged in and changed grades for a single student to higher grades, even in classes that staff member is not responsible for. When asked, the staff member says that they did not perform the action. Which of the following is the most likely way that a student could have gotten access to the staff member’s password?
opts: A keylogger
A rootkit
Spyware
A logic bomb
questions.exp: Nathan should check the staff member’s computer for a keylogger, which would have captured their username and password. A student could have then used the staff member’s credentials to make the changes described. A rootkit would be used to retain access, spyware gathers a variety of data but is not specifically aimed at capturing keystrokes like this, and logic bombs have specific events or triggers that cause them to take action.

questions.q: Amanda notices traffic between her systems and a known malicious host on TCP port 6667. What type of traffic is she most likely detecting?
opts: Command and control
Spyware
A worm
A hijacked web browser
questions.exp: Amanda has most likely discovered a botnet’s command and control channel, and the system or systems she is monitoring are probably using IRC as the command and control channel. Spyware is likely to simply send data to a central server via HTTP/HTTPS, worms spread by attacking vulnerable services, and a hijacked web browser would probably operate on common HTTP or HTTPS ports (80/443).

questions.q: Mike discovers that attackers have left software that allows them to have remote access to systems on a computer in his company’s network. How should he describe or classify this malware?
opts: A worm
Crypto malware
A trojan
A backdoor
questions.exp: Remote access to a system is typically provided by a backdoor. Backdoors may also appear in firmware or even in hardware. None of the other items listed provide remote access by default, although they may have a backdoor as part of a more capable malware package.

questions.q: What is the primary impact of bloatware?
opts: Consuming resources
Logging keystrokes
Providing information about users and devices to third parties
Allowing unauthorized remote access
questions.exp: Bloatware is typically not a significant security threat, but it consumes resources like disk space, CPU, and memory. Unfortunately, some bloatware can be vulnerable and may not get regularly patched, meaning it’s both useless and a potential risk!

questions.q: What type of malware is used to gather information about a user’s browsing habits and system?
opts: A Trojan
Bloatware
Spyware
A rootkit
questions.exp: Spyware is specifically designed to gather information about users and systems and to send that data back to a central collector. Trojans pretend to be useful software and include malicious components, bloatware is preinstalled software that isn’t needed, and rootkits are used to conceal malicious software and retain a foothold on compromised systems.

questions.q: Nancy is concerned that there is a software keylogger on the system she’s investigating. What best describes data that may have been stolen?
opts: All files on the system
All keyboard input
All files the user accessed while the keylogger was active
Keyboard and other input from the user
questions.exp: While keyloggers often focus on keyboard input, other types of input may also be captured, meaning Nancy should worry about any user input that occurred while the keylogger was installed. Keyloggers typically do not target files on systems, although if Nancy finds a keylogger, she may want to check for other malware packages with additional capabilities.

questions.q: Sharif notices that his authentication logs have many different usernames showing failed logins with the same password. What type of attack has he discovered?
opts: Credential harvesting
Impersonation
BEC
Spraying
questions.exp: Sharif has discovered a spraying attack that uses the same password—often a default or common password—with many usernames. Credential harvesting is the process of gathering credentials like usernames and passwords. Impersonation is a social engineering technique used when an attacker pretends to be someone else. BEC, or business email compromise, involves attackers posing as a trusted individual and asking for actions to be performed.

questions.q: While reviewing her logs, Michele notices that a remote system has attempted to log into her server via SSH using the username admin and a variety of passwords like “password” and “ninja.” What type of attack has Michele noticed?
opts: A brute‐force attack
Shoulder surfing
An on‐path attack
Pretexting
questions.exp: Michele has discovered a brute‐force attack, which relies on trying a large number of passwords, often combined with a list of usernames to try. Shoulder surfing attacks involve an attacker watching as a user enters information like a password or credit card data. On‐path attacks intercept data sent via a network, and pretexting is a social engineering attack that relies on a believable reason for attackers to need a victim to take action.

questions.q: Joanna wants to detect password spraying attacks. What type of rule should she deploy through her security systems?
opts: Match attempts to log into many systems with the same username and password.
Match multiple attempts to log into the same user account using different passwords.
Match repeated use of the same password during failed login attempts for multiple usernames.
Match all attempts to use passwords with slight changes for the same account.
questions.exp: Password spraying involves the use of the same password to attempt to log into multiple accounts. Joanna should search for uses of the same password for different accounts.

questions.q: Alaina wants to determine if a password spraying attack was used against her organization. Which of the following indicators would be most useful as part of her investigation?
opts: The time the login attempts happened
The passwords used for failed attempts
The source IP address of the attempts
The number of failed attempts for each user
questions.exp: Password spraying attempts try to use a single common password for many user accounts. Determining if a single password is being used over and over can help catch basic password spraying attempts. The time, source IP, or number of failed attempts do not indicate password spraying.

questions.q: Kyle is conducting a penetration test. After gaining access to an organization’s database server, he installs a backdoor on the server to grant himself access in the future. What term best describes this action?
opts: Privilege escalation
Lateral movement
Maneuver
Persistence
questions.exp: Backdoors are a persistence tool, designed to make sure that the attacker’s access persists after the original vulnerability is remediated. Kyle can use this backdoor to gain access to the system in the future, even if the original exploit that he used to gain access is no longer effective.

questions.q: Frank is investigating a security incident where the attacker entered a very long string into an input field, which was followed by a system command. What type of attack likely took place?
opts: Cross‐site request forgery
Server‐side request forgery
Command injection
Buffer overflow
questions.exp: Buffer overflow attacks occur when an attacker manipulates a program into placing more data into an area of memory than is allocated for that program’s use. The goal is to overwrite other information in memory with instructions that may be executed by a different process running on the system.

questions.q: What type of attack places an attacker in the position to eavesdrop on communications between a user and a web server?
opts: On‐path attack
Session hijacking
Buffer overflow
Meet‐in‐the‐middle
questions.exp: In an on‐path attack, the attacker fools the user into thinking that the attacker is actually the target website and presenting a fake authentication form. They may then authenticate to the website on the user’s behalf and obtain the cookie. This is slightly different from a session hijacking attack, where the attacker steals the cookie associated with an active session.

questions.q: Chris is reviewing evidence of a cross‐site scripting attack where the attacker embedded JavaScript in a URL that a user clicked. The web page then sent the JavaScript to the user in the displayed page. What term best describes this attack?
opts: Reflected XSS
Stored XSS
Persistent XSS
DOM‐based XSS
questions.exp: This is an example of a reflected attack because the script code is contained within the URL. A persistent or stored attack places the content on a web page or other location where a victim may later access it. DOM‐based XSS attacks hide the attack code within the Document Object Model.

questions.q:
Joe checks his web server logs and sees that someone sent the following query string to an application running on the server:

http://www.mycompany.com/servicestatus.php?serviceID=892&serviceID=892'%20;DROP%20TABLE%20Services;--

What type of attack was most likely attempted?
opts: Cross‐site scripting
Session hijacking
Parameter pollution
On‐path
questions.exp: This query string is indicative of a parameter pollution attack. In this case, it appears that the attacker was waging a SQL injection attack and tried to use parameter pollution to slip the attack past content filtering technology. The two instances of the serviceID parameter in the query string indicate a parameter pollution attempt.

questions.q:
Joe’s adventures in web server log analysis are not yet complete. As he continues to review the logs, he finds the request:

http://www.mycompany.com/../../../etc/passwd

What type of attack was most likely attempted?
opts: SQL injection
Session hijacking
Directory traversal
File upload
questions.exp: In this case, the .. operators are the telltale giveaway that the attacker was attempting to conduct a directory traversal attack. This particular attack sought to break out of the web server’s root directory and access the /etc/passwd file on the server.

questions.q: Wendy is a penetration tester who wishes to engage in a session hijacking attack. What information is crucial for Wendy to obtain if her attack will be successful?
opts: Session ticket
Session cookie
Username
User password
questions.exp: Websites use HTTP cookies to maintain sessions over time. If Wendy is able to obtain a copy of the user’s session cookie, she can use that cookie to impersonate the user’s browser and hijack the authenticated session.

questions.q: Joe is examining the logs for his web server and discovers that a user sent input to a web application that contained the string WAITFOR. What type of attack was the user likely attempting?
opts: Timing‐based SQL injection
HTML injection
Cross‐site scripting
Content‐based SQL injection
questions.exp: The use of the SQL WAITFOR command is a signature characteristic of a timing‐based SQL injection attack.

questions.q: What type of cryptographic attack attempts to force a user to reduce the level of encryption that they use to communicate with a remote server?
opts: Birthday
Frequency
Downgrade
Collision
questions.exp: A downgrade attack is sometimes used against secure communications such as TLS in an attempt to get the user or system to inadvertently shift to less secure cryptographic modes. The idea is to trick the user into shifting to a less secure version of the protocol, one that might be easier to break.

questions.q: Shahla recently discovered an attack where the attacker managed to force a network user to use weak encryption and was then able to decrypt that content. What term best describes this attack?
opts: Downgrade
Collision
Homomorphic encryption
Birthday attack
questions.exp: Downgrade attacks try to remove or lower the strength of encryption to allow the decryption of sensitive information. Birthday attacks find collisions where two different inputs produce the same hash value output, but there is no discussion of that in this scenario. Homomorphic encryption is not an attack but a technology that protects privacy by encrypting data in a way that preserves the ability to perform computation on that data.

questions.q: Gabby wants to detect physical brute‐force attempts against her organization. What solution is best suited to this?
opts: Security guards
Locks
Access badges
An intrusion detection system (IDS)
questions.exp: Security guards who can monitor for and understand the signs of a physical brute‐force attempt are the most useful control listed. Locks may show signs of attempts but require careful inspection, access badges would require log review and additional information to detect brute‐force attacks, and an IDS is useful for network attacks.

questions.q: Wayne is concerned that an on‐path attack has been used against computers he is responsible for. What artifact is he most likely to find associated with this attack?
opts: A compromised router
A browser plug‐in
A compromised server
A modified hosts file
questions.exp: Browser on‐path attacks take advantage of malicious browser plug‐ins or proxies to modify traffic at the browser level. They do not involve compromised routers or servers, and a modified hosts file is more likely to be involved in an on‐path attack.
questions.framing_note: On-path attacks (formerly MITM) come in two flavours: network-level (rogue AP, ARP poisoning, compromised router) and browser-level / Man-in-the-Browser (malicious plug-ins or proxies modifying traffic at the browser). A common Security+ instinct goes straight to network-level and picks the compromised router. Sybex tests the browser-level variant here — a malicious browser plug-in IS an on-path attack, just at a different layer. The exam treats both as on-path; let the question's other details (Wayne's "computers he is responsible for", not "his network") tell you which variant is being tested.

questions.q: Mark wants to prevent DNS poisoning attacks. What technology should he implement to counter them most effectively?
opts: DNSSEC
SDNS
SASE
SD‐WAN
questions.exp: DNSSEC validates both the origin of DNS information and ensures that DNS responses have not been modified, making it the best option to help prevent DNS poisoning attacks. SDNS was made up for this question. SASE is used to secure networks in complex multilocation environments, and SD‐WAN allows for dynamic wide area networks defined by software, but neither provides this type of DNS security.

questions.q: Octavia discovers that the contact list from her phone has been acquired via a wireless attack. Which of the following is the most likely culprit?
opts: Bluejacking
An evil maid
Bluesnarfing
An evil twin
questions.exp: Bluesnarfing is the theft of information from a Bluetooth enabled device. If Octavia left Bluetooth on and had not properly secured her device, then an attacker may have been able to access her contact list and download its contents. A bluejacking attack occurs when unwanted messages are sent to a device via Bluetooth. Evil twins are malicious access points configured to appear to be legitimate access points, and an evil maid attack is an in‐person attack where an attacker takes advantage of physical access to hardware to acquire information or to insert malicious software on a device.

questions.q: Kristen discovers missing logs as part of her threat hunting activities. What has most likely happened?
opts: The logs hit the end of their life cycle and were rotated.
The system is a newly deployed system.
An attacker wiped the logs to hide evidence.
An attacker encrypted the logs as part of their process.
questions.exp: Missing logs are often associated with an attacker attempting to hide evidence of their actions. Log rotation will typically remove the oldest log items and replace them with new log items rather than wiping a log, or will archive the old log file and create a new one. A newly deployed system typically has at least some logs from booting and running. Encrypting logs would leave a file in place even if it couldn’t be read.

questions.q: Dana is reviewing her system’s application logs and notices that a full backup of the application was done at 10 a.m. She knows that the job that runs the backup process is set to run overnight. What indicator should she flag this as?
opts: Unexpected logs
Resource consumption
Resource inaccessibility
Out‐of‐cycle logging
questions.exp: This is an example of out‐of‐cycle logging, or logging that occurs at a different time than expected. This may be because an attacker is using the backup tool to acquire data. Unexpected logs are not an indicator found on the Security+ exam outline. There is no indication of resource consumption or inaccessibility in the question.

questions.q: One of Murali’s staff members has malware on their PC. They claim that they downloaded only a spreadsheet tool, and not malware. What type of malware have they encountered if the malware was designed to look legitimate but was actually malicious?
opts: A worm
A virus
A Trojan
A rootkit
questions.exp: Trojans, or Trojan horses, are malware designed to appear legitimate but that are actually malicious. Viruses require human interaction to spread, whereas worms propagate on their own via networks, often targeting vulnerable services. Rootkits help attackers obtain and maintain persistent access to systems.

questions.q: Olivia wants to protect against DNS cache poisoning, and she knows that digitally signing DNS replies from protected zones would be helpful as part of that effort. What can she configure to implement this capability?
opts: SDNS
DNS over IKE
DNSSEC
DNS over TLS
questions.exp: DNSSEC uses digital signatures to validate information provided by a DNS server, helping to prevent issues such as DNS poisoning. None of the other answers are real DNS security solutions; although you could protect DNS queries with TLS, doing so wouldn’t validate the actual DNS information like DNSSEC does.

questions.q: In the following image, a connection between two systems has been redirected by an attacker. The attacker has spoofed ARP packets to make it so that responses to the legitimate server are instead sent to a system that the attacker controls. When traffic is sent to that system, the attacker reads and potentially modifies the traffic before passing it along the server, then sends back responses from the server after reviewing or modifying them as well. What type of attack is this?
opts: An ARPjacking
A disassociation attack
An on‐path attack
A TCP redirect attack
questions.exp: This is one form of an on‐path attack, an attack that redirects traffic to a system or device controlled by the attacker, which can then take action on network traffic originally destined for another system. ARPjacking and TCP redirect attacks are made up. Disassociation attacks focus on causing Wi‐Fi devices to drop their connection and try to reconnect to an access point.

questions.q: Which of the following components is required for an SSL/TLS stripping attack?
opts: An on‐path system
A TLS accelerator card
An SSL accelerator card
An SSL/TLS removal script
questions.exp: SSL stripping (or TLS stripping) relies on making the end user believe that they have a secure connection but instead proxies that connection via an on‐path system that intercepts requests, terminates the SSL or TLS connection, and then passes those requests on to the legitimate server after either capturing or modifying the traffic.

questions.q: Gabby wants to protect against credential theft and knows that there are detection settings that can help prevent the abuse of stolen credentials. What detection and prevention setting relies on geolocation to protect against malicious use of stolen credentials?
opts: Impossible travel time
Privilege escalation
Time‐of‐check (TOC)/time‐of‐use (TOU)
Time‐based login
questions.exp: Risky login detection schemes look at impossible travel times between geographic locations using GeoIP capabilities. This means that they can detect that a user cannot reasonably have logged in from a site in one location and then traveled to a second location and logged in there. Although VPN usage can cause issues with this, in general this is a useful setting to avoid the use of stolen or shared credentials. Privilege escalation attacks attempt to use the rights of more privileged accounts, such as an administrator account. Time‐of‐check (TOC)/time‐of‐use (TOU) exploits are race conditions. Login time restriction is a setting used to prohibit users from logging in outside of specific hours but does not use geographic location.

questions.q: Ben wants to conduct an offline brute‐force attack against a Linux system. What file should he work to obtain a copy of?
opts: John the Ripper
The /etc/passwd file
The /etc/shadow file
He does not need a file; he can use SSH.
questions.exp: The /etc/shadow file contains password hashes for most modern Linux implementations, and Ben can then use a tool such as rainbow tables or John the Ripper to crack passwords. John itself is not a password file or repository, and /etc/passwd is a secure pointer to /etc/shadow and does not actually contain useful information. Finally, an offline password attack implies activity that does not take place over the network, so SSH is not a valid answer.

questions.q: Daniel wants to make users in his organization visit a different site than they intend to. To accomplish this, he falsifies DNS information in the local DNS server’s cache, causing systems that use that DNS server to get incorrect information. What term describes this attack?
opts: ARP spoofing
DNS phishing
DNS poisoning
Name overload
questions.exp: DNS poisoning attacks focus on falsifying DNS information that is then provided as the correct response to systems that rely on the poisoned DNS server. Since this information may be spread to other DNS servers that rely on the poisoned server, it can have a broad impact depending on the server that is poisoned. ARP spoofing involves responding to ARP requests with incorrect information, in essence claiming to be a different system based on the hardware address of the spoofed system or device. DNS phishing and name overload are not common technical or security terms.

questions.q: What type of Trojan is specifically designed to provide administrative control of the systems it is installed on?
opts: A BRT
A RAT
A root horse
A full Trojan
questions.exp: Remote access Trojans (RATs) are Trojans that are specifically designed to provide remote administrative access. The rest of the answers here are made up.

questions.q: Phil is conducting a penetration test and has gained access to a target system. The account he has on that system is a standard user account, and Phil is installing a tool that will allow him to gain root access. What term best describes this activity?
opts: Privilege escalation
Lateral movement
Pivoting
Persistence
questions.exp: Privilege escalation is the act of increasing the level of access that an attacker has to a system. It is a common exploit to launch after gaining initial access to a system in an attempt to gain administrative access (otherwise known as root or superuser access).

questions.q: Which one of the following environments is least susceptible to an injection attack?
opts: LDAP
SQL
CASB
XML
questions.exp: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), Structured Query Language (SQL), and the Extensible Markup Language (XML) all are command‐driven languages that are susceptible to injection attacks. Cloud access security brokers (CASBs) are security platforms that do not typically have injection vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Sherry is concerned that a web application in her organization supports unvalidated redirects. Which one of the following approaches would minimize the risk of this attack?
opts: Implementing multifactor authentication
Restricting redirects to her domain
Encrypting session cookies
Requiring HTTPS
questions.exp: Unvalidated redirects instruct a web application to direct users to an arbitrary site at the conclusion of their transaction. This approach is quite dangerous because it allows an attacker to send users to a malicious site through a legitimate site that they trust. Sherry should restrict redirects so that they only occur within her trusted domain(s).

questions.q: Lori has discovered that a system she is responsible for is sending traffic to an alternate gateway rather than to her organization’s normal gateway. What type of attack is Lori most likely investigating?
opts: A Trojan
An on‐path attack
A replay attack
An amplified DDoS
questions.exp: Lori has likely encountered an on‐path attack that redirects traffic through a system controlled by the attacker. The alternate gateway will be the default route for traffic sent by the system, allowing the attacker to see and potentially manipulate the network traffic. A Trojan is designed to look like a legitimate application or program. A replay attack captures and re‐sends valid authentication data, and an amplified DDoS increases traffic sent to a target using flaws and features of various software that result in more traffic being sent than was received.

questions.q: Todd’s upstream Internet provider informs him that their IPS has detected an attacker who appears to have spoofed his organization’s server IP address to send DNS queries with large responses via UDP to his organization. What type of attack has Todd’s ISP observed?
opts: A reflected DDoS
An amplified, reflected DDoS
An amplified DDoS
A DNS on‐path DDoS
questions.exp: This DDoS is both amplified by the larger responses and reflected because it is spoofed and sent back to the apparent sender. An on‐path attack inserts a system controlled by the attacker into a network path, allowing the attacker to observe and potentially modify traffic.

questions.q: Brian’s security management tool flags multiple usernames for his organization all attempting to log in across systems. When he investigates, he notes that the failed attempts all use the same password. What type of attack has Brian discovered?
opts: A birthday attack
A credential overflow attack
An injection attack
A password spraying attack
questions.exp: Brian has discovered a password spraying attack. Password spraying attacks use the same password across multiple usernames to attempt to log in. Birthday attacks attack encryption, credential overflow attacks were made up for this question, and injection attacks are used against SQL databases.

questions.q: Helen is reviewing network traffic in Wireshark and sees the traffic shown here. What should she identify as a likely network event?
opts: A system dropping its network connection
A denial‐of‐service (DoS) attack
A brute‐force attack
A dictionary attack
questions.exp: This traffic pattern is most likely to indicate a DoS attack involving a SYN flood. This is not a distributed DoS attack because there is only one system sending the SYN packets, so Helen might choose to investigate the system or block it.

questions.q: Ron receives a notification that computers throughout his organization have begun to display a message demanding that money be paid in Bitcoin to allow restoration of access to important business documents and other files. What type of malware often uses this type of behavior?
opts: Worms
Viruses
Ransomware
Spyware
questions.exp: Ransomware demands a ransom paid in Bitcoin to unlock files. Although paying does often result in the files being restored, this can be a dangerous option and does not guarantee results. Secure, independent backups are the best insurance against cryptographic malware taking your business out of operation. Worms spread themselves, but the actions they take vary from worm to worm, as do the actions taken by viruses. Spyware gathers information about user browsing habits but does not demand a ransom.

questions.q: Eve is investigating a security incident where the user of a web application submitted an internal URL to the application and tricked the web server into retrieving sensitive data from that URL and displaying it as output. What term best describes this attack?
opts: SSRF
CSRF
XSS
Command injection
questions.exp: Server‐side request forgery (SSRF) attacks trick a server into visiting a URL based on user‐supplied input. SSRF attacks are possible when a web application accepts URLs from a user as input and then retrieves information from that URL. If the server has access to non‐public URLs, an SSRF attack can unintentionally disclose that information to an attacker. CSRF (cross‐site request forgery) leverages malicious code to cause users to take action via a website they’re already authenticated to. XSS (cross‐site scripting) injects malicious scripts into preexisting websites by getting them to display the scripts, and command injection attacks attempt to run commands on an operating system by leveraging a vulnerable application.

questions.q: Samantha has discovered that an attacker was able to log in to systems using a user’s password. The user did not remember a phishing attack or other event when their password might have been exposed but did note that they checked their email using a computer in a hotel lobby while traveling. What type of malware would Samantha expect to find if she was able to examine that system?
opts: A rootkit
A keylogger
A logic bomb
Bloatware
questions.exp: A keylogger can capture keystrokes and send them to an attacker. The scenario described most likely reflects a keylogger on the hotel lobby computer. A rootkit is used to retain access to a compromised system and to hide the attacker’s actions. Logic bombs wait to execute until conditions are met like a time and date or other event, and bloatware is simply unwanted software often installed on new machines by manufacturers.

questions.q: What type of attack depends on the fact that users are often logged in to many websites simultaneously in the same browser?
opts: Server‐side request forgery
Cross‐site scripting
Cross‐site request forgery (XSRF)
File inclusion
questions.exp: XSRF attacks work by making the reasonable assumption that users are often logged into many different websites at the same time. Attackers then embed code in one website that sends a command to a second website. XSS (cross‐site scripting) injects malicious scripts into preexisting websites by getting them to display the scripts. XSRF (cross‐site request forgery) leverages malicious code to cause users to take action via a website they’re already authenticated to. File inclusion attacks try to take advantage of upload functions that are not properly secured and which can allow programs to be executed or files to be displayed to users.

questions.q: Renee is responding to a cybersecurity incident at her organization in which the attackers used a botnet to disrupt access to the organization’s website, preventing legitimate customers from placing orders. What type of attack took place?
opts: Destruction
Alteration
Denial
Integrity
questions.exp: This is an example of a distributed denial‐of‐service (DDoS) attack that disrupted the availability of the website for legitimate users.

cram.def: Dividing network into isolated segments. Limits lateral movement if one segment is compromised.
Virtual LAN — logical segmentation at Layer 2. Isolates traffic without separate physical hardware.
Isolated network segment for public-facing servers. Between internet and internal network.
Complete physical isolation — no network connection. Used for most sensitive systems.
Only approved applications can run. Default-deny. Strongest application control.
Granular segmentation — each workload isolated. Core Zero Trust architecture component.

matching.prompt: Isolated network for public-facing servers
Logical isolation at Layer 2
Complete physical network isolation
Only approved apps can run
Per-workload isolation in Zero Trust

questions.q: Which BEST captures the primary SECURITY benefit (not operational benefit) of network segmentation?
opts: Limiting lateral movement — if one segment is compromised the attacker must cross additional controls to reach other segments, slowing spread and aiding detection
Encrypting traffic between hosts in different segments via the segment boundary devices, providing built-in confidentiality without needing TLS or IPsec
Blocking all external attacks at the network perimeter by ensuring inbound traffic from the internet cannot reach any internal segment under any condition
Replacing the need for endpoint authentication because segment placement alone determines what each host can access in the environment
questions.exp: The primary SECURITY benefit of network segmentation is limiting blast radius. When the network is divided into segments with controls between them (firewalls, ACLs, microsegmentation policies), an attacker who compromises one segment cannot freely reach others — they must cross another control, and that crossing is detectable and may fail. The encryption distractor confuses segmentation with TLS/IPsec (segmentation does not encrypt). The perimeter distractor confuses segmentation with edge defense (segmentation works on internal traffic too). The authentication distractor confuses placement with identity (placement is one input to access control, not a replacement). Operational benefits (speed, cost, management) are real but secondary.

questions.q: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is used to:
opts: Host public-facing servers in an isolated segment between the internet and internal network
Encrypt all internal east-west traffic between segmented production and management subnets
Store offline disaster-recovery backups in an isolated VLAN protected from production access
Monitor all internal network traffic from a passive sensor mirroring switchport SPAN data
questions.exp: A DMZ exposes public services (web, email) to the internet while protecting the internal network if those services are compromised.

questions.q: An air gap provides the STRONGEST isolation primarily because:
opts: VLAN segmentation combined with strict access control lists provides equivalent isolation by separating broadcast domains at Layer 2 with policy enforcement
A DMZ with a WAF in front provides functionally equivalent isolation by inspecting all inbound traffic at the application layer before it reaches the protected system
The system has absolutely no network connection — there is no path for a remote attacker to reach it over a network at all, removing the entire remote-attack surface
A host-based firewall combined with EDR provides equivalent isolation by blocking unauthorized connections and detecting malicious behavior at the endpoint
questions.exp: The defining property of an air gap is the complete absence of network connection — no Ethernet, no WiFi, no Bluetooth, no USB-bridged data path. That makes remote attacks impossible (the only attack paths are physical: introduced media, supply chain, or insider). DMZ + WAF, VLAN + ACL, and host-firewall + EDR all reduce attack surface but still maintain a network path to the system; with sufficient skill, a determined attacker can find a path through any of them. Air gap is a categorically different control class — it removes the path entirely rather than guarding it.

questions.q: Which BEST explains why an application allow list provides stronger protection than a block list?
opts: Allow lists prevent privileged-user override since administrators cannot bypass the policy to run unapproved binaries, while block lists permit administrators to whitelist exceptions on demand
Allow lists use cryptographic signature verification of every binary while block lists rely on file hashes and content patterns — signatures are cryptographically stronger overall
Allow lists ship with built-in machine-learning detection of anomalous binary behavior while block lists rely only on static signature rules without behavioral analysis

Allow lists implement default-deny — only explicitly approved applications run, so novel and unknown malware is blocked. Block lists implement default-allow — only known-bad is blocked, so any uncataloged malware runs freely
questions.exp: The structural difference is the default policy. Allow list = default-deny: by default nothing runs, only listed applications are permitted. Result: novel malware is blocked by default because it is not on the list. Block list = default-allow: by default everything runs except listed bad items. Result: novel malware runs freely until added to the block list. This is why allow lists are stronger but harder to operate — every legitimate application change requires updating the list. Cryptographic mechanisms (B) are independent of allow vs block; ML detection (C) is independent; admin override (D) is also not the structural difference — most enterprise allow-list implementations (Windows Defender Application Control, Apple Endpoint Security, etc.) DO support administrator overrides for legitimate purposes, and block lists likewise support exceptions.

scenarios.q: A manufacturing company's flat network has all 500 workstations, 20 servers, 15 production line controllers, and corporate WiFi on the same subnet with no internal firewall controls. Ransomware on one workstation encrypts 340 workstations, all 20 servers, and 11 production controllers before being contained. What architectural change would have MOST limited the ransomware's lateral movement?
opts: Implementing network segmentation with VLANs and internal firewall rules isolating workstations, servers, production controllers, and WiFi into separate zones
Deploying antivirus on all workstations
Enabling host-based firewalls on all workstations
Deploying an IDS to detect the ransomware spreading
scenarios.exp: Network segmentation is the core answer. In a flat network, ransomware can reach everything. Segmentation with zone-based firewall rules means workstations can't reach production controllers directly. The blast radius is contained to the segment where infection occurs. The production controller infection was the most serious — OT network segmentation is critical.

scenarios.q: An organization deploys application allow-listing permitting only signed binaries from approved vendors. A red team bypasses this by using mshta.exe (a legitimate, signed Microsoft binary) to execute a malicious HTA file hosted on a remote server. The allow-list is not triggered. What technique bypassed the control, and what additional detection would catch it?
opts: The red team exploited a buffer overflow in the allow-listing software's parser engine
The red team used an unsigned binary that happened to match a known-good file hash collision
Living-off-the-land (LOLBins) — detect via behavioral analytics on signed-but-unusual process invocations
The allow-list was misconfigured to allow all Microsoft-signed binaries, not just the approved subset
scenarios.exp: Mshta.exe is a whitelisted signed binary. The allow-list permits it, but the malicious behavior is what it's doing. Detection: EDR with behavioral rules flagging mshta.exe making external network connections. LOLBins bypass allow-listing by definition — the binary IS allowed. The control works at process creation; it can't control what the allowed process does. Behavioral monitoring catches this: mshta.exe calling out to the internet is anomalous. EDR rules on LOLBin behavior are a necessary complement to allow-listing.

cram.def: Applying vendor-released fixes for known vulnerabilities. Most important ongoing security activity.
Users and processes get only minimum access needed. Limits damage from compromise.
Quarantining compromised or suspicious systems to prevent spread.
Properly retiring and securely wiping end-of-life systems to prevent data exposure.
Automated tools ensure systems maintain secure baseline configurations. Prevents configuration drift.

matching.prompt: Most important ongoing security activity
Users get only minimum necessary access
Quarantining a compromised system
Securely retiring end-of-life systems
Automated enforcement of secure configurations

questions.q: Which mitigation technique MOST directly reduces the risk from known vulnerabilities?
opts: Encryption
Patching
Network segmentation
MFA
questions.exp: Applying vendor-released security fixes. Patching removes the vulnerability — other controls reduce impact but don't fix the underlying flaw.

questions.q: Least privilege as a mitigation technique means:
opts: Granting users and processes only the minimum access necessary to perform their functions — nothing more
Removing all user accounts except administrators — reducing the number of credential-bearing identities
Requiring MFA for every operation — strengthening the trust placed on existing user permissions
Encrypting all user data at rest with role-based key wrapping for confidentiality
questions.exp: Least privilege limits the blast radius of a compromise — an attacker who compromises a limited account has limited access.

questions.q: Which BEST captures why an IR team isolates a compromised system rather than immediately wiping or restoring it?
opts: Preserve the compromised system in its current state strictly for later forensic analysis, with no other operational goal beyond evidence collection
Prevent the spread of malware or attacker access to other systems while preserving the compromised system intact for forensic investigation and root-cause analysis
Immediately remove the malware and attacker tooling from the system so it can be safely returned to production within hours of the initial detection
Trigger an automatic snapshot of the system's memory and disk for offline analysis while the attacker continues to operate normally on the system
questions.exp: Isolation has TWO primary purposes that distinguish it from other IR steps: (1) STOP the spread — the compromised host can no longer reach other systems on the network, blocking lateral movement and exfiltration; (2) PRESERVE the system intact — for forensic investigation, evidence collection, and root-cause analysis. Wiping or restoring (C, D) destroys the evidence needed to understand HOW the compromise happened and WHAT the attacker accessed. Forensics-only framing (B) misses the spread-prevention purpose. The standard NIST IR sequence is contain then eradicate then recover; isolation is containment, not eradication or recovery.

scenarios.q: A security team patches a critical RCE vulnerability in their web application framework within 4 hours of vendor announcement. One week later, they discover their systems were compromised — the attacker exploited the same vulnerability 6 hours before the patch was released. The patch was deployed in time but the system was already compromised. What does this demonstrate?
opts: Patching is ineffective and shouldn't be prioritized

Patching is the most important control for known vulnerabilities, but it cannot protect against exploitation that occurred before the patch existed. Defense-in-depth controls already in place — network segmentation, least privilege, behavioral monitoring — limit damage from zero-day exploitation
The team should have patched faster — 4 hours is too slow
The vendor should have released the patch before the vulnerability was public
scenarios.exp: Patching is essential but not sufficient. Zero-day attacks occur before patches are available. Existing controls — network segmentation, least privilege, behavioral monitoring — determine how much damage a successful pre-patch exploit causes. Patch fast AND maintain layered defenses.

scenarios.q: An analyst receives an alert that a workstation is attempting to connect to 47 different internal IP addresses on port 445 (SMB) within 5 minutes. The workstation belongs to an accountant with no IT duties. The analyst isolates the workstation. What is the NEXT step?
opts: The analyst applied least privilege by revoking the accountant's network permissions, since lateral movement typically requires a compromised account to keep moving sideways through the corporate network

The analyst applied isolation as a containment technique. Next step: preserve forensic evidence (memory dump before shutdown, network connection state) and begin investigation — what executed, was the user socially engineered, are the 47 IPs scanned already compromised?
The analyst applied network segmentation by moving the workstation to a guest VLAN, which adequately limits any further blast radius from the compromise across the broader corporate network
The analyst applied zero trust by requiring re-authentication on the workstation, ensuring any future SMB connections come from a freshly-verified user identity rather than a stale session token
scenarios.exp: Isolation stops the spread (the SMB scanning is consistent with worm behavior or ransomware propagation). But isolation before forensics destroys evidence — the memory dump captures running malware and encryption keys that disappear on shutdown. Then investigate: the 47 IPs scanned may already be compromised.

cram.def: Process of securing a system by reducing its attack surface — removing unnecessary features, services, and access.
First hardening step on any new device — default passwords are publicly known.
UEFI feature verifying boot software is signed and trusted — prevents bootkit attacks.

Advanced endpoint security — detects malicious behavior, provides visibility and response capability.
Systematic process for applying patches promptly and consistently across the environment.
