Advanced endpoint detection and response
Removing unused applications

questions.q: System hardening is BEST described as:
opts: Installing the latest endpoint malware protection on every system before deployment
Reducing a system's attack surface by removing unnecessary features, services, accounts, and access
Encrypting all system data at rest with full-disk encryption tied to a TPM key
Monitoring system logs for anomalies and forwarding suspicious events to the SIEM
questions.exp: Hardening systematically removes anything not needed for the system's intended function — reducing the ways an attacker can exploit it.

questions.q: The FIRST step when hardening a newly deployed network device should be:
opts: Enable all available features
Install the latest firmware
Change all default credentials
Configure network segmentation
questions.exp: Default credentials are publicly known — changing them immediately is the most critical first step in device hardening.

questions.q: Secure Boot mitigates which type of attack?
opts: Application-layer SQL injection attacks targeting database parameter handling at runtime
Password spraying attacks that test one common password against many user accounts
Bootkit/rootkit attacks that modify the boot process before the OS loads
Volumetric DDoS attacks that saturate the network edge with reflected UDP traffic
questions.exp: Secure Boot verifies the cryptographic signature of bootloader and OS — preventing unsigned malicious code from running at boot.

questions.q: Which BEST distinguishes EDR from traditional signature-based antivirus?
opts: EDR only detects known malware signatures and is therefore equivalent to traditional AV with a different name
EDR replaces the need for a SIEM because it correlates logs from network and identity sources directly without any separate platform
EDR provides behavioral detection, continuous endpoint telemetry, and active response (isolation, kill, rollback) — not just file-signature matching
EDR is delivered exclusively as a cloud-only managed service while traditional antivirus runs only on-premises endpoints
questions.exp: Traditional signature-based antivirus matches files against a known-malware-hash database — fast on known threats but misses novel and polymorphic malware. EDR adds behavioral detection (process trees, parent-child anomalies, lateral movement signals), continuous endpoint telemetry streamed to a central plane for hunting and post-hoc investigation, and active response capabilities (isolate the host from network, kill processes, roll back changes). Distractor A is what a student picks if they think EDR is just rebranded AV. EDR does not replace SIEM (they are complementary), and EDR is not cloud-only.

scenarios.q: A new Linux web server is deployed running as root, with all Apache modules enabled, PHP display_errors=On, SSH with password authentication enabled, and the default Apache welcome page visible. A security engineer is asked to harden it before production. What are the HIGHEST PRIORITY hardening actions?
opts: Run the web server process as a non-root dedicated user (privilege containment), disable unused Apache modules (attack surface reduction), disable display_errors in PHP (information disclosure), and disable password SSH authentication in favor of key-based auth
Install antivirus and enable the host firewall
Change the hostname and SSH port to obscure the server's identity
Enable SELinux and configure all policies from scratch
scenarios.exp: Hardening priority: run as non-root (if exploited, attacker gets web server privileges, not root), disable unused modules (each module is an attack surface), display_errors reveals code paths to attackers, password SSH is vulnerable to brute force. These are quick wins with highest impact.

scenarios.q: An organization implements Secure Boot on all new laptops. Six months later, a red team boots a laptop from a USB drive containing a customized OS that bypasses all endpoint controls. Investigation reveals Secure Boot is enabled but the UEFI settings have no password and allow USB to boot first. What failed?
opts: Secure Boot doesn't protect against USB boot attacks at all — the entire premise of Secure Boot is unrelated to boot media
The UEFI firmware has an undisclosed vulnerability that bypasses Secure Boot — vendor patches will be needed across the fleet
Secure Boot was configured correctly but surrounding hardening was incomplete — without a UEFI password and boot-order lock, an attacker can disable Secure Boot or boot USB first
The USB drive had a Microsoft-signed bootloader that Secure Boot accepted, allowing the customized OS to load successfully
scenarios.exp: Layered hardening: an attacker with physical access and no UEFI password can disable Secure Boot or change boot order in 30 seconds. The complete hardening: Secure Boot (verified boot chain) + UEFI password (prevents configuration changes) + boot order locked (prevents USB boot) + full disk encryption (protects data even if they succeed).

questions.q: Brenda’s company provides a managed incident response service to its customers. What term best describes this type of service offering?
opts: MSP
PaaS
SaaS
MSSP
questions.exp: Brenda’s company is offering a technology service to customers on a managed basis, making it a managed service provider (MSP). However, this service is a security service, so the term managed security service provider (MSSP) is a better description of the situation.

questions.q: Helen’s organization is planning to deploy IoT devices across their buildings as part of a HVAC system. Helen knows that the vendor for the IoT devices does not provide regular security updates to the device’s web interfaces that are used to manage the devices. What security control should she recommend to help protect the devices on the network?
opts: Install host‐based firewalls.
Deploy the IoT devices to a protected VLAN.
Install host‐based IPS.
Disable the web interfaces for the IoT devices.
questions.exp: Since the web interfaces are needed to manage the devices, Helen’s best option is to place the IoT devices in a protected VLAN. IoT devices will not typically allow additional software to be installed, meaning that adding firewalls or a HIPS won’t work.

questions.q: What is the primary reason to remove unnecessary software during hardening efforts?
opts: To reduce the attack footprint of the device
To reduce the number of patches that are installed
To reduce the number of firewall rules required for the device
To support incident response (IR) activities
questions.exp: Removing unnecessary software helps to reduce the attack surface of the devices. Not all software runs a service or opens a network port, but installed software provides additional opportunities for attackers to find vulnerabilities. That means that reducing firewall rules is not a primary purpose. While removing it may reduce the number of patches required by a device, that is not the primary driver. Finally, while incident response efforts may point to a need for further hardening to prevent future incidents, removing unnecessary software is not a typical step in support of IR activities.

questions.q: Fred has recently purchased a network router and is preparing to deploy it. Which of the following is a common step in deploying new routers?
opts: Disabling unwanted services
Removing unnecessary software
Installing antivirus
Changing default passwords
questions.exp: Network devices as well as many other devices like printers come with default passwords set. Fred should change the default password as part of the process of setting up his new router.

questions.q: Charlene wants to prevent attacks against her system that leverage flaws in the services that it provides while still keeping the services accessible. What hardening technique should she use?
opts: A host‐based firewall
A host‐based IPS
Encryption
An EDR
questions.exp: A host‐based intrusion prevention system (HIPS) can detect and prevent attacks against services while allowing the service to be accessible. A firewall can only block based on port, protocol, and IP; encryption won’t prevent this; and an EDR is primarily targeted at malicious software and activity, not at network‐based attacks on services.

questions.q: Selah wants to ensure that users in her organization can only install applications that are evaluated and approved by the organization’s security team. What should she use?
opts: A SIEM
An application deny list
An application allow list
sFlow
questions.exp: Application allow lists are used to ensure that only allowed applications are installable on systems. A deny list specifically identifies programs that aren’t allowed. A SIEM doesn’t provide application management capabilities, and sFlow is a flow tool like NetFlow.

questions.q: Mark unplugs the network connection from a system that is part of an incident and places tape over its Ethernet jack with a sign that says, “Do not reconnect without approval from IR team.” How is this method best described?
opts: Containment
Isolation
Segmentation
Zoning
questions.exp: Mark has isolated the system by removing it from the network and ensuring that it cannot communicate with other systems. Containment would limit the impact of the incident and might leave the system connected but with restricted or protected access. Segmentation moves systems or groups of systems into zones that have similar purposes, data classification, or other restrictions on them.

questions.q: Alyssa has identified malware on a system. She removes the system from the network to ensure that it cannot impact other systems. What technique has she used to deal with this system?
opts: Quarantine
Segmentation
Converted it to agentless
Deny listing
questions.exp: Alyssa’s has quarantined the machine, ensuring it cannot reach other systems or impact the rest of her organization. Segmentation would involve putting the system in protected network zone. Agentless tools are used to send data without a separate program or agent deployed to allow that. Deny lists are used to prevent specific programs or files from being used or deployed to systems.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements is not true about compensating controls under PCI DSS?
opts: Controls used to fulfill one PCI DSS requirement may be used to compensate for the absence of a control needed to meet another requirement.
Controls must meet the intent of the original requirement.
Controls must meet the rigor of the original requirement.
Compensating controls must provide a similar level of defense as the original requirement.
questions.exp: PCI DSS compensating controls must be “above and beyond” other PCI DSS requirements. This specifically bans the use of a control used to meet one requirement as a compensating control for another requirement.

questions.q: Terry wants to prevent her users from installing specific games on her organization’s computers. Which feature can she use to prevent known applications from being installed?
opts: Application deny list
HIDS
Application allow list
HIPS
questions.exp: An application deny list feature blocks specific applications or files from being run or installed on a computer. An application allow list allows for the installation and running of the specified applications or files that are allowed. A host intrusion detection or prevention system will not prevent application installation.

questions.q: Vincent discovered the vulnerability shown here when scanning a system on his network. What is the best action he can take to correct this vulnerability?
opts: Add multifactor authentication to the FTP server.
Add an intrusion prevention system.
Require the use of strong passwords.
Remove the FTP server.
questions.exp: The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) is an insecure protocol that should not be used today. Vincent’s best course of action is to remove the FTP server and replace this insecure protocol with a secure alternative, such as FTPS.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between HIDS and HIPS?
opts: HIDSs can only be installed on servers.
HIDSs can stop attacks and HIPSs only log them.
HIPSs can only be installed on servers.
HIDSs only log attacks and HIPSs can stop them.
questions.exp: The primary difference between a host intrusion detection system and a host intrusion prevention system is that a host‐based intrusion prevention system (HIPS) can stop attacks by dropping or modifying traffic whereas a host‐based intrusion detection system (HIDS) will only log and alert on attacks.

cram.def: Provider supplies virtualized compute, storage, networking. Customer manages OS upward. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure VMs.
Provider manages infrastructure + OS + runtime. Customer manages application and data. Examples: Heroku.
Provider manages everything. Customer just uses the application. Examples: Microsoft 365, Salesforce.
IaaS: customer responsible for most. SaaS: provider responsible for most. Security always shared.
Defining and provisioning infrastructure via code (Terraform, CloudFormation). Enables repeatable, auditable deployments.
No server management — code runs in response to events. Provider handles all infrastructure. Examples: AWS Lambda.
Security policy enforcement point between users and cloud services — visibility, compliance, data security.
Combination of public and private cloud — workloads move between environments.

matching.prompt: Provider supplies VMs; customer manages OS upward
Provider manages everything; customer uses app
Defining infrastructure via code files
Code runs on events; no server management
Security enforcement between users and cloud services
Mixed public and private cloud

questions.q: In the IaaS cloud model, the customer is responsible for:
opts: Physical hardware security and hypervisor patching at the cloud provider's data centers
Nothing — the provider handles all security including OS patching and application logic
Only the application data while the provider patches the OS and runtime layers
The operating system, applications, and data
questions.exp: The provider manages physical infrastructure and virtualization. IaaS provides raw compute — the customer manages everything from the OS upward including patching, hardening, and data.

questions.q: Which cloud service model provides the LEAST customer control over the underlying infrastructure?
opts: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
On-premises
questions.exp: SaaS gives customers the least control — the provider manages everything including infrastructure, OS, runtime, and application.

questions.q: A CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) is used to:
opts: Enforce security policies between users and cloud services — providing visibility, compliance, and data security
Provide physical security for cloud data centers including biometric access and video surveillance
Replace network firewalls in cloud environments by handling all packet filtering at Layer 7
Manage cloud billing and costs by aggregating usage data across multiple subscription accounts
questions.exp: CASBs sit between users and cloud services — enforcing DLP, access control, encryption, and compliance policies.

questions.q: A hybrid cloud architecture introduces which unique security challenge?
opts: Securing data and consistent policy enforcement across both private and public cloud environments
Lack of encryption support — hybrid clouds cannot use TLS for data in transit between sites
No access control options exist when private and public infrastructure coexist together
Physical security of data centers fully shifts to the customer once any public cloud is involved
questions.exp: Hybrid clouds require consistent security policies, data classification, and access controls across two different environments.

scenarios.q: A startup is building a new SaaS application. The CTO wants to deploy on AWS and has asked the security engineer to outline who is responsible for what. The engineer draws the line at: AWS is responsible for the physical data centers, networking hardware, and hypervisor; the startup is responsible for the operating system, application code, data, and IAM configuration. Which cloud service model does this describe?
opts: SaaS — the provider manages everything including the application
PaaS — the provider manages the OS and runtime, the startup manages the application
On-premises — no cloud provider is involved
IaaS — the provider manages infrastructure up to and including the hypervisor; the customer manages everything above
scenarios.exp: IaaS shared responsibility: the cloud provider secures the physical infrastructure and virtualization layer. The customer is responsible for everything from the OS upward — OS patching, application security, data protection, and IAM configuration. This is the most customer-managed cloud model.

scenarios.q: A company migrates its entire application stack to AWS and assumes that because AWS is 'secure', they don't need to configure security groups, encrypt their S3 buckets, or audit their IAM roles. Three months later, they suffer a data breach via an exposed S3 bucket. Which fundamental concept did the company fail to understand?
opts: AWS has a bug in their S3 security controls
Cloud providers are always less secure than on-premises
The shared responsibility model
AWS should have blocked the public S3 access automatically without customer configuration
scenarios.exp: AWS secures the infrastructure, but the customer is responsible for what they put on it, including data classification, access control, and encryption configuration. Shared responsibility model failure: AWS secures the platform; the customer secures their configuration and data. S3 bucket ACLs, encryption at rest, and IAM policies are always the customer's responsibility regardless of cloud model. 'AWS is secure' doesn't mean 'my deployment on AWS is secure'.

scenarios.q: An organization's development team deploys Lambda functions for a serverless application. The security team reviews the setup and finds: each Lambda function has an IAM role with AdministratorAccess, environment variables contain database credentials in plaintext, and error messages returned to users include stack traces. Which cloud security concern is MOST immediately critical?
opts: The serverless architecture itself is the vulnerability — migrate to EC2
The stack traces in error messages reveal code structure to attackers and should be disabled
The plaintext credentials in environment variables are critical and should use AWS Secrets Manager instead

The IAM roles with AdministratorAccess are the most critical — if any Lambda function is compromised, the attacker gains full AWS account control. Remediate by applying least privilege to each function's specific permissions
scenarios.exp: Overprivileged IAM roles are the most critical finding: a compromised Lambda function with AdministratorAccess gives the attacker complete control of the AWS account — all services, all data, all regions. Plaintext credentials and stack traces are serious but limited in scope. Least privilege on IAM is the foundational cloud security control.

scenarios.q: A financial services firm uses a SaaS CRM system to store customer contact information and interaction history. The firm's CISO asks the security team to document who is responsible for encrypting the data at rest within the CRM database. What is the correct answer under the shared responsibility model?
opts: The financial services firm — they must deploy their own encryption layer over the SaaS application
It depends on which cloud provider the SaaS vendor uses
The SaaS provider — in SaaS, the provider manages the entire stack including the database and its encryption
There is no encryption responsibility in SaaS — the provider handles all security
scenarios.exp: SaaS shared responsibility: in SaaS, the provider manages everything — infrastructure, OS, application, and database. Database encryption at rest is the SaaS provider's responsibility. The customer's responsibility in SaaS is primarily data governance (what data they put in, who in their organization has access), not infrastructure security.

scenarios.q: A company is deciding between deploying an application using IaaS (EC2 instances they manage) or PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk where AWS manages the OS and runtime). The security team prefers PaaS. What is the BEST security justification for choosing PaaS over IaaS for this workload?
opts: In PaaS, the provider manages OS patching and runtime security — reducing the customer's attack surface and eliminating the risk of unpatched OS vulnerabilities due to missed patching cycles
PaaS is always cheaper than IaaS because the customer doesn't pay for compute time directly — only for application requests handled at flat rates
PaaS prevents all application-level vulnerabilities because the platform automatically scans and blocks insecure code patterns at deployment time
IaaS is inherently insecure because the customer manages too many components — no organization can correctly configure all of them at scale
scenarios.exp: PaaS security benefit: the provider handles OS and runtime patching — one of the most common sources of compromise (unpatched OS vulnerabilities). The customer still owns application code and data security, but the OS attack surface is managed by the provider who has dedicated teams and automation for this purpose.

cram.def: Separates control plane from data plane. Centralized, programmable network control. Rapid policy changes.
Traffic between systems within the same network (internal). Traditional security focused on north-south only.
Traffic entering and leaving the network perimeter. Traditional firewall focus.
Granular per-workload isolation — inspects and controls east-west traffic. Key for Zero Trust.
Running network functions (firewall, IDS, load balancer) as virtual machines rather than dedicated hardware.
Software-defined WAN — uses multiple connectivity types. Centralized management.

matching.prompt: Separates control plane from data plane
Traffic between internal systems
Traffic entering/leaving network perimeter
Per-workload isolation in Zero Trust
Network functions as virtual machines

questions.q: East-west traffic security is important because:
opts: Attackers who breach the perimeter use lateral movement — traditional perimeter firewalls don't inspect internal traffic
It is always encrypted by default and so requires no additional inspection or controls
It travels faster than north-south traffic and overwhelms inspection appliance throughput
It never contains sensitive data because internal applications scrub all PII at egress
questions.exp: Traditional security focuses on north-south (perimeter) traffic. East-west inspection catches lateral movement after a breach.

questions.q: Microsegmentation addresses which limitation of traditional network security?
opts: Perimeter-only security that leaves internal east-west traffic uninspected — enabling attacker lateral movement
Lack of encryption at the network layer between traditional segmented zones in production
High cost of dedicated network appliance hardware in legacy three-tier architectures
Lack of user authentication on internal applications behind the corporate network firewall
questions.exp: Microsegmentation applies granular security policies to east-west traffic — containing breaches to individual workloads.

questions.q: SDN (Software-Defined Networking) improves security management by:
opts: Eliminating the need for firewalls by routing all traffic through SDN-controller policy points
Centralizing network control — enabling rapid, consistent policy deployment across the entire network
Using stronger encryption for all traffic between SDN switches and the central controller
Replacing physical network hardware with software-only switches running on commodity servers
questions.exp: SDN's centralized control plane enables rapid, programmatic security policy changes across the entire network from one place.

scenarios.q: A network architect is designing a new data center. The CEO asks why they need an internal firewall between the server VLAN and the workstation VLAN — 'aren't they both inside the network already?' What is the BEST justification for internal segmentation?
opts: Internal firewalls are required by all compliance frameworks
Internal segmentation limits lateral movement
Internal firewalls make the network faster by segmenting broadcast domains
VLANs alone provide all the security needed without internal firewalls
scenarios.exp: If an attacker compromises a workstation, internal firewall rules prevent them from directly reaching the servers. The perimeter firewall only stops threats entering from outside, not threats already inside. East-west traffic control: traditional perimeter-only security assumes everything inside is trusted. Modern attacks (ransomware, insider threats) compromise one internal system then move laterally. Internal segmentation forces traffic between zones through controls — limiting blast radius if a workstation is compromised.

scenarios.q: A company's web application servers sit on the same network segment as the internal corporate systems. During a penetration test, the tester compromises the web application server and immediately accesses internal HR systems, payroll databases, and Active Directory — all without additional exploitation. What architectural flaw does this reveal?
opts: The web application had too many vulnerabilities — proper application-layer hardening would have made the network-segmentation question moot here
The penetration tester used advanced 0-day techniques against the corporate systems that no defensive control would have stopped reliably
The internal systems had default credentials — credential rotation alone would have prevented the lateral movement entirely
The web application servers are not in a DMZ — they should be in an isolated segment with strict firewall rules allowing only necessary traffic to internal systems
scenarios.exp: DMZ architecture flaw: public-facing web servers should be in a screened subnet (DMZ) isolated from internal systems. If a web server is compromised (expected attack surface), the attacker should face another firewall before reaching internal HR, payroll, and AD. A flat network where web servers can freely reach everything internal is a critical design failure.

scenarios.q: A security architect is implementing microsegmentation for a cloud workload environment. They define policies where each application tier (web, application, database) can only communicate with adjacent tiers on specific ports, and no lateral communication is permitted within a tier (web server to web server, for example). An attacker compromises one web server. What is the MOST significant benefit of this design?
opts: The attacker cannot see any other systems on the network because microsegmentation drops all traffic between any two non-explicitly-paired hosts
The attacker's traffic is automatically encrypted by the microsegmentation platform — even if intercepted, the attacker can't decrypt their own communications
The attacker cannot reach the database tier directly and cannot spread to other web servers — their movement is constrained to the single compromised web server's permitted communication paths
The compromised web server is automatically isolated by the microsegmentation platform within seconds of detecting any unusual outbound activity
scenarios.exp: Microsegmentation benefit: east-west controls limit lateral movement within the environment. The attacker can only communicate on paths the policy explicitly permits. Spreading to other web servers (lateral movement within tier) is blocked. Jumping directly to the database (skipping the application tier) is blocked. Each compromise is contained to that workload's permitted communication paths.

scenarios.q: A company is evaluating SD-WAN to replace their MPLS WAN. The security team has concerns. The network team argues SD-WAN actually improves security posture compared to MPLS. Which argument BEST supports the network team's position?
opts: SD-WAN is always cheaper than MPLS, which frees budget for other security controls and lets organizations spread investment more broadly
SD-WAN enables consistent, centrally-managed security policies across all branches — including integrated branch encryption and direct-to-cloud routing with security applied at the edge
SD-WAN eliminates the need for branch firewalls because the SD-WAN controller handles all security functions centrally including IPS
MPLS is inherently encrypted at the carrier level, so replacing it with SD-WAN reduces the security posture of branch traffic
scenarios.exp: SD-WAN security advantage: centralized policy management with encryption across all WAN links, and the ability to apply security controls (FWaaS, CASB) close to the user rather than backhauling all traffic to a central data center. MPLS doesn't encrypt traffic natively. SD-WAN with SASE provides better cloud-era security than MPLS backhauling.

cram.def: Lightweight application packaging. Containers share host OS kernel. Docker, Kubernetes. Faster than VMs.
Network-connected embedded devices — cameras, HVAC, medical devices. Often lack security controls.
Industrial Control Systems. Control physical processes. Critical infrastructure. Availability top priority.
Hardware and software controlling physical equipment. Different priorities than IT — availability > confidentiality.
Processing data close to where it's generated — IoT devices, edge nodes. Reduces latency, increases attack surface.

Network-connected embedded devices
Control physical industrial processes

Processing data near where it is generated

questions.q: IoT devices present unique security challenges because:
opts: They often lack adequate security controls, have long lifecycles, are difficult to patch, and have limited computational resources
They are always connected via encrypted protocols
They are always behind corporate firewalls
They only connect to internal networks
questions.exp: IoT devices ship with minimal security, default credentials, and rare firmware updates — making them persistent vulnerabilities.

questions.q: ICS/SCADA systems have different security priorities than traditional IT because:
opts: Availability is the top priority — downtime in industrial control systems can have physical, safety, or economic consequences
They use stronger encryption than IT systems by default for all process control data
They are never connected to networks and remain physically air-gapped from corporate IT
They only process non-sensitive data so confidentiality is never a meaningful concern
questions.exp: In OT/ICS, a patch that requires downtime may be unacceptable — availability and safety often outweigh confidentiality concerns.

questions.q: Containerization differs from full virtualization in that:
opts: Containers are always more secure than VMs because their smaller image size limits the attack surface
Containers always run on physical hardware whereas VMs always run inside hypervisor abstractions
Containers cannot be networked together without a heavyweight bridge that defeats their isolation
Containers share the host OS kernel — making them more lightweight but providing less isolation than separate VMs
questions.exp: Containers share the host kernel — a kernel vulnerability can affect all containers on the host. VMs have separate kernels for stronger isolation.

scenarios.q: A hospital's biomedical engineering team connects patient monitoring devices, infusion pumps, and imaging systems to the same network as clinical workstations and the corporate email system. The IT security team flags this as a critical risk. The biomedical team says the devices have never been hacked. What is the BEST explanation of the risk?
opts: Medical devices are too old to be hacked since attackers focus on modern systems — the risk is overestimated and resources are better spent on patching corporate endpoints
Medical devices typically run unpatched embedded OSes with default credentials, optimized for availability — same-network corporate malware can reach life-critical devices and vice versa
The risk only applies if the medical devices are connected to the public internet directly — internal-only network connectivity poses no real attack vector
The biomedical team is correct — dedicated medical devices are secure by design and FDA-regulated equipment manufacturers ship them hardened
scenarios.exp: OT/medical device risk: these devices often run unpatched embedded OSes, have hardcoded credentials, and can't have security software installed. They must be available at all times (patient safety). Placing them on the same network as corporate systems creates a bidirectional risk: malware from corporate reaches medical, or a compromised medical device becomes a pivot to corporate. Network segmentation is the required mitigation.

scenarios.q: A manufacturing company connects its production line PLCs (Programmable Logic Controllers) to the corporate network to enable remote monitoring by management. Six months later, a ransomware infection that entered via a phishing email encrypts several PLC configuration files, halting production for three days. What architectural principle was violated?
opts: The OT (Operational Technology) network should have been air-gapped or at minimum strictly segmented from the IT network — connections between IT and OT create a path for IT-targeting malware to reach production systems
The PLCs should have had antivirus installed on the embedded OS to detect ransomware before it could reach control logic files and disrupt production
The remote monitoring software introduced the ransomware as a payload bundled with a routine vendor update — the root cause is the vendor's build pipeline compromise
The PLCs should have been upgraded to run a modern OS with regular security patches — outdated PLC firmware was the underlying cause of the breach scope
scenarios.exp: OT/IT convergence risk: IT malware (ransomware) crossing into OT is a well-documented attack pattern. The Purdue Model and ISA/IEC 62443 specifically prescribe network demarcation between IT and OT with controlled, monitored interfaces. Unrestricted IT-to-OT connectivity turns every IT phishing email into a potential production outage.

scenarios.q: A large retailer deploys 500 IoT-connected smart thermostats across their stores to enable centralized HVAC management. The devices run a proprietary embedded OS with no update mechanism, use default credentials that the retailer cannot change, and communicate via an unencrypted protocol. Security recommends segregating them on a dedicated VLAN with no path to the corporate network. Operations objects that this would prevent centralized monitoring. What is the BEST architectural compromise?
opts: Accept the risk — HVAC devices cannot be a meaningful attack vector

Place the devices on an isolated IoT VLAN with a one-way data diode or restricted DMZ allowing monitoring traffic to reach the management server but preventing any other communication — particularly no inbound access from IoT devices to corporate systems
Deploy the devices on the corporate network but monitor them closely
Replace all 500 devices with ones that have better security features before deployment
scenarios.exp: IoT segmentation with controlled monitoring path: the devices cannot be hardened (no patch, no credential change). Full isolation prevents monitoring. The architectural compromise is a restricted path — monitoring data can flow from IoT VLAN to the management server, but no other communication is permitted. A data diode or strict firewall rules achieve this. Replacing 500 devices is operationally unrealistic.

scenarios.q: A developer is arguing that containers are just as secure as VMs for their multi-tenant application because 'containers have namespaces and cgroups for isolation.' A security architect disagrees. What is the STRONGEST argument the architect can make?
opts: Containers use more CPU so they're less efficient
VMs are always easier to manage than containers
Containers cannot be monitored by security tools
Containers share the host OS kernel
scenarios.exp: A kernel-level vulnerability exploited from one container can potentially affect all containers on the host. VMs have separate kernels; a kernel exploit in one VM doesn't cross the hypervisor boundary to other VMs. For true multi-tenant isolation where tenants are untrusted, VMs provide stronger security boundaries. Container isolation boundary: namespace/cgroup isolation is a software boundary in the shared kernel. A kernel exploit (like a container escape) crosses this boundary. VMs have hardware-enforced isolation through the hypervisor — each VM's kernel is separate. For hostile multi-tenancy (untrusted tenants), this distinction matters significantly. Many cloud providers run customer VMs, not containers, for this reason.

cram.def: No single point of failure. Redundant components, automatic failover. Measured in nines of uptime.
Maximum acceptable time to restore a system after failure. How quickly must we recover?
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. How much data can we afford to lose?
Average time to repair a failed component. Lower is better.
Average time between failures of a component. Higher is better.
All nodes handle traffic simultaneously — immediate failover, maximum utilization.
One node active, one standby — failover when active fails. Standby capacity wasted.

matching.prompt: Maximum time to restore after failure
Maximum acceptable data loss in time
Average time to repair a failed component
Average time between failures
All nodes active simultaneously
One active, one on standby

questions.q: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines:
opts: How much data the organization can afford to lose measured in time elapsed since the last backup
The maximum acceptable time to restore a system or service after a failure or disaster
How often backup jobs should run against a tier of business-critical production data
The average time between system failures of a given component or subsystem
questions.exp: RTO answers 'how quickly must we recover?' — systems with low RTO require hot standby or rapid failover capabilities.

questions.q: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines:
opts: How quickly systems must be restored after a failure or disaster strikes the data center
The target uptime percentage that the SLA commits to over a calendar month
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time — determining backup frequency
The time required to detect a failure has occurred before recovery efforts begin
questions.exp: RPO answers 'how much data can we afford to lose?' — a 1-hour RPO means backups must run at least hourly.

questions.q: A system with 99.999% availability (five nines) experiences approximately how much downtime per year?
opts: About 5 minutes
About 52 minutes
About 8.7 hours
About 1 hour
questions.exp: Five nines (99.999%) = approximately 5.26 minutes of downtime per year — requires fully redundant failover systems.

questions.q: Active-active clustering provides better performance than active-passive because:
opts: All nodes handle traffic simultaneously
Active-active uses stronger hardware
Active-passive is more expensive
Active-active uses less electricity
questions.exp: Maximizing utilization and providing immediate failover. Active-active uses all nodes for production traffic — when one fails, the others absorb load. Active-passive wastes standby capacity.

scenarios.q: A hospital's electronic health records system has an SLA requiring 99.9% availability. The IT team calculates this allows approximately 8.7 hours of downtime per year. The clinical informatics director rejects this, arguing that the system must be available during all shifts and cannot be down for more than 15 minutes during any clinical period. What RTO and availability tier does the clinical director's requirement describe?
opts: 99.9% availability with a 4-hour RTO — standard for healthcare systems
An RPO of 15 minutes, meaning backups must run every 15 minutes

An RTO of 15 minutes during clinical hours, requiring a high-availability architecture with automatic failover — likely requiring 99.9%+ availability during defined windows. The 8.7-hour annual downtime at 99.9% must be confined to maintenance windows outside clinical hours
Cold site DR with 15-minute maximum recovery time
scenarios.exp: RTO in context: 99.9% aggregate availability distributed poorly still fails clinical requirements. The real requirement is 15-minute RTO during clinical windows — which requires hot standby, automatic failover, and maintenance windows scheduled during off-peak periods. This is an application-of-SLA-to-operational-reality question the exam tests through scenarios.

scenarios.q: An organization runs its critical billing system on a single server with no redundancy. The server fails on a Tuesday morning and takes 6 hours to restore from backup. During this time, $2M in billing transactions cannot be processed. The CTO asks the security architect to explain what metrics they should have defined to prevent this. What TWO metrics are most directly relevant?
opts: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption begins
MTBF and MTTR only — these predict how often failures occur and how long they take to fix
CVSS score and patch cadence — the server was likely unpatched, which is the root concern for the metric question
Uptime percentage and SLA penalties — these are the only metrics that matter financially
scenarios.exp: The maximum acceptable time to restore the system, which 6 hours clearly exceeded — and RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — the maximum acceptable data loss. Together these drive the architecture: RTO drives redundancy decisions; RPO drives backup frequency. RTO and RPO drive DR architecture: RTO = 'how fast must we restore?' — if the answer was 1 hour, the current architecture (6-hour restore) was non-compliant and redundancy was required. RPO = 'how much data can we lose?' — drives backup frequency. Defining these before failure allows right-sizing of the architecture. Discovering them after is expensive.

scenarios.q: A company runs two identical web server clusters in an active-active configuration behind a load balancer. Each cluster can handle 100% of peak traffic independently. During a major DDoS attack, one cluster is overwhelmed and fails. The load balancer automatically redirects all traffic to the surviving cluster, which continues serving all users without degradation. What availability concept does this demonstrate?
opts: Active-passive clustering — one cluster was on standby
Geographic dispersal — the clusters are in different locations
Active-active clustering with automatic failover
Cold site failover — the surviving cluster was previously inactive
scenarios.exp: Both clusters handle traffic simultaneously, and either can absorb 100% load if the other fails, with no manual intervention required. Active-active: both nodes handle production traffic simultaneously, and each is sized to handle full load. Failover is instantaneous — the load balancer redirects without waiting for a cold system to start up. This contrasts with active-passive where the standby is idle. The key indicators: both active simultaneously, automatic failover, no degradation during failure.

scenarios.q: An e-commerce company's payment processing system has the following requirements: transactions during a failure cannot exceed $50,000 in lost data, and the system must be restored within 2 hours of a failure to avoid regulatory reporting obligations. A storage system fails at 2pm. Backups run every 4 hours (last at noon). Recovery completes at 3:45pm. Were the RPO and RTO met?
opts: Both were met — 2 hours recovery and $50,000 data loss are within limits
RPO was met but RTO was breached — 1h45m exceeds 2 hours
Both were breached — the backup gap and recovery time both exceeded limits

RTO was met (3:45pm = 1h45m recovery, under 2 hours), but RPO was breached — the last backup was at noon (2 hours before failure), meaning up to 2 hours of transactions are in the backup gap, potentially exceeding $50,000 in transaction data
scenarios.exp: RPO analysis: $50,000 maximum data loss translates to a maximum backup gap. If 2 hours of transactions exceed $50,000, the 4-hour backup interval is insufficient for this RPO. RTO of 2 hours was met (1h45m recovery). This question tests whether students understand RPO as a data loss tolerance (measured in time/volume), not just a time metric.

questions.q: What major difference is likely to exist between on‐premises identity services and those used in a cloud‐hosted environment?
opts: Account policy control will be set to the cloud provider’s standards.
The cloud service will provide account and identity management services.
Multifactor authentication will not be supported by the cloud vendor.
None of the above.
questions.exp: Most cloud services provide identity and authorization tools for their services. Most, although not all, allow customers to set some or even many of the account policies they will use, and most major vendors support some form of multifactor capability.
questions.framing_note: Both A and B can be true of cloud-hosted identity, which makes this question feel like a 50/50. Sybex resolves it by asking which difference is *defining* rather than *possible*: cloud-hosted IAM exists because the provider runs the identity layer (option B). Option A overstates the constraint — most cloud IAM lets the customer set their own account policies. If you see "what is THE major difference" framing on the exam, pick the answer that defines the service model, not a side-effect that can vary by provider.

questions.q: Felix wants to clone a virtual machine. What should he do to capture a live machine, including the machine state?
opts: A full backup
A snapshot
A differential backup
Live boot media
questions.exp: Virtual machine snapshots capture the machine state at a point in time and will allow Felix to clone the system. A full backup and a differential backup can be used to capture the disk for the machine but typically will not capture the memory state and other details of the system state. Live boot media allows you to boot and run a nonpersistent system from trusted media.

questions.q: Kevin discovered that his web server was being overwhelmed by traffic, causing a CPU bottleneck. Using the interface offered by his cloud service provider, he added another CPU to the server. What term best describes Kevin’s action?
opts: Elasticity
Horizontal scaling
Vertical scaling
High availability
questions.exp: This is an example of adding additional capacity to an existing server, which is also known as vertical scaling. Kevin could also have used horizontal scaling by adding additional web servers. Elasticity involves the ability to both add and remove capacity on demand, and though it does describe this scenario, it’s not as good a description as vertical scaling. There is no mention of increasing the server’s availability.

questions.q: Which one of the following is not an example of infrastructure as code?
opts: Defining infrastructure in JSON
Writing code to interact with a cloud provider’s API
Using a cloud provider’s web interface to provision resources
Defining infrastructure in YAML
questions.exp: Infrastructure as code (IaC) is any approach that automates the provisioning, management, and deprovisioning of cloud resources. Defining resources through JSON or YAML is IaC, as is writing code that interacts with an API. Provisioning resources through a web interface is manual, not automated, and therefore does not qualify as IaC.

questions.q: Brian is selecting a CASB for his organization, and he would like to use an approach that interacts with the cloud provider directly. Which CASB approach is most appropriate for his needs?
opts: Inline CASB
Outsider CASB
Comprehensive CASB
API‐based CASB
questions.exp: API‐based CASB solutions interact directly with the cloud provider through the provider’s API. Inline CASB solutions intercept requests between the user and the provider. Outsider and comprehensive are not categories of CASB solutions.

questions.q: In which of the following cloud categories are customers typically charged based on the number of virtual server instances dedicated to their use?
opts: IaaS only
SaaS only
IaaS and PaaS
IaaS, SaaS, and PaaS
questions.exp: Customers are typically charged for server instances in both IaaS environments, where they directly provision those instances, and PaaS environments, where they request the number of servers needed to support their applications. In an SaaS environment, the customer typically has no knowledge of the number of server instances supporting their use.

questions.q: Brian would like to limit the ability of users inside his organization to provision expensive cloud server instances without permission. What type of control would best help him achieve this goal?
opts: Resource policy
Security group
Multifactor authentication
Secure web gateway
questions.exp: Cloud providers offer resource policies that customers may use to limit the actions that users of their accounts may take. Implementing resource policies is a good security practice to limit the damage caused by an accidental command, a compromised account, or a malicious insider.

questions.q: Ryan is selecting a new security control to meet his organization’s objectives. He would like to use it in their multicloud environment and would like to minimize the administrative work required from his fellow technologists. What approach would best meet his needs?
opts: Third‐party control
Internally developed control
Cloud‐native control
Any of the above
questions.exp: Controls offered by cloud service providers have the advantage of direct integration with the provider’s offerings, often making them cost‐effective and user‐friendly. Third‐party solutions are often more costly, but they bring the advantage of integrating with a variety of cloud providers, facilitating the management of multicloud environments.

questions.q: Kira would like to implement a security control that can implement access restrictions across all of the SaaS solutions used by her organization. What control would best meet her needs?
opts: Security group
Resource policy
CASB
SWG
questions.exp: Cloud access security brokers (CASBs) are designed specifically for this situation: enforcing security controls across cloud providers. A secure web gateway (SWG) may be able to achieve Kira’s goal, but it would be more difficult to do so. Security groups and resource policies are controls used in IaaS environments.

questions.q: Fran’s organization uses a Type I hypervisor to implement an IaaS offering that it sells to customers. Which one of the following security controls is least applicable to this environment?
opts: Customers must maintain security patches on guest operating systems.
The provider must maintain security patches on the hypervisor.
The provider must maintain security patches on the host operating system.
Customers must manage security groups to mediate network access to guest operating systems.
questions.exp: Type I hypervisors, also known as bare‐metal hypervisors, run directly on top of the physical hardware and, therefore, do not require a host operating system.

questions.q: Tony purchases virtual machines from Microsoft Azure exclusively for use by his organization. What model of cloud computing is this?
opts: Public cloud
Private cloud
Hybrid cloud
Community cloud
questions.exp: This is an example of public cloud computing because Tony is using a public cloud provider, Microsoft Azure. The fact that Tony is limiting access to virtual machines to his own organization is not relevant because the determining factor for the cloud model is whether the underlying infrastructure is shared, not whether virtualized resources are shared.

questions.q: In what cloud security model does the cloud service provider bear the most responsibility for implementing security controls?
opts: IaaS
FaaS
PaaS
SaaS
questions.exp: The cloud service provider bears the most responsibility for implementing security controls in an SaaS environment and the least responsibility in an IaaS environment. This is due to the division of responsibilities under the cloud computing shared responsibility model.

questions.q: Wanda is responsible for a series of seismic sensors placed at remote locations. These sensors have low‐bandwidth connections, and she would like to place computing power on the sensors to allow them to preprocess data before it is sent back to the cloud. What term best describes this approach?
opts: Edge computing
Client‐server computing
Fog computing
Thin client computing
questions.exp: This approach may be described as client‐server computing, but that is a general term that describes many different operating environments. The better term to use here is edge computing, which involves placing compute power at the client to allow it to perform preprocessing before sending data back to the cloud. Fog computing is a related concept that uses IoT gateway devices that are located in close physical proximity to the sensors.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about cloud computing is incorrect?
opts: Cloud computing offers ubiquitous, convenient access.
Cloud computing customers store data on hardware that is shared with other customers.
Cloud computing customers provision resources through the service provider’s sales team.
Cloud computing resources are accessed over a network.
questions.exp: One of the key characteristics of cloud computing is that customers can access resources on‐demand with minimal service provider interaction. Cloud customers do not need to contact a sales representative each time they wish to provision a resource but can normally do so on a self‐service basis.

questions.q: Helen designed a new payroll system that she offers to her customers. She hosts the payroll system in AWS and her customers access it through the web. What tier of cloud computing best describes Helen’s service?
opts: PaaS
SaaS
FaaS
IaaS
questions.exp: Helen is using IaaS services to create her payroll product. She is then offering that payroll service to her customers as a SaaS solution.

questions.q: Which cloud computing deployment model requires the use of a unifying technology platform to tie together components from different providers?
opts: Public cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Hybrid cloud
questions.exp: Hybrid cloud environments blend elements of public, private, and/or community cloud solutions. A hybrid cloud requires the use of technology that unifies the different cloud offerings into a single, coherent platform.

questions.q: Which one of the following would not commonly be available as an IaaS service offering?
opts: CRM
Storage
Networking
Computing
questions.exp: Customer relationship management (CRM) packages offered in the cloud would be classified as software‐as‐a‐service (SaaS), since they are not infrastructure components. Storage, networking, and computing resources are all common IaaS offerings.

questions.q: Brian has deployed a system that monitors sensors and uses that data to manage the power distribution for the power company that he works for. Which of the following terms is commonly used to describe this type of control and monitoring solution?
opts: SCADA
SIM
HVAC
AVAD
questions.exp: SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) is a system architecture that combines data acquisition and control devices with communications methods and interfaces to oversee complex industrial and manufacturing processes, just like those used in utilities. A SIM (subscriber identity module) is the small card used to identify cell phones; HVAC stands for heating, ventilation, and air‐conditioning; and AVAD was made up for this question.

questions.q: The organization that Lynn works for wants to deploy an embedded system that needs to process data as it comes in to the device without processing delays or other interruptions. What type of solution does Lynn’s company need to deploy?
opts: An MFP
A HIPS
An SoC
An RTOS
questions.exp: A real‐time operating system (RTOS) is an OS that is designed to handle data as it is fed to the operating system, rather than delaying handling it as other processes and programs are run. Real‐time operating systems are used when processes or procedures are sensitive to delays that might occur if responses do not happen immediately. An MFP is a multifunction printer, a HIPS is a host intrusion prevention system, and an SoC is a system on a chip—which is hardware, which might run an RTOS, but the option does not mention what type of OS the SoC is running.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a common constraint of an embedded system?
opts: Compute
Cost
Network
Authentication
questions.exp: Embedded systems are available at many price points. Understanding constraints that limited resources create for embedded systems helps security professionals identify appropriate security controls and options.
questions.framing_note: This one diverges from a lot of Security+ teaching that lists cost alongside compute, power, and network as embedded-system constraints. Sybex's argument is that embedded systems exist at many price points (from a $3 microcontroller to a multi-thousand-dollar industrial PLC), so cost isn't an inherent constraint of the category — it's a design choice. The exam may frame it either way; if the question is about *inherent technical limits* (resources, footprint, connectivity), cost is the odd one out. If the question is about *deployment constraints* (budget, scale, replacement cost), cost is in. Read the framing carefully.

questions.q: Gary wants to prevent his organization’s most sensitive data from being accessed by network‐based attackers at any cost. What solution should he implement to ensure this?
opts: An air gap
Firewall rules
An IPS
IPSec
questions.exp: Physical isolation like an air gap is used when the additional work to manually transfer files is an acceptable trade‐off against the potential for a security event caused by potential network‐based attackers. Firewall rules, an IPS, or the use of IPSec to protect traffic will not sufficiently address this issue if any services remain accessible on the system.

questions.q: What type of hypervisor requires that the platform operator routinely patch the host operating system?
opts: Type I hypervisor
Type II hypervisor
Type III hypervisor
Type IV hypervisor
questions.exp: A Type II hypervisor is the only type of hypervisor that uses a host operating system. A Type I hypervisor, or bare‐metal hypervisor, runs directly on top of the physical hardware. Type III and IV hypervisors do not exist.

questions.q: Under the shared responsibility model, which component always remains the responsibility of the customer, regardless of the cloud service model used?
opts: Data
Application
Hardware
Datacenter
questions.exp: In the shared responsibility model for cloud computing, the customer always retains either full or partial responsibility for data security. Responsibility for hardware and physical data centers is the cloud provider’s responsibility under all models. Responsibility for applications is the customer’s responsibility under IaaS, the provider’s responsibility under SaaS, and a shared responsibility under PaaS.

questions.q: Kevin is using a service where a cloud provider offers a platform that executes his code in response to discrete events. He is billed based on the actual resources consumed during each code execution event. What term best describes this service?
opts: PaaS
SaaS
IaaS
FaaS
questions.exp: This is an example of function‐as‐a‐service (FaaS) computing, a subset of platform‐as‐a‐service (PaaS). Although both terms may be used to describe the service Kevin uses, the best answer is FaaS, because it is more specific.

questions.q: Rick has been asked to secure a legacy SCADA environment that his organization uses to manage power generation facilities. What recommendation is best suited to a legacy environment that uses a combination of proprietary and open protocols and systems?
opts: Require regular patching and enable local firewalls on all devices to build a zero‐trust environment.
Deploy a HIPS for each device to protect each system from both known and behavioral threats.
Put the SCADA system on an isolated network and strictly control ingress and egress.
None of the above
questions.exp: Aging infrastructure that is tightly coupled to critical systems like a power generation facility is a common issue that enterprise security practitioners encounter in many industries. Placing devices that cannot otherwise be secured onto an isolated network and ensuring that only trusted and inspected access is allowed is a common solution. Since aging devices are often out of support, cannot be patched, and do not have support for firewalls or host‐based intrusion prevention systems (HIPSs), those solutions are often unable to be implemented, particularly for the embedded and specialized devices found in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) and industrial control systems (ICS) environments.

questions.q: Gary has deployed a technology that allows him to manage his network via APIs. He uses the technology to dynamically manage the network as part of his zero‐trust deployment and to ensure appropriate performance from the network. What type of network technology is Gary using?
opts: IoT
Virtualization
Containerization
Software‐defined networking
questions.exp: Software‐defined networking (SDN) uses software‐based controllers and application programming interfaces to control networks. It is frequently used to ensure proper performance by making dynamic changes to networks and is a common element in zero‐trust deployments. IoT (Internet of Things) describes a variety of Internet‐connected smart devices. Virtualization can involve software‐defined networking as part of its environment but goes beyond what is described. Containerization is used to allow applications to move with only their needed components, making them easy to deploy across systems and operating systems.

questions.q: Which one of the following terms best describes the ability of a system to incorporate added capacity as demand increases?
opts: Scalability
Version control
Provisioning
Deprovisioning
questions.exp: Scalability says that applications should be designed so that computing resources they require may be incrementally added to support increasing demand. Version control is used as part of development processes to ensure that the right code versions are worked on and used. Provisioning is part of the identity management life cycle and involves identity and rights creation. It can also refer to creating and providing resources or new systems. Deprovisioning is done at the end of a life cycle to remove rights and privileges for identity management, or resources from other environments.

questions.q: Tina’s organization is operating in a platform‐as‐a‐service (PaaS) environment. Which of the following is a shared responsibility according the shared responsibility matrix in a PaaS environment?
opts: Information and data
Identity infrastructure
Physical hosts
Accounts and identities
questions.exp: PaaS environments commonly rely on customers and providers to maintain identity and directory infrastructure, applications, and network controls. Customers manage information and data, devices, and accounts and identities, whereas providers are responsible for operating systems, physical hosts, networks, and datacenters.

questions.q: In what cloud security model does the cloud service customer bear the most responsibility for implementing security controls?
opts: SaaS
IaaS
PaaS
FaaS
questions.exp: The cloud service customer bears the most responsibility for implementing security controls in an infrastructure‐as‐a‐service (IaaS) environment and the least responsibility in a software‐as‐a‐service (SaaS) environment. This is due to the division of responsibilities under the cloud computing shared responsibility model.

cram.def: Network areas with different trust levels — internet, DMZ, internal, restricted. Traffic controlled at boundaries.
Default firewall rule: deny all traffic not explicitly permitted. Foundation of secure network design.
Fail-open: continues operating if security fails. Fail-closed (fail-secure): blocks all if security fails. Fail-secure preferred.
Minimize exposed components, services, and access points. Less exposed = less risk.

matching.prompt: Network areas with different trust levels
Default-deny all traffic not explicitly permitted
Blocks all traffic if security system fails
Continues operating if security system fails

questions.q: Implicit deny as a default firewall rule means:
opts: All traffic is allowed unless specifically blocked
All traffic from untrusted sources is denied
Only internal traffic is denied
All traffic is denied unless explicitly permitted — a default-deny posture
questions.exp: Implicit deny is the foundation of secure firewall design — only explicitly permitted traffic passes, everything else is dropped.

questions.q: A fail-closed (fail-secure) security device:
opts: Continues to pass all traffic if it fails — prioritizing availability over the security function
Alerts the security operations team but never blocks any traffic regardless of severity
Blocks all traffic if the security function fails — prioritizing security over availability
Fails to a half-open state where TCP handshakes complete but no data passes through
questions.exp: Fail-closed blocks all traffic on failure — sacrificing availability to maintain security. Appropriate for high-security environments.

questions.q: Attack surface reduction involves:
opts: Adding more security monitoring tools so every event has multiple detection signals
Increasing system redundancy so a primary system failure has a hot standby waiting
Minimizing exposed services, components, and access points — anything not needed is removed or disabled
Deploying more firewalls along every internal segment to inspect east-west traffic
questions.exp: Every unnecessary service, port, or account is a potential entry point — removing them reduces the ways an attacker can gain access.

scenarios.q: A security architect is designing a network for a financial firm. They propose: all traffic between network zones must pass through a firewall, all firewall rules default to deny unless explicitly permitted, and any security device failure results in all traffic being blocked until the device is restored. A junior engineer asks why traffic isn't automatically allowed during a device failure 'so users can keep working.' What security principle does the architect's design enforce?
opts: Availability over security — the architect is wrong to block traffic during failures
Fault tolerance — the design ensures the firewall never fails
Implicit deny and fail-closed (fail-secure) design
Redundancy — the design creates backup network paths
scenarios.exp: A security system that fails open is no longer providing security. An attacker who can cause a security device to fail gains unrestricted access. Fail-closed prioritizes security over availability, which is appropriate for a financial firm's critical segments. Fail-closed/fail-secure: if a security control fails and traffic flows freely, the attacker's strategy becomes 'cause the security device to fail.' Fail-closed means a failure state is also a secure state — no traffic passes. The cost is availability during failure; the benefit is that attackers cannot bypass security by crashing it. Appropriate for high-security environments.

scenarios.q: During a network audit, a consultant finds that the organization has a firewall between the internet and the DMZ, and a firewall between the DMZ and the internal network. However, there are no controls between the workstation VLAN, the server VLAN, and the finance VLAN — all internal traffic flows freely. A ransomware infection on one workstation encrypts all file servers and the finance database within 20 minutes. What architectural gap enabled this?
opts: The DMZ firewall was misconfigured
The absence of internal network segmentation
The workstations should have had better antivirus
The ransomware exploited a zero-day vulnerability that no control could have stopped
scenarios.exp: Without east-west controls between VLANs, a compromised workstation can reach all servers and all VLANs directly. The perimeter firewall only addresses north-south traffic (entering/leaving the network). Internal threats, insider attacks, and lateral movement after perimeter breach are all unrestricted. East-west gap: perimeter firewalls address external threats. Internal segmentation addresses lateral movement. The absence of internal controls means any compromised internal device can reach any other — ransomware spreads freely. The 20-minute total encryption time is consistent with unrestricted network access. VLANs with internal firewall rules would have contained the infection.

scenarios.q: A security team is implementing security zones for a manufacturing company. They propose five zones: Internet (untrusted), DMZ (public-facing services), Corporate IT (employee systems), OT Network (production systems), and a Management Zone (security tools, jump servers). All inter-zone traffic is denied by default, with explicit permit rules for required flows. An operations manager argues this is overly complex. What is the STRONGEST justification for this design?
opts: Zone-based architecture with explicit permit rules implements implicit deny across all inter-zone boundaries — each zone failure or compromise is contained to that zone. A ransomware infection in Corporate IT cannot directly reach OT systems. A compromised DMZ server cannot reach internal corporate data. The explicit rules also provide an auditable record of all permitted communication paths
Complexity is good — more complex networks are harder for attackers to understand
The five-zone design is required by all security frameworks
Zone-based firewalls are faster than rule-based firewalls
scenarios.exp: Zone-based design with implicit deny is defense-in-depth: each zone boundary is a control point. Compromise of one zone doesn't automatically grant access to others. The explicit permit rules are also valuable for security operations — they define exactly what's expected, making anomalous traffic visible.

cram.def: Passive — detects and alerts on suspicious activity. Does not block. Tap or span port.
Active — detects AND blocks malicious traffic inline. Can cause legitimate traffic disruption.
Compares traffic/behavior against known attack patterns. Effective for known threats; misses novel attacks.
Baselines normal behavior and alerts on deviations. Catches novel threats; higher false positives.
Legitimate traffic flagged as malicious — can block valid users.
Malicious traffic not detected — attack succeeds undetected. More dangerous than false positive.

matching.prompt: Passive — detects and alerts only
Active — detects and blocks inline
Known attack pattern matching
Deviations from normal behavior baseline
Legitimate traffic flagged as malicious
Malicious traffic not detected

questions.q: How does an IPS differ from an IDS?
opts: IPS actively blocks malicious traffic inline; IDS only detects and alerts without blocking
IPS uses signature detection; IDS uses anomaly detection
IPS is always cloud-based; IDS is on-premises
IDS is more effective than IPS
questions.exp: IPS is active (inline — blocks traffic). IDS is passive (out-of-band — detects and alerts only, no blocking).

questions.q: Signature-based IDS/IPS is limited because:
opts: It requires too much processing power to inspect all traffic at typical network rates
It cannot detect unknown or novel threats that have no matching signature
It produces too many false positives by matching benign traffic to malicious patterns
It requires constant manual tuning to adjust thresholds for each unique environment
questions.exp: Signature-based detection only catches known threats — zero-days and novel malware with no signature will go undetected.

questions.q: A false negative in IPS is more concerning than a false positive because:
opts: A false negative means a real attack succeeded undetected — a false positive only blocks legitimate traffic
False negatives are easier to fix once the SOC tunes the IPS signature feed monthly
False positives cause more financial damage when blocked legitimate traffic is business-critical
They both have equal impact and consume comparable analyst time during alert triage
questions.exp: False negatives allow attacks through undetected. False positives are disruptive but don't result in successful attacks.

scenarios.q: A company deploys a network IPS inline between the internet-facing firewall and the internal network. After one week, the security team notices the IPS is blocking legitimate traffic from a key business partner's IP range due to a false positive on their encrypted VPN traffic. The operations team wants to disable the IPS entirely. What is the BEST approach?
opts: Disable the IPS — the risk of blocking legitimate traffic outweighs the security benefit
Accept all traffic from the partner's IP range as trusted and bypass IPS inspection
Replace the IPS with a firewall rule blocking all partner traffic
Move the IPS to a passive (IDS) mode — it will monitor and alert without blocking, then tune the rules using the alerts before re-enabling blocking mode
scenarios.exp: IPS tuning process: false positives on legitimate traffic are common when first deploying IPS. The correct response is not to disable it, but to tune — moving to detection-only (IDS mode) while tuning rules, then re-enabling blocking once rules are refined. Disabling entirely removes the protection. Bypassing all partner traffic creates a blind spot the attacker can exploit by spoofing the partner's IP range.

scenarios.q: A SOC analyst is reviewing IDS alerts and notices that a specific rule fires 2,000 times per day, but after reviewing 200 samples, all are legitimate network management traffic that happens to match the signature. The analyst asks whether to tune the rule or disable it. The security architect advises tuning. What is the difference between tuning and disabling, and why does it matter?
opts: Tuning and disabling are functionally the same — both stop noisy alerts from firing in the SOC, with no meaningful difference in detection coverage
Tuning requires purchasing additional IDS licenses for the advanced rule-editor module — most organizations skip it for that licensing cost
Disabling is more precise than tuning and is preferred — surgical removal of one noisy rule is cleaner than adding many exception conditions
Tuning adds conditions to the rule (e.g., exclude specific source IPs/protocols) so it fires on genuinely suspicious traffic. Disabling removes detection — creating a blind spot
scenarios.exp: Rule tuning vs disabling: a high-volume false positive rule seems useless but may catch real attacks with slightly different characteristics. Tuning (exclude the known-good management traffic by source IP or context) keeps the detection logic active for cases where a real attacker uses the same technique. Disabling tells attackers they can use that technique freely.

scenarios.q: An organization uses signature-based IDS to monitor their network. A red team conducts an assessment and successfully exfiltrates 50GB of data over 3 weeks using a novel technique that doesn't match any existing IDS signatures. The organization asks the IDS vendor why the data loss wasn't detected. What is the fundamental limitation the vendor would cite, and what additional control could have detected this?
opts: Signature-based IDS only detects known attack patterns — novel techniques without signatures are invisible. Anomaly/UEBA detection, which baselines normal behavior and alerts on deviations like unusual outbound data volumes, would have detected this
The IDS was misconfigured for the customer's network and should have detected the exfiltration — proper deployment in tap mode would have caught the slow-and-low pattern
The IDS needed more frequent signature updates — daily rather than weekly updates would have included the latest exfiltration patterns released by major threat-intel feeds
The data was encrypted in transit so the IDS couldn't inspect packet contents — this is a fundamental TLS visibility limitation that no amount of signature updates can address
scenarios.exp: Signature-based blind spot: novel techniques have no signatures. 50GB exfiltrated over 3 weeks at unusual hours would likely trigger anomaly-based detection (baseline deviation in data volume/timing) even without a specific signature. This is the core argument for layering anomaly-based and behavioral detection alongside signature-based IDS.

cram.def: Secure intermediary for accessing systems in protected network segments. Single point of access for admin.
Intermediary for client requests. Forward proxy: client to internet. Reverse proxy: internet to server.
Distributes traffic across multiple servers — improves availability and performance. Can perform SSL offloading.
One-way network device — data flows in one direction only. Used in high-security/OT environments.
Stateful firewall + application awareness + IPS + SSL inspection + user identification.

matching.prompt: Secure admin access to protected network segments
Intermediary between clients and internet
Intermediary between internet and internal servers
One-way data flow device
Stateful + app awareness + user ID + IPS

questions.q: A jump server (bastion host) is used to:
opts: Provide a single, secured, monitored access point for administrators to reach systems in protected network segments
Distribute web traffic across servers
Block malicious traffic at the network perimeter
Store authentication credentials
questions.exp: Jump servers are the single authorized path for administrative access to sensitive segments — all admin activity is logged and monitored.

questions.q: A data diode is used when:
opts: Data must only flow in one direction — preventing any return path that could be used for exfiltration or attack
Bidirectional traffic is required between paired control-system endpoints with low latency budgets
High-speed networking is required at line rate beyond what conventional firewalls can sustain
All traffic must be encrypted before crossing the security boundary, with key escrow
questions.exp: Data diodes physically allow only one-way data flow — used in OT/critical infrastructure to receive data without allowing anything back.

questions.q: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) differs from a traditional stateful firewall by:
opts: Being significantly faster but markedly less secure than the stateful firewall it replaces
Adding application awareness, user identification, SSL inspection, and integrated IPS to traditional stateful inspection
Using only signature-based detection without any session state tracking or anomaly checks
Operating at Layer 2 only and so unable to enforce policy on routed network traffic
questions.exp: NGFWs understand applications (not just ports), identify users, inspect encrypted traffic, and include integrated IPS.
