In active-active, both sites handle live traffic — failover is immediate. In active-passive, the passive site is idle and failover requires detection, activation, and data sync, adding minutes to the RTO. For real-time apps, that delay may be unacceptable
Active-passive cannot achieve 99.99% availability under any circumstances since failover delay always exceeds the 52-minute annual downtime budget allowed under that service-level tier
scenarios.exp: Active-active vs active-passive RTO: active-active failover is instantaneous — the load balancer redirects traffic to the surviving site immediately. Active-passive requires failure detection plus site activation time. For applications with sub-minute RTO requirements, even a 2-3 minute failover in active-passive is unacceptable. The cost saving must be weighed against the availability degradation.

scenarios.q: An organization uses a cold site as their disaster recovery option. The cold site has power, cooling, and network connectivity, but no hardware. During a disaster, the organization must purchase or lease servers, ship them to the cold site, install and configure them, restore data from offsite backups, and bring applications online. The process takes 5 days. What type of organization would find a cold site acceptable, and what type would not?
opts: Cold sites are never acceptable — all organizations should have hot sites
Cold sites are the most secure DR option because they have no equipment to be hacked
Cold sites are only used by government agencies

A cold site is acceptable for organizations with non-critical systems and RTO measured in days rather than hours — a small non-profit whose website downtime is tolerable, for example. It is unacceptable for organizations with strict RTO requirements (healthcare, financial trading, emergency services, e-commerce) where hours of downtime cause patient harm, financial loss exceeding the cost of a hot site, or regulatory violation. DR site tier must match the RTO derived from the BIA
scenarios.exp: Cold site fit: the BIA determines the acceptable RTO, which determines the DR site tier. Cold site = days of RTO (acceptable for low-criticality, cost-constrained). Warm site = hours. Hot site = minutes. The site type isn't a security classification — it's an availability investment calibrated to business criticality. A $500/month cold site for a critical hospital system is an under-investment; a hot site for a once-a-year charity fundraiser website is an over-investment.

cram.def: Ensuring sufficient resources (people, technology, infrastructure) to meet current and future demands.
Third-party security operations — SOC monitoring, threat intelligence, incident response.
Ability to increase capacity on demand. Cloud enables elastic scaling.

matching.prompt: Third-party security operations provider
Ability to increase resources on demand

questions.q: Capacity planning in security context addresses:
opts: Ensuring sufficient people, technology, and infrastructure resources to maintain security operations under normal and peak load
Only server hardware requirements forecasted from projected growth in compute workloads
Only budget planning for next year's security tooling and staffing line items
Only network bandwidth forecasting for production WAN links between data centers
questions.exp: Capacity planning covers all three dimensions: people (SOC analysts), technology (SIEM, compute), and infrastructure (power, space, cooling).

questions.q: An MSSP (Managed Security Service Provider) is used when:
opts: An organization wants to eliminate all security staff
An organization has unlimited security budget
An organization needs to augment its security capabilities with external expertise, 24/7 monitoring, or specialized skills
An MSSP replaces all security technology
questions.exp: MSSPs provide SOC monitoring, threat intelligence, and incident response — particularly valuable for organizations without large internal security teams.

scenarios.q: A growing e-commerce company's security operations team of 3 analysts is struggling to manage alerts from 15 security tools, monitor 24/7, investigate incidents, maintain security policies, conduct vulnerability assessments, and keep up with threat intelligence. The CISO asks for recommendations. What capacity planning solution BEST addresses this situation?
opts: Engage an MSSP (Managed Security Service Provider) for 24/7 alert monitoring and initial triage, freeing the internal team to focus on incident response, policy, and strategic security work that requires organizational context. Simultaneously implement SOAR to automate repetitive response tasks, reducing the manual workload the MSSP and internal team handle
Implement SOAR to automate all security operations without any analysts
Hire 50 additional security analysts immediately
Replace all 15 security tools with a single platform
scenarios.exp: People capacity through MSSP + automation: three analysts cannot sustainably cover 24/7 monitoring, incident response, and strategic security. MSSPs provide 24/7 SOC coverage with economies of scale; the internal team retains ownership of incidents, policies, and strategic decisions requiring internal knowledge. SOAR reduces mechanical workload for both the MSSP and internal team. This is a realistic capacity solution for a growing company.

scenarios.q: A company plans to migrate from on-premises infrastructure to cloud. The security architect notes that the migration will require the existing security team to develop new skills in cloud security, IAM, and CSPM tools, while simultaneously maintaining security operations for the on-premises systems during the transition. What capacity planning risk does this represent?
opts: No risk — cloud security is simpler than on-premises security
A skills and bandwidth capacity risk
Cloud migrations automatically improve security posture so the risk is overstated
The risk only applies to large enterprises, not mid-sized companies
scenarios.exp: The team must run two parallel operational environments (on-premises and cloud) during transition while upskilling in cloud-specific security disciplines. Without additional capacity (temporary contractors, MSSP coverage for routine monitoring, or a phased migration that doesn't overwhelm the team), security posture degrades in one or both environments during the transition period. Migration capacity risk: the 'two-speed operation' problem — maintaining existing systems while building new capability simultaneously. Security teams that are stretched thin during migrations make mistakes in both environments. Planning options: phased migration to reduce parallel operation duration, temporary contractor support for specific cloud skills, or MSSP coverage to free internal analyst time for upskilling.

cram.def: Discussion-based DR simulation — team talks through response to a scenario. No actual systems involved.
Recovery systems brought online alongside production — both running simultaneously. Validates recovery without risk.

audit_d_review.note: Parallel test; 3.4 Recovery Testing IS umbrella; parallel test is a recovery test type.

sybex_reference.section: Testing Resilience and Recovery Controls and Designs

Tabletop exercises are index-confirmed at p.284 (Ch 9 §Testing Resilience); parallel test is a sibling test type in the same section. Term may be in chapter prose. partial-depth retained.

cram.def: Production actually fails over to recovery — real outage. Most realistic, highest risk and cost.

audit_d_review.note: Full interruption test; same as item 9 (3.4 Recovery Testing umbrella).

sybex_reference.section: Testing Resilience and Recovery Controls and Designs

cram.def: Practicing specific DR scenarios — more realistic than tabletop but less disruptive than full test.
After any test or real incident — document what worked, what didn't, and update plans accordingly.

matching.prompt: Discussion-based scenario walkthrough
Recovery systems brought up alongside production
Production actually fails over — highest risk
Post-incident review of what worked/failed

questions.q: A tabletop exercise differs from a full interruption test in that:
opts: Tabletop tests use real systems and require failover of production traffic to recovery
Full interruption tests are cheaper and lower risk than tabletop discussions are by far
A tabletop exercise is discussion-based — no actual systems are involved or tested
They test different scenarios with no overlap in the threats or failures they address
questions.exp: Tabletop = talk through the plan. Full interruption = actually fail over production. Tabletop has no real-world impact.

questions.q: A full interruption test is the MOST realistic DR test because:
opts: It uses the most complex scenarios that include compounding failures and cyber incidents
Production actually fails over to recovery systems — revealing real-world issues that tabletop or parallel tests miss
It involves the most people because the entire IT organization must be physically on-site
It tests only network connectivity between primary and secondary sites at the WAN edge
questions.exp: Full interruption tests actual failover of production — the highest fidelity but also the highest risk and cost.

questions.q: DR plans should be tested:
opts: Only after a real disaster occurs, so that lessons learned go into the next plan revision
Never — testing risks causing an outage that could disrupt production for paying customers
Only when the board requests it as part of a regulatory or compliance review cycle
Regularly (at least annually) and after any significant infrastructure change
questions.exp: Untested DR plans often fail when needed — regular testing finds gaps before a real disaster. Annual minimum; test after major changes.

scenarios.q: A company conducts an annual disaster recovery tabletop exercise. The exercise scenario is: 'The primary data center has suffered a flood and is completely unavailable.' The IT director walks through the DR plan step by step with the team. After the exercise, the team reports the plan 'seems solid.' Six months later, a real disaster occurs and recovery takes 3 days instead of the planned 4 hours. What did the tabletop exercise fail to reveal?
opts: Tabletop exercises are always sufficient — the 3-day recovery was due to unforeseeable complications outside the scope of any test methodology that could have been applied earlier
The IT director should not have led the exercise — independent facilitation is required to surface hard truths that internal leadership would suppress during a friendly walkthrough
The tabletop exercise was conducted incorrectly — proper methodology calls for surprise scenarios delivered without prior notice, which weren't used in the company's annual exercise

Tabletop tests the plan on paper but doesn't reveal practical execution failures: stale replication, broken restore procedures, departed personnel, third-party dependencies, network differences. Parallel or full-interruption testing would have revealed these gaps
scenarios.exp: Tabletop vs operational testing: tabletop exercises reveal plan logic gaps and communication issues. They don't reveal whether the technical recovery actually works. The only way to know if backups restore correctly in the expected time is to restore them. The only way to know if the DR site comes up correctly is to bring it up. Annual tabletop only, with no actual recovery test, is a false sense of assurance.

scenarios.q: An organization conducts a parallel DR test — they bring up their recovery site while production remains running. The test is declared successful because all systems came online at the DR site. Three months later during a real failover, they discover their critical Oracle database had a 6-hour data lag because the replication was misconfigured after a DR test cleanup. What does this reveal about their parallel testing process?
opts: Parallel tests are less valuable than tabletop exercises since they can't surface plan-level coordination problems among the leadership team and stakeholders during the test scenario
The Oracle database should have been excluded from DR planning given how complex its replication is to validate without disrupting production traffic on the actual live application servers
Replication failures are undetectable until a real disaster — the only way to confirm replication is to actually fail over and accept the data-loss-or-no-loss outcome at runtime

The parallel test revealed systems could come up at the DR site but didn't validate data currency — a critical gap. Successful startup is not the same as successful replication. The test should have validated replication lag, data integrity, and post-test cleanup
scenarios.exp: Test scope vs test completeness: bringing systems online is necessary but not sufficient. Data currency, replication health, and post-test environment hygiene are equally important to validate. A DR test should explicitly verify: (1) systems boot, (2) data is current to within RPO, (3) applications function with DR data, (4) the test cleanup restores production replication correctly. Each of these can fail independently.

scenarios.q: A financial services firm's DR plan has never been tested with a full interruption test because management is concerned about the risk of a test-induced outage. The CISO argues an untested DR plan is more dangerous than the risk of a test. How should the CISO frame this argument?
opts: A DR plan that has never been tested provides false assurance — it may contain errors, outdated information, or technical failures that are only discovered during an actual disaster when the stakes are highest. The risk of a planned, controlled full interruption test (with rollback procedures, done during a low-traffic window) is calculable and manageable. The risk of discovering the plan doesn't work during an actual disaster is catastrophic and uncontrolled. Untested DR is effectively no DR
The CISO is wrong — testing DR plans always causes outages that justify never testing
Full interruption tests should be done daily to ensure readiness
The CISO should be overruled by operations management on this decision
scenarios.exp: Testing risk vs untested DR risk: a controlled test has known risks with prepared mitigations (rollback plan, test window, staff on standby). A real disaster with an untested plan has unknown risks at the worst possible time. The CISO's framing: 'we're choosing between a small, known risk now and a large, unknown risk when we can least afford it.' Most boards understand this once framed in business continuity terms.

cram.def: Complete copy of all data. Slowest to create, fastest to restore. Baseline for all other backup types.
Only data changed since LAST BACKUP (full or incremental). Fastest to create, slowest to restore.
All data changed since LAST FULL BACKUP. Slower to create than incremental, faster to restore.
3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite. Industry best practice.
Backup not connected to network — ransomware cannot reach it. Essential for ransomware resilience.
Regularly verify backups are complete and can be restored. An untested backup is not a backup.

matching.prompt: All data changed since last full backup

audit_d_review.note: Differential backup; 3.4 Backups IS umbrella; differential backup is a backup type.

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: A type of backup that stores all files that have been modified since the

sb_fix_2.note: STRONG T1 (glossary entry). Differential backup.

matching.prompt: All data changed since last backup of any type
Complete copy of all data
3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite
Not connected to network — ransomware-proof

questions.q: Which backup type backs up only data changed since the LAST FULL backup?
opts: Incremental
Full
Differential
Snapshot
questions.exp: Differential backs up everything changed since the last full — grows larger each day but restores with only 2 sets (full + latest differential).

questions.q: Which backup type is slowest to restore after a failure?
opts: Full backup
Incremental backup
Differential backup
Snapshot
questions.exp: Incremental restore requires the full backup plus every incremental since — the more incrementals, the longer the restore.

questions.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule states:
opts: Back up 3 times per day, to 2 locations, within 1 hour
Test 3 times, with 2 tools, in 1 year
Use 3 backup types, 2 vendors, 1 cloud provider
Keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with at least 1 copy stored offsite
questions.exp: 3-2-1: 3 copies (original + 2 backups), 2 media types (disk + tape), 1 offsite (protects against site disasters).

questions.q: Why are offline (air-gapped) backups essential for ransomware resilience?
opts: They are cheaper than online backups because tape media costs less per terabyte than cloud-stored object data
They comply with all regulations including HIPAA, PCI DSS, and GDPR backup retention requirements
Offline backups restore faster because tape sequential reads outpace random network access patterns
Ransomware cannot encrypt backups it cannot reach — network-connected backups are often encrypted by ransomware
questions.exp: Ransomware specifically targets backup systems — offline/air-gapped backups are the only way to guarantee recovery without paying ransom.

questions.q: An organization discovers their backup files are corrupted when they try to restore after a ransomware attack. This highlights the importance of:
opts: More frequent backups so the recovery point objective is much shorter than today
Regularly testing backups by actually restoring them — an untested backup provides false confidence
Using a different backup software vendor that offers better hardware sensor monitoring
Storing backups on faster media to reduce the duration of any future restore window
questions.exp: An untested backup is not a backup — regular restore testing is essential to confirm backups are complete and recoverable.

scenarios.q: A company takes daily full backups at midnight. A ransomware attack encrypts all file servers at 4pm on Wednesday. The company restores from Tuesday midnight's backup. After restoration, the IT director declares the incident resolved. The business team objects. What data loss has occurred, and was the RPO met?
opts: No data loss — the backup was from last night and any work done after the backup but before the encryption is recoverable from the user's local browser and application caches
The company should pay the ransom to recover Wednesday's data because no backup-based recovery can match the granularity needed for transactional data integrity in production
The backup was from Tuesday, which is more than 24 hours old — the RPO was definitely breached and the company has no defense against a regulatory complaint or audit finding

About 16 hours of data loss: files modified between Tuesday midnight and Wednesday 4pm aren't in the backup. If the RPO is 24 hours, 16 is within RPO — but if business RPO is stricter, the loss is real
scenarios.exp: RPO in practice: 16 hours of lost data (midnight to 4pm) is the actual loss. Whether this breaches RPO depends on the defined RPO value. If RPO = 24 hours, it's technically met. But business-critical data created Wednesday morning (orders, customer records, financial transactions) may not be recoverable — highlighting that IT RPO and business data criticality must be aligned. The business objection suggests the RPO was never properly defined with business input.

scenarios.q: A small accounting firm backs up all client data to an external hard drive stored in the server room. The firm's office suffers a fire that destroys both the primary server and the backup drive. The owner argues they had a backup strategy. What backup principle was violated, and what was the minimum required change?
opts: No principle was violated — any backup is better than none, and the firm at least had something to recover from in the event of pure data corruption affecting the primary copy
Two backup drives in the server room would have been sufficient redundancy — the multiple-copy requirement is satisfied without geographic separation between the copies on storage
The backup drive was the wrong type — tape backup would have survived the fire because tape cartridges are more thermally resistant than spinning disks under typical fire-ground temperatures

The 3-2-1 rule was violated, specifically the 1-copy-offsite part. On-site backups mean a site disaster destroys both primary and backup. Minimum fix: store one copy offsite — cloud, safety deposit, or partner location. The 'S' in 3-2-1 exists for site disasters
scenarios.exp: 3-2-1 rule — the '1 offsite' requirement: the purpose of the offsite copy is specifically to survive site-level disasters. Any backup stored at the same site as primary data is vulnerable to the same physical threats (fire, flood, theft, earthquake). Offsite doesn't need to be expensive — cloud backup services cost very little for small businesses and provide site-level disaster protection that no amount of on-site redundancy can provide.

scenarios.q: A company tests their backup restoration quarterly by restoring a sample of files and verifying they're accessible. During an actual ransomware incident, they attempt a full server restore and discover the backup job had been failing silently for 3 weeks due to a storage quota exceeded error — no alerts were configured for backup failures. The most recent restorable backup is 3 weeks old. What backup management failure occurred?
opts: The backup software had a bug that should be fixed by the vendor
The 3-week-old backup is acceptable — the company should restore from it and accept the data loss
The company should have used a different backup solution

Two failures: (1) no monitoring or alerting on backup job failures — backup jobs must have success/failure alerting so failures are discovered immediately, not during a disaster; (2) the restore testing methodology was insufficient — restoring sample files doesn't validate complete server restore capability or catch systematic backup failures. Both failures allowed 3 weeks of silent backup degradation to go undetected
scenarios.exp: Backup monitoring and testing gaps: backup jobs fail silently when no alerting is configured — this is one of the most common real-world DR failures. The second gap: file-level restore testing doesn't catch systematic failures (quota exceeded, job timeout, corruption) that would affect a full restore. Comprehensive backup testing must include: (1) automated success/failure alerting, (2) full restore exercises (not just file samples), and (3) validation that restored data is consistent and complete.

scenarios.q: An organization uses continuous replication to a secondary data center as their primary DR strategy, with no traditional backup. A database administrator accidentally runs a DROP TABLE command on the production database, deleting a critical table. The command replicates immediately to the secondary data center, which was the point-in-time source for recovery. What recovery limitation does this reveal about replication-only DR?
opts: Replication is always superior to backup — this scenario is not possible
The secondary data center should have had a read-only replica
Replication replicates data AND errors
The database administrator should not have had permission to run DROP TABLE
scenarios.exp: The accidental deletion propagated immediately to the replica. Without a point-in-time backup (such as database snapshots taken at regular intervals or a log-based backup allowing point-in-time recovery), the organization has no version of the table from before the deletion. Replication is excellent for site failure recovery but provides no protection against logical errors or user mistakes that propagate. Backups and replication serve different failure scenarios and both are needed. Replication vs backup for different failure types: replication protects against hardware/site failure. Backups protect against logical corruption, accidental deletion, malware encryption, and any error that replicates. A DROP TABLE replicates immediately — replication makes it worse (both sites lose the table). Point-in-time recovery (PITR) from backup allows restoration to the moment before the drop. Both mechanisms serve essential but different DR roles.

cram.def: Battery backup providing immediate power during outages — bridges gap until generator starts. Minutes of runtime.
Provides extended power during prolonged outages. Typically diesel. Takes time to start.
UPS provides instant power; generator provides extended power. Standard data center power resilience.
Full redundancy — two complete independent power systems. If one fails entirely, the other supports all load.
Critical equipment connected to two separate power circuits — one fails, other continues.

matching.prompt: Immediate battery power during outage
Extended power for prolonged outages
Full redundancy — two complete independent power systems
Critical equipment on two separate circuits

questions.q: The primary purpose of a UPS in a data center is:
opts: Providing power for extended outages lasting many hours when no generator is available
Regulating voltage during normal operation by smoothing the AC waveform on the utility feed
Providing immediate battery power to bridge the gap between power failure and generator startup
Distributing rack PDUs across redundant power paths inside each cabinet for cabling neatness
questions.exp: UPS provides instant power on failure — generators take time to start. UPS bridges this gap (typically minutes).

questions.q: 2N power configuration means:
opts: Two UPS units installed in series so a single failure trips the next downstream battery
Two backup generators sharing a common load bus with manual transfer between them
Power from two utility providers feeding the same single power distribution path
A completely redundant power system — every component duplicated, no shared paths between primary and backup
questions.exp: Two independent power paths for every component. 2N means double everything — two complete, independent power systems. If one fails entirely, the other supports all load.

questions.q: Dual power feeds for critical servers protect against:
opts: Power surges from utility provider lightning strikes during summer thunderstorm seasons
Single power circuit failure — if one feed loses power, the other continues delivering to the same critical load
Generator failure when the primary diesel generator's fuel pump seizes during operation
UPS battery depletion during multi-hour utility outages exceeding the runtime budget
questions.exp: If one circuit fails, the server continues on the second. Dual power feeds provide path redundancy at the equipment level — one feed fails, the other automatically takes full load.

scenarios.q: A company's data center has a single UPS providing battery backup for all servers. During a power failure, the UPS activates but fails after 4 minutes due to a faulty battery — the generator hasn't started yet. All servers crash, causing data corruption on 3 databases and a 6-hour recovery. What redundancy improvements would have prevented this outcome?
opts: Two issues: (1) UPS battery wasn't tested or maintained — UPS batteries degrade and must be tested under load; (2) single UPS is a single point of failure. Improvements: dual UPS, regular battery testing
Replace the UPS with a larger one — capacity was the issue and the existing unit simply didn't have enough kVA to bridge a 4-minute generator startup window during the failure event
Generators should start faster — 4 minutes is too slow and modern systems can transfer load in under 30 seconds with proper auto-start configuration of the transfer switch and starter battery
The servers should have been shut down gracefully before the power failure — a UPS-triggered automated shutdown would have prevented the 4-minute outage entirely if scripted in advance
scenarios.exp: UPS reliability requires maintenance: batteries degrade over time — a UPS reporting 10 minutes of runtime may only deliver 4 minutes on degraded batteries. Testing under load annually (or per manufacturer recommendation) reveals actual runtime. N+1 or 2N UPS design means no single UPS failure causes a complete power event. The generator start time must be less than the verified UPS runtime — not the rated runtime on degraded batteries.

scenarios.q: A financial trading firm requires its trading systems to have zero tolerance for power interruptions — even a 100ms power fluctuation can cause trading system crashes and corrupted transaction logs. The firm is evaluating power infrastructure options. Which power architecture BEST addresses this requirement?
opts: A single large UPS with a 4-hour runtime

2N power infrastructure: two completely independent power feeds from different utility substations, two independent UPS systems (each capable of carrying full load), a generator that starts within the UPS runtime, and servers with dual power supplies connected to separate PDUs fed from separate UPS systems — any single component failure results in no power interruption because the redundant path carries full load immediately
A generator without UPS — generators are more reliable than batteries
Standard N+1 UPS configuration with a single utility feed
scenarios.exp: 2N power for zero-tolerance environments: financial trading requires uninterrupted power at every level. 2N means: dual utility feeds (different substations), dual UPS (each full capacity), dual PDUs, and servers with dual PSUs. A utility feed failure, UPS failure, or PDU failure each result in zero interruption because the fully independent parallel path takes over instantly. This is the standard for Tier IV data centers and financial trading floors.

scenarios.q: During a security assessment, an auditor finds that a hospital's data center has a UPS that hasn't been tested in 3 years, a generator that was last exercised 18 months ago (fuel tank level unknown), and no written procedure for power failure response. The data center runs systems that support patient monitoring. What is the RISK ASSESSMENT of this finding?
opts: Low risk — power failures are rare and unlikely to occur, especially in a hospital with utility-grade redundancy provided by the regional power network and the grid as a stable infrastructure baseline

Critical risk: untested UPS may not provide expected runtime (batteries degrade silently); untested generator may fail to start (fuel contamination, mechanical issues, dead battery). For a hospital with patient monitoring, cascading UPS/generator failure is a patient safety event requiring action

Medium risk — the hospital has never had a power failure before, so the historical record suggests the existing equipment posture is adequate for the realistic likelihood of failure events under normal conditions

The risk is acceptable because the hospital has insurance covering operational interruptions — financial recovery from any single incident outweighs proactive maintenance investment by the facility-management department
scenarios.exp: Power resilience risk in healthcare: untested power infrastructure in a patient-critical environment is a patient safety issue, not just an IT risk. UPS batteries fail silently. Generators fail to start if not exercised. Three years without testing means unknown actual runtime. The combination of UPS, generator, and no procedure means a power failure could cascade into total failure with no fallback — a life-safety event for patients on monitoring equipment.

questions.q: Naomi wants to handle increasing load by scaling cloud‐hosted resources as needed while having the change remain transparent to users. She also wants to allow for upgrades and system replacements transparently. What solution should she select?
opts: Load balancing
Clustering
Geographic diversity
A hot site
questions.exp: Naomi should select a load balancing solution. Load balancers allow multiple systems or services to appear like a single resource and can take systems out of the load‐balanced pool to allow for upgrades or changes in resources required. Clustering is used to allow groups of computers to perform the same task, but without a load balancer cannot provide the same transparent service appearing as the same system. Geographic diversity and hot sites are concepts used to provide resilience but don’t provide this capability.

questions.q: Ellen is concerned about her company’s resilience and wants to ensure it can handle either changing loads or support disaster recovery and business continuity efforts if a primary location or datacenter were taken offline. Which of the following should she primarily focus on during her capacity planning?
opts: People, technology, and infrastructure
A generator and a UPS
RAID 0, 1, 5, and 10
Incremental, differential, and full backups
questions.exp: Resilience requires capacity planning to ensure that capacity—including staff, technology, and infrastructure—is available when is needed. Although a generator, UPS, various RAID levels, and backups have their place in disaster recovery and contingency planning, they are not the primary focus of resiliency and capacity planning.

questions.q: Madhuri has deployed a replication tool that copies data over to a secondary hot site in real time. What type of replication has she deployed?
opts: Synchronous replication
Journaled replication
Asynchronous replication
Snapshot‐based replication
questions.exp: Synchronous replication occurs in real time, whereas asynchronous replication occurs after the fact but more regularly than a backup. Journaled and snapshot‐based replication are not specific types of replication.

questions.q: How does technology diversity help ensure cybersecurity resilience?
opts: It ensures that a vulnerability in a single company’s product will not impact the entire infrastructure.
If a single vendor goes out of business, the company does not need to replace its entire infrastructure.
It means that a misconfiguration will not impact the company’s entire infrastructure.
All of the above.
questions.exp: Technology diversity helps ensure that a single failure—due to a vendor, vulnerability, or misconfiguration—will not impact an entire organization. Technology diversity does have additional costs, including training, patch management, and configuration management.

questions.q: Scott sends his backups to a company that keeps them in a secure vault. What type of backup solution has he implemented?
opts: Nearline
Safe
Onsite
Offsite
questions.exp: Scott has implemented an offsite backup scheme. His backups will take longer to retrieve because they are at a remote facility and will have to be sent back to him, but they are likely to survive any disaster that occurs in his facility or datacenter. Onsite backups are kept immediately accessible, whereas nearline backups can be retrieved somewhat more slowly than online backups but faster than offline backups. “Safe backups” is not an industry term.

questions.q: Florian wants to test his high‐availability designs but does not want to interrupt his organization’s normal work. Which of the following is the least disruptive testing scenario?
opts: A failover exercise
A tabletop exercise
A partial failover exercise
A simulation
questions.exp: A tabletop exercise is the least disruptive form of exercise. Even simulations have some risk if an employee does not fully realize that the scenario is simulated and takes action. Failover, even partial, involves the potential for disruption.

questions.q: Rick performs a backup that captures the changes since the last full backup. What type of backup has he performed?
opts: A new full backup
A snapshot
An incremental backup
A differential backup
questions.exp: Differential backups back up the changes since the last full backup. Incremental backups back up changes since the last backup, and snapshots are a live copy of a system. This is not a full backup, because it is capturing changes since a full backup.

questions.q: Gurvinder identifies a third‐party datacenter provider over 90 miles away to run his redundant datacenter operations. Why has he placed the datacenter that far away?
opts: Because it is required by law
Network traffic latency concerns
Geographic dispersion
Geographic tax reasons
questions.exp: Geographic dispersion helps ensure that a single natural or human‐made disaster does not disable multiple facilities. This distance is not required by law; latency increases with distance; and though there may be tax reasons in some cases, this is not a typical concern for a security professional.

questions.q: What type of recovery site has some or most systems in place but does not have the data needed to take over operations?
opts: A hot site
A warm site
A cloud site
A cold site
questions.exp: Warm sites have systems, connectivity, and power but do not have the live or current data to immediately take over operations. A hot site can immediately take over operations, whereas a cold site has space and power, and likely connectivity, but will require that systems and data be put in place to be used. Cloud sites are not one of the three common types of recovery sites.

questions.q: Ben wants to test his warm site to verify that it will take over operations successfully. What type of testing is this?
opts: Parallel processing
Simulation
Failover
A tabletop exercise
questions.exp: Testing that involves an actual failover to another site or service is failover testing. Parallel processing runs both sites or services at the same time; simulation and tabletops both review what would happen without making the actual change.

questions.q: Sally is working to restore her organization’s operations after a disaster took her datacenter offline. What critical document should she refer to as she restarts systems?
opts: The restoration order documentation
The TOTP documentation
The HOTP documentation
The last‐known good configuration documentation
questions.exp: A documented restoration order helps ensure that systems and services that have dependencies start in the right order and that high‐priority or mission‐critical services are restored first. TOTP and HOTP are types of one‐time password technology, and last‐known good configurations are often preserved with a snapshot or other technology that can allow a system to return to a known good status after an issue such as a bad patch or configuration change.

questions.q: Alecia wants to ensure that her backups cannot be accessed by third parties while stored in an offsite storage location. What should she do to secure her backups?
opts: Hash the backup data.
Avoid the use of offsite storage locations.
Employ security guards.
Encrypt the backup data.
questions.exp: Encryption is commonly used to ensure that backup media or data that is exposed is not accessible to third parties. This does mean that Alecia must carefully secure the encryption keys for the backup. Hashing that data would not keep it secure, and if only hashes were stored the data would be unrecoverable. Security guards are expensive and not a complete solution if data is inadvertently exposed, and offsite, secure storage locations are a useful and common solution for organizations that want to have remote backups.

questions.q: Fred wants to be able to recover his database transactions at any point in time if a physical disaster occurs involving his datacenter. His organization uses daily backups. What additional solution should he select to support this need?
opts: Onsite journaling
Onsite snapshots
Offsite journaling
Offsite snapshots
questions.exp: Offsite journaling will allow transactions to be recorded and to remain available if a significant event occurred that involved his datacenter. Snapshots are useful at a point in time but do not retain a transaction log between snapshots.

questions.q: Madhuri is designing a load‐balancing configuration for her company and wants to keep a single node from being overloaded. What type of design will meet this need?
opts: A daisy chain
Active/active
Duck‐duck‐goose
Active/passive
questions.exp: Active/active designs spread traffic among active nodes, helping ensure that a single node will not be overwhelmed. Active/passive designs are useful for disaster recovery and business continuity, but they do not directly address heavy load on a single node. There are many load‐balancing schemes, but daisy chains and duck‐duck‐goose are not among them.

questions.q: Janet is the cybersecurity lead for a medium‐sized company located in a hurricane‐prone region. She’s been tasked with designing a plan to ensure the company’s systems remain available and functional, even during a natural disaster. What strategy should she prioritize to maximize resilience and support continuity of operations?
opts: Store all company data on physical servers in a highly secure location.
Use a highly sophisticated cryptographic solution for all systems.
Establish backup datacenters at least 90 miles apart and in a non‐hurricane‐prone region.
Depend solely on uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems for power‐related contingencies.
questions.exp: A resilient cybersecurity strategy would emphasize multiple, distributed redundancies to prevent any single point of failure. Therefore, having backup datacenters located at least 90 miles apart and in a region not prone to hurricanes helps guard against geographically based disasters. Using a single data storage location or relying on a single cryptographic solution doesn’t provide this redundancy, making these strategies insufficient for maximizing resilience. Lastly, while UPS systems are essential for power continuity, they only provide backup power for short periods; thus, relying solely on them won’t fully address longer‐term power outages or wider network and system failures.

questions.q: Simon is a system administrator for a technology firm. His organization has high data modification and transaction rates. They need a RAID solution that offers high read speeds, has a fault tolerance for at least one disk failure, and does not require double the storage. Which RAID level should Simon choose for his organization?
opts: RAID 0
RAID 1
RAID 5
RAID 10
questions.exp: Simon should choose RAID 5. This RAID level stripes data across drives with one drive used for parity (checksum) of the data. It offers high read speeds and can sustain a single drive failure without losing data, which aligns with the requirements of Simon’s organization. It does not require double the storage, unlike RAID 1, which is a significant advantage in a high data transaction environment. RAID 0, while providing better I/O performance, is not fault tolerant—all data is lost if a drive fails; hence it is not suitable for Simon’s requirements. RAID 10 is similar to RAID 5 but adds additional performance benefits. However, it does require double the storage of a non‐RAID solution because it uses mirroring. Therefore, it does not meet Simon’s requirements.

questions.q: Brianna is concerned about undervoltage events and short power outages for her systems in a datacenter. What type of power protection should she put in place to help keep her systems online?
opts: A generator
Dual‐power supplies
PDUs
A UPS
questions.exp: A UPS (uninterruptible power supply) relies on batteries or other stored power to keep systems online during short power outages, and it can also provide stable power during power sags and undervoltage events. A generator is needed for longer outages, because most UPS systems are intended to stay online for only a few minutes. Dual‐power supplies are used to ensure that a single power supply failing or a single power source failing does not take down a server. A power distribution unit (PDU) is used to deliver power to devices. Dual‐power supplies are used to ensure that a single power supply failing or a single power source failing does not take down a server.

questions.q: As part of her organization’s response and recovery controls, Charlene has implemented a remote site that has all the systems needed to operate her company’s IT infrastructure. In the event of a major outage or issue, she would need to bring copies of data to the site. What type of disaster recovery site has she set up?
opts: Cold site
Warm site
Hot site
Availability zone
questions.exp: A warm site has all the hardware and networking needed to run essential operations, but it does not have the data ready to go. A cold site is essentially just space to bring in equipment, networking, and data. A hot site has everything you need, and you may have to bring just the last data update. Availability zones are a cloud computing concept used by Amazon.

questions.q: Sarah’s security team has recommended that she place the offsite storage facility for her organization’s backups at least 90 miles away from the primary office location. What is the primary driver of this recommendation?
opts: Placing the offsite storage facility 90 miles away prevents theft by making the backups hard to get to for local thieves.
Ninety miles away is the minimum distance to prevent latency issues for backups.
Placing the offsite storage facility 90 miles away means a single disaster won’t destroy both the main facility and the backups.
Placing the offsite storage facility 90 miles away ensures that different local jurisdiction laws will apply, making it harder for a single legal case to involve the primary data and the backups.
questions.exp: Geographic diversity is an important concept for redundant sites and backup locations. Although the minimum distance considered safe varies based on the guidelines you choose to follow, a distance like this is intended to ensure that a single disaster cannot destroy both the primary datacenter or storage location and the backups. Although the remainder of the answers may sound reasonable, they are not actual reasons for this type of geographic dispersion.

questions.q: Hank has purchased servers that have dual power supplies. How should he connect the power supplies to ensure that systems stay online?
opts: Connect both power supplies to the same UPS or power distribution system.
Connect the power supplies to different UPS or power distribution systems.
Leave one power supply disconnected so that it can be enabled in case of an issue.
Leave one power supply disconnected to avoid providing too much power to the system.
questions.exp: A dual power supply system is typically connected to two different power infrastructures to ensure that, if one side fails, the server or system will remain online. This is part of designing and building a fully redundant power infrastructure.

questions.q: Chris operates a database‐driven e‐commerce website and wants to be able to restore his backups to the point in time when an outage occurs, resulting in a very short recovery point objective (RPO). What type of backup capability will he need to be able to do this without losing data?
opts: Disk‐based backup
Cloud‐based backup
Journaling
Snapshots
questions.exp: Organizations that want to restore databases to a point in time due to a small or short recovery point objective will deploy journaling technology. This will replay transactions to restore a database to a given point in time after it is restored from a backup point. Snapshots, disk, and cloud‐based backups can be used for the underlying backup, but journaling provides the to‐the‐moment restoration capability desired to lose minimal transactions.

questions.q: Which of the following types of exercises is most similar to a real event?
opts: Failover
Parallel processing
Simulations
Tabletop exercises
questions.exp: Failover exercises require organizations to actually switch to the backup systems or location. This is the closest to a real event of the four answers. Parallel processing, simulations, and tabletop exercises come next by similarity to a real event.

questions.q: Bart runs a backup service for his organization, and every day he backs up the changes since the last backup operation he performed. If today’s only backed up the changes since the last backup operation, what type of backup is he performing?
opts: Differential
Full
Incremental
Partial
questions.exp: Bart is conducting an incremental backup. Differential backups back up all data that has changed since the last full backup. Incremental backups back up the changes since the last full or incremental backup. Full backups back up all data, and partial backups are not a defined technical term.

cram.def: Minimum security configuration a system must meet. Starting point for all deployments.
Systems gradually diverging from secure baseline through undocumented changes.
Security Content Automation Protocol — NIST standard for automated security configuration assessment.
Prescriptive configuration guides used as security baselines.
Apply via GPO, MDM, Ansible, Puppet, Chef.

matching.prompt: Minimum security configuration all systems must meet
Systems diverging from secure baseline
NIST standard for automated config compliance checking

questions.q: A security baseline defines:
opts: The minimum security configuration required for all systems in the environment
The maximum security controls allowed
The average security level across systems
Security policies for administrators only
questions.exp: A security baseline is the minimum standard — every deployed system must meet or exceed it.

questions.q: Configuration drift is:
opts: Systems gradually diverging from their secure baseline through undocumented changes
Systems becoming progressively more secure over time as patches and updates are applied
The formal change process for updating an established secure baseline configuration
Migrating systems from one operating system version to another newer release
questions.exp: Drift occurs as changes accumulate — moving systems away from the known-good baseline.

questions.q: SCAP is used to:
opts: Automate security configuration assessment and compliance verification against defined standards
Conduct external penetration tests against perimeter-facing services on a quarterly basis
Monitor real-time network traffic flow patterns for anomalies on internal segments
Manage user identities and group memberships across federated directory environments
questions.exp: SCAP provides a standardized, automated way to check whether systems meet security configuration requirements.

scenarios.q: An organization deploys 300 new Windows workstations using a golden image. Six months later, a vulnerability scan reveals that 47 workstations have weak TLS cipher suites enabled, 23 have SMBv1 active, and 12 have the local administrator account enabled with a known default password. The security team thought the golden image hardened all of these. What most likely caused this drift?
opts: The golden image was never hardened correctly
The vulnerability scanner produced false positives
Configuration drift
The workstations received a Windows update that changed security settings
scenarios.exp: After deployment, workstations were modified by local administrators, software installs, or troubleshooting procedures that changed settings from the baseline. Group Policy enforcement was likely not configured to continuously reapply and remediate settings that drift from baseline. Configuration drift cause: hardened images start secure, but post-deployment changes accumulate. Local admin access, troubleshooting steps, and software installations change settings. Group Policy with enforcement (not just application at login) continuously remediate drift. Without continuous enforcement and monitoring (SCAP scanning, GPO enforcement), systems gradually diverge from the known-good baseline.

scenarios.q: A compliance auditor reviews a company's server baseline configuration and finds it was created 4 years ago, before a major cloud migration, and has not been updated since. The baseline still references on-premises-specific settings (local user accounts, physical NIC configurations) but says nothing about cloud security groups, IAM roles, or metadata service configuration. What is the security impact?
opts: No impact — baselines only need to be created once
The auditor should accept the baseline as-is since the company completed the migration
Baselines should be recreated every week to stay current

The baseline is outdated and no longer reflects the current threat model or environment — systems are being 'baselined' against irrelevant criteria while actual cloud-specific attack surfaces (IMDSv1 misconfiguration, overprivileged IAM roles, open security groups) go unaddressed. A baseline must be maintained and updated as the environment evolves, incorporating current threats and technology
scenarios.exp: Baseline currency: a baseline that doesn't match the current environment gives false assurance — systems pass the 'baseline check' on irrelevant criteria while real vulnerabilities go unmeasured. Baselines must evolve with the environment, be reviewed after major changes (cloud migration, new technology), and incorporate current framework guidance (CIS Benchmarks release new versions as threats evolve).

scenarios.q: A security team uses SCAP content to automatically assess workstation compliance against CIS Benchmark Level 2 for Windows 10. The scan reports 91% compliance across 500 workstations. The team marks this as 'acceptable' and moves on. A security architect reviews and disagrees. Why?
opts: 91% compliance is excellent — the architect is being too strict

91% means 9% of controls fail across 500 workstations — that could be 45 workstations each missing a single control, or 5 workstations each missing 9 controls. The team needs to understand WHICH controls are failing and on WHICH systems. A single critical control failure (e.g., BitLocker disabled on a laptop) on 5 systems is more serious than 45 minor UI setting deviations. Aggregate compliance percentages hide individual risk — the team must review the specific failures
The SCAP tool is not approved for this use
CIS Benchmark Level 2 is too strict for workstations
scenarios.exp: Compliance percentage analysis: aggregate numbers mask individual risk. The right question is: what specifically is failing? A 9% non-compliance rate on trivial UI settings is different from 9% non-compliance on encryption or patching controls. Security teams must triage by control criticality, not just percentage. A single critical control failure on 5 systems may be more urgent than 100 minor configuration deviations.

cram.def: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH not Telnet, update firmware.
Minimal OS install, disable unnecessary services, patch promptly, host-based firewall.
Air gap where possible, patch carefully (availability priority), segment from corporate network.
MDM enrollment, container separation of corporate/personal data, remote wipe capability.
Network segmentation is most important — isolate in separate VLAN.

matching.prompt: Hardening first step — network devices
Encrypted admin for network devices
Air gap or strict segmentation for

questions.q: When hardening a new network switch, the FIRST action should be:
opts: Enable all available switch features so monitoring tools have maximum visibility from day one
Configure 802.1Q VLANs and trunk ports to match the network architecture immediately
Update the switch firmware to the latest vendor release before doing anything else
Change all default credentials — vendor-supplied admin/root passwords are publicly known and must be replaced first
questions.exp: Default credentials are publicly known — changing them immediately is the critical first hardening step.

questions.q: ICS/SCADA hardening differs from standard IT hardening because:
opts: ICS systems use stronger encryption protocols by default than standard IT systems do
ICS systems never need patching because their firmware is provably secure by design
Availability is the top priority — patches and downtime must be planned carefully to avoid disrupting critical processes
ICS systems cannot be networked to corporate IT environments under any circumstances
questions.exp: In ICS/SCADA, disruption of physical processes is unacceptable — security changes must be planned around operational windows.

questions.q: Which hardening technique is most important for IoT devices with limited security features?
opts: Installing endpoint protection software on each constrained IoT device's onboard storage
Full disk encryption on every IoT device's flash storage using hardware-rooted keys
Network segmentation — isolating IoT devices on dedicated VLANs
Deploying a host-based firewall directly onto each IoT device's microcontroller stack
questions.exp: Isolating IoT devices in a separate VLAN away from critical systems. IoT devices often cannot be hardened directly — isolating them in a separate network segment limits the damage if they're compromised.

questions.q: An organization is hardening three different asset classes: enterprise servers, employee mobile devices, and IoT sensors deployed in a manufacturing plant. Which hardening priority is MOST distinctive to IoT (i.e. the priority that most differentiates IoT hardening from server or mobile hardening)?
opts: Strong password complexity policies — IoT devices benefit from the same password rules used for enterprise servers and managed laptops
Full-disk encryption — IoT devices must have encrypted local storage in a way that servers and mobile devices typically do not require for routine deployments
Disabling unnecessary services and changing default credentials — IoT devices ship with well-known defaults cataloged in attack tools, and run services not needed in the deployed environment
Frequent operating-system patching via the device vendor — IoT vendors push patches monthly the same way Microsoft and Apple do for their fleets
questions.exp: IoT hardening's most distinctive characteristic is that devices ship with well-known default credentials (often documented publicly and built into bot-net tools like Mirai), and many run services that are not needed in the deployed environment — so changing defaults and disabling unneeded services is the highest-leverage IoT-specific action. Password complexity helps but applies broadly. Full-disk encryption is more critical for mobile/laptop than for stationary IoT sensors. IoT vendors are notoriously irregular about patches — many devices receive no patches after the first year — so patching is harder, not easier, than for servers and mobile.

scenarios.q: A healthcare organization connects medical imaging devices (MRI, CT scanners) to the hospital network. These devices run Windows XP Embedded with no available patches, cannot have antivirus installed, and must be available 24/7. A security engineer proposes a compensating control strategy. Which combination BEST reduces risk without disrupting clinical operations?
opts: Disconnect all imaging devices from the network permanently
Install antivirus on the Windows XP systems using a third-party solution
Upgrade all devices to Windows 10 before reconnecting to the network

Network segmentation placing imaging devices on an isolated VLAN with strict firewall rules permitting only the specific ports required for imaging workflows (DICOM protocol to the PACS server), combined with enhanced monitoring of all traffic to/from the imaging VLAN for anomalies
scenarios.exp: IoT/medical device hardening via compensating controls: devices that cannot be patched or have AV installed must be protected at the network level. VLAN isolation limits what the device can reach if compromised; strict firewall rules limit inbound attack surface; DICOM-specific rules ensure only legitimate imaging traffic is permitted. Monitoring detects anomalies. This is the standard approach for unhardenable embedded systems.

scenarios.q: A company deploys a fleet of Android tablets for retail employees to process customer transactions. The tablets are enrolled in MDM, which enforces screen lock, encryption, and prevents sideloading. An employee reports their tablet was left unlocked on a counter and a customer may have accessed it. The security team reviews MDM logs. What hardening control would have automatically protected the tablet after the employee walked away?
opts: Screen auto-lock with a short timeout (e.g., 30 seconds of inactivity) enforced by MDM policy — an unlocked tablet left unattended automatically locks itself, requiring re-authentication before the next transaction. This is a fundamental mobile device hardening control that doesn't rely on employee behavior
Remote wipe — the device should have been wiped immediately
Full disk encryption — encrypted tablets cannot be accessed by customers
A more complex PIN — the customer couldn't have guessed a complex PIN
scenarios.exp: Auto-lock timeout: the simplest and most effective control for unattended device scenarios. MDM-enforced auto-lock after 30 seconds means even if an employee forgets to lock manually, the device locks itself. No amount of encryption or complex PINs helps if the device is left unlocked — the auto-lock is the last line of defense for physical access scenarios.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester is assessing a company's network device security. They use the default credentials 'admin/admin' to log into a core switch, then 'cisco/cisco' to access a router, and find a firewall still accessible on its management interface from the internet using the vendor default username and password. The company's IT team says these are 'internal devices' and assumed they were secure. What does this assessment demonstrate?
opts: The penetration tester used advanced techniques — these attacks cannot be prevented

Default credential attacks are the most trivially executed class of attack — they require no technical skill, only the ability to find vendor default credentials in publicly available documentation. 'Internal' doesn't mean 'secure from an attacker who has compromised any internal system.' Every network device must have its default credentials changed before production deployment, and management interfaces must not be accessible from untrusted network segments
The company should have used a VPN to protect management interfaces
Default credentials are acceptable for internal devices not facing the internet
scenarios.exp: Default credentials are trivially exploitable: vendor defaults are published online. Any attacker with internal network access (via phishing, physical access, or supply chain) immediately tries defaults. 'Internal only' is not a security boundary — it's a network constraint that can be crossed. Changing defaults is step zero of device hardening, non-negotiable for every device regardless of network position.

cram.def: Physical survey to plan AP placement, measure signal strength, identify interference.
Company owns device but allows personal use. Better control than BYOD.
Employee selects from company-approved device list. Company manages selected device.
Restricts device functionality based on geographic location.
Manages individual applications rather than the whole device — more granular than MDM.

audit_d_review.note: MAM; 4.1 Securing Wireless and Mobile IS umbrella; MAM is a mobile management specific.

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: Application management allows enterprise control of applications

sb_fix_2.note: STRONG T1 (glossary entry + index 445-448). MAM (Mobile Application Management).

matching.prompt: Physical survey planning AP placement
Company owns device, allows personal use
Employee chooses from approved device list
Restricts device based on geographic location

questions.q: A wireless site survey is performed to:
opts: Test network speed only by running iperf bandwidth tests at each candidate access point location
Scan for rogue access points broadcasting unauthorized SSIDs near the corporate facility
Plan optimal access point placement and measure signal coverage before and after deployment
Test wireless encryption strength by attempting WPA2 handshake captures at each location
questions.exp: Site surveys map signal strength, identify interference, and optimize AP placement for coverage, performance, and security.

questions.q: COPE (Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled) differs from BYOD in that:
opts: The company owns the COPE device
COPE allows any personal device
COPE devices cannot have personal apps
COPE is more expensive than BYOD always
questions.exp: Giving greater control than BYOD while allowing limited personal use. COPE: company buys and owns the device, allowing personal use. BYOD: employee's own device. COPE provides more corporate control.

questions.q: Geofencing is used in mobile device management to:
opts: Track device GPS coordinates continuously for asset management inventory reporting only
Improve wireless signal strength to enrolled corporate devices in the same geographic region
Restrict device functionality or access based on geographic location — blocking corporate access outside defined areas
Monitor battery usage patterns to detect compromised devices reporting unusual telemetry
questions.exp: Geofencing can disable corporate apps or access when the device leaves defined geographic boundaries.

questions.q: An organization is documenting three mobile device deployment models that it offers to different employee groups: (1) employees can use their personal smartphones for work email and corporate apps; (2) the company buys smartphones for sales staff and explicitly allows personal use too; (3) employees choose from a company-approved list of laptops, which the company purchases and owns. Which set of model labels matches in order?
opts: (1) BYOD; (2) COPE; (3) CYOD
(1) COPE; (2) BYOD; (3) CYOD
(1) CYOD; (2) BYOD; (3) COPE
(1) BYOD; (2) CYOD; (3) COPE
questions.exp: BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) — employee-owned, employee-managed (with optional MDM enrollment for corporate data); selective wipe is the typical data-removal authority (corporate data only, personal data untouched). COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally-Enabled) — corporate buys the device but explicitly allows personal use; full MDM and full-device wipe authority. CYOD (Choose Your Own Device) — employee selects from a company-approved list of devices that the company buys and owns; full MDM and full-device wipe. The three models distinguish primarily by ownership and data-wipe authority.

scenarios.q: A company's BYOD policy allows employees to use personal smartphones for work email and calendar access via a corporate MDM profile. An employee is dismissed for cause and their access is revoked. The IT team uses MDM to perform a 'selective wipe,' removing the corporate MDM profile and associated data. The employee calls to confirm their personal photos and apps are unaffected. What should the IT team confirm?
opts: The selective wipe removed only the corporate MDM container — corporate email, calendar, contacts, and corporate app data were removed, but personal photos, apps, and data outside the MDM profile are untouched. This is the designed purpose of MDM containerization for BYOD — corporate data can be removed without touching personal data
All data has been wiped — selective wipe removes everything for security
The employee must factory reset their device to verify
The MDM logs will show which files were deleted
scenarios.exp: MDM selective wipe for BYOD: containerization separates corporate and personal data. Selective wipe removes only the corporate container. This is the legal and practical compromise for BYOD — employees accept MDM to access corporate resources, but the organization commits to only touching corporate data. Full device wipe on personal devices raises legal issues; selective wipe on containerized data does not.

scenarios.q: A sales team uses COPE (Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled) smartphones. The company pays for the devices and plans, allows personal use, and manages them via MDM. A salesperson notices the MDM can track their GPS location continuously. They raise a privacy concern. The IT team explains this is necessary for asset tracking. What is the BEST policy response that balances security and employee privacy?
opts: Continuous GPS tracking is required and employees must accept it
Disable GPS tracking entirely — it creates too much legal risk
Replace COPE with BYOD — BYOD gives employees more privacy

Configure MDM location tracking to be active only during business hours (or disable it entirely on COPE devices, relying on device remote wipe as the primary asset recovery tool), document the tracking policy clearly in the acceptable use agreement, and ensure employees acknowledge it at enrollment. For COPE devices used for personal activities outside work hours, continuous location tracking is disproportionate to the security benefit
scenarios.exp: COPE privacy policy: employees bring personal lives to corporate devices in COPE programs. Continuous GPS tracking of off-hours location is a significant privacy intrusion with limited security benefit (remote wipe achieves device control without tracking). The appropriate control: time-limited or opt-in tracking, transparent AUP acknowledgement, and proportionate controls (remote wipe > constant surveillance). This is increasingly a legal requirement in jurisdictions with strong employee privacy laws.

scenarios.q: During a wireless site survey of a new office space, the survey team discovers significant RF interference in the 2.4GHz band from neighboring tenant equipment, but clean spectrum in the 5GHz band. The team also finds three dead zones near the server room where the metal walls attenuate signal. What should the site survey report recommend?
opts: Deploy all APs on 2.4GHz since it has better range
Install a Faraday cage around the server room to eliminate the attenuation
Use fewer APs with higher transmit power to compensate for dead zones

Deploy APs on 5GHz to avoid the interference from neighboring tenants, add APs or adjust placement to eliminate dead zones near the server room, and document the physical layout and RF measurements for future reference. Consider band steering to direct capable devices to 5GHz while maintaining 2.4GHz for legacy devices that don't support 5GHz
scenarios.exp: Site survey findings drive design: the survey exists to reveal exactly these issues before deployment. 5GHz recommendation addresses the interference; additional AP placement addresses dead zones. Site surveys are not just signal strength maps — they inform AP count, placement, channel planning, and band selection decisions. Deploying without acting on survey findings defeats the purpose.

scenarios.q: A company allows BYOD for employee smartphones. An employee enrolls their personal iPhone in the corporate MDM to access email and Slack. Six months later, the employee leaves the company. The MOST appropriate action by the IT team for the device is:
opts: Full device wipe — restore the iPhone to factory defaults so all data (corporate AND personal) is removed, ensuring no corporate residue remains anywhere
Selective wipe via MDM — remove only the corporate profile, corporate apps, and corporate data (email, Slack, certificates); the employee's personal photos, contacts, and apps remain untouched
Demand the employee surrender the personal device for forensic imaging before any wipe occurs, since the device may contain evidence of company data
Take no action — the employee's personal device is their property and the company has no authority to act on it after departure under any circumstances
scenarios.exp: For BYOD, the appropriate scope of corporate authority is the corporate data only — the device remains the employee's property, so a full wipe (which would destroy personal photos, contacts, apps) is not authorized and is also unnecessary. Selective wipe via MDM removes only the corporate profile, corporate apps, and corporate data (email, Slack, certificates) while leaving personal data intact. Demanding forensic imaging of a personal device is not warranted by routine departure (it would require legal cause). Taking no action leaves corporate data on the device, which is unacceptable. The selective-wipe capability is exactly why MDM enrollment is required for BYOD.

cram.def: Latest wireless security. SAE replaces PSK. Resistant to offline attacks. Perfect forward secrecy.
Pre-shared key (PSK). Single password for all users.
802.1X with RADIUS. Per-user authentication. Unique session keys per user.
WPA3 replacement for PSK. Resistant to offline dictionary attacks.
Requires certificates on both client and server. Strongest EAP method.
8-digit PIN can be brute-forced in ~11,000 attempts. Disable WPS entirely.

matching.prompt: WPA3 replacement for PSK
Per-user authentication using RADIUS
EAP type requiring certificates on both sides
Single PSK shared by all users

questions.q: WPA3-Personal improves on WPA2-Personal primarily because:
opts: It uses longer passwords by mandating a 16-character minimum on every WPA3 PSK
It uses AES-256 instead of AES-128 by default for all session encryption traffic
SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces PSK — preventing offline dictionary attacks
It requires X.509 client certificates instead of any pre-shared secret material
questions.exp: Providing resistance to offline dictionary attacks and perfect forward secrecy. WPA3's SAE protocol prevents offline cracking of captured handshakes and provides PFS.

questions.q: WPA2-Enterprise is more secure than WPA2-Personal because:
opts: It uses stronger AES encryption with a longer key length than WPA2-Personal AES-128 CCMP
Per-user authentication via 802.1X/RADIUS — each user has unique credentials and unique session keys
It is faster because session keys are pre-computed and cached at the access point during boot
It doesn't require any passwords because every user's device is enrolled by serial number
questions.exp: Enterprise: each user authenticates individually — no shared PSK. Unique session keys per user improve isolation.

questions.q: Disabling WPS on wireless access points mitigates:
opts: Evil twin attacks where a rogue AP impersonates a legitimate corporate SSID to capture clients
Deauthentication attacks that flood the channel with spoofed 802.11 management frames
Encryption downgrade attacks that force WPA2-AES sessions back down to WEP-RC4 ciphers
Brute-force attacks against the WPS PIN (which has a fundamental design flaw allowing ~11,000 attempts)
questions.exp: WPS PIN can be brute-forced in ~11,000 attempts due to its design — disabling WPS entirely is the only mitigation.

questions.q: WPA3-Personal replaces WPA2-Personal's 4-way PSK handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals). The PRIMARY vulnerability that SAE was designed to fix is:
opts: WPA2-PSK transmitted the pre-shared key in plaintext over the air during association
WPA2-PSK's 4-way handshake exposed material that allowed offline dictionary attacks against the captured handshake
WPA2-PSK lacked any form of authentication entirely, allowing any client to associate without a password
WPA2-PSK used DES encryption, which has been deprecated since the early 2000s for being computationally weak
questions.exp: SAE (a Dragonfly key exchange) provides forward secrecy and resistance to offline cracking even when the password is weak — its central improvement is eliminating the offline-dictionary-attack window that WPA2-PSK's 4-way handshake exposed (an attacker who captured the handshake could brute-force the PSK offline at unlimited speed). WPA2-PSK never transmits the PSK in plaintext, it does authenticate via PSK derivation, and it uses AES-CCMP (not DES). The KRACK family of attacks against the 4-way handshake is the historical context for SAE's design.

questions.q: An organization protecting classified or highly sensitive data over its wireless network is choosing between WPA3-Personal (SAE) and WPA3-Enterprise with the 192-bit mode. The PRIMARY reason to choose WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit over WPA3-Personal in this scenario is:
opts: WPA3-Personal (SAE) and WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit have identical security properties — only the marketing names differ; either mode is suitable for classified data handling
WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit is intended for guest networks while WPA3-Personal is intended for employee networks — the 192-bit mode is specifically a guest-isolation feature
WPA3-Personal (SAE) is faster than WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit, and the performance advantage is the primary reason it is chosen for high-sensitivity wireless networks

WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit pairs 802.1X per-user authentication with a 192-bit cryptographic suite (AES-256-GCM, BIP-GMAC-256) meeting CNSA-tier requirements; WPA3-Personal uses a shared SAE password and a lower-tier cryptographic suite
questions.exp: WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode requires a 192-bit cryptographic suite — typically AES-256-GCM for unicast traffic and BIP-GMAC-256 for management frames — and uses 802.1X authentication with per-user credentials. The combination meets the US government's Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) suite requirements for handling sensitive and classified data over wireless. WPA3-Personal (SAE) uses a shared password and a lower-tier cryptographic suite; while SAE itself defeats offline dictionary attacks, the shared-credential model and lower crypto are not appropriate for classified data. Naming alone does not capture the difference, performance is not the structural distinction, and the 192-bit mode is not a guest-network feature.

scenarios.q: A company is migrating their wireless network from WPA2-Personal to WPA2-Enterprise. The project manager asks why the migration takes months rather than days, given it's 'just a different authentication method.' What does the migration actually require?
opts: WPA2-Enterprise requires faster access points with newer 802.11ac/ax chipsets that must be purchased and installed before any migration can begin
The migration is simple — it just requires updating the SSID password and pushing the new password to every connected device manually
WPA2-Enterprise requires replacing all current access points with new enterprise-grade hardware that's specifically compatible with 802.1X
WPA2-Enterprise requires 802.1X infrastructure: a RADIUS server, certificate or AD integration, supplicant configuration on every device, and user training. It's an identity infrastructure project
scenarios.exp: WPA2-Enterprise migration complexity: the 'just change authentication' framing understates the infrastructure required. RADIUS server deployment, PKI for certificates, supplicant configuration at scale across all devices (requiring GPO, MDM, or manual configuration), and potential user training are all real project components. Project managers need accurate scoping — underestimating this leads to incomplete deployments where some devices fall back to WPA2-Personal.

scenarios.q: A wireless network uses WPA2-Personal with a pre-shared key. An employee who is leaving the company is concerned about retaining access after departure. The IT team rotates the PSK. Three other employees immediately call the helpdesk because their devices stopped connecting. What architectural limitation does this reveal, and what is the long-term solution?
opts: The PSK was set incorrectly — check the configuration
The employee should be physically prevented from accessing the building instead
WPA2-Personal should use a longer PSK to prevent this issue
