WPA2-Personal has a fundamental architectural limitation: all users share the same PSK. Revoking one user's access requires changing the key for everyone, then reconfiguring all devices. The long-term solution is WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X — each user authenticates with individual credentials. Revoking access means disabling that user's account in AD/RADIUS, which immediately prevents their wireless access without affecting any other user
scenarios.exp: PSK rekeying impact is a WPA2-Personal design limitation: one key for everyone means any access change affects everyone. This is why Enterprise authentication exists — per-user credentials allow per-user revocation. The helpdesk calls after a PSK rotation are a real operational pain that organizations regularly experience, and it's a compelling business argument for migrating to 802.1X.

scenarios.q: A red team discovers that a company's wireless network uses EAP-PEAP for authentication. They set up a rogue access point broadcasting the same SSID without a server certificate validation requirement. A Windows laptop connects to the rogue AP and attempts PEAP authentication. The rogue AP captures the user's username and a MSCHAPV2 challenge-response. What attack is being conducted, and what configuration change would have prevented the credential capture?
opts: A WPS PIN attack — disable WPS on all access points
An RFID cloning attack — use certificate-based authentication instead
A deauthentication attack — enable management frame protection
An evil twin PEAP credential capture
scenarios.exp: When clients don't validate the server certificate, they'll authenticate against any AP claiming the correct SSID. The MSCHAPV2 response can be cracked offline. Prevention: configure clients to validate the server certificate and reject authentication if the certificate is not from the trusted corporate CA — this is done via supplicant configuration (GPO on Windows) so clients refuse to authenticate to rogue APs presenting unexpected certificates. PEAP without certificate validation: PEAP's server certificate is the client's way to verify it's connecting to the legitimate RADIUS server. Without validation, any rogue AP can intercept PEAP authentication. The fix is supplicant configuration — tell Windows/mobile devices which CA to trust for the RADIUS server certificate, and refuse connection if the certificate doesn't match. This is a deployment step many organizations skip, leaving them vulnerable to this exact attack.

scenarios.q: A small office of 25 employees uses WPA2-Personal with a single pre-shared key (PSK) for all employees. An employee with a documented grievance is terminated on Friday and their network access (Active Directory account, VPN, email) is revoked the same day. On Monday, the security team observes unfamiliar devices associating with the wireless network from the parking lot. The MOST appropriate immediate action AND the MOST appropriate longer-term remediation are:
opts: Immediate: rotate the WPA2-PSK and re-distribute to all employees. Long-term: continue with WPA2-Personal but rotate the PSK quarterly going forward.
Immediate: do nothing — the terminated employee no longer works at the company so legally they cannot use the wireless network. Long-term: continue with WPA2-Personal.

Immediate: rotate the WPA2-PSK and re-distribute to all employees. Long-term: migrate to WPA2-Enterprise (or WPA3-Enterprise) with per-user 802.1X authentication so revoking an individual's identity revokes their wireless access.
Immediate: disable wireless entirely until an investigation completes. Long-term: continue with WPA2-Personal but require that every employee sign a non-disclosure agreement covering the PSK.
scenarios.exp: WPA2-Personal's PSK is shared by every user, so revoking the terminated employee's individual accounts does not revoke their wireless access — they (or anyone they shared the PSK with) can still associate. The immediate action is to rotate the PSK; the structural fix is to migrate to an Enterprise mode that uses 802.1X with per-user credentials, so identity revocation at the IdP also revokes wireless access. Quarterly rotation helps marginally but does not solve the structural problem. Doing nothing ignores the active threat. Disabling wireless entirely is disproportionate, and an NDA does not technically prevent access.

cram.def: Verifying all user input before processing. Whitelist (accept known good) preferred over blacklist.
Analyzing source code without executing it. Finds vulnerabilities early in development.
Testing running application. Sends inputs, observes behavior. Finds runtime vulnerabilities.
Sending random/unexpected input to find crashes and vulnerabilities.
Digitally signing application code — verifies publisher identity and detects tampering.
Security integrated into every phase of software development.

matching.prompt: Verifying user input before processing
Testing running application with attack inputs
Analyzing source code without running it
Sending random inputs to find crashes
Digitally signing software to verify publisher

questions.q: Input validation is the PRIMARY defense against:
opts: DDoS attacks targeting application bandwidth saturation at upstream peering links
Injection attacks (SQL injection, XSS, command injection) by ensuring user input cannot be interpreted as code
Brute force password attacks where attackers guess passwords through repeated login attempts
Physical security threats including tailgating into restricted server rooms after hours
questions.exp: Validating input prevents malicious data from being processed as code — the root cause of most injection vulnerabilities.

questions.q: SAST differs from DAST in that:
opts: SAST is significantly more expensive to license per developer seat than DAST tooling
SAST is always automated by integration into the CI pipeline; DAST is always manual
SAST analyzes source code without execution
DAST finds more vulnerabilities than SAST because runtime testing covers every input path
questions.exp: Finding vulnerabilities early in development; DAST tests the running application. SAST = source code analysis (no execution). DAST = running app testing (finds runtime issues SAST misses).

questions.q: Fuzzing involves:
opts: Manually reviewing source code for vulnerabilities by walking each function with a checklist
Sending random, unexpected, or malformed inputs to an application to discover crashes and security vulnerabilities
Scanning the application binary for known vulnerability signatures from a vendor CVE feed
Testing network protocols by capturing and replaying traffic to verify request handling
questions.exp: Fuzzing automates vulnerability discovery by bombarding the application with unexpected inputs — finding edge cases developers miss.

scenarios.q: A developer submits code to a repository. The CI/CD pipeline automatically runs SAST, dependency vulnerability scanning (SCA), and unit tests. The SAST tool flags a potential SQL injection in a new API endpoint. The pipeline fails and the code is blocked from merging. The developer argues the finding is a false positive. What is the correct process?
opts: The security team reviews the flagged code with the developer — if confirmed as a false positive, the specific finding is suppressed with documented justification; if confirmed as a real vulnerability, the developer fixes it before merging. The key principle is that security gates in CI/CD pipelines must not be bypassed based solely on developer assertion — all security findings require review and documented disposition before code can merge
Allow the code to merge since the developer says it's a false positive
Override the pipeline and merge immediately to avoid development delays
Remove SAST from the pipeline — false positives slow development
scenarios.exp: Security gate process: developer assertion of false positive is the starting point for investigation, not the end. SAST findings must be reviewed and formally dispositioned — confirmed real vulnerabilities are fixed; confirmed false positives are suppressed with documentation. Bypassing security gates on assertion alone defeats the purpose of automated security testing and creates liability if the vulnerability turns out to be real.

scenarios.q: A web application accepts file uploads. Users can upload profile pictures. The developer validates that uploaded files have image extensions (.jpg, .png, .gif) by checking the file extension in the filename. A penetration tester uploads a file named 'shell.php.jpg' — the server accepts it because the extension is .jpg, but the web server executes it as PHP when accessed. What input validation failure occurred, and what is the correct fix?
opts: The file extension check was performed correctly — the server has a misconfiguration
Block the .php extension in the filename blacklist

Extension-only validation is insufficient — attackers control the filename. The correct fix is multi-layered: (1) validate the MIME type by inspecting the file's magic bytes (the actual file header, not the extension), (2) strip the filename and rename uploaded files server-side to a generated safe name with the correct extension, (3) store uploaded files outside the web root or in a separate domain so they cannot be executed by the web server, (4) configure the web server to not execute scripts in the upload directory
Require users to prove they are uploading real images by previewing them
scenarios.exp: File upload validation depth: extension checking is easily bypassed. Actual content validation (magic bytes), server-side renaming (remove attacker control of filename), storage outside web root (prevent execution), and server configuration (no script execution in upload directories) are all required layers. A file named shell.php.jpg that gets stored as shell.php.jpg in the web root and has PHP execution enabled is a web shell — a complete application takeover.

scenarios.q: A security team is performing a code review and finds the following in a Python Flask application: 'query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + user_id' where user_id comes from a URL parameter. They also find the application displays full Python stack traces in the browser on errors, and the debug mode is set to True in production. Rank these three findings by severity.
opts: SQL injection via string concatenation is critical (allows database extraction or destruction); debug mode in production is high (enables the Werkzeug debugger which allows arbitrary code execution via the browser); verbose stack traces are medium (information disclosure revealing code structure, file paths, and library versions). Fix order: disable debug mode immediately (active RCE risk), fix SQL injection (use parameterized queries), then suppress error details in production responses
Stack traces are most severe, debug mode is medium, SQL concatenation is low
Debug mode is most severe since it enables the REPL
Stack traces are most severe since they reveal the entire codebase
scenarios.exp: Severity ranking for web app findings: debug mode with Werkzeug in production is a critical RCE risk — the interactive debugger allows arbitrary Python execution from the browser. SQL injection is critical but requires the specific vulnerable endpoint to be reached. Stack traces are information disclosure (serious but not directly exploitable). The exam expects students to reason about relative severity and impact, not just identify vulnerability classes.

questions.q: Adam is conducting software testing by reviewing the source code of the application. What type of code testing is Adam conducting?
opts: Mutation testing
Static code analysis
Dynamic code analysis
Fuzzing
questions.exp: Adam is conducting static code analysis by reviewing the source code. Dynamic code analysis requires running the program, and both mutation testing and fuzzing are types of dynamic analysis.

questions.q: Tom is a software developer who creates code for sale to the public. He would like to assure his users that the code they receive actually came from him. What technique can he use to best provide this assurance?
opts: Code signing
Code endorsement
Code encryption
Code obfuscation
questions.exp: Code signing provides developers with a way to confirm the authenticity of their code to end users. Developers use a cryptographic function to digitally sign their code with their own private key, and then browsers can use the developer’s public key to verify that signature and ensure that the code is legitimate and was not modified by unauthorized individuals.

questions.q: Charles is worried about users conducting SQL injection attacks. Which of the following solutions will best address his concerns?
opts: Using secure session management
Enabling logging on the database
Performing user input validation
Implementing TLS
questions.exp: Charles should perform user input validation to strip out any SQL code or other unwanted input. Secure session management can help prevent session hijacking, logging may provide useful information for incident investigation, and implementing TLS can help protect network traffic, but only input validation helps with the issue described.

questions.q: What purpose would Linux file permissions set to rw-r—r-- serve?
opts: To allow the owner to read and write the file, and for the owner’s group and others to be able to read it
To allow all users to read and write the file, and for the group and owner to be able to read it
To allow system administrators to read and write the file, and for users and all others to be able to read it
To prevent reading and writing for all users, and to prevent reading by groups and a specific user
questions.exp: Linux file permissions are read left to right, with the first three characters indicating read, write, and execute permissions (rwx) for the owner of the file, the second three apply to the group, and the last three to all other users. Any indicated with a – are not allowed for that set.

questions.q: Allan is preparing to harden his organization’s network switches. Which of the following is not a common hardening technique for network devices?
opts: Removing unnecessary software
Installing patches
Administrative VLANs
Changing default passwords
questions.exp: Unlike computers and mobile devices, switches and other network devices typically do not have additional software that can be removed. Installing patches, placing administrative interfaces on protected VLANs, and changing default passwords are all common hardening techniques for network devices like switches.

questions.q: Chris wants systems that connect to his network to report their boot processes to a server where they can be validated before being permitted to join the network. What technology should he use to do this on the workstations?
opts: UEFI/Trusted boot
BIOS/Trusted boot
UEFI/Measured boot
BIOS/Measured boot
questions.exp: Chris knows that BIOS‐based systems do not support either of these modes, and that trusted boot validates every component before loading it, whereas measured boot logs the boot process and sends it to a server that can validate it before permitting the system to connect to the network or perform other actions.

questions.q: Naomi has discovered the following TCP ports open on a system she wants to harden. Which ports are used for unsecure services and thus should be disabled to allow their secure equivalents to continue to be used?
opts: 21 and 80
questions.exp:
The services listed are:

21—FTP
22—SSH
23—Telnet
80—HTTP
443—HTTPS

questions.q: What is the most frequent concern that leads to GPS tagging being disabled by some companies via an MDM tool?
opts: Chain of custody
The ability to support geofencing
Privacy
Context‐aware authentication
questions.exp: Geotagging places a location stamp in documents and pictures that can include position, time, and date. This can be a serious privacy issue when pictures or other information are posted, and many individuals and organizations disable GPS tagging. Organizations may want to enforce GPS tagging for some work products, meaning that the ability to enable or disable it in an MDM tool is quite useful. Chain of custody is a forensic concept, the ability to support geofencing does not require GPS tagging, and context‐aware authentication may need geolocation but not GPS tagging.

questions.q: Bart wants to use a cellular hotspot to provide Internet connectivity via Wi‐Fi. What type of network has he set up for his laptop and phone to connect to?
opts: Ad‐hoc
NFC
Point‐to‐point
RFID
questions.exp: This is an ad‐hoc network set up to allow devices to connect to the access point provided by the cellular modem. NFC is a short range, low bandwidth connection method used for payments and similar purposes. Point‐to‐point connections are used to bridge two networks together or for single connections, this is a multi‐device network. RFID uses tags and readers.

questions.q: Susan wants to ensure that the threat of a lost phone creating a data breach is minimized. What two technologies should she implement to do this?
opts: Wi‐Fi and NFC
Remote wipe and FDE
Containerization and NFC
Geofencing and remote wipe
questions.exp: Susan’s best options are to use a combination of full‐device encryption (FDE) and remote wipe. If a device is stolen and continues to be connected to the cellular network, or reconnects at any point, the remote wipe will occur. If it does not, or if attackers attempt to get data from the device and it is locked, the encryption will significantly decrease the likelihood of the data being accessed. Of course, cracking a passcode, PIN, or password remains a potential threat. NFC and Wi‐Fi are wireless connection methods and have no influence on data breaches due to loss of a device. Geofencing may be useful for some specific organizations that want to take action if devices leave designated areas, but it is not a general solution. Containerization may shield data, but use of containers does not immediately imply encryption or other protection of the data but simply that the environments are separated.

questions.q: Jerome wants to allow guests to use his organization’s wireless network, but he does not want to provide a preshared key. What solution can he deploy to gather information such as email addresses or other contact information before allowing users to access his open network?
opts: WPS capture mode
Kerberos
WPA2
A captive portal
questions.exp: Jerome should deploy a captive portal that requires users to provide information before being moved to a network segment that allows Internet access. WPS capture mode was made up for this question, Kerberos is used for enterprise authentication, and WPA2 supports open, enterprise, or PSK modes but does not provide the capability Jerome needs by itself.

questions.q: Amanda wants to create a view of her buildings that shows Wi‐Fi signal strength and coverage. What is this type of view called?
opts: A channel overlay
A PSK
A heatmap
A SSID chart
questions.exp: Amanda wants to create a heatmap, which shows the signal strength and coverage for each access point in a facility. Heatmaps can also be used to physically locate an access point by finding the approximate center of the signal. This can be useful to locate rogue access points and other unexpected or undesired wireless devices. PSK stands for preshared key, a channel overlay is not a commonly used term (although channel overlap is a concern for channels that share bandwidth), and SSID chart was made up for this question.

questions.q: Megan wants to prevent access to phones that are misplaced by members of her organization. Which of the following MDM control options is least likely to help her protect phones that are misplaced?
opts: PINs
Device encryption
Remote wipe
Application management
questions.exp: Managing applications won’t help protect a misplaced phone from being accessed. PINs, device encryption, and remote wipe will all help keep her organization’s data and devices secure.

questions.q: Gurvinder wants to select a mobile device deployment method that provides employees with devices that they can use as though they’re personally owned to maximize flexibility and ease of use. Which deployment model should he select?
opts: CYOD
COPE
BYOD
MOTD
questions.exp: Gurvinder’s requirements fit the COPE (corporate‐owned, personally enabled) mobile device deployment model. Choose your own device (CYOD) allows users to choose a device but then centrally manages it. BYOD allows users to use their own device, rather than have the company provide it, and MOTD means message of the day, and is not a mobile device deployment scheme.

questions.q: Fred’s company issues devices in a BYOD model. That means that Fred wants to ensure that corporate data and applications are kept separate from personal applications on the devices. What technology is best suited to meet this need?
opts: Biometrics
Full‐device encryption
Context‐aware authentication
Containerization
questions.exp: Using a containerization system can allow Fred’s users to run corporate applications and to use corporate data in a secure environment that cannot be accessed by other applications outside of the container on the device. Containerization schemes for mobile devices typically use encryption and other isolation techniques to ensure that data and applications do not cross over. Biometrics and context‐aware authentication are useful for ensuring that the right user is using a device but don’t provide this separation. Full‐device encryption helps reduce the risk of theft or loss of a device resulting in a data breach.

questions.q: Michelle has deployed iPads to her staff who work her company’s factory floor. She wants to ensure that the devices work only in the factory and that if they are taken home they cannot access business data or services. What type of solution is best suited to her needs?
opts: Context‐aware authentication
Geofencing
Geolocation
Unified endpoint management (UEM)
questions.exp: Geofencing will allow Michelle to determine what locations the device should work in. The device will then use geolocation to determine when it has moved and where it is. In this case, the correct answer is therefore geofencing—simply having geolocation capabilities would not provide the solution she needs. Context‐aware authentication can help by preventing users from logging in when they aren’t in the correct location, but a device that was logged in may not require reauthentication. Finally, UEM, much like mobile device management, can be used to enforce these policies, but the most correct answer is geofencing.

questions.q: Ivan is running an enterprise wireless network and his heatmap shows that two access points are likely conflicting with each other. What will the enterprise access controller most likely do to handle this conflict?
opts: Increase the broadcast power of one of the access points.
Change the SSID for one of the access points.
Disable one of the access points.
Decrease the broadcast power of the access points.
questions.exp: When access points conflict, enterprise wireless network management tools will typically decrease the power for both access points until the issue is resolved. Simply increasing power will cause more conflicts, changing the SSID would not serve typical enterprise models that use a single SSID to allow roaming, and disabling an access point may leave coverage gaps.

questions.q: Daniel knows that WPA3 has added a method to ensure that brute‐force attacks against weak preshared keys are less likely to succeed. What is this technology called?
opts: SAE
CCMP
PSK
WPS
questions.exp: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) is used to establish a secure peering environment and to protect session traffic. Since the process requires additional cryptographic steps, it causes brute‐force attacks to be much slower and thus less likely to succeed while also providing more security than WPA2’s preshared key (PSK) mode. WPS is Wi‐Fi Protected Setup, a quick setup capability; CCMP is the encryption mode used for WPA2 networks. WPA3 moves to 128‐bit encryption for Personal mode and can support 192‐bit encryption in Enterprise mode.

questions.q: Isabelle needs to select the EAP protocol that she will use with her wireless network. She wants to use a secure protocol that does not require client devices to have a certificate, but she does want to require mutual authentication. Which EAP protocol should she use?
opts: EAP‐FAST
EAP‐TTLS
PEAP
EAP‐TLS
questions.exp: Isabelle should select PEAP, which doesn’t require client certificates but does provide TLS support. EAP‐TTLS provides similar functionality but requires additional software to be installed on some devices. EAP‐FAST focuses on quick reauthentication, and EAP‐TLS requires certificates to be deployed to the endpoint devices.

questions.q: Theresa has implemented a technology that keeps data for personal use separate from data for her company on mobile devices used by members of her staff. What is this concept called?
opts: Storage segmentation
Multifactor storage
Full‐device encryption
Geofencing
questions.exp: Storage segmentation is the concept of splitting storage between functions or usage to ensure that information that fits a specific context is not shared or used by applications or services outside of that context. Full‐device encryption encrypts the entire device, geofencing is used to determine geographic areas where actions or events may be taken by software, and multifactor storage was made up for this question.

questions.q: Tom has documented the set of security settings and procedures used to configure systems before they are deployed in his organization. What industry term describes this sort of documentation?
opts: A lockdown guide
A config FAQ
A secure baseline
A nonrepudiation guide
questions.exp: Secure baselines are used to document the settings and procedures used to configure systems or devices. The other answer choices are not common industry terms.

questions.q: What significant improvement in Personal mode wireless was included in WPA3?
opts: Simultaneous authentication of equals
Support for dictionary attacks
Added WPS3
Removed support for AES encryption
questions.exp: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) is a major addition to WPA3’s Personal mode, and it actually helps prevent dictionary attacks. AES encryption remains in use, but Wi‐Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is being removed.

questions.q: Frank needs to choose a mobile device deployment option for his organization. He wants to allow users to use devices that his organization selects and purchases for their own use. Which mobile solution should he select?
opts: BYOD
COPE
CYOD
VDI
questions.exp: The corporate‐owned, personally enabled (COPE) model allows end users to use their devices for personal as well as corporate use while providing corporate control and management of the mobile devices. BYOD is a bring‐your‐own‐device model, which can create challenges when users manage and maintain their devices. CYOD, or choose your own device, allows users to select their own device. Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) runs applications on a remote system, allowing separation of data and systems while providing functionality to remote devices but is heavily bandwidth and application dependent.

questions.q: Maria is considering a BYOD device deployment and wants to enroll the devices in an MDM application. What key concern will she likely need to address with her users in the event that a device is lost and the organization wants to respond to ensure no corporate data is lost?
opts: Full‐device encryption
Remote wipe
VDI
Storage segmentation
questions.exp: Users in Maria’s organization are likely to be concerned about what would be wiped if the device was remotely wiped in the event it was lost. If the organization’s policy is to immediately fully wipe the device, and it is then recovered, their personal data may be lost. Organizational policies for BYOD devices can be complex, and many organizations choose to separate user and corporate data more completely via storage segmentation and other capabilities to avoid this scenario. Full‐device encryption can help protect the data but would not typically be a concern for users—most will appreciate it. Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) would not have a direct impact on users.

questions.q: Dan needs to select a mobile device deployment model to fit his organization’s needs. He wants to have the maximum amount of control over the devices selected but wants users to be able to install applications they need to make the devices useful to them. What model should he use?
opts: BYOD
COPE
CYOD
COBO
questions.exp: The corporate‐owned, personally enabled (COPE) model provides devices to users but allows them to use the device for their own use as well. BYOD (bring your own device) simply uses personally owned devices, while CYOD (choose your own device) allows users to select typically from a limited set of devices that the organization purchases and provides. COBO (corporate owned, business only), while not found in the current exam outline, is a common model in high‐security environments.

questions.q: Dana needs to deploy and manage applications on mobile devices for her organization and knows that a broad variety of tools support this. Which of the following is not a common tool for this purpose?
opts: MDM
MAM
MARS
UEM
questions.exp: Mobile device management (MDM), mobile application management (MAM), and universal endpoint management (UEM) tools are all commonly used to manage applications on mobile devices. Although MARS isn’t a common acronym, Cisco’s MARS product is a monitoring and analysis tool used to manage network devices, not mobile devices.

questions.q: When Lucca wants to test a potentially malicious file, he uploads it to a third‐party website. That website places the software in a secured testing environment and documents what it does, and then uses antimalware tools to try to identify it. What is that type of secure testing environment called?
opts: A software jail
A sandbox
A litterbox
A root dungeon
questions.exp: Running software in an isolated, instrumented, and protected sandbox is a useful technique when testing unknown, potentially malicious software. Sandboxing techniques are used by many malware analysis tools and companies to allow them to determine what a new malicious application does. The remaining options are made up.

questions.q: Emily wants to check on the success of her organization’s system‐hardening process. What information‐gathering process is frequently used to quickly validate whether unneeded services have been disabled?
opts: A port scan
A vulnerability scan
A Registry scan
An Opal review
questions.exp: A quick port scan is often used to check if unnecessary and unwanted services remain accessible. Although a vulnerability scan can be used, a port scan will be faster. A Registry scan might be used, but it wouldn’t work for Linux systems or other non‐Windows devices. Opal is an encryption standard for encrypted drives.

questions.q: Ujama is deploying a wireless access point for a small business that won’t use enterprise authentication for wireless. What WPA3 feature ensures that the initial key exchange for personal mode is more secure?
opts: MAC
PSK
SAE
IKE
questions.exp: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) provides a more secure initial key exchange process than PSKs (preshared keys) did in WPA2. Ujama should implement a WPA‐3 personal mode network to meet this need. MAC (Media Access Control) addresses are the hardware addresses used for networked devices. IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is part of the IPSec protocol but is not used for this.

questions.q: What device deployment model is least likely to support an agent‐based NAC solution?
opts: Corporate‐owned
Bring your own device (BYOD)
Corporate‐owned, personally enabled
Choose your own device
questions.exp: BYOD environments are less likely to find general acceptance of agent‐based NAC solutions since they require the installation of an agent that can be obtrusive. That means that agentless NAC solutions are more common when security needs must still be met without an agent being installed.

questions.q: Arun wants to determine the best placement for new Wi‐Fi access points. What process is typically done to determine where access points should be placed?
opts: A Wi‐Fi map
A directional map
A site survey
A SSID survey
questions.exp: Site surveys are done to map existing installations and to create wireless signal heat maps to determine where a new access point may be needed or where coverage is weak. Wi‐Fi maps, directional maps, and SSID surveys are not common terms used for this purpose.

questions.q: Cynthia has defined a boundary around her organization in the MDM tool she uses, and users are unable to access institutional data when their mobile devices are outside of that boundary. What is this technique called?
opts: Geofencing
GeoIP
Geotagging
Geolocation
questions.exp: Geofencing places a boundary around a location using geolocation services. Actions are taken based on where a device is in relation to the geofence. A geoIP system attempts to match IP addresses to a geographic location or region. Geotagging marks a specific spot, and geolocation is the ability to locate a device or system.

cram.def: Repository of all IT asset information and relationships. Foundation for change and incident management.
Securely removing data from media before disposal or reuse. Methods: overwriting, degaussing, destruction.
Using magnetic field to erase magnetic media (HDD, tape). NOT effective on SSDs.
Shredding, pulverizing, incineration. Most thorough. Required for SSDs.
Document proving media was securely destroyed — required for compliance.
End of Life / End of Support Life — vendor stops providing security updates.

matching.prompt: Repository of all IT assets and their relationships
Magnetic field erasing magnetic media
Most thorough sanitization — guaranteed unrecoverable
Required for SSD sanitization
Vendor stops providing security patches

questions.q: Why is degaussing NOT effective for sanitizing SSDs?
opts: Degaussing is too slow for SSDs to be operationally practical at any scale
SSDs use flash memory, not magnetic storage — a magnetic field has no effect on flash memory cells
Degaussing is too expensive for SSDs because of the specialized equipment needed
SSDs are always encrypted with built-in self-encrypting-drive features, making degaussing unnecessary
questions.exp: Degaussing works on magnetic media. SSDs use NAND flash — degaussing has zero effect. Physical destruction is needed.

questions.q: Which media sanitization method provides the STRONGEST assurance of data unrecoverability?
opts: Overwriting with zeros (single-pass disk wipe)
Degaussing the drive with a strong magnetic field
Physical destruction (shredding/incineration)
Formatting the drive from the operating system
questions.exp: Physical destruction guarantees media cannot be read — used for high-sensitivity data.

questions.q: An organization is disposing of old laptops with confidential data. The MOST appropriate action is:
opts: Simply deleting files and donating the laptops
Securely wiping or physically destroying storage media and obtaining a certificate of destruction
Formatting the drives and reselling them
Storing the laptops in a locked room indefinitely
questions.exp: Secure disposal requires verifiable sanitization and documentation (certificate of destruction) for compliance.

questions.q: An asset management program tracks a laptop through its full lifecycle. Which of the following correctly orders the major asset lifecycle stages?
opts: Acquisition → Decommissioning → Assignment → Disposal → Operation/Maintenance
Disposal → Acquisition → Assignment → Operation/Maintenance → Decommissioning
Acquisition → Assignment → Operation/Maintenance → Decommissioning → Disposal/Sanitization
Assignment → Acquisition → Operation/Maintenance → Disposal → Decommissioning
questions.exp: The standard asset lifecycle moves Acquisition (procurement, intake, tagging) → Assignment (issuance to a custodian/user) → Operation/Maintenance (ongoing tracking, patching, configuration management) → Decommissioning (formal removal from active service) → Disposal/Sanitization (data sanitization first, then physical disposal, resale, or destruction). The other orderings violate the natural flow — disposal before acquisition, decommissioning before assignment, and assignment before acquisition are all out of order. Knowing the stage names and their order is exam-tested directly.

questions.q: A company maintains a hardware inventory of 5,000 assets and a software inventory generated by an asset-discovery tool that scans the network monthly. The asset-management team needs to verify that physical assets in the warehouse match the hardware inventory, and that deployed devices in the network match both inventories. Which combination of asset-tracking mechanisms is MOST appropriate for these two distinct verification needs?
opts: Use only barcodes everywhere — RFID is unnecessary, and software-discovery tools are unreliable for asset matching at any scale
RFID for warehouse cycle counts; barcodes for shelf-level audits; software-discovery for deployed-device reconciliation against hardware inventory
Use only RFID for both warehouse and network — RFID readers can detect deployed devices on the network as well as in storage areas
Manual visual inspection of every asset quarterly — automated tracking systems are not sufficiently accurate for asset management at any scale
questions.exp: Different verification needs call for different mechanisms. RFID enables bulk read from a distance — ideal for warehouse cycle counts (a single pass with a handheld reader inventories shelves of devices). Barcodes are line-of-sight and per-item — appropriate for shelf-level spot checks and tagging at intake. Software-discovery tools enumerate deployed devices via network presence (DHCP, agent check-in, etc.) and reconcile against the hardware inventory to flag missing or unknown assets. Each tool fits a distinct verification axis. Single-tool approaches leave gaps. Manual inspection does not scale to 5,000 assets and is error-prone.

scenarios.q: An IT team discovers a server running critical financial reporting software that is not in the CMDB, has not received patches in 18 months, is not covered by any backup policy, and is only known to one employee who set it up before leaving the company. The server is running Windows Server 2008 R2 which reached end of life in January 2020. What risk does this represent, and what immediate actions are required?
opts: Low risk — the server has been running fine for 18 months without incident
The server should be immediately powered off

This is a ghost/rogue asset representing multiple critical risks: (1) EOL OS with no security patches for years — known exploitable vulnerabilities will never be patched; (2) not in asset management so it receives no patching, monitoring, or backup coverage; (3) single point of knowledge creates operational risk. Immediate actions: add to CMDB, assess what data it holds and its network exposure, implement emergency compensating controls (network isolation, enhanced monitoring), engage the business to plan migration to a supported platform
Remove the server from the network and ignore it since it's not officially managed
scenarios.exp: Ghost asset risk: undiscovered assets in production are blind spots — they receive no patching, monitoring, or backup coverage. An EOL OS compounds this with permanent unpatched vulnerabilities. The single-employee knowledge dependency creates an operational continuity risk independent of security. Asset discovery scanning should have found this — the fact that it didn't indicates gaps in asset management processes.

scenarios.q: A company is disposing of 200 decommissioned laptops. Some were used by executives and contain sensitive financial data. The IT team proposes reformatting the hard drives (quick format) before donating the laptops to a local school. A security officer objects. Why, and what is the correct disposal procedure?
opts: Quick format is sufficient — it deletes all user data
Donating laptops with corporate data is always illegal

Quick format only removes file system references — the actual data remains on the drive and is recoverable with freely available tools. For laptops that contained sensitive financial data, the correct procedure is: (1) secure overwrite (DoD 5220.22-M or equivalent multi-pass overwrite) for functional drives, or (2) physical destruction (shredding) for maximum assurance, or (3) cryptographic erasure if the drives are encrypted. A certificate of destruction should be obtained for audit purposes
The laptops should be physically destroyed regardless of data sensitivity
scenarios.exp: Data remanence after quick format: quick format (and even full format) leaves data recoverable. The FAT/NTFS structures are reset but sectors are not overwritten. For drives containing sensitive data, overwriting or destruction is required. The appropriate method depends on data sensitivity — executives' financial data warrants at minimum secure overwrite and potentially physical destruction. Donating un-sanitized drives is a data breach.

scenarios.q: During an audit, an assessor finds that the organization has 847 active software licenses tracked in the CMDB, but vulnerability scans identify 1,243 unique software installations across the network. The delta of 396 unlicensed installations includes several applications with known critical vulnerabilities. What does this demonstrate, and what control addresses it?
opts: The vulnerability scanner is producing systematic false positives — the 396 applications are likely duplicates of legitimately tracked CMDB entries
Unlicensed software is a legal concern only, not a security concern — the licensing audit can be addressed separately from any security review
Shadow IT plus software asset management gaps: 396 apps are installed but not in CMDB — no patch management, no vulnerability tracking. Allow-listing plus full asset management closes the gap
The CMDB needs to be updated to add the 396 applications as approved entries — once they're tracked, the vulnerability gap automatically closes
scenarios.exp: Software asset management security impact: untracked software isn't just a license compliance issue — it's a security gap. Untracked applications aren't included in patch management cycles, so vulnerabilities go undetected and unpatched indefinitely. Allow-listing prevents installation of unapproved software; CMDB tracking ensures approved software is covered by patch management. The 396 gap represents 396 potential attack vectors with no remediation path.

scenarios.q: A company is decommissioning storage from three different sources: (1) 50 spinning-platter (HDD) drives from a file server, (2) 20 SSDs from developer workstations, and (3) 10 hybrid laptops with built-in self-encrypting SSDs that have been encrypted with a strong key for the entire device lifetime. The data classification is 'Restricted.' For each source, which sanitization method is MOST appropriate?
opts: (1) Degauss; (2) Degauss; (3) Degauss — degaussing is the universal answer for all magnetic and solid-state media
(1) Single-pass overwrite; (2) Single-pass overwrite; (3) Single-pass overwrite — overwrite is sufficient for all media types when followed by verification
(1) Degauss or destroy; (2) Cryptographic erase if the SSD supports it, otherwise destroy; (3) Cryptographic erase by destroying the encryption key (crypto-shred), then dispose
(1) Cryptographic erase; (2) Degauss; (3) Single-pass overwrite — match each method to the most aggressive option for each technology
scenarios.exp: HDDs (spinning platters) are vulnerable to degaussing and can also be physically destroyed; both are appropriate for Restricted data. SSDs do NOT respond to degaussing because their data is held in NAND flash, not magnetic media; the correct approach is the SSD's built-in cryptographic erase (sanitize command), or physical destruction if the device does not support it. Self-encrypting devices that have always been encrypted can be sanitized by destroying the encryption key (crypto-shred), which renders the underlying ciphertext unrecoverable. Universal overwrite is unreliable on SSDs due to wear leveling. Universal degaussing does not work on SSDs at all.

questions.q: Elaine wants to securely erase the contents of a tape used for backups in her organization’s tape library. What is the fastest secure erase method available to her that will allow the tape to be reused?
opts: Using a degausser
Wiping the tape by writing a random pattern of 1s and 0s to it
Incinerating the tape
Wiping the tape by writing all 1s or all 0s to it
questions.exp: A degausser is a quick and effective way to erase a tape before it is reused. Wiping a tape by writing 1s, 0s, or a pattern of 1s and 0s to it will typically be a slow operation and is not a common method of destroying data on a tape. Incinerating the tape won’t allow it to be reused!

questions.q: Alex has been handed a flash media device that was quick‐formatted and has been asked to recover the data. What data will remain on the drive?
opts: No data will remain on the drive.
Files will remain but file indexes will not.
File indexes will remain, but the files will be gone.
Files and file indexes will remain on the drive.
questions.exp: Quick‐formatting a drive removes the file indexes but leaves the file content on the drive. Recovery tools look for those files on the drive and piece them back together using metadata, headers, and other clues that help to recover the files.

questions.q: Isaac needs to sanitize an SSD that uses full‐disk encryption and that has been encrypted for its full service life with the company he works for. What is the most effective means of making the data on the SSD no longer retrievable?
opts: Completely overwrite the drive with binary 0s.
Reformat the drive using a full format.
Completely overwrite the drive with random patterns of binary 1s and 0s.
Destroy the encryption key for the drive and then use the SATA secure erase command.
questions.exp: Isaac can simply destroy all copies of the encryption key for the drive to make the data very difficult to access. Using the built‐in secure erase command will ensure that the data is no longer recoverable under any normal circumstances. Overwriting SSDs and other flash media that are overprovisioned with additional space for wear leveling purposes is likely to miss remnant data in spare or replaced space. Formatting a drive simply removes the file indices and does not remove the data.

questions.q: Garrett is attempting to manage the cloud server instances used by his organization. They do not currently tag cloud resources with the identity of the responsible individual. What is the primary risk of not better controlling this situation?
opts: VM escaping
Hypervisor breach
Improper permissions
VM sprawl
questions.exp: Virtual machine (VM) sprawl occurs when IaaS users create virtual service instances and then forget about them or abandon them, leaving them to accrue costs and accumulate security issues over time. Organizations should maintain instance awareness to avoid VM sprawl issues. VM escaping is where an attacker escapes the isolation of a virtual machine and gets access to the underlying operating system and other VMs on the same physical machine. Hypervisor breaches are cases where an attacker is able to compromise the hypervisor of a virtualization platform and gain access to virtual machine and/or the underlying operating system. Improper permission settings occur when users receive privileges not necessary to carry out their job functions.

questions.q: Helena wants to ensure that a drive is properly sanitized before being reused. What process is typically used for a hard drive?
opts: A secure erase
The drive is pulverized.
The drive is incinerated.
The drive is reformatted.
questions.exp: Secure erase utilities are frequently used for hard drives. Pulverizing and incinerating drives destroys them, preventing them from being reused. Reformatting does not completely erase data.

cram.def: Automated tool identifying known vulnerabilities. Examples: Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS.
Scanner logs into systems — deeper, more accurate results. Finds local vulnerabilities.
External perspective — what an unauthenticated attacker sees. Finds exposed services.
Reported vulnerability that doesn't actually exist. Wastes remediation effort.
Real vulnerability not detected. Dangerous — gives false confidence.

matching.prompt: Scanner authenticates to systems for deeper results
External unauthenticated perspective
Real vulnerability not detected by scanner
Reported vulnerability that doesn't exist

questions.q: A credentialed vulnerability scan provides more accurate results because:
opts: It scans more IP addresses across the corporate range than a non-credentialed scan does
It uses more attack signatures from the vendor's premium signature feed library
The scanner authenticates to systems — direct visibility into installed packages, not just network probing
It runs faster because cached fingerprint data avoids the need for service interrogation
questions.exp: Finding local vulnerabilities, missing patches, and misconfigurations invisible externally. Credentialed scans see what's inside the system — local patch status, user rights, registry settings — not just externally exposed services.

questions.q: False negatives in vulnerability scanning are MORE dangerous than false positives because:
opts: A false negative means a real vulnerability was missed — giving false confidence while the vulnerability remains exploitable
False negatives are easier to fix than false positives once they're discovered later in the cycle
False positives waste less time than false negatives because they only cause noise alerts in triage
They both have equal impact on security since both indicate fundamental scanner accuracy issues
questions.exp: False negatives are the unseen danger — you think you're safe but the vulnerability is real and exploitable.

questions.q: A security team is selecting a vulnerability scanning approach for a fleet of 800 servers, including some that are isolated from the management network (no inbound network access from the scanner's subnet). Which scanning approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Network-based credentialed scan from the central scanner — most accurate, and credentials let the scanner enumerate installed packages without local agent installation
Network-based unauthenticated scan from the central scanner — least intrusive, no credentials needed, and works on any network-reachable host
Manual host-by-host inspection by a system administrator — most accurate of all because a human reviews each system in person
Agent-based scan with a lightweight agent installed on each host — accurate package enumeration, works on hosts the central scanner cannot reach, and reports back over outbound connections
questions.exp: Agent-based scanning is the right choice when some hosts are unreachable from the central scanner: the agent runs locally and reports outbound, bypassing the inbound-blocked constraint, and gives accurate package-level enumeration. Network-based credentialed scanning is excellent when the scanner can reach the host but fails on the isolated hosts described. Unauthenticated scans are less accurate because they only see what is exposed on the network. Manual inspection is impractical at 800 hosts. Many enterprises deploy a hybrid: agent-based for unreachable assets, credentialed network-based for the rest.

scenarios.q: A security team runs a credentialed vulnerability scan of their web servers and gets 847 findings. The same servers scanned without credentials produce 23 findings. The team has been reporting the non-credentialed scan results to management as their vulnerability posture. What is wrong with this approach, and why does the gap between 23 and 847 findings exist?
opts: The non-credentialed scan only shows externally visible vulnerabilities (open ports, exposed services, banner information) — what an unauthenticated attacker from outside sees. The credentialed scan authenticates to the server and sees everything an insider or attacker with credentials would see: unpatched OS components, vulnerable locally-installed software, misconfigured services, weak file permissions. Reporting only non-credentialed results drastically underrepresents actual risk — most vulnerabilities are internal and invisible to unauthenticated scans
The credentialed scan is producing false positives — use the non-credentialed results
The credentialed scan has a bug — contact the vendor
Both scan types are unnecessary — use a WAF instead
scenarios.exp: Credentialed vs non-credentialed scope: the 824-finding gap represents real vulnerabilities that exist but are invisible to an external scanner. Most software vulnerabilities (unpatched OS components, third-party apps) are not exposed externally — they require authenticated access to discover. Organizations that report only non-credentialed scan results give management a false picture of security posture.

scenarios.q: A vulnerability scanner reports a critical finding on a server: 'OpenSSL 1.0.1e — Remote Code Execution (CVE-XXXX-XXXX).' The system administrator says the finding is a false positive because they manually upgraded OpenSSL three weeks ago. The scanner is still reporting the old version. What is most likely happening, and what should be verified?
opts: The scanner is correct and the administrator is mistaken — vulnerability scanners cannot be wrong about installed software versions on hosts they enumerate
Mark all findings on this server as false positives in the vulnerability tracking system, since the administrator has confirmed the upgrade is complete
The scanner should be reconfigured to trust administrator assertions about installed software, overriding what it detects automatically on the host

The scanner may be reading OpenSSL version from a stale banner or registry entry, or multiple versions exist on the system. Verify by checking actual binary version and confirming services link the new library
scenarios.exp: False positive investigation process: scanner findings on patched vulnerabilities require verification, not automatic dismissal. Manual upgrades can leave old binaries in non-standard locations; scanners may read version info from sources that weren't updated. Verification must be done against the actual running binary and the actual library the service loads — not just what was installed. This is a common real-world scenario the exam tests through vulnerability management scenarios.

cram.def: Evidence-based knowledge about threats — TTPs, IoCs, threat actors.
Open Source Intelligence — publicly available information.
Information Sharing and Analysis Center — sector-specific threat sharing organizations.
Standardized formats for sharing threat intelligence between organizations.
Proactive searching for threats — assumes breach, looks for hidden adversary activity.

matching.prompt: Publicly available threat information
Sector-specific threat sharing organization
Standardized threat intel sharing format

audit_d_review.note: STIX/TAXII; 4.3 Threat Intelligence IS umbrella; STIX/TAXII is a threat intel sharing format.

sybex_reference.quote_excerpt: Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information

sb_fix_2.note: STRONG T1 (TAXII glossary entry + index 41 for both STIX and TAXII).

questions.q: OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) uses:
opts: Classified government intelligence reports shared through cleared partner channels only
Publicly available sources including news sites, social media, vulnerability databases, and public forums
Only commercial threat feeds purchased from vendors with paid signature subscriptions
Only dark web sources accessed through a Tor exit node from a cleanroom workstation
questions.exp: OSINT leverages openly available information — no special access required.

questions.q: Threat hunting differs from reactive security monitoring in that:
opts: Threat hunting assumes the organization is already compromised and proactively searches for hidden adversary activity
Threat hunting uses automated tools; monitoring uses humans
Threat hunting only looks at network traffic
Monitoring is more effective than threat hunting
questions.exp: Threat hunting is proactive — hunters look for stealthy attackers who have evaded automated detection.

scenarios.q: A financial institution's threat intelligence team receives a STIX feed containing indicators of compromise (IoCs) from a sector ISAC: 47 malicious IP addresses, 12 domain names, and 8 file hashes associated with a banking trojan actively targeting financial institutions. What is the MOST operationally valuable immediate action with these IoCs?
opts: Ingest IoCs into operational controls immediately: IPs to firewall and SIEM, domains to DNS/proxy filtering, hashes to EDR. Check historical logs for existing matches — a hit indicates ongoing compromise
Store them in a threat intelligence database for future reference — they'll be useful as background knowledge for the team's analysts if needed later on
Publish the IoCs on the company website to warn other organizations and enable broader industry sharing of the threat information that arrived
File a report with law enforcement about the threat indicators and let federal investigators handle any active intrusion that's underway elsewhere
scenarios.exp: Threat intel operationalization: IoCs have a short shelf life — malicious infrastructure changes frequently. The value is in immediate ingestion into controls (firewall, DNS, EDR) and retrospective hunt (did we already see this?). Threat intel that sits in a database without being operationalized provides no protection. The ISAC sharing model exists specifically to enable rapid defensive action across the sector.

scenarios.q: A threat hunter reviews network logs and notices an employee's workstation has been connecting to a domain registered 4 days ago at regular 5-minute intervals, even outside business hours. The connections return small amounts of data. The employee reports no unusual activity. Threat intelligence feeds show no information about the domain. What threat hunting hypothesis should guide the investigation?
opts: The domain is likely a legitimate cloud service consumed by the workstation's installed software — no further action needed beyond noting it
The 5-minute interval indicates a legitimate software update check from a vendor's auto-updater running quietly in the background as a service
The employee is violating acceptable use policy by accessing personal websites with random subdomain generation features designed for ad evasion in private browsing

Pattern consistent with malware beaconing: regular intervals, newly-registered domain, out-of-hours, small returns. Hunt the process making the connection, memory forensics, and what was installed at start
scenarios.exp: Threat hunting methodology: the hypothesis drives the investigation. Beaconing behavior (regular intervals + new domain + out-of-hours + small data) is a well-documented C2 pattern. The absence of threat intel hits for a newly registered domain is itself suspicious — attackers register new domains specifically to avoid existing blocklists. EDR process investigation will identify what's making the connection; memory forensics may find the injected code.

scenarios.q: A company receives a threat intelligence report that a nation-state actor is targeting organizations in their industry using spear phishing emails with malicious Word documents. The TTPs include: initial access via phishing, living-off-the-land techniques (PowerShell, WMI), lateral movement using pass-the-hash, and exfiltration via DNS tunneling. The CISO asks which controls to prioritize. What is the correct prioritization?
opts: Block all PowerShell execution — this stops the attack chain entirely

Layered controls mapped to the attack chain: (1) anti-phishing (email gateway, DMARC, user training) to reduce initial access success rate; (2) PowerShell logging and constrained language mode to detect/limit LOLBin abuse; (3) network segmentation and credential hygiene to limit pass-the-hash lateral movement reach; (4) DNS monitoring for tunneling patterns and restricting direct internet DNS to the internal resolver. No single control stops the entire chain — the goal is to fail the attacker at multiple stages
Purchase cyber insurance — nation-state attacks cannot be defended against
Block all outbound traffic — this prevents exfiltration
scenarios.exp: TTP-mapped defensive prioritization: intelligence about adversary TTPs allows defenders to map controls to the kill chain. Each phase of the attack chain has corresponding defensive measures. The goal isn't to find one magic control — it's to make each stage harder, forcing the attacker to work harder and creating more detection opportunities. This is how threat intelligence drives strategic security decisions.

cram.def: Authorized simulated attack to identify and demonstrate exploitable vulnerabilities.
No prior knowledge of target. Simulates external attacker. Most realistic.
Full knowledge of target. Most thorough coverage.
Partial knowledge — simulates insider or attacker with some reconnaissance.
Document defining scope, timing, allowed techniques, and off-limits systems.
Offensive team simulating real attackers.
Red and blue teams working together — sharing findings in real-time.

matching.prompt: No prior knowledge — simulates external attacker
Full knowledge — most thorough coverage
Defines scope, timing, and rules before testing
Red and blue working together in real-time

questions.q: Penetration testing differs from vulnerability scanning in that:
opts: Pen testing uses automated tools; scanning uses humans
Pen testing actively exploits vulnerabilities to demonstrate real impact; scanning only identifies potential vulnerabilities
Scanning is more comprehensive than pen testing
Pen testing is always automated
questions.exp: Vulnerability scanning identifies potential weaknesses. Pen testing actually exploits them — proving they're real and demonstrating business impact.

questions.q: Rules of Engagement (RoE) define:
opts: The scope, timing, permitted techniques, and off-limits systems — legally protecting both tester and organization
The payment terms for the test engagement including hourly rate and final report deliverables
The reporting format including required sections, risk-rating taxonomy, and executive summary length
The vulnerabilities to be found before the test starts so that scope is locked down at outset
questions.exp: RoE establishes the legal framework — preventing the tester from being prosecuted and the organization from unexpected disruption.

questions.q: A purple team exercise is most valuable for:
opts: Having red and blue teams collaborate in real-time — sharing findings immediately to improve detection capabilities
Finding additional vulnerabilities the red team missed during their independent engagement
Reducing the cost of security testing engagements by combining red and blue work
Simulating sophisticated nation-state attacks against the organization's defenses
questions.exp: Purple teaming: red shares attack techniques, blue improves detection. Both teams learn and defenses improve immediately.

scenarios.q: A penetration tester has been engaged for a black box test. They conduct passive reconnaissance for two weeks, discovering the company's IP ranges, employee names and titles from LinkedIn, email format from a data breach database, and a forgotten subdomain (dev.company.com) hosting a staging version of the application. They haven't touched any of the company's systems yet. What phase are they in, and why is this phase valuable even before any active testing?
opts: Active reconnaissance — touching the target's systems has already begun via subdomain probing
Social engineering — using LinkedIn data directly constitutes an attack
Exploitation — the subdomain has begun to be actively attacked through unauthenticated probing
Passive reconnaissance — only public information without touching target systems directly
scenarios.exp: All information was gathered from public sources without touching the target's systems. This phase is valuable because it replicates what real attackers do before launching attacks — attackers don't immediately start scanning, they first understand the target. The forgotten dev subdomain is a significant finding (staging environments often have weaker controls and real production data). This intelligence shapes the entire active test — the tester now knows where to focus, what credentials to try, and which systems may be more vulnerable. Passive recon phase value: attackers invest significant time in passive recon before touching a target. The dev subdomain discovery through DNS enumeration and Google dorking is a zero-touch finding that real attackers regularly exploit. Pen testers who skip passive recon miss findings that may be the most critical — forgotten systems with no monitoring, exposed development environments, and intelligence that dramatically improves active phase effectiveness.

scenarios.q: A penetration test engagement has Rules of Engagement specifying: scope includes the company's production web application (192.168.1.0/24), testing window is weekdays 9am-5pm, destructive testing is prohibited, and social engineering requires written CISO approval for each campaign. During testing, the tester discovers a server at 192.168.2.50 that appears to be a domain controller — outside the defined scope but potentially accessible. What should the tester do?
opts: Test the domain controller immediately — it's too valuable a finding to ignore
Test the domain controller after hours to avoid the testing window restriction
Note the finding and include it in the final report without testing it

Stop testing the out-of-scope system and immediately notify the client in writing that a potentially significant system was discovered adjacent to the scope boundary. The client decides whether to expand scope through a written amendment to the Rules of Engagement. Testing out-of-scope systems without explicit authorization — even in a penetration test — is unauthorized computer access. The RoE is the legal document protecting both parties
scenarios.exp: RoE as legal boundary: the RoE defines what is authorized. Testing out-of-scope systems — even during an authorized penetration test — is not covered by the engagement authorization and could constitute unauthorized access. The tester's professional and legal obligation is to notify the client and await explicit written authorization to expand scope. This is a real ethical and legal distinction the exam tests.

scenarios.q: A company conducts an annual penetration test that finds the same 12 critical vulnerabilities year after year. The CISO argues the penetration test program is broken. The security team argues they've been patching but the vulnerabilities reappear. What does this pattern indicate, and what root cause should be investigated?
opts: The penetration testing firm is incompetent at finding new vulnerability classes — hire a different firm with broader testing methodology and tooling overall

Recurring findings indicate systemic remediation failure: patching applied to instances but not root cause (vulnerable software in base image), incomplete change management, or false closure of findings without verification
The vulnerabilities are unfixable in the current system architecture — accept them as documented residual risk and continue with normal operations as-is
Switch from annual penetration testing to quarterly automated vulnerability scanning only — the recurring findings will surface much more quickly that way
scenarios.exp: Recurring pen test findings as process indicators: the same vulnerabilities year after year indicate a systemic issue, not just a patching backlog. Common causes: vulnerable base images (new deployments start vulnerable), patch management not covering all systems, or inadequate remediation validation. Root cause analysis of recurring findings is more valuable than the findings themselves — fix the process, not just the instances.

cram.def: Common Vulnerability Scoring System. 0-10 severity score. 9.0-10 = Critical.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. Public database with CVE-YYYY-XXXXX identifiers.
National Vulnerability Database. NIST augments CVE with CVSS scores and patch info.
Exploit Prediction Scoring System. Probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild.

matching.prompt: 0-10 vulnerability severity score
Public database with CVE-YYYY-XXXXX identifiers
Probability vulnerability will be exploited
CVSS score for Critical severity

questions.q: CVSS is used to:
opts: Identify specific named vulnerabilities by their unique CVE identifiers
Monitor live network traffic for in-progress exploit attempts targeting the environment
Patch discovered vulnerabilities automatically without administrator approval
Provide a standardized 0-10 severity score to prioritize vulnerability remediation
questions.exp: CVSS gives each vulnerability a standardized score (0-10) — organizations use scores to prioritize which vulnerabilities to fix first.

questions.q: A CVSS score of 9.5 indicates:
opts: Low severity
Critical severity — patch immediately
High severity
Medium severity
questions.exp: CVSS 9.0-10.0 = Critical. These require immediate remediation.

questions.q: EPSS improves vulnerability prioritization by:
opts: Adding the probability that a vulnerability will be actively exploited in the wild — helping focus on likely real-world threats
Replacing CVSS as the primary scoring framework used by every vulnerability scanner output
Automating patch deployment timelines based on the predicted exploitation probability score
Calculating the expected financial impact of each unpatched vulnerability per asset class
questions.exp: CVSS measures severity; EPSS measures likelihood of exploitation. Combining them improves prioritization.

audit_d_review.note: EPSS; 4.3 Analyzing Vulnerabilities IS umbrella; EPSS is a vulnerability scoring system.

sb_fix_2.note: Chapter-level Tier 3. T2 grep (EPSS|exploit prediction) returned zero matches. Ch 5 §Vulnerability Management p.87 is the natural home (CVSS adjacency); EPSS not in glossary/index, page approximate. Term may be in chapter prose. partial-depth retained.

questions.q: CVSS scores are computed from three metric groups: Base, Temporal, and Environmental. Which statement about these groups is CORRECT?
opts: Base metrics describe characteristics that change over time; Temporal describe inherent attack characteristics; Environmental describe organization-specific factors
Base metrics describe organization-specific factors; Temporal describe inherent attack characteristics; Environmental describe characteristics that change over time
Base, Temporal, and Environmental all measure the same dimensions and are computed identically — they are interchangeable groupings used by different vendors

Base metrics describe inherent attack characteristics that do not change; Temporal describe characteristics that change over time (e.g. exploit code maturity); Environmental describe organization-specific factors
questions.exp: Base metrics capture intrinsic, time-invariant properties of the vulnerability — attack vector, attack complexity, privileges required, user interaction, scope, and CIA impact. Temporal metrics capture characteristics that change over time — exploit code maturity, remediation level, and report confidence. Environmental metrics let an organization tailor the score to their specific deployment — modified base metrics plus impact subscore weights for CIA. Options A and D scramble the assignments; option C confuses the groups, which are deliberately distinct so a score can be progressively refined from inherent severity to organization-specific risk.

questions.q: A new vulnerability is discovered in a widely-used open-source library. Which sequence BEST describes the typical CVE workflow from discovery to remediation?
opts: Vendor advisory issued → CVE-ID assigned → discovery → CVSS scored → remediation deployed
Discovery → CVSS scored → patch deployed → CVE-ID assigned → vendor advisory issued
Remediation deployed → vendor advisory issued → discovery → CVE-ID assigned → CVSS scored
Discovery → CVE-ID assigned by a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority) → CVSS Base score computed → vendor advisory and patch issued → consumers remediate
questions.exp: The standard CVE workflow runs: a researcher or vendor DISCOVERS the vulnerability → a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority, e.g. MITRE or a participating vendor) ASSIGNS a CVE-ID → CVSS Base score is COMPUTED (often by the vendor or NVD) → the vendor issues an ADVISORY and patch → consumers REMEDIATE. CVE-IDs serve as the cross-vendor reference identifier; CVSS provides the severity scoring; vendor advisories are the actionable consumer-facing communication. The other options scramble the order — advisories cannot be issued before discovery, and remediation cannot precede CVE assignment.

scenarios.q: A vulnerability management team receives scan results showing 3,400 vulnerabilities across their environment. The CISO demands they all be patched within 30 days. The team says this is impossible. They propose a risk-based prioritization approach. How should they prioritize, and what factors determine which vulnerabilities are addressed first?
opts: Patch in strict alphabetical order by CVE ID to ensure fairness across all teams
Patch the most expensive applications first — these are the most important assets
Always patch the newest CVEs first — newer vulnerabilities are more dangerous
Risk-based prioritization — combining CVSS, exploit availability, and asset criticality to drive patch order
scenarios.exp: (1) Critical/High CVSS score AND actively exploited in the wild (check CISA KEV catalog and EPSS score) on internet-facing or critical-asset systems — patch within 24-72 hours; (2) Critical/High CVSS on internal systems — patch within 7-14 days; (3) Medium CVSS — patch within 30 days; (4) Low CVSS — patch in next scheduled maintenance window. A CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on an isolated test server with no internet exposure is lower priority than a CVSS 7.0 vulnerability with a public exploit on an internet-facing payment system — context and exploitability matter as much as score. Risk-based vulnerability prioritization: CVSS score alone is insufficient context. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog flags CVEs actively exploited in the wild — these have immediate urgency regardless of CVSS score. EPSS provides exploitation probability. Asset criticality and internet exposure multiply risk. This is how mature vulnerability management programs triage — not by score alone, but by score × likelihood × asset criticality.

scenarios.q: A CVSS 9.8 critical vulnerability is announced in a widely-used web application framework. Your organization runs 47 instances of the affected version. The vendor releases a patch the same day. Your patch management process requires a 2-week testing cycle before deployment. The vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild within 48 hours of the announcement. What should happen?
opts: Invoke emergency change management: compress testing on the exploit vector, implement temporary WAF rules on internet-facing instances, deploy the patch within 24-48 hours, and document the change record
Follow the standard 2-week testing cycle — process discipline must be maintained even for critical CVE-9.8 emergencies that affect production
Wait for the standard 2-week testing cycle and accept the risk of compromise during that 14-day window as an acceptable cost of process discipline
Disable all 47 instances until the standard 2-week testing cycle completes — pure availability sacrifice for guaranteed safety from this CVE
scenarios.exp: Emergency patching for actively exploited critical vulnerabilities: the 2-week cycle exists to prevent bad patches from breaking production — not to delay security for weeks during active exploitation. Emergency change management compresses but doesn't eliminate the process: rapid staging test focusing on the exploit scenario, compensating controls as a bridge, and rapid deployment with rollback plan. The alternative — 2 weeks of known critical exposure during active exploitation — is unacceptable for internet-facing systems.

scenarios.q: A vulnerability management team is prioritizing two findings from the same scan. Vulnerability X has a CVSS Base score of 9.1 (critical) but an EPSS score of 0.4% (very low probability of exploitation in the next 30 days). Vulnerability Y has a CVSS Base score of 7.2 (high) but an EPSS score of 38% (high probability of exploitation in the next 30 days). The team has resources to remediate ONE this sprint. Which should be remediated first AND why?
opts: Vulnerability X — its CVSS score of 9.1 is higher, and CVSS is the only authoritative severity standard; EPSS is just a vendor metric

Vulnerability Y — although its CVSS is lower, its 38% probability of exploitation indicates active or imminent threat in the wild, so the real-world risk is meaningfully higher than the theoretically more severe X
Vulnerability X — CVSS critical is always remediated first regardless of any other factor, by NIST policy
Either is fine — the two metrics are equivalent and either choice would produce the same risk reduction
scenarios.exp: CVSS measures inherent severity (what could happen if exploited); EPSS measures the probability of exploitation in the wild within a short window. They answer complementary questions and prioritization should weigh both. Vulnerability Y has lower theoretical severity but a much higher probability of being actively exploited, so the expected risk (severity × probability) is higher in the immediate term. CVSS-alone prioritization misses the real-world exploitation signal. EPSS is published by FIRST, not a vendor. Many organizations now combine CVSS thresholds with EPSS thresholds in their prioritization rules.

cram.def: Primary remediation. Vendor-supplied fix removes the vulnerability.
Alternative security measures when patching isn't possible.
Formally documenting accepted risk — with management sign-off and periodic review.
After remediation, verify the vulnerability is actually fixed — rescan, retest.

matching.prompt: Primary remediation — removes the vulnerability
Formally accepting a vulnerability with management sign-off
Verifying vulnerability is fixed after remediation
Alternative control when patching not possible

questions.q: After applying a patch for a critical vulnerability, the next step should be:
opts: Validate the remediation — rescan or retest to confirm the vulnerability is actually fixed
Mark the vulnerability as closed immediately because the vendor patch installed without errors
Apply the same patch to all other systems immediately without testing in a staging environment
Report to management with a brief description of the patch deployment and an SLA confirmation
questions.exp: Patches can fail or be misapplied — validation confirms the vulnerability is actually remediated before closing the finding.
