Add more character type requirements — require at least 3 special characters in every password to defeat any pattern-matching attempts based on simpler templates used by current attackers in their wordlist generation
scenarios.exp: Policy-driven weak passwords: complexity requirements create minimum-viable-password thinking; forced rotation creates predictable increments. NIST's guidance, based on research into how users actually behave under password policies, recommends length over complexity, no forced rotation (change only on compromise), and breach database checks. The observed 'Password1!' pattern is the direct result of 8-character complexity requirements — users satisfy the policy with the shortest, easiest-to-remember combination.

scenarios.q: A systems administrator is configuring a new service account for a database that will be used by an application server to query the database. They propose using the password 'ServiceAcct2024!' and rotating it manually every 6 months. A security architect rejects this approach. What is the better solution and why?
opts: The proposed approach is fine — service accounts don't need strong passwords
Service accounts need simpler passwords because applications have strict password requirements

Managed service accounts or secrets management solutions are the correct approach: (1) Windows Managed Service Accounts (MSA/gMSA) automatically rotate the password on a schedule without requiring manual updates and without the password being visible to any human; (2) a secrets management vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) generates a strong random password, stores it securely, provides it to the application at runtime, and can rotate it automatically. Both eliminate: human-chosen passwords (which are weaker than random), manual rotation (which gets deferred or forgotten), and password exposure during rotation. Service accounts are high-value targets — they typically have broad database permissions and their compromise is often undetected for long periods
Service accounts should use the same credentials as the DBA for simplicity
scenarios.exp: Service account credential management: human-chosen, manually-rotated service account passwords are a systemic weakness. They're often weak (complexity requirements aren't enforced at account creation), rotation is deferred, and when rotated the new password must be updated in every application config file (creating outage risk). MSAs/gMSAs (managed by AD) or secrets vaults (automatic rotation injected at runtime) eliminate all these problems — the password is machine-generated, automatically rotated, and never seen by a human.

questions.q: Angela has chosen to federate with other organizations to allow use of services that each organization provides. What role does Angela’s organization play when they authenticate their users and assert that those users are valid to other members of the federation?
opts: Service provider
Relying party
Authentication provider
Identity provider
questions.exp: Angela’s organization is acting as an identity provider (IdP). Other members of the federation may act as a service provider or relying party when they allow her users to access their services. Authentication provider is not a named role in typical federation activities.

questions.q: Which of the following biometric technologies is most broadly deployed due to its ease of use and acceptance from end users?
opts: Voice print recognition
Gait recognition
Retina scanners
Fingerprint scanner
questions.exp: Fingerprint scanners are found on many mobile devices and laptops, making them one of the most broadly deployed biometric technologies. Facial recognition is also broadly deployed, but it is not mentioned in this question or offered as an option.

questions.q: Adam want to increase his organization’s passwords resistance to attacks in the event that the password hash database is stolen by attackers. Which of the following password security settings has the largest impact on password cracking if his organization’s current passwords are 8 characters long?
opts: Password complexity
Password length
Password reuse limitations
Preventing the use of common words in passwords
questions.exp: Password length has the largest impact on preventing password cracking. When paired with a strong password hash algorithm and proper use of technology like salting, long passwords are much harder to crack. Complexity is the next most important option, as preventing simple repeated characters and similar problematic passwords helps reduce the probability of easily cracked passwords being used. Reuse limitations and preventing common words are less useful.

questions.q: A PIN is an example of what type of factor?
opts: Something you know
Something you are
Something you have
Something you set
questions.exp: PINs and passwords are both examples of something you know. Something you set is not a type of factor. Biometric factors are an example of something you are, and a physical USB token would be a common example of something you have.

questions.q: Marie is implementing a PAM solution and wants to ensure that root passwords are available in the event of an outage. Which PAM‐related tool is most likely to be useful in this situation?
opts: Ephemeral accounts
Just‐in‐time permissions
Password vaulting
Token‐based authentication
questions.exp: Password vaulting, which stores passwords for use with proper authentication and rights, is the most appropriate solution for Marie’s needs. Ephemeral accounts and just‐in‐time permissions are typically used under normal circumstances to provide least privilege access as needed. Token‐based authentication is not specifically a PAM solution.

questions.q: Jill sets her files on a Windows file share to allow Fred to access the files. What type of access control system is she using?
opts: Mandatory access control
Rule‐based access control
Attribute‐based access control
Discretionary access control
questions.exp: Jill is able to make decisions about the rights she grants on her files, meaning this is a discretionary access control system. A mandatory access control system relies on labels to set access control rules. Rule‐based access control systems rely on rules to define access, and attribute‐based access control systems grant access based on attributes like job roles or locations.

questions.q: Lisa sets up an account on a website that allows her to log in with Google. When she logs in, Google provides an access token to the website that confirms that she is who she says she is but doesn’t provide the site with her password. Which of the following technologies has she used?
opts: LDAP
OAuth
MITRE
RADIUS
questions.exp: OAuth is an authentication protocol that allows services to receive authentication tokens from an identity provider without needing the user’s password. LDAP is a directory service and is often used as part of SSO processes. MITRE is a nonprofit organization, and RADIUS is an authentication technology.

questions.q: Kyle has been asked to provide his government‐issued ID as part of the creation of his user account. What process should he assume it is being used for?
opts: Biometric enrollment
Just‐in‐time permission creation
Identity proofing
Federation
questions.exp: Kyle can assume that his government‐issued ID is being used as part of an identity proofing process to validate that he is who he claims to be. Biometric enrollment typically requires interaction with an enrollment process to scan or capture biometric information. Just‐in‐time permission creation is done when access is requested and does not require government ID, and federation connects identity providers with service providers, which is not described here.

questions.q: What key concept below best describes only providing the permissions necessary to perform a role?
opts: Least privilege
Best practice
Ephemeral accounts
Mandatory access control
questions.exp: The principle of least privilege means that users should only be given the permissions necessary to perform their role. Best practice is a general term describing commonly recommended and accepted industry practices. Temporal accounts are ephemeral, or short‐lived accounts. Mandatory access control is an access control scheme.

questions.q: Nina has recently left her organization. What should the organization do with her account?
opts: Transfer it to her replacement.
Reprovision it for another user.
Deprovision her account.
Change the password and preserve the account.
questions.exp: Without other factors that would require the account to be retained, deprovisioning accounts that belonged to users who have left the organization is a best practice. Transferring accounts or reprovisioning them may expose data to new users or provide them with rights that they should not have.

questions.q: A person’s name, age, location, or job title are all examples of what?
opts: Biometric factors
Identity factors
Attributes
Account permissions
questions.exp: A person’s name, age, location, job title, and even things like their height or their hair color are all attributes that may be associated with a person’s identity. None of these describe biometric factors used for authentication, and identity factors are something you are, something you have, or somewhere you are. Account permissions determine what you can do, not attributes like these.

questions.q: Which of the following technologies is the least effective means of preventing shared accounts?
opts: Password complexity requirements
Requiring biometric authentication
Requiring one‐time passwords via a token
Requiring a one‐time password via an application
questions.exp: Password complexity requirements do not prevent sharing of complex passwords, making it the least effective option from the list. Biometric authentication measures will require the enrolled user to be there, although in some cases such as fingerprint systems, multiple users could each enroll a valid fingerprint for a single account. Both types of one‐time passwords could be shared but make it harder and less convenient to share accounts.

questions.q: What type of access control scheme best describes the Linux filesystem?
opts: MAC
RBAC
DAC
ABAC
questions.exp: Linux users can change who can read, write, or execute files and directories they own, which is discretionary access control (DAC). Mandatory access control (MAC) would enforce settings set by the systems administrator without users having the rights to make their own decisions. While role‐based access control is involved, DAC best describes the access control scheme. ABAC is not a default method for setting rights for the Linux filesystem.

questions.q: Amitoj wants to ensure that her organization’s password policy does not allow users to reset their password multiple times until they can reuse their current password. What setting is used to prevent this?
opts: Complexity
Length
Expiration
Age
questions.exp: Password age is set to prevent users from resetting their password enough times to bypass reuse settings. Complexity, length, and expiration do not influence this.

questions.q: Which type of multifactor authentication is considered the least secure?
opts: HOTP
SMS
TOTP
Biometric
questions.exp: SMS messages are not secure and could be accessed by cloning a SIM card or redirecting VoIP traffic, among other possible threat models. Both HOTP and TOTP tokens and applications as well as biometric factors are generally considered more secure than an SMS‐based factor.

questions.q: Geeta has been issued a USB security key as part of her organization’s multifactor implementation. What type of implementation is this?
opts: A hard token
A biometric token
A soft token
An attestation token
questions.exp: A USB security key is an example of a hard, or physical, token. An application is an example of a soft token. A biometric factor might be a fingerprint or faceprint. Attestation is a formal verification that something is true. Attestation tokens were made up for this question.

questions.q: Michelle enables the Windows picture password feature to control logins for her laptop. Which type of attribute will it provide?
opts: Somewhere you are
Something you know
Something you are
Someone you know
questions.exp: Picture password asks users to click on specific, self‐defined parts of a picture. This means that clicking on those points is something you know. Something you are involves biometric traits, and somewhere you are relies on geographic locations.

questions.q: Theresa wants to implement an access control scheme that sets permissions based on what the individual’s job requires. Which of the following schemes is most suited to this type of implementation?
opts: ABAC
DAC
RBAC
MAC
questions.exp: Role‐based access control (RBAC) sets permissions based on an individual’s role, which is typically associated with their job. Attribute‐based access control (ABAC) is typically matched to other attributes than the job role. Discretionary access control (DAC) and mandatory access control (MAC) are commonly implemented at the operating system level.

questions.q: What are the two most commonly deployed biometric authentication solutions for mobile devices?
opts: Voice recognition and face recognition
Fingerprint recognition and gait recognition
Face recognition and fingerprint recognition
Voice recognition and fingerprint recognition
questions.exp: Current mobile device implementations have focused heavily on facial recognition via services like Apple’s Face ID and fingerprint recognition like Android’s fingerprint scanning and Apple’s Touch ID. Gait recognition is not a widely deployed biometric technology and would be difficult for most mobile device users to use. Voice recognition as a biometric authenticator has not been broadly deployed for mobile devices, whereas voice‐activated services are in wide usage.

questions.q: The authentication token that Susan uses generates codes based on an algorithm that relies on the current time. What type of token does Susan have?
opts: HOTP
Timestamp
TOTP
Time offset
questions.exp: Susan has a time‐based OTP (TOTP) token. HMAC‐based one‐time password (HOTP) tokens use a mathematical function that increments based on an event such as the click of a button. Time stamp and time offset are used for forensic and log analysis but are not types of tokens.

questions.q: Thomas has configured UEFI boot attestation on the servers that he is responsible for. What occurs during boot attestation?
opts: Each boot component is checked against a list of signed and known software before it is loaded.
The system builds a chain of trust from component to component as it loads during boot.
The system attests to a verification platform about the trustworthiness of the software it is running after it completes the boot process.
All of the above.
questions.exp: Boot attestation provides information about the software that it booted with to an attestation verification platform or system after boot, unlike secure boot, which uses a chained verification process to ensure that each component is signed and acceptable before it is loaded.

questions.q: The biometric authentication system that Patricia has deployed has been allowing users to authenticate whose fingerprints do not match the users who they are authenticating as. What type of error is this called in biometric systems?
opts: CER
False rejection
False acceptance
The efficacy rate
questions.exp: This type of problem is an issue with false acceptance and can be a major issue for biometric systems. Patricia needs to tune the system to reduce the false acceptance rates while minimizing false rejection rates. The crossover error rate (CER) is the point at which the false acceptance rate (FAR) and false rejection rate (FRR) cross over. Efficacy rate simply means how effective something is at performing its desired function.

questions.q: Xavier is implementing multifactor authentication and wants to ensure that he is using different factors. The authentication system he is setting up requires a PIN and a biometric factor. What types of factors are these?
opts: Something you know and something you are
Something you have and something you are
Something you know and something you have
They are both the same factor and cannot be used for multifactor authentication.
questions.exp: A PIN is something you know, and a biometric factor is something you are. Xavier is correctly using two different types of factors for his authentication scheme. If he was using a PIN and a password, he would be using two of the same type of factor, reducing the overall security for his environment.

questions.q: Joanna wants to implement an access control schema for her organization and needs to identify staff members based on their job title, their location, and whether they are a member of a specific team. What type of access control mechanism should she choose?
opts: ABAC
DAC
MAC
RBAC
questions.exp: ABAC (attribute‐based access control) is based on attributes of subjects. In this case, each of the items listed is an attribute that can be used to grant permissions or access. Discretionary access control (DAC) gives resource owners the rights to decide what others can do with their resources. MAC enforces access control at the system or OS level, requiring the administrator to make those choices. RBAC can be either rule‐ or role‐based access control. Here, there are more than roles involved, and no rules were mentioned.

questions.q: Adam wants to deploy one‐time passwords to his staff, and he wants to be able to support many different sites while also providing the ability to enroll users using his MDM system. What tool should he select?
opts: Hardware tokens
Static codes
An authentication application
Phone‐based push authentication
questions.exp: Adam should select an authentication application. Tools like Google Authenticator, Duo, and Microsoft Authenticator all provide the capabilities that he is looking for. Some hardware tokens can handle multiple sites but are not manageable via MDM. Static codes are just that—printed‐out codes. Phone‐based push authentication could support multiple sites but is far less secure and, again, is not managed via MDM.

questions.q: Klara wants to implement a biometric factor for a multifactor authentication system. What concern should she raise if the biometric system is noted to have a high FRR?
opts: Users who shouldn’t be able to authenticate may be able to.
Users who should be able to authenticate may be rejected.
Users may not be able to successfully enroll in the biometric system.
Users may not be able to change their biometric identifiers.
questions.exp: FRR (false rejection rate) describes what happens when a biometric system does not accept a valid biometric factor. Klara should look for a low FAR (false acceptance rate) as well as a low FRR (false rejection rate).

questions.q: Bea wants to establish a password standard. Which of the following organizations does not provide commonly used password guidelines?
opts: NIST
Microsoft
NSA
IEC
questions.exp: The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Microsoft, and the National Security Agency (NSA) all provide regularly updated password guidelines to help organizations build password policies. The IEC (International Electrical Commission) creates standards for electrical devices, not passwords.

cram.def: Speed (faster than human response), consistency (no human error), scalability (handles volume).
Security Orchestration, Automation, Response — automates security workflows and executes playbooks.
Documented sequence of steps for responding to a specific security incident type.
Security testing integrated into CI/CD pipelines — finds vulnerabilities during development.
Automated, repeatable infrastructure provisioning. Version-controlled security configs.

matching.prompt: Automates security workflows and tool integration
Documented steps for responding to an incident type
Security testing integrated into CI/CD pipeline
Automated version-controlled infrastructure provisioning

questions.q: The PRIMARY security benefit of automation over manual processes is:
opts: Automation is always more accurate than humans because the underlying logic never has bugs
Automation is always cheaper than human analysts at every scale of security operations workload
Speed and consistency — automated tasks execute identically every time
Automated tools need no maintenance because vendor-managed pipelines update playbooks invisibly
questions.exp: Automated responses execute in seconds without human error or delay. Automation responds in milliseconds vs hours for humans — and applies the same logic every time.

questions.q: A SOAR playbook is:
opts: A vendor product manual describing each module's GUI options and configuration screens
A type of firewall rule that combines multiple ACL entries into a single grouped policy
A documented, automated sequence of steps that executes in response to a specific type of security incident
A network diagram showing the SOC architecture and data flows between security tools and the SIEM
questions.exp: Playbooks encode response procedures — SOAR executes them automatically on alert trigger.

questions.q: DevSecOps integrates security into CI/CD pipelines by:
opts: Replacing developers with security analysts during the software development cycle entirely
Adding security testing (SAST, DAST, SCA) at every stage of the software development pipeline — finding vulnerabilities early
Removing all automated testing from the CI/CD pipeline to reduce build delays and developer friction
Running penetration tests only at release time, after all development is fully complete
questions.exp: DevSecOps: shift security left — find vulnerabilities during development when they're cheap to fix.

questions.q: A security team is comparing automation and orchestration in the context of their SOAR platform. Which statement BEST distinguishes the two?
opts: Automation and orchestration are different vendor names for the same concept; they can be used interchangeably with no real distinction between them in any product literature or training
Automation runs on-premises; orchestration runs in the cloud — they are deployment models for the same fundamental capability of scripted task execution across security operations workflows

Automation = single-task script (reset password, run scan, block IP); orchestration = multi-system workflow combining automated tasks across tools (when SIEM alerts, isolate endpoint via EDR, capture forensic image, open ticket, notify on-call)
Automation is for security operations only; orchestration is for IT operations only — they apply to different teams within an organization with no overlap in tooling or shared workflow definitions
questions.exp: Automation is the unit task — a single script or action that replaces a manual step (reset a password, block an IP, run a scan). Orchestration is the workflow that strings multiple automated tasks across multiple systems into a coordinated, conditional process — typically encoded as a SOAR playbook with branching logic. The distinction is scope: automation = one task; orchestration = multi-step, multi-tool workflow. Vendor terms are not equivalent. Deployment location does not differentiate them. Both are used in security and broader IT.

questions.q: A security team is identifying high-value candidates for security automation. Which set of tasks is BEST suited for automation (high-volume, repetitive, well-defined input/output, low judgment required)?
opts: Manual penetration testing with novel exploitation paths; red-team campaign design and execution; security awareness training content authorship for adult learners
Strategic security architecture decisions; vendor selection negotiations; incident communication with regulators and the press; threat-actor attribution analysis under uncertainty
Code review approvals that require deep judgment; legal contract review with negotiation; executive briefings on emerging risks; security policy authorship from scratch

User account provisioning/deprovisioning when HR posts a hire/termination event; routine ticket creation when a SIEM alert exceeds a threshold; vulnerability scan triage that closes false-positive findings matching known patterns; IR playbook composition that orchestrates standard containment steps
questions.exp: Good automation candidates share four characteristics: high-volume (worth the build cost), repetitive (the same operation many times), well-defined input/output (clear contract), and low judgment (humans not adding value). Account provisioning, ticket creation, false-positive triage, and IR playbook composition all match. Strategic decisions, communications, and contract review require judgment, context, and accountability that automation cannot supply. Manual pen testing and content authorship are creative and exploratory. Choosing the right targets is the most important automation decision; automating the wrong things wastes effort and creates new failure modes.

scenarios.q: A security team's SOAR playbook automatically blocks IP addresses that appear in threat intelligence feeds. One morning, a major cloud provider's IP address (used by a business-critical SaaS application) is added to a threat feed after being used in an attack on other organizations. The SOAR automatically blocks the IP, and the business-critical SaaS application becomes inaccessible. The CEO cannot access their email. What does this incident reveal about SOAR automation?
opts: SOAR automation is too dangerous and should be replaced with manual processes — the cost of an incorrect automated action outweighs response speed gains in the SOC across all known scenarios analyzed
The threat intelligence feed provider is responsible for this incident — they sent a bad indicator and the SOC's automation acted as expected on it without any local-context evaluation by the SOC

Automated response requires safeguards for high-impact actions: auto-blocking is appropriate for clearly malicious low-profile IPs, but high-profile IPs (cloud providers, CDN, partners) need human approval or an exception list. Automation needs guardrails for high-impact actions

All SOAR actions should require manual approval — automation is the entire problem and removing the automation step eliminates this class of incident permanently from the SOC operational risk register
scenarios.exp: SOAR guardrails for high-impact actions: automation without guardrails creates its own availability incidents. Best practice: tiered automation — high-confidence, low-impact actions (block unknown IP, quarantine email to sandbox) execute automatically; low-confidence or high-impact actions (block a cloud provider IP, isolate a critical server) require human approval. Exception lists for known-good high-profile IP ranges, and a 'soft block' (alert without action) option for suspicious-but-uncertain indicators, prevent this class of false positive.

scenarios.q: A company's security team writes a Python script that automatically retrieves vulnerability scan results, correlates them with asset criticality data from the CMDB, generates a prioritized remediation report, and emails it to the appropriate system owners every Monday morning. Before this script, a security analyst spent 8 hours every Monday doing this manually. What automation benefit does this represent, and what risks should the team manage?
opts: This automation has no meaningful security benefit

This is a clear automation efficiency gain: consistent weekly reporting that previously took 8 person-hours now executes in minutes, freeing the analyst for higher-value work (threat hunting, incident investigation). The risks to manage: (1) script error handling — if the scan API fails or the CMDB data is stale, the script should alert rather than silently produce incorrect reports; (2) access control — the script likely has credentials to vulnerability scanner and CMDB APIs that must be secured (secrets vault, not hardcoded); (3) output validation — automated reports should include data freshness indicators so recipients know if source data was current; (4) change management — updates to the script should go through code review to prevent introducing errors into a business-critical process
Automation should never be used for security reporting — humans must review all data
The analyst's 8 hours should be reallocated to more automation development
scenarios.exp: Automation benefits and risks: efficiency gain is real — repetitive, well-defined tasks are ideal automation candidates. The risks are also real: automated processes fail silently if not properly instrumented (error handling, alerting on failures), credentials used by automation must be managed as privileged secrets, and unvalidated automated output can propagate errors faster and wider than manual processes. Automation amplifies both correct processes and incorrect ones.

scenarios.q: A SOC team is automating endpoint isolation in response to high-severity SIEM alerts. The playbook will: (1) parse the alert, (2) identify the affected endpoint, (3) call the EDR API to isolate the endpoint from the network. The team is concerned about a buggy detection rule auto-isolating dozens of production servers in a single false-positive cascade. The MOST appropriate guardrails are:
opts: No guardrails — the automation should run as fast as possible to maximize containment speed; any false positives can be reverted manually after the fact without consequence to the SOC operations posture

Disable EDR API access entirely so the automation cannot run at all and no risk of cascade exists in the environment under any circumstances now or in the future once the API is fully turned off at the platform level

Run the automation only quarterly so any cascade is naturally rate-limited by the long delay between successive playbook executions in the SOC and the operational risk is contained by the long delay between runs

Validation (require alert severity match, log the planned action), rate-limiting (cap isolations per hour), approval gates for high-impact targets (servers tagged 'production critical'), and rollback (auto-revert if a follow-up signal indicates false positive within X minutes)
scenarios.exp: High-impact automation needs guardrails proportional to the blast radius. The four standard guardrails are: VALIDATION (verify the trigger meets strict criteria before acting), RATE-LIMITING (cap the number of actions per time window so a buggy rule cannot cascade), APPROVAL GATES for high-impact targets (require human approval before acting on critical assets), and ROLLBACK (auto-revert the action if a follow-up signal indicates false positive). No-guardrails automation invites the exact cascade the team fears. Quarterly automation is too slow for active threats. Disabling the API entirely defeats the whole point. The guardrails-first design is what makes high-impact automation safe enough to deploy.

questions.q: Chris is creating a script that will automatically screen any user requests and flag those that exceed normal thresholds for manual review. What term best describes this automation use case?
opts: User provisioning
Guard rails
Ticket creation
Escalation
questions.exp: This is an example of the guard rails use case for automation. Cybersecurity professionals can use scripting to automatically review user actions and block any that are outside of normal parameters.

questions.q: Which one of the following is not a common drawback of automating cybersecurity operations?
opts: Reducing employee satisfaction
Creating single points of failure
Costs
Complexity
questions.exp: Automation normally increases employee retention. The common drawbacks to automation include complexity, cost, creating single points of failure, incurring technical debt, and creating challenges to ongoing supportability.

questions.q: Every time Susan checks code into her organization’s code repository, it is tested and validated, and then if accepted, it is immediately put into production. What is the term for this?
opts: Continuous integration
Continuous delivery
A security nightmare
Agile development
questions.exp: Although this example includes continuous integration, the key thing to notice is that the code is then deployed into production. This means that Susan is operating in a continuous deployment environment, where code is both continually integrated and deployed. Agile is a development methodology and often uses CI/CD, but we cannot determine if Susan is using Agile.

questions.q: Which one of the following is not an advantage of automation in cybersecurity operations?
opts: Enforcing baselines
Technical debt
Employee retention
Standardizing infrastructure configurations
questions.exp: The main benefits of automation are efficiency and time savings, enforcing baselines, standardizing infrastructure configurations, scaling in a secure manner, retaining employees, reducing reaction time, and serving as a workforce multiplier. Technical debt is one of the potential drawbacks of automation.

cram.def: 1. Preparation. 2. Detection and Analysis. 3. Containment, Eradication, Recovery. 4. Post-incident Activity.
IR plan, team, tools, training — BEFORE an incident.
Stop the spread. Short-term (isolate) and long-term (block C2, patch vector).
Remove malware, close vulnerabilities exploited, eliminate attacker persistence.
Restore systems to production. Validate before returning to service.
Lessons learned, report, update IR plan, improve defenses.

matching.prompt: IR Phase 1 — before an incident
IR Phase 3a — stopping the spread
IR Phase 3b — removing malware and persistence
IR Phase 3c — returning to production
IR Phase 4 — lessons learned

questions.q: Which NIST IR phase involves removing malware and closing vulnerabilities?
opts: Eradication
Containment
Detection and Analysis
Recovery
questions.exp: Eradication removes the attacker's presence — malware, backdoors, compromised accounts — and addresses the vulnerabilities that enabled the attack.

questions.q: The purpose of the containment phase is to:
opts: Identify who conducted the attack by correlating IOCs with known threat-actor TTPs
Restore systems to production immediately so business operations continue without interruption
Stop the spread of the incident to other systems while investigation continues
Document lessons learned and brief stakeholders on the response so playbooks improve over time
questions.exp: Containment limits damage — isolating compromised systems prevents lateral movement.

questions.q: Evidence preservation during incident response requires:
opts: Immediately reformatting compromised systems so the malware persistence path is destroyed
Capturing memory dumps and forensic images BEFORE remediation — preserving evidence for investigation and potential legal action
Deleting all malware binaries immediately so the attacker can no longer use them on the host
Notifying all users that an incident has occurred and is being remediated by the SOC team
questions.exp: Remediation destroys forensic evidence — capture memory and disk images first, then clean.

questions.q: Post-incident activity (lessons learned) is important because:
opts: It satisfies legal requirements only with no operational benefit beyond regulatory paperwork
It closes the incident ticket so the SOC dashboard returns to a green-status overview
It assigns blame to responsible parties so consequences can be applied during the next review cycle
It identifies what worked and what failed — improving the IR plan, controls, and defenses to reduce impact of future incidents
questions.exp: Lessons learned drives continuous improvement — every incident teaches something that makes the next response faster.

questions.q: At 11pm, a SOC analyst confirms a high-severity ransomware incident on a production server. Which escalation/communication order is MOST consistent with standard IR practice?
opts: SOC analyst → public press release on the company website immediately to maintain transparency; THEN internal notifications follow to leadership and the board
SOC analyst → board of directors directly, bypassing all middle management, because the board has ultimate authority over the technical and stakeholder response

SOC analyst → IR lead takes command → CISO/security leadership → CIO/IT leadership → executive leadership (CEO, legal, comms, CFO) → board if material → external counsel before any external statement → regulators per applicable law
SOC analyst → law enforcement first, before any internal company notification, because external law-enforcement involvement should precede company communications
questions.exp: Active-incident communication has both legal and operational ordering. The IR lead takes command of the technical response. Internal escalation runs UP the management chain (CISO → CIO → executive leadership → board if material) so each layer has the context they need to make decisions in their lane. External counsel is engaged BEFORE any external statement to manage privilege and regulatory exposure. Regulators are notified per the applicable law (HIPAA 60-day, GDPR 72-hour, state breach laws, SEC for material events). Premature external comms create legal exposure and may pre-empt a coordinated response. Bypassing management cuts off the people who need to authorize spend and reach customers. Notifying law enforcement before internal escalation is appropriate in narrow cases but is not the default order.

scenarios.q: At 3am, a SOC analyst receives an alert that a server is generating large volumes of outbound network traffic to an IP address in an unfamiliar country. The analyst determines this is likely data exfiltration. They want to immediately shut down the server to stop the exfiltration. A senior analyst advises against this. Why?
opts: The junior analyst is correct — stop the exfiltration immediately by any means available, including hard shutdown of the affected server regardless of any forensic preservation considerations at this point in the incident
The alert is likely a false positive — no action should be taken at 3am until the senior analyst can review the alert in the morning during normal business hours after coffee and a full inbox review

Exfiltration should be allowed to continue temporarily to gather more intelligence about the attacker's methodology and infrastructure for future defensive countermeasures and threat-intelligence sharing

Shutdown destroys forensic evidence: volatile data in RAM (malware code, encryption keys, active connections, in-memory credentials) is lost. Sequence: (1) network-isolate to stop exfiltration without destroying state; (2) collect volatile evidence; (3) eradicate
scenarios.exp: Containment vs forensic preservation: immediate shutdown stops the bleeding but destroys the crime scene. Network isolation (firewall block, switch port disable, EDR network isolation) achieves containment while keeping the system running for forensic collection. The volatile memory dump taken from a running system contains the malware code, decryption keys for encrypted communications, and the complete attack toolset — information that is gone forever after shutdown. Collect first, then contain.

scenarios.q: An organization suffers a ransomware attack. The IR team follows their playbook, which was written 3 years ago. They discover: the playbook lists a DRP contact who left the company 2 years ago, it references a backup system that was replaced 18 months ago, and it specifies an isolation procedure for a network architecture that no longer exists. The recovery takes 4x longer than the RTO because the team has to improvise. What IR program failure does this represent?
opts: The IR playbook was fine — ransomware recovery always takes longer than expected
The ransomware was particularly sophisticated — no playbook would have helped
The IR team improvised well — 4x RTO is an acceptable outcome for ransomware
IR playbook maintenance failure — playbook references systems and people no longer in place
scenarios.exp: Playbooks must be living documents — reviewed and updated after major infrastructure changes, personnel changes, and after every significant incident or exercise. A playbook that references departed contacts, replaced systems, and obsolete architecture is worse than no playbook in some ways — the team trusts it and discovers the errors at the worst possible moment. Best practice: playbooks reviewed quarterly, updated after every significant infrastructure change, and tested (tabletop or simulation) annually to verify they reflect current reality. IR playbook lifecycle management: a playbook written once and never updated provides false readiness. The discovery of obsolete information during an actual incident is the highest-cost way to learn that the playbook is outdated. Quarterly review cycles, change-triggered updates (when the backup system is replaced, update the playbook immediately), and annual testing (tabletop minimum, simulation preferred) catch gaps before they're discovered under pressure.

scenarios.q: A company suffers a data breach where customer PII is exfiltrated. The IR team successfully contains and eradicates the threat in 36 hours. The legal team then informs the IR team that GDPR requires notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach. The IR team says they needed the 36 hours to understand the scope of the breach before they could notify. They notify on hour 37. Was the notification requirement met?
opts: Yes — 37 hours is well within the 72-hour window
No — GDPR notification only applies if more than 500 individuals are affected
No — GDPR requires notification within 1 hour of any suspected breach

Yes — 37 hours from initial awareness (when the breach was confirmed and scope was understood) is within the 72-hour window IF the 72 hours is measured from the point of awareness. However, if the organization was 'aware' of the breach at hour 0 (when the alert fired) and waited until hour 36 to notify (after investigation), the clock started at hour 0 and 37 hours of investigation may consume most of the notification window. GDPR does allow initial notification 'without undue delay' when full information isn't yet available — a preliminary notification stating 'breach suspected, investigation ongoing, further details to follow' can be filed within 72 hours even before full scope is known, with supplementary notifications as information develops
scenarios.exp: GDPR breach notification nuance: the 72-hour clock starts when the organization becomes aware of a breach — not when investigation is complete. 'Aware' means reasonable certainty that a breach occurred, not certainty about scope. GDPR explicitly allows for initial notification with incomplete information, followed by supplementary reports. IR teams should plan for parallel workflows: containment/investigation AND notification preparation, rather than sequential (investigate fully, then notify). A preliminary notification preserves the timeline; detailed investigation continues after.

scenarios.q: At 2pm on a business day, a SOC analyst confirms that an internal-facing finance application server is actively being exfiltrated from — outbound traffic to a known-malicious IP, ongoing for the past 30 minutes. The application is mid-quarter-close and is being used by 200 finance staff right now; isolating the host will halt the close. The CFO has asked the security team to 'wait until end of day' to isolate. The MOST appropriate immediate action is:
opts: Wait until end of day as the CFO requested — the business impact of stopping the close mid-day outweighs additional 4 hours of exfiltration
Do not isolate; instead block the outbound destination IP at the firewall and continue monitoring, accepting that the attacker may pivot to a different destination
Isolate the host from the network immediately, escalate the business impact and recovery plan to the CFO and CIO in writing, and engage the IR plan; document the decision and the executive escalation
Shut the host down completely without isolation so the attacker stops, even though shutdown destroys volatile evidence in memory
scenarios.exp: Active exfiltration is an ongoing data-loss event; allowing it to continue for hours to preserve a business deadline is generally not defensible — every additional minute increases the data loss. The right action is to isolate the host (containment), escalate to the executive chain in writing with the recovery options and timeline, and follow the IR plan. Pure firewall blocking is brittle — the attacker can switch destinations. Full shutdown destroys volatile forensic evidence (memory, network state). Waiting prioritizes business continuity over an active loss event without proper authority — and the IR plan typically gives the IR lead authority to contain regardless of business pressure, with mandatory executive notification.

cram.def: Discussion-based simulation. Team talks through response to a scenario. No systems involved.
Identifying the fundamental cause of an incident — not just the symptom. Prevents recurrence.
Broad plan for maintaining business operations during/after disruption. Parent of DRP.
Technical plan for recovering IT systems after disaster. Subset of BCP.

matching.prompt: Discussion only — no systems involved
Finding the root reason an incident occurred
Technical plan for IT system recovery
Broad plan for business survival during disruption

questions.q: Root cause analysis (RCA) after an incident is used to:
opts: Identify the fundamental cause of the incident to prevent recurrence — not just treat the symptom
Assign blame to the responsible individuals so consequences are applied during quarterly reviews
Calculate financial losses by aggregating downtime cost across all affected revenue streams
Complete the incident report by adding final timeline timestamps and ticket close-out fields
questions.exp: RCA finds why the incident happened — fixing the root cause prevents the same attack from succeeding again.

questions.q: A DRP (Disaster Recovery Plan) is a subset of BCP because:
opts: DRP specifically covers IT system recovery; BCP covers all business operations including non-IT
DRP covers all business functions including HR, facilities, communications, and supply chain
BCP is only for large organizations with multi-site footprints and dedicated continuity teams
They are the same plan with different titles used by different industry verticals interchangeably
questions.exp: BCP covers the broader goal of maintaining all business operations. BCP is the strategic framework for business continuity. DRP is the tactical IT-specific recovery plan that fits within the broader BCP.

questions.q: A company is planning incident response exercises and is choosing among four formats: tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, and full-interrupt. Which statement correctly characterizes the formats?
opts: Tabletop is discussion-based with no systems touched; walkthrough is a step-by-step review of the IR plan; simulation involves role-play with realistic injects but production systems are not disrupted; full-interrupt actually disrupts production systems to test live response (highest realism, highest risk)
Tabletop disrupts production; walkthrough involves role-play; simulation is discussion-based; full-interrupt is a step-by-step plan review
All four exercise types are functionally identical — the labels differ by industry tradition only
Tabletop and full-interrupt are the same thing; walkthrough and simulation are the same thing — there are only two distinct categories
questions.exp: The four exercise types are arrayed along an intrusiveness/realism axis. Tabletop is the lowest — purely discussion-based, no systems touched; useful for validating decision-making and roles. Walkthrough is a structured step-by-step review of the IR plan against a scenario. Simulation involves role-play with realistic scenario injects (often with a facilitator playing external parties) but production is not disrupted. Full-interrupt is the most realistic — it actually disrupts production systems (e.g. takes a database offline) to test live response, and carries the highest operational risk. Higher intrusiveness gives higher realism but higher business risk; most organizations cycle through all four as their program matures.

questions.q: An incident response team is conducting a post-mortem and is choosing among three root-cause-analysis frameworks: 5 Whys, Fishbone (Ishikawa), and Apollo. Which statement BEST distinguishes them?
opts: The three frameworks are equivalent and interchangeable — the choice is purely team preference with no methodological difference between them in practice for any incident category being analyzed

5 Whys: ask 'why' iteratively until reaching a root cause whose fix prevents recurrence; Fishbone (Ishikawa): categorical cause-mapping (people, process, technology, environment) for visual exploration; Apollo: structured causal-chain method linking effect to causal conditions
5 Whys is for technical incidents only; Fishbone is for process incidents only; Apollo is for cultural incidents only — they are not interchangeable across categories of incidents analyzed
All three frameworks yield the same root cause when applied correctly — they differ only in visual presentation style and report formatting for the post-mortem document published afterward
questions.exp: The frameworks are real methodological alternatives with different strengths. 5 Whys is fast and conversational — ask 'why' iteratively until you hit a root cause that, when fixed, prevents recurrence; risk is shallow analysis if the team stops too soon. Fishbone (Ishikawa) is a categorical visual exploration — branches for people, process, technology, environment, etc. — useful when the team needs to canvas a broad space of possible causes. Apollo Root Cause Analysis is more structured and detailed — every effect links to its causal conditions AND the actions that caused it. The frameworks complement rather than substitute. The symptom-fix vs root-cause distinction matters across all three: patching the same issue repeatedly without RCA is symptom-fix.

scenarios.q: A company's IR plan states that in the event of a significant security incident, the CISO should notify the CEO within 1 hour and the board within 24 hours. During a real ransomware incident, the CISO is on vacation with limited connectivity, the documented backup contact is also unavailable, and nobody else is sure who has authority to notify the CEO or board. The CEO first hears about the incident from a news reporter 6 hours later. What communication plan gap does this expose?
opts: The plan has single points of failure: it designates specific individuals without alternates or escalation. A robust plan: primary + 2 backup contacts per role, escalation chains (if X unavailable for 30 min → contact Y), authority matrix, out-of-band methods
The CISO should never take vacations during critical periods — communication continuity should be guaranteed by ensuring senior leaders remain available during high-risk windows
The board should have been monitoring security news directly — they could have learned of the breach independently and pursued action without waiting for formal notification
Communication plans are not necessary for organizations with experienced security teams — informal notification networks within an experienced team work effectively in incidents
scenarios.exp: Communication plan resilience: key personnel will sometimes be unavailable during incidents — vacations, medical emergencies, travel. The communication plan must designate alternates, specify escalation chains with time triggers (if primary unreachable in 30 minutes, escalate to backup), and document authority delegation (who can notify the board in the CISO's absence). Testing the communication plan during exercises specifically tests whether the backup chain works.

scenarios.q: After a security incident involving data exfiltration, the incident response team completes their forensic investigation and writes a lessons learned report. The report identifies root causes, recommends 7 technical and 3 process improvements, and is filed in the security team's document management system. Six months later, a different analyst checks on implementation status and finds that 8 of the 10 recommendations were never implemented. What post-incident activity failure occurred?
opts: Lessons learned reports are informational only — implementation is not expected
The analyst should not have checked on implementation — lessons learned reports are historical documents
Lessons learned reports should be destroyed after 90 days for liability reasons

The lessons learned process lacked an ownership and tracking mechanism: identifying recommendations without assigning owners, timelines, and a follow-up mechanism guarantees they won't be implemented. Best practice: each recommendation in a lessons learned report must have (1) a named owner responsible for implementation, (2) a due date, (3) integration into the organization's task/project tracking system (not just a document), and (4) a scheduled review date to verify completion. The CISO or IR program owner should track open recommendations as active risk items until closed
scenarios.exp: Lessons learned implementation tracking: the value of post-incident analysis is in the improvements implemented — not in the quality of the report. A well-written report that sits in a document system delivers zero security improvement. Embedding recommendations into project tracking, assigning owners with accountability, and scheduling completion reviews converts lessons learned from a compliance exercise into actual security improvement. Unimplemented recommendations are a form of known, accepted risk that should be formally tracked.

cram.def: Collect most volatile evidence first. CPU registers/cache → RAM → swap → disk → remote logs → physical.
Documentation tracking who handled evidence, when, and how — essential for legal admissibility.
Exact bit-for-bit copy of storage media including deleted files and unallocated space.
Hardware device preventing any writes to evidence drive — preserving integrity during imaging.
Preserving all relevant data for anticipated litigation — suspends normal deletion policies.

matching.prompt: First thing to collect — most volatile evidence
Documentation tracking evidence handling
Exact bit-for-bit copy including deleted files
Prevents writes to evidence drive during imaging
Preserving data for litigation

questions.q: The order of volatility in digital forensics dictates that:
opts: The most volatile (short-lived) evidence
Physical media is collected first
Disk is always collected first because it contains the most evidence
Order doesn't matter as long as everything is collected
questions.exp: CPU registers, RAM, network state — is collected before less volatile evidence like disk. RAM disappears when powered off — collect it first. Disk persists — collect later. Most volatile to least volatile.

questions.q: Chain of custody is required to:
opts: Speed up the investigation by allowing forensic analysts to skip image-verification steps
Prevent unauthorized access to evidence by restricting the lab to forensic-team members only
Store evidence securely in a sealed cabinet inside a locked forensic lab on the corporate site
Document every person who handled the evidence and how — ensuring it's admissible in court and hasn't been tampered with
questions.exp: Unbroken chain of custody is required for legal admissibility — any gap raises doubt about whether evidence was tampered with.

questions.q: A write blocker is used to:
opts: Block write permissions for suspects on their workstation accounts during an active investigation
Speed up the imaging process by parallelizing reads across multiple SATA channels at once
Encrypt the evidence drive with a forensic-team-owned key during imaging to prevent leaks
Prevent any writes to the evidence drive during imaging — preserving the original state and maintaining integrity
questions.exp: Without a write blocker, merely mounting the drive may modify it — inadvertently altering evidence.

scenarios.q: A forensic investigator is called to examine a server suspected of being compromised. When they arrive, the on-site IT administrator has already rebooted the server 'to clear whatever was causing the performance issues,' deleted a suspicious directory they found, and run a full disk format on an external drive that was attached to the server. The investigator is asked to determine what happened. What evidence has been lost and what can still be recovered?
opts: All evidence is intact — disk forensics can recover everything
The reboot is the only significant issue — the other actions are recoverable
Nothing is lost — forensic tools can recover all data from any state

Significant evidence is lost: (1) All volatile memory contents (running malware, network connections, encryption keys, credentials) are gone permanently — reboot clears RAM; (2) The deleted directory contents may be partially recoverable from disk (deleted files leave traces until overwritten) but directory metadata is gone; (3) The external drive that was formatted — data may be partially recoverable (format doesn't always overwrite all data) but will require significant forensic effort and may be incomplete. What can still be attempted: disk forensic imaging of the server's storage (recover deleted files, examine artefacts in unallocated space), event logs if not cleared, file system metadata (creation times, access times, modification times), and network logs from other sources (firewall, SIEM). The IT administrator's actions are textbook evidence destruction — responders must be trained to preserve, not remediate, before forensics are complete
scenarios.exp: Evidence preservation failures: each 'helpful' IT action destroyed a category of forensic evidence. Reboot = volatile memory gone. Deleted directory = file system artefacts partially gone. Formatted drive = external evidence significantly degraded. IR training must reach IT responders, not just the security team — the first people on scene are often IT staff who are trained to fix problems, not preserve evidence. The first responder's role is to isolate and photograph/document the state, not remediate.

scenarios.q: A company's legal team instructs the security team to preserve all data from a specific employee's workstation related to a potential lawsuit. The security team creates a forensic image of the hard drive and stores it on a network share. Two weeks later, the legal team asks for the hash value of the image to verify its integrity. The security team realizes they never recorded a hash of the image at the time of creation. What is the evidentiary problem?
opts: Hash values are optional for forensic evidence — this is not an issue and the image's network-share storage location is sufficient for legal admissibility under any chain-of-custody rules used in court today

The network share storage is the problem — forensic images must be stored on tape media to satisfy any criminal or civil chain-of-custody legal requirements that come up during litigation discovery proceedings

Without a hash recorded at image creation, there's no proof the stored image matches the original. Anyone with share access could modify it. Procedure: hash the original (write-blocker), hash the image immediately, document both, re-verify at each handling step

Hash values only matter for criminal investigations, not civil lawsuits — civil discovery rules don't impose chain-of-custody hashing requirements on either party in any common jurisdiction in the country
scenarios.exp: Hash verification for evidence integrity: the forensic hash is the chain of custody's technical backbone. Without it, the defense can argue the image was modified after collection. Standard procedure: (1) image the drive with a write-blocker (prevents any writes to the original), (2) hash the original device, (3) hash the forensic image, (4) verify the two hashes match (proving the image is a perfect copy), (5) store the hash with the image and document it in the chain of custody record, (6) re-verify before any analysis step. Every handling of evidence requires hash verification.

scenarios.q: A forensic investigator collected a hard drive from a suspect's workstation, imaged it with a write blocker, and stored the image in evidence. Two weeks later, while preparing for trial, the investigator discovers that the chain-of-custody log has a 6-hour gap during which the original hard drive was unaccounted-for in the evidence room (the entry/exit log was not signed for that period). The MOST appropriate disclosure and recovery action is:
opts: Disclose the chain-of-custody gap to opposing counsel and the court, document the gap in writing, and let the judge rule on admissibility — the integrity of evidence handling depends on accurate disclosure even when the disclosure damages the case
Do not disclose the gap — fix the log retroactively to fill the gap with plausible entries so the trial proceeds without complication for the prosecution
Destroy the evidence to avoid the embarrassment of admitting the gap to the court at all and start the case over with new evidence
Re-image the original hard drive now and use the new image as evidence, ignoring the gap in the original chain because the data is the same
scenarios.exp: Chain-of-custody integrity depends on accurate disclosure of every gap, error, or anomaly. Fabricating retroactive entries is evidence tampering — a far more serious offense than an honest gap disclosure. Destroying evidence is also a serious offense (spoliation). Re-imaging now does not fix the historical gap and may itself constitute spoliation if the evidence has been altered in the gap window. The correct action is to disclose the gap to opposing counsel and the court, document it in writing, and let the judge rule on admissibility — possibly the evidence is still admissible with appropriate weight reduction, possibly it is excluded. The investigator's credibility and the case integrity both depend on the disclosure.

questions.q: Selah wants to ensure that malware is completely removed from a system. What should she do to ensure this?
opts: Run multiple antimalware tools and use them to remove all detections.
Wipe the drive and reinstall from known good media.
Use the delete setting in her antimalware software rather than the quarantine setting.
There is no way to ensure the system is safe and it should be destroyed.
questions.exp: In most malware infection scenarios, wiping the drive and reinstalling from known good media is the best option available. If the malware has tools that can infect the system BIOS/UEFI, even this may not be sufficient, but BIOS/UEFI resident malware is relatively uncommon. Multiple antivirus and antimalware tools, even if they are set to delete malware, may still fail against unknown or advanced malware packages. Destroying systems is uncommon, expensive, and unlikely to be acceptable to most organizations as a means of dealing with a malware infection.

questions.q: Which one of the following security assessment techniques assumes that an organization has already been compromised and searches for evidence of that compromise?
opts: Vulnerability scanning
Penetration testing
Threat hunting
War driving
questions.exp: Threat hunting is an assessment technique that makes an assumption of compromise and then searches the organization for indicators of compromise that confirm the assumption. Vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, and war driving are all assessment techniques that probe for vulnerabilities but do not assume that a compromise has already taken place.

questions.q: The following figure shows the Security+ incident response cycle. What item is missing?
opts: Planning
Reporting
Monitoring
Preparation
questions.exp: The first item in the incident response cycle used by the Security+ exam is preparation.

questions.q: Which team member acts as a primary conduit to senior management on an IR team?
opts: Communications and public relations
Information security
Management
Technical expert
questions.exp: Members of management or organizational leadership act as a primary conduit to senior leadership for most incident response teams. They also ensure that difficult or urgent decisions can be made without needing escalated authority. Communications and PR staff focus on internal and external communications but are typically not the direct conduit to leadership. Technical and information security experts do most of the incident response work itself.

questions.q: Jayne wants to determine why a ransomware attack was successful against her organization. She plans to conduct a root cause analysis. Which of the following is not a typical root cause analysis method?
opts: Root/branch review
Five whys
Event analysis
Diagramming
questions.exp: Five whys, event analysis, and diagramming are all common methods of performing root cause analysis. Root/branch review is not a typical process for this.

questions.q: Hitesh wants to keep a system online but limit the impact of the malware that was found on it while an investigation occurs. What method from the following list should he use?
opts: Containment
Isolation
Segmentation
Black holing
questions.exp: Containment activities focus on preventing further malicious actions or attacks. In this case, Hitesh might opt to prevent the malware from spreading but leave the system online due to a critical need or a desire to preserve memory and other artifacts for investigation. Isolation walls a system or systems off from the rest of the world, whereas segmentation is frequently used before incidents occur to create zones or segments of a network or system with different security levels and purposes.

questions.q: What phase in the incident response process leverages indicators of compromise and log analysis as part of a review of events?
opts: Preparation
Containment
Eradication
Identification
questions.exp: The Analysis phase focuses on using various techniques to analyze events to identify potential incidents. Preparation focuses on building tools, processes, and procedures to respond to incidents. Eradication involves the removal of artifacts related to the incident, and containment limits the scope and impact of the incident.

questions.q: The company that Ben works for wants to test its incident response plan. Ben gathers the incident response team in a room and walks through a scenario to validate the organization’s processes and procedures. What type of event has Ben hosted?
opts: A checklist exercise
A simulation
A tabletop exercise
A fail‐over exercise
questions.exp: Ben’s organization is conducting a tabletop exercise. Tabletop exercises are conducted with more flexibility—team members are given a scenario and asked how they would respond and what they would do to accomplish tasks they believe would be relevant. Checklist exercises are not a specific type of exercise. A simulation exercise attempts to more fully re‐create an actual incident to test responses. Fail‐over exercises are conducted by actually failing a datacenter over to a hot location.

questions.q: Felix wants to make an exact copy of a drive using a Linux command‐line tool as part of a forensic acquisition process. What command should he use?
opts: df
cp
dd
ln
questions.exp: dd is a copying and conversion command for Linux and can be used to create a forensic image that can be validated using an MD5sum or SHA1 hash. The other commands are df for disk usage, cp for copying files, and ln to link files.

questions.q: What legal concept determines the law enforcement agency or agencies that will be involved in a case based on location?
opts: Nexus
Nonrepudiation
Jurisdiction
Admissibility
questions.exp: Jurisdiction is the legal authority over an area or individuals based on laws that create the jurisdiction. Nexus defines whether a relationship or connection exists, such as a local branch or business location. Non‐repudiation ensures that evidence or materials can be connected to their originator. Admissibility determines whether evidence can be used in court.

questions.q: Michael wants to acquire the firmware from a running device for analysis. What method is most likely to succeed?
opts: Use forensic memory acquisition techniques.
Use disk forensic acquisition techniques.
Remove the firmware chip from the system.
Shut down the system and boot to the firmware to copy it to a removable device.
questions.exp: Firmware can be challenging to access, but both memory forensic techniques and direct hardware interface access are viable means in some cases. Firmware is not typically stored on the disk and instead is stored in a BIOS or UEFI chip. Removing the chip from the system will leave it unable to run and thus this is not a preferred method. Also, many chips are not removable. Shutting down the device and booting it to the firmware does not provide a means of copying the firmware for most devices. Although the firmware is likely to allow updates, most do not allow downloads or copying.

questions.q: Charles needs to know about actions an individual performed on a PC. What is the best starting point to help him identify those actions?
opts: Review the system log.
Review the event log.
Interview the individual.
Analyze the system’s keystroke log.
questions.exp: Although it may be tempting to use a technical answer, interviewing the individual involved is the best starting point when a person performed actions that need to be reviewed. Charles can interview the staff member, and then move on to technical means to validate their responses. System and event logs may have some clues to what occurred, but normal systems do not maintain a keystroke log. In fact, the closest normal element is the command log used by both Windows and Linux to allow command‐line input to be recalled as needed.

questions.q: Maria has acquired a disk image from a hard drive using dd, and she wants to ensure that her process is forensically sound. What should her next step be after completing the copy?
opts: Securely wipe the source drive.
Compare the hashes of the source and target drive.
Securely wipe the target drive.
Update her chain‐of‐custody document.
questions.exp: Once a copy is made, hashes for the original and target drive should be compared to ensure that the copy was successful. After that, the chain‐of‐custody document can be updated to note that a copy was made and will be tracked as it is analyzed while the original is preserved. Wiping either drive after a copy is not part of the process, although a target drive may be wiped after a case is complete.

questions.q: Alaina wants to maintain chain‐of‐custody documentation and has created a form. Which of the following is not a common element on a chain‐of‐custody form?
opts: Item identifier number
Signature of the person transferring the item
Signature of the person receiving the item
Method of transport
questions.exp: Chain of custody tracks who has an item, how it is collected, where it is stored and how, how it is secured or protected, who collected it, and transfers, but it does not typically include how the items were transported because that is not relevant if the other data is provided.

questions.q: Henry is following the EDRM model and is preparing to review data. What two key tasks occur during this stage?
opts: Validating that time stamps match between systems and that data is properly hashed to confirm that original data is sent
Validating that the legal hold request is valid and that all documented items are included
Validating that the desired data is included and that information that should not be shared is not included
Validating that chain of custody is ensured and that malicious files are not included
questions.exp: It is important to ensure that data prepared for e‐discovery only contains what it is supposed to, and that information that should not be shared is not included. Time stamps, hashing, chain of custody, and ensuring malicious files are not included are not part of the EDRM model. Validating that a legal hold is valid should happen before preservation, but validating that documented items from the hold are included if they exist should occur.

questions.q: Theresa’s organization has received a legal hold notice for their files and documents. Which of the following is not an action she needs to take?
opts: Ensure that changes to existing documents related to the case are tracked and that originals can be provided.
Preserve all existing documents relevant to the case.
Delete all sensitive documents related to the case.
Prevent backups that contain files related to the case from being overwritten on their normal schedule.
questions.exp: Removing information relevant to a legal hold is exactly what the hold is intended to prevent. Theresa’s organization could be in serious legal trouble if they were to intentionally purge or change related information.

questions.q: Gurvinder wants to follow the order of volatility to guide his forensic data acquisition. Which of the following is the least volatile?
opts: RAM
Data on the hard drive
Backups
Remote logs
questions.exp: Backups are the least volatile of these options according to the order of volatility. Backups will be kept until they are aged out, which may be days, weeks, or even months in some cases. From most to least volatile, these are RAM, data on the hard drive, remote logs, and then backups.

questions.q: Greg is preparing a forensic report and needs to describe the tools that were used. What should he report about the tools in addition to their names?
opts: The type of system the tools were installed or run on
The training level or certifications of the team that uses the tools
Any known limitations or issues with the tools
The patch level or installed version of the tools
questions.exp: If there are known limitations or issues with the tools used, this should be included in the report. The type of system the tool was installed on may influence performance but should not influence the report or output. Training and certification may be listed as part of a team description but are not required as part of tool description. Finally, patch levels or installed versions are not critical unless there are known issues that would have been described as such.

questions.q: Gabby is preparing chain‐of‐custody documentation and identifies a gap in hand‐off documentation for an original source forensic drive. What issue should she expect to encounter due to this gap?
opts: The evidence may not be admissible in court.
The forensic activities may need to be repeated.
The staff involved may have to re‐create the missed log.
The chain of custody may need to be edited to note the problem.
questions.exp: If forensic evidence was not properly handled, it may not be admissible in court. Repeating forensic activities won’t reverse mishandling, staff can’t go back and re‐create logs, and noting the issue will not resolve it.

questions.q: Mike’s organization has recently moved to a SaaS cloud service and needs to collect forensic data from the cloud service. What process can Mike use to gather the information he needs?
opts: Install forensic imaging software on the cloud service’s servers.
Identify the log information available and request any other desired information from the cloud service provider.
Engage law enforcement to acquire the forensic data.
Request the forensic information from third‐party auditors.
questions.exp: Mike’s best option is to identify the log information available from the provider and to request any additional information knowing that he may not receive more detail unless there is contractual language that specifies it. SaaS vendors typically won’t allow installation of forensic tools, law enforcement does not perform forensic acquisition for third parties upon request, and auditors don’t provide forensic data acquisition either.

questions.q: Charles wants to obtain a forensic copy of a running virtual machine. What technique should he use to capture the image?
opts: Run dd from within the running machine.
Use FTK Imager from the virtual machine host.
Use the VM host to create a snapshot.
Use WinHex to create a copy from within the running machine.
questions.exp: Creating a snapshot will provide a complete copy of the system, including memory state that can then be analyzed for forensic purposes. Copying a running system from a program running within that system can be problematic, since the system itself will change while it is trying to copy itself. FTK Imager can copy drives and files, but it would not handle a running virtual machine.

questions.q: Melissa wants to capture network traffic for forensic purposes. What tool should she use to capture it?
opts: A forensic suite
Wireshark
dd
WinHex
questions.exp: Even though Wireshark is not a dedicated network forensic tool, since network traffic is ephemeral, capturing it with a packet sniffer like Wireshark is Melissa’s best option. Forensic suites are useful for analyzing captured images, not capturing network traffic, and dd and WinHex are both useful for packet capture, but not for network traffic analysis.

questions.q: Frank is concerned about the admissibility of his forensic data. Which of the following is not an element he should be concerned about?
opts: Whether the forensic source data has remained unaltered
Whether the practices and procedures would survive review by experts
Whether the evidence is relevant to the case
Whether the forensic information includes a time stamp
questions.exp: Forensic information does not have to include a time stamp to be admissible, but time stamps can help build a case that shows when events occurred. Files without a time stamp may still show other information that is useful to the case or may have other artifacts associated with them that can provide context about the time and date.

questions.q: What is the document that tracks the custody or control of a piece of evidence called?
opts: Evidence log
Audit log
Event report
Chain of custody
questions.exp: Chain‐of‐custody documentation tracks evidence throughout its life cycle, with information about who has custody or control and when transfers happened, and continues until the evidence is removed from the legal process and disposed of. The other terms are not used for this practice.

questions.q: Isaac is performing a forensic analysis on two systems that were compromised in the same event in the same facility. As he performs his analysis, he notices that the event appears to have happened almost exactly one hour earlier on one system than the other. What is the most likely issue he has encountered?
opts: The attacker took an hour to get to the second system.
One system is set to an incorrect time zone.
The attacker changed the system clock to throw off forensic practitioners.
The forensic tool is reading the time stamps incorrectly.
questions.exp: The most common cause of an hour of difference between two systems in an environment is an incorrectly set time zone. Isaac should check the time zone settings, and then correct his findings based on the time zones set on the systems if necessary.

questions.q: Lucca needs to make a forensic copy of a Linux system. What built‐in Linux command‐line tool can she use for that purpose?
opts: dd
md5sum
cat
grep
